name: Washington State Standard
title: Commentary: Fixing WA’s housing crisis won’t be easy, but predictable policy would help
description: As lawmakers plan for the 2027 legislative session, they will do so amid significant economic uncertainty and difficult choices about the state budget. Meanwhile, Washington’s housing crisis remains unresolved. These challenges are interconnected. A strong economy depends on having enough homes for the people who work here, while homebuilding generates jobs [...]
text:
Housing construction in Duvall, Washington in 2021. (Ian Dewar Photography/Shutterstock)As lawmakers plan for the 2027 legislative session, they will do so amid significant economic uncertainty and difficult choices about the state budget. Meanwhile, Washington’s housing crisis remains unresolved. These challenges are interconnected. A strong economy depends on having enough homes for the people who work here, while homebuilding generates jobs and ongoing tax revenue that support state and local services. 
Homebuilders play an important role in supporting our state’s economy, but that contribution cannot be taken for granted. Building homes requires significant private investment, and investment decisions depend on whether projects are financially feasible. Policymakers’ decisions can either encourage investment in new housing or drive it elsewhere.
Good housing policy is essential to economic development. There are practical, tangible policy tools our Legislature can advance in 2027 to expand housing choices, improve affordability and support economic growth. Chief among them are simplifying land division for housing and stabilizing building codes. But just like the tools in any carpenter’s toolbox, nothing will happen unless we pick them up and use them effectively. We don’t need more process because policymakers must make progress decisively on the plans already in place. Washington’s workers and businesses cannot afford to wait for more housing to effectively compete economically.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
I am encouraged by Governor Ferguson’s convening of his Economic Development Council and former Governor Gregoire’s leadership at Challenge Seattle, together with the engagement of other state and local leaders. These efforts give me hope that housing will remain central to Washington’s economic conversation.
The benefits of common-sense housing policy extend beyond the walls of a new home. An economic analysis found that every 100 new single-family homes built in Washington generate on-going benefits totaling $6.8 million in income for residents and $2.5 million in state and local tax revenue.  The benefits are similar for multifamily construction. Homebuilding not only provides the housing our communities and workforce need; it supports jobs, generates public revenue and contributes to our economic vitality.
As a homebuilder, I focus on building the homes our region needs while navigating an ever-shifting patchwork of regulatory requirements. A major choke point is land. It is very expensive, especially in existing communities near jobs, transit and schools. We must use limited buildable land efficiently. Yet despite recent reforms, the processes governing land division remain unnecessarily complex and often duplicate other requirements.
The Legislature should simplify land division to create a streamlined process that encourages more opportunities for housing within urban growth areas. One practical change would raise the short plat threshold to 30 lots, allowing streamlined land division in urban areas – which have already undergone extensive planning and environmental review under the Growth Management Act – to be approved administratively. This would not change the underlying zoning or how much development is allowed. It would simply make it easier for new homes, including middle housing, to reach the market sooner.
Modernizing the land division process would complement existing state efforts to streamline environmental review, improve permitting efficiency, lower development costs, and accelerate delivery of new homes.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
That commitment to predictability should extend to building codes. Constant code update cycles add cost and uncertainty. A period of stability would give builders, local governments, and consumers greater predictability while allowing time to evaluate the costs and impacts of existing requirements. Five other states have already delayed or adjusted their code adoption cycles to improve affordability and ease implementation. Washington should do the same.
More broadly, policymakers should consider any new regulatory standards for housing in the context of existing requirements. Too often, it is not any single regulation that prevents a home from being built, but the cumulative effect of fees, regulatory requirements, delays, and uncertainty that drives up housing costs and can make otherwise viable projects financially infeasible.
Washington faces difficult choices in 2027. We need more homes people can afford, an economy that continues to create opportunities and sustainable revenues to support the public services our communities rely on. Homebuilding can contribute to all three, but only if we create the conditions that make investment in new housing possible
Builders are ready to do their part. Now we need lawmakers to do theirs by making practical policy decisions that reduce unnecessary costs, restore predictability, and give builders the confidence to invest in Washington’s future.
We have the tools. It’s time to put them to work so everybody has a place to call home.
Trevor Johnson is the CEO & Co-founder of Blackwood Homes, a local homebuilder. He currently serves on Governor Ferguson’s Economic Development Council and is a past president of the Master Builders Association of King and Snohomish Counties.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: 2 Massive Fuel Leaks In 5 Years. Has Hawaiʻi Learned Anything?
description: Though officials have assured the public that the latest environmental disaster poses no threat to the island's drinking water, parallels between Red Hill and H-Power are hard to ignore.
text:
As Civil Beat’s journalists came into the newsroom on Thursday, many of us were thinking about the toxic legacy of Hawaiʻi’s most harmful fuel spill.
It was the fifth anniversary of the week jet fuel from the Navy’s massive World War II-era storage complex at Red Hill gushed some 20,000 gallons into its underground tunnels, located directly over Oʻahu’s drinking water supply. Our top story that day recounted how the disaster sickened thousands of people, some of whom are still struggling with health impacts. 
Then, mid-morning, we learned there had been an even bigger leak of 400,000 gallons of diesel — 20 times larger than Red Hill — at H-Power, the city-owned incinerator in Kapolei. The parallels are hard to ignore: Like at Red Hill, there had been an apparent failure in leak detection and a delay in informing the public, and there are big questions about contamination, accountability and remediation.  
In H-Power’s case, the city contractor, Reworld, discovered that fuel had been spewing from an underground pipeline for months, from January through May, soaking fuel into the soil around the facility. Mayor Rick Blangiardi says he didn’t find out the full scope of it until Tuesday of this week. The public learned at a mayoral press conference on Thursday. 

Civil Beat: 
400K-Gallon Fuel Leak In Hawaiʻi Kept From Public For Months

Officials answered the most obvious question: Is our drinking water at risk? 
Ernie Lau, the chief engineer of the Honolulu Board of Water Supply, assured the public he has no reason to believe the H-Power fuel leak could jeopardize the area’s drinking water, in part because the nearest well is located a few miles away and is uphill.
Lau earned a lot of public trust during the Red Hill debacle, but with so much at risk, folks aren’t necessarily taking his word for it. Incoming City Council Chair Tyler Dos Santos-Tam and Councilwoman Andria Tupola are both calling for independent environmental testing and required public notification going forward.

Civil Beat: 
EPA Fines At Site Preceded Incinerator Fuel Leak As Questions Mount

Officials said much less about possible impacts to the ocean, either from fuel-tainted groundwater or runoff from contaminated soil. Blangiardi only said he doesn’t expect there to be shoreline impacts. Some experts are already expressing concern to Civil Beat about that.
Mayor Rick Blangiardi held a press conference Thursday morning to announce roughly 400,000 gallons of fuel oil was spilled at the city’s H-Power waste-to-energy plant earlier this year.  (Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026)
Much is still unknown about the H-Power incident. But as journalists, we can look to the past to chart the course forward for our news coverage. 
Some of the topics we’ll be asking about in coming weeks:

The hydrogeology of Kapolei. As we learned in this story about Red Hill, much of how water travels through Oʻahu’s aquifers is unknown, which can make it challenging to know how pollution will travel underground. Kapolei’s landscape is different than at Red Hill, and we’re trying to get a better understanding of it.
Fuel tracking systems. At Red Hill, the Navy had had problems keeping track of how much fuel was where. That allowed for some 20,000 gallons of fuel to go unaccounted for in a May 2021 leak. That fuel reappeared months later and contaminated the drinking water in November 2021. H-Power’s contractor also apparently was losing fuel for months before it realized what was happening. We want to know how their leak detection system was supposed to work and how it failed.
Accountability. To our knowledge, the military leaders at Red Hill faced few consequences for running the facility in a manner that sickened thousands of people. Some got letters of censure. Two civilian employees were criminally charged with conspiracy and making false statements to regulators. They pleaded not guilty, and their case is pending. Who will be held responsible for the mess at H-Power? The EPA, which enforces the Clean Water Act, is already investigating.

As a reporter, I ran point on Civil Beat’s coverage of Red Hill — we’ve published 244 stories, columns and community voices to date — and now, as an editor, I’m using that experience to guide our team as we cover another environmental mess.
We’ll be using the lessons we learned in the last fuel disaster, as well as new research and reporting, to inform our questions about the H-Power fuel leak. If you have questions you want us to ask or suggestions about where to look for information, please shoot us a note at news@civilbeat.org. 
Delayed Disclosure, Deja Vu 
First, a recap. 
On the day of the disastrous Red Hill leak — Saturday, Nov. 20, 2021 — fuel spewed into the Red Hill well, which supplied drinking water to some 90,000 people on Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. Workers struggled to stop or contain it. Fuel rained down for 34 hours straight. For days, the military didn’t tell anyone their water was at risk. 
“There are no signs or indication of any releases to the environment,” a Navy press release said on the Monday following the leak, “and the drinking water remains safe to drink.” 
Tim Walsh holds a bottle of water labeled ‘poison’ that contains water collected after he and his wife smelled fuel odors while living in Makalapa Navy Housing. (Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2021)
So, the week of Thanksgiving 2021, people drank the fuel-tainted water. After family meals of turkey and mashed potatoes, they washed their dishes in it. They bathed their children in it. 
And people started getting sick. They threw up. They had vertigo. Kids had rashes. Some went to the hospital. They didn’t know what was going on and were being told everything was fine. Later, they felt gaslit. 
The public only got confirmation they weren’t crazy when the state health department published a notice on Nov. 29 — more than a week after the catastrophic spill. The Navy didn’t admit there was a problem until three days later. 
The Navy’s denial in those early days caused irreparable damage to public trust. People still talk about it years later. 
The (obvious) lesson learned: People want to know right away when there is a possible threat to public health. 
In the case of the H-Power incident, Blangiardi said he will be assessing why he didn’t find out about the scope of the problem sooner. As for the state health department, Director Ken Fink said his subordinates didn’t post about the leak in the public database called iHEER – run by the Hazard Evaluation and Emergency Response Office — because the case is still open. 
We plan to ask experts whether it makes sense for the health department to wait for a case to be closed before telling the public about a major contamination incident. 
The Public Has A Right To Public Information 
Our reporting on Red Hill was greatly helped by people willing to stick their necks out and explain to us, both on and off the record, how the facility worked and where things went wrong. Some brave soul even gave us the only video the public has ever seen of the leak itself. 


I’d like to pause to personally thank those sources for helping us get to the bottom of things on behalf of our readers. 
A lot of other information stayed hidden. I made many Freedom of Information Act requests that the military simply ignored. 

Civil Beat: 
The Military’s Public Information Black Hole

This keeps public information hidden and further erodes public trust. 
The lesson: The public wants transparency. 
In the hours after we learned of the H-Power leak, Civil Beat journalists combed through public records that are readily available online. We found EPA and OSHA violation notices and a scathing decade-old city audit that says the contractor, Reworld, was able to secure a 20-year extension on its contract, apparently without city officials realizing what they were agreeing to. 
Since then, Civil Beat has filed public records requests to learn more about H-Power’s operations, Reworld’s contract records, how this fuel spill was able to go on undetected. Essentially: Who knew what when? We hope government agencies will err on the side of disclosure. 
See Something, Say Something 
It’s important to remember that even after the Red Hill leak sickened thousands of people, the Navy still intended to keep the facility open. They wanted to continue using it for fuel storage above Oʻahu’s drinking water aquifer. 
Meanwhile, Civil Beat continued to cover the risks and impacts and victims and activists banded together, using our journalism as fodder for their demands. “Shut Down Red Hill” became a rallying cry at protests and a message found on bumper stickers and cafe posters. 

Civil Beat: 
How Hawaii Activists Helped Force The Military’s Hand On Red Hill


Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2021
David Croxford/Civil Beat/2022
David Croxford/Civil Beat/2024
Protest played a role in shutting down Red Hill. 
Only in the face of overwhelming public and political pressure did the defense secretary at the time say they would close it. And that was a big deal, because the Navy had said for years that Red Hill was an essential national security asset. (See here in a 2015 press release that hasn’t aged well.)
The lesson: Journalism informs not just officials but everyday people, who have the power to band together and demand change and accountability — and it can make a big difference. 
If you have information about H-Power, Reworld or other environmental risks to our community, we want to talk to you. It could be the start of something important.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Neal Milner: Green Should Idle His Indignation Machine, Look Hard At Kauhale
description: Can the state’s homeless policy be saved from the awesome clutches of The Indignation Machine? All that indignation has come about from state auditor Les Kondo’s critical assessment of Gov. Josh Green’s flagship kauhale tiny house homeless program.  It’s turned into a morality play, good melodrama but awful governance. It is diverting us from the […]
text:
Can the state’s homeless policy be saved from the awesome clutches of The Indignation Machine?
All that indignation has come about from state auditor Les Kondo’s critical assessment of Gov. Josh Green’s flagship kauhale tiny house homeless program. 
It’s turned into a morality play, good melodrama but awful governance. It is diverting us from the main question: Do kauhale do the job?
No one really has an answer to this, except for the governor. He thinks the kauhale program is working great and is so confident that he dismisses anyone, such as the auditor, who has the gall to point out problems. 
There is plenty to be indignant about. Green’s angry self-martyrdom aside – he’s accused State Auditor Less Kondo of carrying out a “personal vendetta” against him – the final auditor’s report is even more damning than its preliminary one. 
Kondo’s task was limited and defined by the rules of his job: Find out whether kauhale money has been spent appropriately — what Kondo did.
By auditor standards, the defenses of the governor’s homeless team are pitifully weak. 
Green’s mandate is different from the auditor’s. The difference is at the heart of the anger.
It’s time for some serious anger management in order to confront the homeless issue head-on. 
Three steps: 
Take a breath. Take another look. Take a closer look.
Take A Breath
Green needs to get out of his defensive posture. He just won reelection by a bigger margin than any other governor in Hawai‘i’s history. So he has a cushion, giving him a chance to reflect on just how counterproductive his stance on kauhale has become. 
Most of all, he needs to accept the fact that Kondo is not simply a roadblock but someone who has a legitimate, helpful role.
State Auditor Les Kondo speaks during a Senate hearing on the state’s Kauhale Initiative on Nov. 12 at the State Capitol in Honolulu. The hearing focused on reviewing the administration and financial oversight of Governor Josh Green’s Kauhale Initiative. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
As for Kondo taking a breath: he’s done his job and done it well. His work is done here. The problem is about the homeless, not about him.
Legislators also need to take a breath and remind themselves about the limits of legislative indignation. 
The recent hearings show that the legislators were really good at finding fault with kauhale’s slipshod ways. Fine, as far as it goes.
But there’s a big difference between anger and successful legislative oversight.
Anger and threats alone change nothing, easier to fulminate than fulfil. The best recent example of this is the dunderheaded administration of the Convention Center repairs. Legislators have been criticizing the center’s construction and destruction from its very beginning, yet the mess is getting bigger.
Take Another Look: Emergency Proclamations
The basis for the governor’s actions is an emergency proclamation. Hawai‘i law is typical in that it allows the governor or mayor to determine when an emergency exists.
The governor used an emergency proclamation to create the kauhale program. 
The legislators’ main control is their ongoing kauhale investigation.
Let’s face it. The homeless issue is so awful and complicated, that emergency powers are the only way to go.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

Keep in mind how often you complain about how badly things get done in Hawai‘i – you know, delays, broken deadlines, stuff that drives you nuts, and how upset you become when you see a homeless person in your neighborhood.
But emergency power is not absolute power. It is not more important than the auditor’s power. The two powers run alongside one another.
“Get it done!” and “Do it right!” are a complicated mixture requiring more than dueling kuleana.
Take A Closer Look
We know almost nothing about kauhale’s effectiveness. Green confidently claims it has reduced the percentage living on the streets by 13%.
That’s an assertion based on flawed assumptions. The last homeless count did show a 13% reduction, but there’s no evidence that kauhale was the key reason. And there is so much more to know.
There’s been nothing close to a careful evaluation of kauhale’s impact. A Portland State University study of a similar situation in Portland would be a good model to follow. 
It was done not by advocates but by a group specializing in homeless research.
It compared shelters – considering costs, residents’ experiences and housing outcomes.
It found some very encouraging things about kauhale-like villages in Portland. People in these situations are more likely to find permanent housing. Earlier research had shown that people in the villages were quite satisfied with their housing but worried about food insecurity.
Most of all, though, the assessment asked all the right questions: 
What were the programs trying to accomplish? Who benefitted and who was left out? What happens to the residents over time? How, if at all, does life improve? What’s the cost?
And finally, how is public money protected? Do emergency powers improve the government’s response?
The best thing about this kind of assessment is it takes place in an atmosphere protected from the Indignation Machine.
It also combines the auditor’s side of things with the “emergency powers” side, that complicated mix.
Take A Bated Breath
I wish I could say things look promising.
Last week in his interview with Civil Beat, Green had this to say about his homeless policy. Good advice, he said, isn’t going to come from the tiny house critics “because the auditor and those folks have not yet understood the catastrophic problem and how good it has to have thousands of people off the streets.” 
Green plans to have a “really big conversation” with them “because now I can be a little more vocal.”
So patronizing. Such disdain. It sounds like mansplaining. Call it governorsplaining.
Still no recognition of the proper role of an auditor, more fuel to the Indignation Machine. And no expressed willingness to — as good as kauhale advocates think they are — look at what could make them even better.
And that’s so sad because Gov. Green is the key. Homeless policy is in his hands, and Kauhale has good potential. 
His emergency powers give him a great opportunity to use his initiative if he does his part to turn off the spigot of the Indignation Machine. 
Take a deep-deep breath, governor. Look in the mirror and repeat one of the famous management consultant Peter Drucker’s keys to effective leadership: 
“Listen first, speak last.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: The Sunshine Blog: Hawaiʻi Elections Commission Derailed Again
description: xx
text:
Electoral dysfunction: Well, that didn’t last very long. Earlier this month it seemed the Hawaiʻi Elections Commission was back on track after a five-month hiatus, thanks to the intervention of the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court. It held a public meeting and elected a temporary chair.
But within the first minutes of its next meeting, this one on Thursday, one of the eight commissioners challenged Tamara McKay’s authority to be the pro tem chair. Jeffrey Osterkamp also argued — or tried to, before he was cut out of the Zoom meeting at the insistence of McKay, who said Osterkamp was out of order because his point or order was not part of the meeting’s agenda — that the Elections Commission was dominated by election deniers.
You can read Osterkamp’s written statement below, which he emailed to The Blog. “It probably will be stricken from the record, as we now have an election denier as the invalidly elected Chair Pro Tem,” he wrote in an email.
Another commissioner, Barbara Dalton — like Osterkamp, appointed to the commission by Democrats — then left the meeting, too. “A hui ho,” she said before signing off.
That left the four remaining commissioners — all appointed by Republicans — without a quorum, meaning they could not deliberate nor make decisions per the state’s Sunshine Law. Two other Democrat-appointed commissioners, John Sabas and Liana Horovitz, did not attend the meeting.
The meeting nonetheless continued for more than two and a half hours, dominated by testifiers that included some of the commissioners themselves. McKay and Co. did manage to take care of some administrative business that Deputy Attorney General James Paige determined was allowed: The commission plans to advertise for a permanent chair and reconvene in January.



A Special Commentary Project
Civil Beat is focusing on transparency, accountability and ethics in government and other institutions. Help us by sending ideas and anecdotes to sunshine@civilbeat.org.





Read More

Regarding the search for a new chair, Judith Mills Wong, president of the League of Women Voters of Hawaiʻi, had some advice. She told the commission it was important to select a nonpartisan chair, who would also be the commission’s ninth member.
“The role of the commission is not to represent the party or a position, but to fairly evaluate and advise on matters concerning the electoral process, and we would ask that there be no conflict of interest, not candidates, not people who have run for office, not people who are planning to run for or in the process of running for office, or their staff, and no one who is in conflict with the state who is suing the state for the electoral process,” she said.
Six members of the Hawaiʻi Elections Commission meeting via Zoom on Thursday before two of them suddenly left the meeting, depriving their colleagues of a quorum. 
That would seem to include McKay, who is a past chair of the Hawaiʻi Republican Party, and Cushnie, who along with McKay has sued the state over the electoral process. Both applied for the chair gig in June but could not muster enough support from other commissioners.
Excuses, excuses: During and after every election, the Hawaiʻi Campaign Spending Commission combs over candidate finance reports to make sure they correctly include contributions and expenditures. And during and after every election the CSC invariably finds errors in multiple reporting and doles out appropriate remedies — usually monetary fines.
That happened a half-dozen times at the commission’s Wednesday meeting, although a few candidates pleaded for leniency. The fines went to unsuccessful Honolulu City Council candidate Tara Malia Gregory, who was fined $1,200 for a late filing, even though she told commissioners that she had made her filings “in good faith” but was confused about filing deadlines. Commissioner Barbara Polk did not accept that excuse, saying it was important candidates be transparent when it comes to campaign spending. 
Honolulu City Councilwoman Val Okimoto was fined $781.25 for her late filing and will pay up. Rep. Darius Kila was on the hook for $300 for his own late filing, one that he paid later that same day. Both were reelected this year.
Tara Malia Gregory speaking to the Hawaiʻi Campaign Spending Commission Wednesday. 
Meantime, unsuccessful state Senate candidate Christy MacPherson was fined $1,500 for failing to report expenditures, even though campaign treasurer Garrett Iha argued that he had indeed reported the expenses through the online filing system; for some unexplained reason, he said, they just did not take. And unsuccessful state House candidate Tam Hunt was fined $800 for several reporting errors.
Commissioners also rejected a request on behalf of Ryan Yamane, a former state representative, who was seeking clarification as to whether he could use his campaign funds to pay for legal fees. Yamane served in the House from 2004 to 2023 and then went to work as director of the Department of Human Services in the Green administration.

Former state Rep. Ryan Yamane is accused of taking bribes. 

He retired from that post in May and then was indicted in July on bribery and conspiracy charges. You might have read about that. But Yamane has kept his House campaign filing open and has about $33,000 in it. 
“I respectfully request a formal advisory opinion interpreting the relevant provisions ofHawaii campaign-finance law and Commission rules as applied to the facts described above,” said Isaac Choy, who made the inquiry on behalf of Yamane. Choy is a former state rep who has recently been part of a whistleblower case involving the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority and the Green administration. You might have read about that too.
The Campaign Spending Commission rejected Choy’s request, saying that using the campaign funds was prohibited unless the legal proceedings were somehow related to an elections proceeding or administrative agency action.
Nerd alert: Jared Kuroiwa is the City and County of Honolulu’s new chief data officer. Mayor Rick Blangiardi made the appointment last week.
Kuroiwa will head the Office of the Managing Director, where he will lead efforts to strengthen the city’s use of data, technology, and artificial intelligence “to improve operations, support informed decision-making, and drive innovation across city departments,” says a press release.

Jared Kuroiwa.  (City and County of Honolulu)

The Blog welcomes Kuroiwa to his new gig. Way back in 2012 he developed on his own a searchable database of Hawaiʻi campaign finance information. He also co-founded Hawaiʻi Open Data, dedicated to expanding public access to government information. 
His background also includes roles at aio Hawaiʻi, Oceanic Time Warner Cable, PBS Hawaiʻi, the University of Hawaiʻi Mānoa and the Cancer Research Center of Hawaiʻi.
Agreeing to disagree: Gov. Josh Green was on the road last week, traveling to Santa Fe, New Mexico, and Park City, Utah, for meetings of the Western Governors’ Association and the National Governors Association.
He’s also co-starring in a new video from Disagree Better, which bills itself as a nonpartisan nonprofit “focused on helping Americans navigate political differences more constructively.”
“Green joins outgoing Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) to show how leaders from opposing parties can disagree respectfully, find common ground and work together to solve problems,” says a press release.
You can read more about Green’s views on bipartisanship in a recent Civil Beat Q&A.
Coming soon: Republican state Rep. Lauren Matsumoto and Democratic state Sen. Troy Hashimoto of Hawaiʻi are “teaming up” for an upcoming Disagree Better video, “part of a broader national effort bringing together elected leaders from both parties to model respectful disagreement and cooperation.”

title: Nick Minicucci Becomes University of Delaware’s All-Time Leading Touchdown Passer, Leads Team to Bowl Eligibility with Win over New Mexico State
description: Nick Minicucci threw his program leading 62nd career touchdown in the University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (6-5, 4-3 CUSA), 42-30, win over the New Mexico State Aggies (3-8, 2-5 CUSA), November 21.   Delaware quarterback Nick Minicucci took the shotgun snap with tight end Scott Moore to his left and running back Jo Silver to his right. Minicucci receive[...]
text:
Fightin’ Blue Hen quarterback, Nick Minicucci, warming up before UD’s game against Missouri State on October 20. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
Nick Minicucci threw his program leading 62nd career touchdown in the University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (6-5, 4-3 CUSA), 42-30, win over the New Mexico State Aggies (3-8, 2-5 CUSA), November 21.
 
Delaware quarterback Nick Minicucci took the shotgun snap with tight end Scott Moore to his left and running back Jo Silver to his right. Minicucci received the snap as Moore ran across his face to the right flat. Silver ran the opposite direction and faked like he was receiving the handoff. Minicucci pulled the ball, rolled out right and fired a pass to Moore in the flat.
Moore caught the ball on the run and continued into the endzone. The routine play action pass gave Delaware a two possession lead with a little over a minute remaining in the third quarter, but there was more significance to the simple ten-yard score. The touchdown pass was Minicucci’s 59th of his career. One more than former Blue Hen Matt Nagy and the most for a University of Delaware quarterback all-time.
Minicucci’s record breaking touchdown pass was one of three he threw in the second half of the Blue Hens’, 42-30, victory over New Mexico State, Saturday evening. 
“A lot [is] special about Nick,” head coach Ryan Carty said postgame on the ESPN+ streaming broadcast. “I think the most special thing is something we talked about prior to this game is his work ethic, right, and he’s a guy that’s going to do everything for the team first. He’s unselfish. He is unwavering in his commitment to making sure that he’s going to be the most prepared person in the stadium.” 
Minicucci’s record setting throw not only etched his name in Blue Hen history, but also gave Delaware some breathing room ahead of the fourth quarter. Delaware’s signal caller increased the lead on the Blue Hens’ next possession with a touchdown pass on a screen play to fourth year tight end, Josh Humes, which he ran 47 yards downfield into the left side of the endzone. Minicucci ended his day with a 20-yard touchdown pass to Moore making him the first Delaware receiver with three touchdown receptions in a game since 2022 and gave Delaware a 42-24 lead with less than two minutes remaining in the game. 
The Aggies scored two touchdowns in their fourth quarter comeback attempt on a pair of touchdown passes from third year quarterback Trey Hedden. Hedden connected with third year receiver TJ Pride for both scores, but the pair’s comeback attempt fell short. 
The Blue Hens led the final 20 minutes of the game after a 30-yard touchdown run by fifth year running back Kaderris Roberts returned the lead to Delaware in its opening possession of the third quarter. The Aggies led, 16-14, at halftime after the team scored 13 unanswered points in the last eight and a half minutes of the first half. New Mexico State never led after that.
The Blue Hens finished the game with 523 total yards of offense and their fourth game this season scoring 40 or more points. Minicucci led the passing offense with 31 completions on 41 attempts, 398 passing yards and the five passing touchdowns — all of which were caught by tight ends. Wide receivers Sean Wilson and Bryson Graves combined for 13 catches and 153 yards receiving, and Roberts finished the game as the Blue Hens’ leading rusher with 45 yards and the Blue Hens only rushing touchdown.
Delaware’s win improves its conference record to 4-3 and its overall record to 6-5, making the program bowl eligible in its second straight FBS season. The Blue Hens are one of four CUSA schools to be bowl eligible this season. That total can increase to five if Kennesaw State defeats Western Kentucky in its season finale on November 28.
“I can’t be more proud of that, you know. As somebody who went to this university and played, to be able to usher in you know our phase, jumping up into FBS football is just so amazing,” Carty said on the broadcast.
The Blue Hens have one more game remaining on their schedule against Jacksonville State at home on November 28. Jax State sits in second place in CUSA and will be the team taking on Liberty in the CUSA championship game in December. Jax State lost in the championship last year against Kennesaw State.
Delaware’s home finale will be played at Delaware Stadium with kick-off scheduled for 3:30 p.m. The Blue Hens can match their win total from a season ago — seven wins — with a victory Saturday afternoon. The game will be nationally televised on CBS Sports Network as well.

name: VTDigger
title: After downtime, Killington and Mikaela Shiffrin up for return of World Cup
description:
Back from a 2025 break, Vermont’s biggest ski resort and the most-winning Alpine racer in history are set to reunite with 20,000 spectators and 2 million television viewers this Thanksgiving weekend.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After downtime, Killington and Mikaela Shiffrin up for return of World Cup.
text:
U.S. Olympians Paula Moltzan (left) and Mikaela Shiffrin, pictured at a World Cup race in Austria on Oct. 24, are set to compete at the Killington ski resort this Thanksgiving weekend. Photo by Marco Trovati/AP
Skier Mikaela Shiffrin was on the rise two years ago when she rode up Killington ski resort’s Superstar lift in hopes of scoring an unprecedented 100th World Cup racing win.
Then came the fall — and, set for this coming weekend, the long-awaited return.
The Vermont-schooled athlete slipped, somersaulted and slammed into a fence 12 seconds from the finish line on Nov. 30, 2024, leading to months of physical rehab and recovery. Killington soon followed with its own World Cup break, closing the event’s lift for most of 2025 to install a $12 million replacement.
But that was then. Vermont’s biggest ski area is working to welcome the international circuit back to the Green Mountain State when 100 top female Alpine skiers are scheduled to compete this coming Saturday and Sunday.
Snowmaking crews have spent the month battling warm weather similar to that before the last World Cup, when the temperature hit 56 degrees on Veterans Day, only for 2 feet of snow to fall on Thanksgiving.
“Early season weather tested us once again this year, but our snowmaking team has again shown why they’re the best in the business,” Jordan Spear, Killington’s vice president of mountain operations, said in a statement. “During our most recent snowmaking window, we were able to operate 147 snow guns at once just on Superstar, a new record.”
World Cup officials visited the racecourse Thursday and confirmed the event would take place.
“The challenging weather conditions initially raised doubts,” Peter Gerdol, of the International Ski and Snowboard Federation, said in a statement. “However, following a thorough assessment of the current conditions and the weather forecast for the days leading up to the races, we are confident that the races can go ahead.”
A crowd of some 20,000 spectators and 2 million television viewers are expected to watch Shiffrin — a Burke Mountain Academy graduate who scored her third Olympic gold at the 2026 Milano Cortina Winter Games — as well as teammates including Paula Moltzan, a newly awarded bronze medalist now living in Waitsfield.
Shiffrin has won the Killington event’s slalom — a race down and around a series of gates — for six of its eight years (she placed fifth in 2022 and was sidelined in 2024). Many fans worried she might not return this year when she recently announced her desire to focus on other contests such as giant slalom (a longer version of the slalom) and super-G (short for super giant slalom, which adds the speed of downhill).
“I am currently planning that the Killington slalom would be my first slalom race of the season,” she went on to reassure Vermonters, breaking the news on her “What’s the Point” podcast.

A groomer prepares Killington ski resort’s Superstar trail for World Cup racing this Thanksgiving weekend. Photo courtesy of Killington

Better still for the resort, Shiffrin is inviting the public to a special live taping of her show Friday at 4:45 p.m. on a stage outside the K-1 base lodge.
“Killington feels like home and this crowd is a huge reason why,” Shiffrin said in a statement. 
NBC and Peacock are scheduled to air the giant slalom Saturday at 12:30 p.m. and slalom Sunday at 1:30 p.m.
The live coverage promises to showcase the resort, whose opening this past Tuesday was the first in the eastern United States this ski season.
Local owners at the Killington Independence Group have spent $80 million since purchasing the resort in 2024 to raise the capacity and reduce the energy consumption of their 9-million-gallon-a-day snowmaking system. They recently announced plans to invest another $200 million in other upgrades over the next decade.
“It’s almost sometimes hard to believe,” Killington CEO Mike Solimano said of financial figures unmatched in his 25 years there.
Then again, the mountain’s partners are facing some ups and downs.
The town of Killington, population 1,407, has seen headline-grabbing turnover in its municipal government and is seeking to fill a host of positions, including town manager, finance director, zoning administrator and fire chief. That has caused delays in constructing and accounting for road and water infrastructure improvements approved by residents in 2023.

READ MORE

For its part, Canada’s Great Gulf real estate group is still obtaining permits for a 450-acre retail and residential slopeside village proposed in 2023. Developers had hoped to break ground as soon as this year, but design changes and local and state review have sparked delays, with an updated schedule yet to be announced.
The town turnover and village’s unsettled timeline have fueled misinformation on social media. In response, the Killington Selectboard recently said it was expanding the municipal staff search through online ads, while Great Gulf reiterated its commitment to the area as a major sponsor of this week’s World Cup.
“It reflects our long-term vision for the base village as a vibrant, four-season destination,” Michael Sneyd, head of Great Gulf’s resort residential division, said in a statement.
Ski area leaders, for their part, say they remain on course. 
“I know when you go to Facebook, everyone loves to fight about everything, and the village is not moving as fast as we’d like, but it’s not slowing us down,” Solimano said at a recent community meeting.
Killington is considering whether to limit its World Cup hosting to every other year due to the $2 million annual cost. The resort, now surveying the public and staff, has yet to reveal a decision.
“We want to see what people think,” Solimano said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s blue wave has red edges
description:
Democrats flipped red states by focusing on kitchen table issues, not progressive ideology. Vermont lawmakers should take the same lesson and get to work on affordability.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s blue wave has red edges.
text:
Dear Editor,
Democrats have flipped seats across the country in the latest election, but “flipping blue” means different things in different states, including Vermont.
Even in the best of times, Democrats don’t walk in lockstep. When discussing internal politics for Democrats at all levels, the phrase “herding cats” comes to mind. As Walt Whitman put it, “Do I contradict myself? Very well, then I contradict myself. I am large. I contain multitudes.”
That diversity of opinion is both the best of Democrats and the worst, and keeps our pulses elevated.
What we seem to agree on, going back to the off-year gubernatorial elections in Virginia and New Jersey in 2025, and now into the most recent midterms this November, is that kitchen table issues are front and center of people’s minds. 
Working people are digging into their couch cushions for loose change to fill their gas tanks, and the cost of heating oil is stretching budgets to the breaking point. People see friends and family of the current president filling dump trucks with money, and you get election results like we just saw. Even an ounce of compassion from the White House might have stemmed the blue wave, but Republicans paid the price for their “let them eat cake” — or, as a viral Democratic ad put it, “pick another protein” — attitude, and state after state flipped blue. 
But what does that really mean? Those claiming it’s a progressive mandate seem oblivious to the fact that Mississippi, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa and Alaska — all of which flipped blue — are not hotbeds of progressivism. 
Anyone who saw the law-and-order TV ad by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom will have no doubt he means business about putting crime at the top of his agenda. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton knew he wouldn’t get far talking up Medicare for All. And let’s not forget Mary Peltola’s populist message in Alaska: “Fish, family, freedom.”
Even here in Vermont, moderate Democrats made the difference and reelected Gov. Phil Scott. Many Democrats elected to the Vermont House and Senate are moderate. Expectations of a purely progressive agenda should be moderated by looking at the electoral map that elected Scott. The deep blue of Burlington and Brattleboro was exceeded by the purple and red throughout the rest of the state.
As on the national scene, kitchen table issues will probably dominate the agenda. With fuel oil soaring from under $3.50 per gallon last year to more than $6 this year, it’s enough to scare even those of more than modest means. Food, housing and healthcare costs continue to soar, and Vermonters’ ability to address them will hinge on how much help we get from Congress. Balancing property taxes with ensuring our children get a quality education that prepares them for life in the 21st century will be a high-wire act. 
What portends well for us in Vermont is that we don’t carry campaign rancor into the Legislature. 
In my volunteer work with the National Institute for Civil Discourse, one concern we see in workshops across the country that inhibits working together better is hard-core, nasty election campaigns.
With Vermont campaigns keeping it civil for the most part, as we especially saw in our gubernatorial debates, I hope legislators and the governor can work together to make Vermont more affordable and make a positive difference for Vermonters. 
And now, let’s get to work. 
Mike MrowickiPutney, Vt.

title: 2026 marks a plentiful year for apple crops
description:
Apple growers look back at a successful harvest and apple season.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  2026 marks a plentiful year for apple crops.
text:
Champlain Orchards in Shoreham saw a record crop this year, and some apple varieties were still available for picking at the orchard last week. Other area orchards also reported a positive pick-your-own season, noting favorable weather and good quality fruit. Photo by Steve James/Addison

This story by Marin Howell was first published in the Addison Independent on Nov. 12, 2026.
Favorable weather made for an abundant apple season at orchards around Addison County this fall. With the season winding down — or already wrapped up at some spots — local growers reported plentiful crops and expressed gratitude for community members’ support.
“It was wonderful,” Kathleen Stine, of Monkton’s Stine Orchard, said of the season. “In the beginning there were some important days that were rainy, but after that it was a gorgeous season. The fruit was plentiful, the doughnuts never stopped, and the cookies never stopped.”
Stine and her husband, Aaron, co-own Stine Orchard, where they grow over 20 varieties of apples, along with pears and plums. Kathleen Stine said all of the orchard’s apple varieties fared well this year.
“People’s favorites are typically (McIntosh) and Honeycrisps, but we have some cult followings for the Northern Spy, for example,” she said.
As of early November, Stine Orchard had closed for the season but planned to be open on select Saturdays for doughnuts, with community members able to pick from what’s left on the trees for 50 cents per pound.
The orchard team was also busy gearing up for Thanksgiving, with orders coming in for goods like pies and cider doughnuts and a pickup day planned for the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.
Vergennes area
This year’s season has also wrapped up at Woodman Hill Orchard in Ferrisburgh. Run by Steph Lowe and Rob Rogers, the orchard grows several varieties of apples at 175 Plank Road just outside Vergennes.
The orchard’s season went well overall, according to Rogers and Lowe.
“It was a successful harvest, we made mountains of doughnuts and hosted many field trips, which is always such a joy,” they told the Independent. “It’s an intense two months, but we feel very fulfilled … and ready for a break!”
They noted how this year’s weather made for a positive pick-your-own season.
“It was a bit dry to start but we had good rain earlier this summer so the apple quality didn’t suffer,” they said. “We were lucky that the cold nights in October didn’t get cold enough to bring apple picking to an end and we were able to sell through the end of the month. It was a good, long picking season this year.”

An orchard visitor has an abundance of options to choose from while picking Empire apples at Woodman Hill Orchard in Ferrisburgh. The orchard had a successful harvest this year, echoing other area growers in reporting a good apple crop and positive pick-your-own season. Photo by Lee Kron

Woodman Hill was among the local orchards hit by a spring freeze in 2023 that damaged crops. They noted the freeze put the orchard on “a strong even-year trend.”
“So this year, like 2024, was a boom and all our trees were loaded with fruit, in all varieties. And the quality was good too,” Lowe and Rogers said.
The orchard officially closed Nov. 1 but was open Nov. 8 for a customer appreciation day. On that day, community members could pick fruit for free for themselves or the food shelf.
“This was such a fun day for us where we got to see our returning customers one more time and even meet some folks who had never been here before,” the owners said.
In Shoreham
The pick-your-own season was winding down at Champlain Orchards in Shoreham in early November.  The orchard, which acquired Douglas Orchards several years ago, grows 300 acres of tree fruit, including over 140 varieties of apples.
Champlain Orchards owner Bill Suhr said his spread saw favorable weather and a record crop this year. A damaging freeze that impacted orchards from Virginia to New York didn’t hurt Champlain Orchards, and no hail affected his crop, Suhr said.
“Fruit size is good, fruit color is good, and fruit flavor is fantastic,” he told the Independent.
Suhr noted the EverCrisp apple variety is growing in popularity and he was also pleased with this year’s peach crop. In addition to apples, the orchard grows a variety of stone fruit (including 17 types of peaches), berries, pears, medlars, quince and currants.
Suhr said nearly every crop did well this year, and the orchard harvested 7 million pounds of fruit.
“That mimics a crop from two years ago, but is significantly higher than last year,” he said, adding that the orchard opts to keep fruit in the orchard rather than harvest beyond customer demand. 
With the harvest season ending, the team at Champlain Orchards was pivoting its attention to orchard cleanup, preparing for winter and supporting newer orchards. The team was also busy putting together mail order gift boxes that carry the orchard’s fruit, cider and other goods to customers near and far.
Like other area growers, Suhr was appreciative of community members’ support for locally grown produce.
“It’s great that Vermonters care about where their food is from and are checking in with their farmers,” he said.

title: Cabot to hold January referendum on closing its high school
description:
Voters have opted to keep Cabot’s high school open four times. Now, for the first time, the school board is bringing a vote that will decide its future.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Cabot to hold January referendum on closing its high school.
text:
Cabot School on November 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger

In March, the Cabot School board of directors got some surprising news.
Full-time high school attendance was unexpectedly going to drop by nearly 30% for the upcoming school year, with fewer than 25 students attending the small preK-12 school’s upper grades.
The rest, 22 high school age students, are either attending early college, other public or independent high schools via the state’s regional high school choice program or are part-time at Cabot’s high school and part-time in career and technical education programs.
That news, along with the state’s nascent district merger process, led the board to conclude unanimously in July that the high school is “not sustainable” with so few students, according to school board member Ellen Cairns. While closing the school likely will not save money or reduce the tax rate, the board says sending students elsewhere would increase academic and social opportunities for them.
On Jan. 6, Cabot voters are set to decide whether to close their high school next June and tuition the remaining students out to the public high school or independent school of their choice come next fall. Cabot School would continue to operate its preK-8 grades.
If the majority of the town’s approximately 1,200 voters do not support the closure, then the school board would pursue a merger with the nearby preK-12 Danville School, Tormey said — a process that would span several years. The board already looked to expedite that option with Danville, but found that a fast-tracked merger was not possible.
Cabot’s vote comes as small schools in Vermont are under increased pressure to make changes and curb costs. Act 170, passed this spring, outlines a process for districts and supervisory unions to consider merging with each other to save on administrative and maintenance costs. Act 73, passed in 2025, aims to shift school budgeting decisions away from districts and to the state. The law also established class size minimums.
Cabot’s high school, which focuses on project-based learning, has survived four community-petitioned votes about its existence over the past 14 years. However, this will be the first vote brought by the school board itself, which has spent much time and effort over the past decade to research and educate the community about its options.
“We’re getting to the point where I think the status quo is not something we’re looking forward to maintaining,” Tormey, who has been on the school board since 2004, said earlier this month.
The board is not taking a position on the question of closing the high school versus pursuing a merger.
“I think it’s important at this point to check in with the community,” the school board chair said.
The cost of sending Cabot’s high school students to other schools next year would be slightly more than the savings from staff reductions and reduced facilities costs related to closing the high school, preliminary estimates from the school administration show.
The actual cost would depend on tuition costs for the schools chosen by Cabot’s high school students. Announced tuition rates for next school year at nearby high schools, including the historic independent schools Lyndon Institute and St. Johnsbury Academy, range from $19,500 to $26,588 per student. The cost would also depend on how many members of Cabot’s currently homeschooled community might decide to take advantage of future high school choice.
The cost of a merger with Danville School — located about 20 minutes away from Cabot School — is uncertain, though transportation to the merged school would be provided for all students. In a school choice scenario, transportation is typically up to the student and their family.
While Tormey says the higher-than-usual number of students taking advantage of opportunities outside of the high school this year is a compliment to their abilities and education, he also acknowledges a “very, very unusual set of circumstances” in school leadership that may have led to it.
In the spring of 2024, Cabot residents voted to keep the high school open by a 367-239 margin. Following that vote, the school board hired a new principal — Jennifer Blake — to lead Cabot School, school board member Cairns wrote in this month’s edition of the Cabot Chronicle. Blake “led some popular changes at the school,” and some students who had attended other schools or were homeschooled enrolled in the high school, Cairns wrote, improving numbers and morale.
However, after just a year, Blake resigned for “personal and professional reasons,” she wrote in her letter of resignation, and two part-time interim principals led Cabot School last year. The school board terminated the contract of the principal hired for this year, Darin Carney, just two weeks prior to the start of the school year.
“Being a principal at a K-12 building is always a challenge,” said Caledonia Central Supervisory Union Superintendent Matt Foster, who oversees Cabot as well as Danville, Twinfield, Walden, Waterford, Peacham and Barnet schools.
“The Vermont political environment around closures adds to the difficulty of attracting and retaining good building administrators,” Foster wrote in an email earlier this month.

READ MORE

A new principal, Paul Grimaud, is slated to start this month, and Tormey said that all are looking forward to having a “much more stable leadership situation at the school.” Grimaud is a longtime educator who most recently was the principal of an American school in the United Arab Emirates.
In the meantime, leadership responsibilities at Cabot School have been shared by four Supervisory Union staff who are certified to serve as principal.
Initial opinions among community members on closing the high school versus continuing a merger with Danville School have been split.
A community survey earlier this fall showed that 58% of the 137 respondents were most supportive of closing the high school and 34% of respondents wanted to continue operating the high school while exploring a merger. A slight majority of the nine current students who responded to the survey, 57%, were supportive of closing the high school and transitioning to school choice. However, the survey has been criticized by community members for not being distributed widely enough and lacking adequate information about the district’s options.
“I don’t want to see the high school go,” said Erica Fucello, a Cabot resident who previously served on the school board for a year and a half, in a September meeting. Her three children — a senior participating in early college, a freshman and a third-grader — are very happy at Cabot School, she said.
Several community members at the September meeting spoke about the toll that the uncertain future of the high school is having on students and stressed the importance of a clear path forward.
Rory Thibault, a former longtime school board member, said that he and his wife spend a lot of time trying to shield his eighth grader from the ongoing discussions.
“It’s unavoidable,” he said. “The question of ‘where am I going next year?’ is overwhelming.”
The board is working on an updated version of financial projections that will be mailed to all voters in December to inform as many residents as possible about the school’s options.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Trump’s plan sparked anger, but beef imports had already been rising as US cattle numbers fell
description: President Donald Trump has angered ranchers by allowing more foreign beef into the country, but the United States was importing beef before he began his second stay in the White House.  In 2024, during the final year of President Joe Biden’s administration, U.S. beef imports reached a then-record 4.64 billion pounds, and they’ve continued to […]
text:
As the sun rises near Artesian, South Dakota, on Sept. 17, 2026, Trevor Olson is out in a pasture with a bucket of pellets in hand, scattering feed for his cattle. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight) President Donald Trump has angered ranchers by allowing more foreign beef into the country, but the United States was importing beef before he began his second stay in the White House. 
In 2024, during the final year of President Joe Biden’s administration, U.S. beef imports reached a then-record 4.64 billion pounds, and they’ve continued to go up. 
Falling U.S. cattle numbers are part of the reason. The nation’s cattle numbers have declined from a recent peak of about 95 million cattle in 2019 to an estimated 86 million, which is a 75-year low, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Meanwhile, the number of U.S. farms or ranches with cattle has declined from more than a million in the 1970s to about 600,000.
Brett Kenzy, a rancher from Gregory, said the reasons for those declines are many, and so are the ideas to reverse the trends. He said abrupt changes in import policies are not helping.
“What’s required to build our cattle herd up is confidence — confidence in the market, and we don’t have that right now,” Kenzy said.


Trump’s action and responses
In August, Trump announced a plan to allow 661 million pounds of lean beef trimmings into the country at a lower tariff rate. He said it would lower beef prices for consumers. Yet since the plan took effect, the targeted imports have been slow to arrive and beef prices have remained high.
Trump’s announcement also sent the cattle futures market lower, according to Scott Kolousek, a farmer and rancher from Wessington Springs. 
“When this news comes out of Washington, the markets are up and down, up and down,” Kolousek said. 
He said his operation feeds calves to roughly 750 to 800 pounds. That means a $10-per-hundredweight decline in the market reduces an 800-pound calf’s value by about $80. For a producer selling 200 calves, that’s a $16,000 difference that “you can lose in a matter of minutes,” Kolousek said. 
Producers say raising cattle takes years of planning, while government policy and market expectations can change overnight. A rancher deciding whether to retain heifers for breeding must invest in raising those animals before they can produce calves. Those calves then need additional time to reach market weight.
Kenzy said that makes it difficult for ranchers to invest in expanding their herds if they fear future policy decisions could undermine their operations.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As one proposal to bolster American cattle numbers, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins announced the Ranchers First Initiative on Aug. 31, after blowback about the administration’s move to allow more beef imports. One part of the proposal is an insurance option to encourage ranchers to keep young heifers for breeding. It would provide financial protection over a two-year period if a heifer’s slaughter value exceeds the value of retaining the heifer for breeding. 
The administration also announced proposals including allowing disaster recovery assistance on some federally protected grasslands, expanding support for beginning ranchers and prioritizing American beef in government programs. 
Some cattle producers want a further step, called Mandatory Country of Origin Labeling. It would require labels identifying where an animal was born, raised and slaughtered. Supporters say it would give consumers more transparency about where their meat comes from and encourage them to buy U.S beef, which could motivate ranchers to grow their herds.
The policy was implemented in 2009, but after Canada and Mexico threatened tariffs on U.S. exports in response, Congress removed the labeling requirements in 2016. 
The U.S. Senate Agriculture Committee approved Majority Leader John Thune’s American Beef Labeling Act amendment in August, which includes a pathway to reinstate labeling in the pending farm bill. The bill passed out of the committee in September and is awaiting further action in the Senate, where Thune, a South Dakota Republican, will soon become minority leader instead of majority leader as Democrats take control of Congress following their wins in the general election.
Consolidation
Kenzy said even if cattle numbers grow and the market becomes more stable, the lack of competitive buyers for cattle would remain a significant problem. Only four companies control 85% of the U.S. beef processing market.
Kenzy said the U.S. has spent decades becoming more concentrated in cattle feeding and meatpacking, and “we’ve lost a huge number of independent packing plants and feeders in this country.” That’s meant more producers have to take whatever’s offered. 
“Anybody who’s thoughtful would know that herd building without a long-term fair price mechanism is not going to work,” Kenzy said.
Kolousek said the lack of fair markets is contributing to the decline in ranches and cattle numbers.
“People are getting out of the cattle business,” Kolousek said. “The government doesn’t have our backs. The markets don’t work the way they should.”
Federal officials have made some efforts to address concentration in the meatpacking industry. 
Under former President Biden in 2022, the U.S. Department of Agriculture invested in expanding independent meat processing via grants to help small facilities increase capacity. President Trump’s administration also announced $500 million in assistance for smaller and midsize beef processors this year. 
Additionally, the Department of Justice has been investigating potentially anticompetitive practices in the meatpacking and retail industries. 
Kenzy is among the cattle producers who advocate requiring major packers to purchase more cattle through negotiated cash sales and further strengthening antitrust enforcement. 

Cattle graze in a pasture straddling Mellette and Todd counties in south-central South Dakota. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Competing with crops
Kenzy said all of that is only one part of the challenge facing U.S. cattle numbers.
Across the Great Plains, about 36 million acres of grassland were converted from 2012 through 2023, with row-crop expansion identified as the leading cause, according to a World Wildlife Fund analysis.
Federal crop insurance subsidies and other federal agricultural programs can reduce the financial risks of growing crops, Kenzy said, while cattle producers remain more exposed to market swings. He argued that difference can make crop production more attractive than raising cattle.
Crop farmers benefit from several taxpayer-funded programs that reduce financial risk. The federal government subsidizes crop insurance that protects against losses from drought, flooding and other natural disasters. Other programs provide direct payments when crop prices or revenues fall below certain levels, while government-backed loans help farmers manage financial pressures. The federal government also mandates a minimum amount of biofuels to be mixed into the nation’s fuel supply, incentivizing the growing of crops such as corn to make ethanol.
Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, has proposed legislation to make cattle production more attractive. The Rebuilding America’s National Cow Herd Act would pay farmers to convert less-productive cropland back to grass and allow livestock to graze the acres all season, with an enrollment cap of 20 million acres. 
But more robust subsidies for crop producers are not the only thing leading ranchers to become farmers.  
Ranching’s physical toll
Kenzy also pointed to ranching’s physical demands, compared with the increasingly automated nature of crop farming, as another factor.
“Raising cattle is physical,” Kenzy said. “My shoulders are shot.”
Darrell Raschke has spent his life in the cattle industry. He grew up on a ranch and still has some cattle on his Beadle County farm, where he primarily raises crops. He said automation in farming has allowed farmers to do a lot more with less labor.
“One man, two guys can farm an awful lot of acres with the equipment we have today,” Raschke said.
Meanwhile, cattle demand year-round attention, including feeding, calving and maintaining water supplies through harsh winters, Raschke said. Producers may need herds of 500 to 700 cattle to earn a living, requiring more workers than many operations can afford.
“People used to have eight, nine kids to help out with all those chores,” he said.
Raschke said he is skeptical there is a solution. Kenzy said policies that ensure stability for future generations would help keep young people ranching.  
Trevor Olson is a 27-year-old who raises cattle near Letcher. He sticks with ranching, he said, because “it just feels like the way of life.”
“I’ve grown up doing it,” he said. “I’ve always found that it’s those certain moments throughout a year that really make you appreciate it. Those moments that you feel nothing but pride in knowing the hard work was worth it.”
Olson said if political leaders can figure out how to help grow American cattle numbers, the customers will be there.
“At the end of the day, ranchers work for the consumers, and they have shown us their demand for beef is real,” he said.
