name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico agency seeks funding boost for wildfire-detection cameras
description: The New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department seeks to expand a network of artificial intelligence-enabled wildfire detection cameras to cover the state’s 100-most wildfire-prone communities, department leaders told the Legislative Finance Committee this week.
text:
The New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department is seeking $1 million from the New Mexico Legislature to expand its array of AI-enabled wildfire detection cameras across the state, department leaders said Nov. 19, 2026. Currently, 59 such cameras are installed across the state, illustrated above. (Photo courtesy of EMNRD)
The New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department seeks to expand a network of artificial intelligence-enabled wildfire detection cameras to cover the state’s 100-most wildfire-prone communities, department leaders told the Legislative Finance Committee this week.
The department is seeking an additional $1 million in its general budget fund request for the upcoming fiscal year for a wildfire early detection camera system. The 360-degree cameras would be stationed in wildfire-prone areas and use AI to detect wildfire starts and smoke.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The department currently oversees a pilot program with the company Pano AI, which has installed approximately 20 cameras on mountaintops and cell phone towers primarily in and around Bernalillo County. Large electrical utilities like PNM, along with some New Mexico towns such as Raton, also have their own cameras.
In total, according to the department, 59 cameras are stationed across the state, including in southeast New Mexico and the Gila National Forest. 
But significant gaps remain across the state, New Mexico State Forester Laura McCarthy told lawmakers Thursday, particularly in 684 communities statewide that the department has identified as wildfire-prone. 
If the department could deploy cameras to detect wildfire starts in the 100-most wildfire prone communities in the next fiscal year, McCarthy said, that would mark an “amazing start for New Mexico.”
While the department is still analyzing the benefits of the cameras, McCarthy said, “We are definitely seeing a reduction in the response time for firefighters to get on scene, and they are coming with the right resources because they have more situational awareness.”
The $1 million would go for cameras and related installation and subscription costs, estimated to cost $37,000 each annually, but McCarthy noted that the department can keep its options open in future fiscal years as technology improves and more companies seek the state’s business.
“We have vendors coming to us every week, and honestly, it’s a bit overwhelming to determine what exactly is our best need,” she said. “What we’re doing with the cameras right now is, it’s one year at a time. If there’s a better, newer, better technology that we should pivot to, we’re not obligated to go beyond that one-year period.”
The $1 million request for cameras is part of a roughly $8 million increase in general fund dollars for which the department is seeking legislative approval at the upcoming 60-day session beginning Jan. 19. The department, in total, is seeking $56 million from the state, which is a 13.7% increase from the previous year.

name: VTDigger
title: A week of tech disruptions explained — sorta
description:
A UVM computer science professor thinks the outages might be emblematic of a broader technological shift as AI empowers companies to find bugs hidden in their infrastructure faster.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A week of tech disruptions explained — sorta.
text:
A person types on a keyboard. Photo via Adobe Stock

David Adkins stood in an Australian hotel elevator as Microsoft systems went berserk. He was on vacation. But others in the elevator were there for a technology conference. 
“They were actually absolutely crippled,” said Adkins, a Middlebury College faculty member who also happens to be a cybersecurity expert. 
“There was a guy who was about to present, and his whole presentation was up in OneDrive. And, you know, it was just amazing how people have made the assumption that all this stuff is always going to work all the time.”
Microsoft’s outage was one of several technological failures, shutdowns and cyberattacks across the country this week. In the U.S., the technology troubles felt nonstop. Planes stopped flying, emails stopped sending, Apple Pay and banks experienced delays. The National Security Agency, charged with protecting the nation, wasn’t able to communicate internally. 
Across New England, breakdowns disrupted the work of a New Hampshire hospital and a Maine city hall. Here in Vermont, the state’s own law enforcement records management and dispatch system, as well as the Public Utility Commission website, have been taken offline due to a potential security threat and suspicious activity, respectively. 
Federal, state and company officials have said that none of the recent tech snafus appear to be connected. But they raise a question for anyone — maybe everyone — who counts on these systems to work. 
What happens when the very changes meant to make technology more reliable can also bring them down? After all, when many people depend on similar computer systems, a single failure can affect a lot of people.
The state’s investigation into a “potential security threat” to Valcour, the emergency services records system, is ongoing, Agency of Digital Services Interim Secretary Andrea DeLaBruere told VTDigger Friday. 
The system has been offline since Tuesday morning, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation is now involved, Gov. Phil Scott said in a press conference Thursday evening. 
“We’ll just let the investigation continue until we come to conclusion,” Scott told reporters.
State officials are not jumping to conclusions as to whether or not the threat to Valcour was a cyberattack, DeLaBruere said. She said broader technological outages are concerning to her as both a chief information officer and Vermonter, though.
Still, some Americans are concerned. 
“4Chan is probably busy,” Adkins said of the anonymous online bulletin known to incubate conspiracy theories. 
U.S. National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross left his post this week following the string of outages. President Donald Trump said the outages are not unusual, telling reporters during his trip to the Philippines and China this week that “things like that happen. It’s fine.”
U.S. Sen. Peter Welch D-Vt. wrote in a statement to VTDigger Thursday that he’s disappointed in the response from White House officials. 
“These outages are a real concern — and so is the drip drip of information we’re getting from the White House,” Welch wrote. “The Administration owes it to the public to be up front about what’s going on here, and what they’re doing to protect consumers’ safety and security.”
No one can say for certain whether separate bugs, hacks or programming errors caused the outages, UVM computer science professor Joe Near said. He thinks they might be emblematic of a broader technological shift as AI empowers companies to find bugs hidden in their infrastructure faster.
“I think it has to do with the rate at which we’re trying to change things, and like every time you change something, you might mess it up,” Near said. “I don’t think it’s because the new technology is worse in some way or something.”
State Rep. Scott Campbell, D-St. Johnsbury, vice-chair of the House Energy and Digital Infrastructure Committee, said he believes the national issues aren’t connected, but that Vermont’s public and private sector systems are overly antiquated. 
“We’ve been running systems that are decades old,” he said. “With the advent of these AI systems, AI agents that are able to basically jiggle a lot of digital door handles all at the same time, millions of millions of jiggles, and find one that they can Jimmy open. 
“You know, this is going to be a big, big issue.”
System changes are typical and can lead to temporary failures, Adkins said, pointing to a website that tracks user reports of service outages. But patching bugs is necessary to prevent nefarious cyberactivity, he said. 
“Bad actors have the same access to AI that the good actors have, and so it really has become an arms race,” Adkins said. “But that arms race no longer takes years to develop a nuclear warhead. Now it’s like minutes.”
However, when a large company like Microsoft goes offline, it can impact cross-country operations, he added. 
“Look at the infrastructure of the U.S. and (what) we, as a free market capitalist society, have,” he said. “We have a very innovative and very complex technical environment, which delivers great value when it does, but it’s a little, I don’t want to say more rickety, it’s just by its nature very, very interrelated.”
Oddly enough, though, the week-long — so far — slew of outages and suspicious online activity may have a positive outcome, however, according to Near. 
“In the longer term, we really will maybe find all the bugs and fix them, and actually we may end up with more secure, resilient systems at that point than we’ve ever had before,” he said. “Maybe the AI will get so good that the systems are unhackable.”
DeLaBruere said that the state has thwarted approximately 300 billion cyber threats this year with the help of artificial intelligence systems.
“I think technology in general, and not just specifically AI, has advanced so much that the time between when we’re notified about an issue and the time that we have to fix the issue, it’s a much shorter window than we had in the past,” she said. “So we have to be able to be proactive as much as we can, and then respond in a meaningful way quickly so that we can secure our systems.”
But, as new systems replace the old, service outages are bound to persist, Campbell said.
“This takes years to do,” he said. “So this is going to be an ongoing problem, it seems to me.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Supreme Court denies appeal on clean energy zoning rules, agrees to hear another
description: The Michigan Supreme Court Friday issued a major decision involving the state’s 2023 clean energy zoning law, declining to hear an appeal from nearly 80 localities who argued that state energy regulators had acted outside their authority in their efforts to implement the new policy. In November 2024, 72 townships and seven counties filed a […]
text:
Stock photo/Getty ImagesThe Michigan Supreme Court Friday issued a major decision involving the state’s 2023 clean energy zoning law, declining to hear an appeal from nearly 80 localities who argued that state energy regulators had acted outside their authority in their efforts to implement the new policy.
In November 2024, 72 townships and seven counties filed a challenge against the Michigan Public Service Commission, arguing the regulatory body had violated the state’s rulesmaking procedures by “unlawfully and unreasonably” redefining key terms and and creating processes and procedures “that violate the Legislature’s express and unambiguous intent.”
The appeal came nearly a year after Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signed the Clean Energy and Jobs Act, Public Act 233 and 234, into law. As part of a package of clean energy bills passed by the Democratic-led Legislature, the laws gave the Michigan Public Service Commission authority over permitting renewable energy and battery storage projects above a certain size.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Public Act 233 requires energy companies and power producers to engage with localities whose clean energy permitting process matches the one put in place by the state, those companies can apply for permitting through the commission if a community fails to approve or deny the local application in a timely manner, if the local zoning process is stricter than what state law prescribes, or if a project meets the requirements laid out by the permitting law, but is denied.
The Michigan Court of Appeals agreed with the localities on two points, finding that the commission had erred by only including units of government with zoning authority in its definition of an “affected local unit.” It also determined that the commission’s timeline for an affected local unit to notify a developer that they have a “compatible renewable energy ordinance” did not match the definition laid out in state law. Beyond those terms, the court largely upheld the Michigan Public Service Commission’s order implementing the law.
In their appeal to the Michigan Supreme Court, the localities presented a single question: Did the Public Service Commission unlawfully and unreasonably exceed its authority in issuing all or parts of the Oct. 10 order implementing the permitting law?
How Ann Arbor, Michigan, is creating its own clean energy utility

While the localities argued it had, the high court denied the application for leave to appeal, “because we are not persuaded that the question presented should be reviewed by this Court.”
However, the Supreme Court’s Friday order moves forward on some questions raised in a cross-appeal filed by the Michigan Public Service Commission and a collective of clean energy industry and advocacy groups. Those questions concern the Court of Appeals decision on the notification timeline and a company’s ability to move forward with a project if local elected officials do not respond to their offer to meet within 30 days, or if a meeting is never held. 
While the court declined to consider other questions raised by the commission and the intervenors, it instructed the Clerk of the Court to schedule oral arguments on the approved questions for January 2027.
In a statement, Advanced Energy United, Clean Grid Alliance and the Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council, which intervened in the case, applauded the court’s decision to deny the local governments’ appeal, allowing the commission to move forward in implementing the permitting law. 
“Michigan needs to generate more energy to keep energy costs down as demand continues to surge. The Clean Energy and Jobs Act ensures business leaders have certainty to invest in Michigan, building the projects that power the state’s grid and create jobs,” Trish Demeter, senior managing director at Advanced Energy United, said in a statement. “We look forward to the Michigan Supreme Court ensuring there remains a clear, transparent statewide process that everyone can follow so we can generate the energy needed to affordably meet demand.”
In a news release, Foster Swift Collins and Smith, PC, the law firm representing the local governments, noted their disappointment in the court’s decision not to hear their appeal. However, the firm also cheered its decision to uphold the Court of Appeals ruling around the definition of an “affected local unit.”
“This is an important win for counties and other local governments that may not exercise zoning authority over a project site but will nevertheless experience the project’s impacts,” Michael D. Homier, the leader of Foster Swift’s municipal practice group said in a statement. “The decision confirms that those communities cannot be excluded from the rights and protections the Legislature provided under PA 233 simply because another local government exercises zoning jurisdiction.”
In a statement, the Michigan Public Service Commission offered appreciation to the Supreme Court  for “providing clarity on what it will review in this matter.”
“We look forward to making our case,” the commission stated.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s $80M IT overhaul pause lengthens as ‘shocking’ audit finds more concerns
description:
“It just feels like we're — we're doing this over and over again,” said one lawmaker at a meeting of the Legislature’s technology oversight committee.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s $80M IT overhaul pause lengthens as ‘shocking’ audit finds more concerns.
text:
Rep. Monique Priestley, D-Bradford, speaks during a meeting of the Joint Information Technology Oversight Committee at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Friday, January 19, 2024. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Vermont’s wide-reaching $80 million IT modernization project has effectively been on pause since April. 
Now, a new audit has branded the state’s progress on the issue “unsatisfactory,” and Gov. Phil Scott’s administration is setting aside six more months to prepare for the transition and address the sweeping concerns outlined by the independent report. Estimates of the project’s overall cost, previously hovering at $70 million, have also ticked up, according to state officials.
The yearslong project, which is among the most expensive such undertakings in the state’s recent history, seeks to replace five existing state IT systems, including human resources and finance software, with the multi-use platform Workday. Crucial questions about how the new system will replace and interact with the old state software, as well as the timeline and cost for the effort, “remain unanswered,” the auditors said. 
Sen. Rob Plunkett, D-Bennington, who chairs the Joint Information Technology Oversight Committee, called the findings “shocking” in a meeting of the panel Friday.
“How can you help us, like, not be freaking out about this?” asked Rep. Monique Priestley, D-Bradford, of state officials at the meeting. “It just feels like we’re — we’re doing this over and over again.”
Indeed, it’s not the first time an independent analyst has raised the alarm over the project’s framing.
Lisa Gauvin, an IT consultant for the state’s Legislative Joint Fiscal Office, told lawmakers 18 months ago that the Agency of Digital Services had not done sufficient analysis to determine which functions can and cannot be replaced by Workday.
Then-Digital Services Secretary Denise Reilly-Hughes disagreed at the time, saying that while there were always unknowns in the early phases of such an undertaking, her team had done multiple “gap analyses” to confirm the new system’s ability to fill the state’s needs.
In April, officials shifted their approach to implementing Workday — potentially causing delays and cost increases, they said — and paused their work on the project. 
Reilly-Hughes left her role in mid-October to take a job at Microsoft.

READ MORE

Projects like this one generally take states between two and four years to complete, according to Jim Kreiser, a principal at CliftonLarsonAllen, the financial consulting firm who conducted this month’s audit at the request of State Auditor Doug Hoffer. That in itself makes Vermont, already about six years into its modernization effort according to Gauvin, something of an “outlier,” he said.
Given the audit’s findings, the state’s basis for selecting Workday may itself be in question, Kresier added.
“You may be at an inflection point of deciding: Have we even made the right decision?” he said.
Sean Brown, the state’s deputy secretary of administration, said his team was largely in agreement with many of the audit’s findings. Several areas of the project, he said, carry “substantial risk” currently.
Brown said the next step would be a 24-week period of work to address the audit’s concerns and prepare to implement the new system. At that point, he said, officials will “come back with a proposed timeline to restart the project.”
All parties agreed that the stakes are high. Kreiser’s team said bungling the new software’s implementation could corrupt data, cause costly delays and disrupt the normal functioning of government.
Other states have experienced significant bumps in the road implementing Workday, including Rhode Island and Oregon.
Priestley also raised questions about whether it would be responsible for lawmakers to continue funding the project when so many key factors are up in the air. In order to greenlight more money, she said over text Friday, she would need to see a detailed plan about how the new system would replace particular functions performed by the old ones and ensure access to existing data.
“From my perspective, we’re past the point of assurances,” Priestley said. “The bar is high for a reason.”
The Legislature has approved roughly $25 million so far, of which the state had spent about $17 million at the end of October, according to Chrissy Gilhuly, a spokesperson for the Agency of Administration.
“Every time there’s a delay in this project,” said Gauvin at Friday’s meeting, “that’s another cost.”
Kreiser said the project’s budget estimates are “certainly part of what needs to be reevaluated” in the coming months.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s $80M IT overhaul pause lengthens as ‘shocking’ audit finds more concerns.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CSCU votes on tuition hikes, PURA OK’s settlement with Eversource: CT politics news
description: Plus: A pride flag defaced at a Middletown church, Adoption Day saw 66 children find homes and the U.S. lost its measles elimination status.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
CSCU Regents approve controversial budget proposal
The Connecticut State Colleges and Universities Board of Regents voted Friday morning to approve a budget proposal for fiscal years 2028 and 2029, with one “no” and one abstention.
The proposal envisions a 3% tuition hike and unspecified cuts, which prompted student and faculty pushback Thursday. It requests over $300 million more in state funding in the next two years — a decision for the General Assembly in 2027.
Interim chair Ari Santiago said the board remains open to suggestions about other ways to close its budget gap. The board will vote on whether to actually raise tuition in December.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Pride flag defaced at Middletown church
Last Sunday during morning services at First Church Middletown UCC, a single protester tore down a trans-inclusive version of the LGBTQ+ Pride Flag outside of the church, then entered the sanctuary and interrupted services with a series of derogatory and anti-LGBTQ+ comments, many aimed specifically at the transgender community.  They were ultimately removed from the service, and worship continued. 
The incident came at the beginning of Transgender Awareness Week, which culminates Friday in Transgender Day of Remembrance or TDOR. Tonight, vigils for the 62 known trans people who have died in the past year are planned across the state; read more about that here.   
Sen. Matt Lesser, who represents Cromwell, Middletown, Newington, Rocky Hill and Wethersfield, denounced the violence in a statement sent out Friday morning.  “It is abhorrent that someone would deface someone else’s property and spread hateful rhetoric, let alone interrupt a place of worship to do so,” he said in the statement. “First Church Middletown UCC is a warm and welcoming place of faith and an important part of our community. I stand firmly with the church, its parishioners and our LGBTQ+ community.”
— Lucy Gellman, Arts & Culture Editor
Tong joins coalition supporting Black and Hispanic homeownership programs
Connecticut Attorney General Wiliam Tong is defending loan programs intended to support racial equity in homeownership as the federal government investigates banks offering the support.
On Wednesday, Tong joined a coalition of 20 attorneys general in sending a letter to Wells Fargo, explaining the legality of the bank’s Special Purpose Credit Program, which expands access to credit to disadvantaged groups. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development challenged the program in October, arguing that the focus on marginalized groups violates the Fair Housing Act’s antidiscrimination protects.
The attorneys general counter that the program provides necessary assistance to groups that have been historically denied access to homeownership. They add that even as the HUD probe continues, Wells Fargo must abide by state fair housing and lending laws.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Students for a Dream defend CT laws
Connecticut Students for a Dream announced on Friday that the group had submitted an amicus brief defending its wins on in-state tuition and institutional financial aid laws in the state.
The brief was filed in the U.S. Department of Justice’s lawsuit challenging Connecticut laws on higher education benefits, laws that allow immigrant students without permanent status to receive in-state tuition and financial assistance at public colleges and universities.
“Our members helped write this history. Undocumented students shared their stories publicly, organized their communities, and spent years at the Capitol fighting for access to college,” CT Students for a Dream said in a statement.
— Laura Tillman, Human Services Reporter
Himes: No evidence recent outages caused by cyberattacks
Amid confusion and fears over recent tech disruptions, U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said he’s seen no evidence “to suggest any of these outages were the result of a malicious actor.”
Himes, who hopes to become the chairman next year, noted that the owners of the systems that experienced outages like Microsoft, airlines and banks said they were “caused by internal actions.” Still, he warned that IT infrastructure needs to be prepared.
“Stepping back, the risk of disruptive or even damaging cyberattacks is very real,” Himes said in a statement, “and we need to do more to harden our critical infrastructure against attack.”
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
PURA OK’s settlement with Eversource over old storm costs
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority signed off on a settlement agreement on Wednesday with Eversource that ended a long-running dispute over the terms of a previous agreement that the utility reached with regulators in 2018.
The new settlement will allow Eversource to collect $8.1 million in costs related to several storms that took place during the negotiations over the old settlement. That amount is half what Eversource argued it was owed under the terms of the prior deal.
The agreement, which was brokered by Eversource and the Office of Consumer Counsel, will result in a temporary, .07-cent per kilowatt-hour increase to electric rates from Dec. 1, 2026 until June 30, 2027. 
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter
CT education commissioner elected president of national organization
Connecticut Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker has been elected president of the Council of Chief State School Officers board of directors.
CCSSO is a nationwide professional organization for K-12 education department heads. It provides support through “leadership, advocacy and service” to those officers and the organizations they supervise.
In a statement, Russell-Tucker said a central part of education leaders’ work today is “ensuring that every student sees themself as a learner, a problem-solver, an innovator, and realizes opportunities they may never have imagined possible.”
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Health disparities in Connecticut
The Connecticut Health Foundation released a wide-ranging report on racial and ethnic health disparities in Connecticut. Among the findings: Black residents have a life expectancy of 76.5 years, nearly five years shorter than the state average. They are more likely to face asthma, diabetes and certain cancers.
These disparities result from factors like unequal access to care, healthy food and transportation, but also disparate treatment from health providers and biased screening and testing. The report highlighted Connecticut’s efforts to improve disparities — including expanding coverage for undocumented children — and areas where the state could improve, like funding a 2023 law enacting Medicaid coverage for community health workers.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
US loses measles elimination status
The Pan American Health Organization announced this week that the U.S. lost “measles elimination status” — a designation that a country has gone at least 12 months without continuous spread of a single strain of the disease. Measles had been declared eliminated in the U.S. since 2000.
In a statement, Connecticut Department of Public Health Commissioner Manisha Juthani credited the state’s high vaccination rate with keeping cases low in the state. “Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles,” she said. “If you or your child are not up to date, now is the time to talk with your healthcare provider.”
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
CSCU extends contract for current interim chancellor
Natalie Braswell will continue serving as CSCU interim chancellor until June 2028.
At Friday’s Board of Regents meeting, interim chair Ari Santiago cited “the importance of stability and continuity” for the system and said faculty, staff, students and administrators had urged the board to put the search for a permanent chancellor on hold. “This is a pause, not an end,” Santiago said.
Braswell was appointed after the previous interim chancellor, John Maduko, resigned amid an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment. CSCU’s last permanent chancellor, Terrence Cheng, resigned after a spending controversy.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Rural remote patient monitoring grants extended
The state announced $1.8 million in grants to expand remote patient monitoring as part of the Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion federal effort aimed at improving rural healthcare in the U.S.
Remote patient monitoring will help identify emerging health concerns earlier and coordinate care before conditions require more intensive or costly care. The grantees are eDermatology, Hartford HealthCare Medical Group, Robinhood Health and StayWell Health Care.
Connecticut received a total of $154 million through the federal grant in 2026. In September, the state awarded grants totaling $46 million to four rural hospitals.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
Annual UConn economic forum focuses on AI’s local impact
A crowd of industry, academic, and local economic experts gathered for the University of Connecticut’s third annual economic forum this week.
This year’s event, held at Rentschler Field in East Hartford, focused on the local impacts of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, with university leaders emphasizing that UConn is a key player in the state’s growing tech-oriented economy, which is expanding to include biotech, quantum, and other industries.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
October jobs report shows unchanged unemployment rate, labor force growth
For the tenth month in a row, Connecticut’s unemployment rate stands above the national average, remaining at 5.1% according to the state’s latest jobs report.
The report, released on Thursday, also notes that the state continues to see increases in payroll jobs, which reached a record high in October. That employment growth has been particularly strong in the state’s manufacturing sector, which has grown 4.2% compared to the national rate of .06%.
Groups like the CBIA Foundation note that the latest report suggests that the recent growth in the state’s labor force is possibly more stable than earlier data suggested. Still, the organization said in a Thursday statement that it remains concerned about the fact that more than 40,000 workers have left the labor force since the beginning of the year.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT Adoption Day
The Department of Children and Families and Gov. Ned Lamont celebrated Connecticut Adoption Day on Friday with 66 children adopted.
The event is a chance for DCF to raise awareness about what Lamont called “one of the most loving, selfless acts a person can do.” The theme for this year’s National Adoption Month is “A Home for Every Child,” which DCF said “underscores the collective responsibility to shorten time spent in care and create lasting connections for children and youth.”
DCF said that there are 42 children with complex needs awaiting permanency. They are featured in the Heart Gallery.
— Laura Tillman, Human Services Reporter

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico culture secretary tells lawmakers agency reaching ‘breaking point’ due to understaffing
description: The New Mexico cultural affairs department secretary told lawmakers Thursday that current staff vacancies are pushing state museums and historic sites to a “breaking point” and requested a $4.3 million budget increase to fill positions and additional $5.5M in one-time funding for museum and program upgrades.
text:
New Mexico Department of Cultural Affairs Secretary Debra Garcia y Griego told lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee on Nov. 19, 2026, that staffing vacancies have brought museums and historic sites to a breaking point. Above: The "Telling New Mexico" exhibit at the New Mexico History Museum, which the agency is requesting funding to update. (Photo courtesy of the New Mexico History Museum)The New Mexico cultural affairs department secretary told lawmakers Thursday that current staff vacancies are pushing state museums and historic sites to a “breaking point” and requested a $4.3 million budget increase to fill positions. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Department of Cultural Affairs operates 16 museums and historic sites statewide; the New Mexico State Library; along with preservation and archaeological efforts. In FY26, the department served 1.6 million people in its museums and historic sites; reached 957,000 children statewide through arts programs and school tours; and oversaw 4.5 million digital transactions through the New Mexico State Library online portal, according to DCA data. 
But DCA Secretary Debra Garcia y Griego told lawmakers during the interim Legislative Finance Committee meeting in Santa Fe that lack of funding to fill staff vacancies is leading to the “end of the line” before the department must change services.
“We are in fact reaching a breaking point,” Garcia y Griego added. “We can no longer continue to hold these vacancies and not fill these positions that we have without directly impacting our services and programs to the public.”
According to DCA data, the department has a 17.6% vacancy rate, or 91 unfilled positions. The museums and historic sites alone have 72 vacancies, which has a “direct work impact on curatorial work, visitor hours and site maintenance,” Garcia y Griego said. DCA’s Preservation Division has a nearly 30% vacancy rate, which hinders its work on mandated archaeological and architectural reviews, DCA’s presentation noted.
To fill the vacancies, DCA requested a $4.3 million funding increase for FY27, with over half of the requested funds going to fill vacant positions. Garcia y Griego added that past increases haven’t kept pace with rising costs and DCA having to manage that on top of vacancies “is no longer effective and we will start having to cut services and hours to do that.”
DCA also requested $5.5 million in one-time funding for programs and museum upgrades: $460,000 expansion for the New Mexico Women’s Historic Markers; program; $2 million for the final phase of Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act compliance, $1.5 million for the Navajo Code Talker Museum in Farmington; $1 million to update the “Telling New Mexico” exhibit at the New Mexico History Museum; and $500,000 for restoration costs related to the Apollo 11 exhibit at the New Mexico Museum of Space History in Alamogordo.
Several lawmakers sounded sympathetic to the department’s needs, as well as some of the specific projects it hopes to fund.
Rep. Charlotte Little (D-Albuquerque) said DCA’s work on the final phase of Native American grave repatriation — during which the DCA will determine who the repatriating tribe is, secure the objects and deliver them to the designated tribe — was “so important to the culture, not just of all of New Mexico, but also our tribal communities here.”
LFC Chair Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces) told Garcia y Griego that the committee “looks forward to continuing to support that work, even as we navigate obviously strong budget demands.”
Sen. Nicole Tobiassen (R-Albuquerque) told Garcia y Griego that she’s “always supported your department and facilities, and I’m so thrilled with what you’re doing and the progress you’re making. Especially with the New Mexico Women’s Historic Marker Program. That’s thrilling to see.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Data center developer responds to questions as Mandan voters consider ban
description: The developer of a proposed Mandan data center answered questions from the public this week ahead of a Dec. 15 vote that could ban such projects within the city.  Residents of Mandan petitioned for a special election to vote on a measure that would ban data centers over 25 megawatts within city limits. More than […]
text:
Michael Whalen, managing director of digital infrastructure for Stark Power, speaks to attendees of a data center forum in Mandan on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The developer of a proposed Mandan data center answered questions from the public this week ahead of a Dec. 15 vote that could ban such projects within the city. 
Residents of Mandan petitioned for a special election to vote on a measure that would ban data centers over 25 megawatts within city limits. More than 700 residents signed the petition submitted this fall amid debate over data center ordinances in Mandan and Morton County. Stark Power proposes a 300-megawatt data center in Mandan. 
If city residents vote in favor of the ban, there would be “no path forward” for the project, said Michael Whalen, managing director of digital infrastructure for Stark Power. But rejecting a ban does not necessarily mean this project would advance, he added.
“It gives us an opportunity to submit an application and for there to be public debate,” Whalen said during a public forum.
The discussion was hosted by the Bismarck Mandan Chamber EDC, which prior to the event announced the group’s board of directors had voted to oppose the ban.
“Anytime you put a ban on anything, it takes away the opportunity to have the conversation,” said Brenda Nagel, president of the Bismarck Mandan Chamber EDC. “We are for economic development.”
Residents voice concerns over Mandan data center during town hall

She added any ban could scare off developers and future projects in other industries from coming to the area based on the public’s sentiment over data centers.
Local elected officials could still reject the project across multiple permitting and zoning steps, if the ban is defeated, Nagel said. She also stressed the chamber is not for or against data centers, but is opposed to bans that could affect development of the area.
Jane and Clayton Feist live in the extraterritorial zone just outside the Mandan city limits, but adjacent to the proposed data center site. The city of Mandan has zoning authority for extraterritorial areas up to 2 miles outside of city limits. 
“We can’t even vote on it even though it affects us,” Jane Feist said, since they don’t live within the city.
Clayton Feist said he worries about the standby electric generators that could produce noise at odd hours to power the facility, which could affect animals in the area and his ability to sleep.
“Some of us built for retirement,” Clayton Feist said. “If I try to sell you my home there, and there’s noise, are you going to buy it? I got 16 acres there.”
Michael Whalen, left, managing director of digital infrastructure for Stark Power, speaks next to Clint Cyr, center, lead engineer in acoustics at Epsilon Associates Inc., and Mike Brandt, right, development services engineer and shareholder at Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc., during a data center forum in Mandan on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Wahlen made a presentation to the attendees during the meeting that highlighted a sound modeling study showing the noise would be limited to 45 decibels at the proposed facility’s property line.
The data also showed the noise outside of three schools within a mile of the proposed campus would be between 29 to 39 decibels and even lower once inside the school buildings.
According to the American Academy of Audiology, a 30-decibel sound is equivalent to a whisper while 40 decibels compares to a quiet library. A 50-decibel sound is comparable to a moderate rainfall.
Whalen said Stark Power plans to sell the facility after the permitting process is complete to a company, such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google or Meta, that would occupy the building and operate the data center.
Eden Stramer of Mandan lives about a mile and a half away from the data center site and said she will vote in favor of the data center ban. She said she asked Whalen after the meeting about any assurances Stark Power could give the community after that sale takes place.
“There are no assurances. You can’t control what the next person does,” Steamer said. “We don’t even know who’s going to buy it, who’s interested in buying it.”
Whalen said the conditions for the data center will be bound to their permits, if the project moves forward, regardless of who the operator ends up being.
“When another end user takes ownership of the project, they have to adhere to those same conditions or they are subject to revocation of the permit,” he said. “They are binding conditions.”
Whalen listed the potential benefits to the community and commitments, if the project was able to move forward. 
The $3.4 billion project would sit across multiple buildings of a 300-acre campus on a 700-acre property. Stark Power projects the facility will generate $526 million in public revenue over 20 years to be spent on schools, parks and initiatives in Mandan and Morton County. 
That impact includes a community benefit agreement providing $10 million to a community-controlled fund once the data center reaches its capacity. An annual $1 million stipend would be added to the fund after launch, the company says.
Brenda Nagel, president of the Bismarck Mandan Chamber EDC, speaks during a data center forum in Mandan on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The city on its website says project-specific benefits or impacts have not been confirmed by city officials because no formal application has been submitted.
During peak construction between 2028 to 2031, it’s expected to employ more than 1,200 construction workers. Once operational, the data center is projected to add 210 permanent jobs with an average wage of about $80,000 per year.
The data center would use a closed-loop cooling system that would not draw water from the city, and the project would pay for road upgrades and repairs before construction begins, according to the company’s presentation.
Tom Hansen of Mandan attended the meeting and said he will vote against the data center ban.
“I say build it right now,” Hansen said after the meeting. “Why handcuff somebody because you are not 100% sure?”
Rob Bauer of Mandan said he thought the public forum was a promotion for the data center. He said his mind was not changed during the meeting and plans to vote for the data center ban.
“You hear about all the benefits of having one, and it’s mostly economic, and I don’t know of any other benefit than the economic one,” Bauer said. “I still don’t think there’s enough information to go forward with it.”
The Mandan special election will run from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Dec. 15. Votes can be cast at the Spirit of Life Roman Catholic Church at 801 First St SE. Absentee ballots can also be obtained from the city of Mandan.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: National
title: National outages, emergency alerts become fodder for doomsday conspiracy theories
description: Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days. Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst. The supposed warning signs? A nationwide […]
text:
Cases of bottled water are displayed for sale at a Costco in Burbank, Calif. A recent wave of doomsday conspiracy theories has fueled online calls for Americans to stockpile food, water and emergency supplies amid unfounded predictions of widespread blackouts and other catastrophes. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days.
Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst.
The supposed warning signs? A nationwide flight shutdown, disruptions to banking and technology services and a routine federal emergency alert test — seemingly unrelated events that some online users portrayed as evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or impending emergency.
The doomsday predictions lack credible evidence. But the speculation comes as the nation’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats — raising legitimate questions about the country’s preparedness for major disruptions. 
Federal officials have said they found no evidence that the latest disruptions were connected or that a nationwide emergency was imminent.  And some emergency management experts warn that false alarms can undermine public trust in official warnings and complicate disaster response when real emergencies strike.
FAA grounds all US flights due to air traffic control issue

Still, the attention surrounding these unfounded predictions does not necessarily mean they have gained widespread acceptance.
Joseph Uscinski, a political science professor at the University of Miami who studies conspiracy theories, cautioned against interpreting viral posts as evidence of a broader shift in public beliefs.
“Your average conspiracy theory dies on the vine,” he said, noting that many fade as the news cycle moves on.
Uscinski described the reaction as a recurring pattern: A major event sparks conspiracy theories, those claims attract attention and then eventually fade, only for the cycle to repeat when another event captures the public’s attention.
Some of the latest rumors appeared to gain traction ahead of Tuesday’s nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which interrupted television and radio broadcasts across the country. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, and the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, had announced the Nov. 17 test in September as part of routine efforts to evaluate the nation’s emergency warning infrastructure. Federal rules require nationwide testing at least once every three years.
The timing of the test, combined with recent outages and national security concerns, fueled speculation that the government was preparing Americans for a major catastrophe. 
FEMA addressed the claims on Facebook, saying the test was scheduled in advance and unrelated to any impending disaster. 
“We love a good fan theory as much as anyone, but there is no secret emergency happening here,” the agency’s post read.
From technical glitches to doomsday warnings
The online speculation followed several high-profile disruptions this month, including a major Microsoft service outage Nov. 12-14, and a nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Nov. 13.
Microsoft attributed its disruptions to technical problems. And the FAA blamed work by a contractor upgrading a router in Arkansas.
But this week brought more disruptions: to several major banks Monday,  to Apple services and the National Security Agency’s internal network Tuesday. Those also were separate technical issues, officials said.
Adding to the national security concerns, CNN reported Monday that U.S. intelligence suggested Iran was developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials with a radioactive “dirty bomb” or chemical weapon in Washington, D.C.
US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that he did not believe there was an imminent threat to Washington. Iran also denied the allegations.
During a congressional hearing Wednesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers that threats from Iran against Americans at home and abroad had increased substantially. Asked specifically about the reported dirty-bomb plot, Clayton declined to discuss the intelligence but acknowledged that threats involving weapons capable of causing mass casualties were not new.
Despite those explanations, social media posts increasingly portrayed the events as connected.
Some TikTok videos warned of a 90-day nationwide blackout that was to begin Nov. 17, while other videos encouraged viewers to stockpile emergency supplies, including water, food and medicine.
One widely circulated video manipulated footage of President Donald Trump speaking at a Nov. 9 news conference to make it appear that he had announced an impending blackout, according to a PolitiFact investigation. 
Trump made no such announcement. The account sharing the manipulated footage also promoted cryptocurrency purchases ahead of the supposed national emergency.
Other online posts pointed to a federal Department of Defense initiative announced in September to help military installations operate independently of civilian power grids for at least 90 days. The initiative, known as FORTRESS America, is intended to strengthen military readiness during potential disruptions.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also dismissed the online warnings, telling Fox News that Americans did not need to stockpile supplies in anticipation of widespread disruptions to electricity or to food and water sources. 
Vice President JD Vance similarly sought to ease concerns Monday, saying Americans did not need to build bunkers or rush to stockpile food and water in response to the recent outages. “We do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News. 
Other countries, including the United Kingdom, France and Germany, have urged residents to prepare for severe weather, cyberattacks and other emergencies –– adding to confusion among some Americans about whether they should take similar precautions. The UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign in October suggesting a three-day supply in case of emergency.
Real vulnerabilities
The conspiracy theories have emerged against a backdrop of genuine concerns about the nation’s aging infrastructure and growing cybersecurity threats, which have exposed vulnerabilities in systems Americans rely on for electricity, transportation, healthcare and emergency services.
The American Society of Civil Engineers gave U.S. infrastructure an overall C grade in its 2025 report card, a slight improvement from the C- awarded in 2021. The national report card is released every four years.
FEMA chief, US House members push for emergency management changes

But the organization warned that significant vulnerabilities remain. The nation’s energy and aviation infrastructure each received a D+, and the report estimated a $3.7 trillion gap between planned infrastructure investments and what is needed to bring the country’s systems into good working order.
The recent disruptions also drew scrutiny on Capitol Hill on Thursday, where lawmakers questioned Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, about the nation’s ability to withstand cyberthreats.
“American citizens are jittery,” Michigan Democratic U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said during the Senate Homeland Security Committee hearing, raising concerns about the Trump administration’s elimination of more than 1,000 positions at the agency. 
The nominee, Michael LoSapio, declined to assess the agency’s current resources but said he would evaluate potential gaps and request additional funding if necessary.
Cyberattacks are a growing concern for critical infrastructure operators, as hackers target hospitals, utilities, government agencies and other essential services. 
“Modern society is effectively built on interdependence and high levels of complexity of technologies supporting human systems, and so when you get kind of a localized failure, it can very quickly cascade to more strategic problems,” said Charles Harry, an associate research professor at the University of Maryland who specializes in cybersecurity risk and previously worked for the National Security Agency.
Harry pointed to healthcare and transportation as examples of sectors where interconnected systems can allow disruptions to spread far beyond their original source.
Hundreds of thousands of cyberattacks occur every day, but most attract little public attention because they cause minimal disruption, Harry said.
The landscape is evolving as artificial intelligence gives cybercriminals, state-sponsored hackers and even less sophisticated attackers new tools,  putting additional pressure on organizations to address security weaknesses before they can be exploited.
“Over the last 12 months, we’ve seen just an explosion in this type of activity, and it means that we’re going to have more frequent attacks, more consequential attacks,” Harry said. 
When misinformation becomes a public safety threat
Beyond the latest doomsday predictions, the spread of false information presents a broader challenge for state and local emergency management agencies, which rely on public trust to communicate accurate information during disasters.
FEMA chief decries rumors, disinformation about hurricane recovery as worst ever

During an actual emergency, false or misleading information can divert critical resources, delay response efforts and create confusion about evacuation routes, available shelters and government assistance.
“Sometimes (misinformation) can even mask itself as being something that comes from us, so you really have to dig deep, look at where the messages are coming from,” said Marc Pappas, the president of the National Emergency Management Association and director of the Rhode Island Emergency Management Agency.
The consequences have already played out during real emergencies.
Following Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024, conspiracy theories shared online alleged that the federal government had deliberately created or steered the storms toward certain communities. Other false claims accused federal officials of withholding disaster assistance, confiscating property and preventing private organizations from delivering supplies.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, publicly debunked the weather manipulation claims, emphasizing that no technology exists to create or steer hurricanes. FEMA also launched an online “rumor response” page to counter misinformation and reassure survivors that assistance remained available.
The challenges facing emergency officials come as the Trump administration considers shifting more disaster response responsibilities to state and local governments. During a U.S. House hearing Thursday, FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton called for significant changes to the agency, arguing that stronger states would make the nation more prepared and resilient. Some lawmakers questioned whether states have the resources to take on additional responsibilities.
“Emergency management is ready. We continue to be ready and prepared for emergencies, threats that happen to occur across the nation,” Pappas told Stateline, arguing that state agencies are well equipped to take on additional disaster response responsibilities.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: More state money is reaching NC childcare centers, but families are still struggling
description: For Cassandra Brooks, the owner of Little Believer’s Academy in Raleigh, the state’s new, higher childcare subsidies have meant more money to invest in her classrooms, hire staff and give longtime workers raises.  Like many states, North Carolina pays childcare centers a set amount of money for each child of a low-income family who qualifies […]
text:
Preschoolers learn Spanish in a classroom at Little Believer's Academy in Raleigh, N.C. (Photo by Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)For Cassandra Brooks, the owner of Little Believer’s Academy in Raleigh, the state’s new, higher childcare subsidies have meant more money to invest in her classrooms, hire staff and give longtime workers raises. 
Like many states, North Carolina pays childcare centers a set amount of money for each child of a low-income family who qualifies for subsidies. The subsidy helps offset the cost to make childcare more affordable for those families.
But even with the additional state support, Brooks said many families are still struggling to afford childcare, while providers face staffing shortages and rising costs. 
“It’s one step forward with this, and I’m thankful for that, but we still have a ways to go,” Brooks said during a visit Thursday. 
She was joined by Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt, D-NC, and Sen. Jim Burgin, R-Harnett, co-chairs of the state’s Task Force on Child Care and Early Education. The panel was created by Democratic Gov. Josh Stein to find ways to expand access to affordable childcare across the state. 
Stein announced Thursday that he had signed an executive order extending the bipartisan task force through Dec. 2027. 
“With costs climbing, affordable childcare helps families start a family and stay in the workforce,” Stein said. “I look forward to the task force’s continued work to lower costs and help parents raise their children.” 
The extension gives the task force another year to develop recommendations as state lawmakers prepare for future budget talks. 
The task force’s visit highlighted the implementation of a new statewide floor for childcare subsidy reimbursements, a recommendation the task force first made in June 2025.
NC budget offers rural childcare businesses financial help they’ve sought for years

The state budget included an additional $160 million to raise subsidy payments and to set a statewide minimum rate. The governor’s office said North Carolina is the first state in the country to set one. 
Beginning Oct. 1, providers in counties with subsidy reimbursement rates lower than the new statewide minimum got a raise. For Brooks, whose Little Believer’s Academy operates two locations, the additional funding is already making a difference.
At the Raleigh location, Brooks estimated that between 85% and 90% of enrolled children receive childcare subsidies. At the academy’s Clayton location, she said the share is closer to 50%.
The additional revenue has helped the center purchase new classroom supplies and toys, bring in additional staff and provide raises to employees who have worked at the center for years.
But the funding has not eliminated the financial challenges facing families. Brooks said even with subsidies, some parents still face monthly copayments of $300 to $400, depending on their circumstances.
She described one family whose child had to leave the program after the mother was injured at work and could no longer afford a $300 monthly copayment. The mother was receiving workers’ compensation and was homeless. 
“We have multiple stories just like that,” Brooks said.
Cassandra Brooks (right) and Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt. (Photo by Tre Spencer/NC Newsline)
Staffing is still another challenge for the center. The academy spent thousands of dollars advertising open positions, but struggled to find and retain employees.
The center offers medical, dental, and vision insurance and pays licensed teachers hourly wages ranging from $14 to $24. Despite those efforts, employee retention at the location is still only around 60%.

To address the shortage, Brooks obtained approval to hire nine workers through the federal H-2B visa program. The workers arrived in October and will stay through May. 
Brooks called the additional workers a “saving grace,” saying they have helped provide more consistent staffing and given employees more support in managing classroom needs.
Burgin said staffing shortages are affecting centers across the country, and the task force plans to keep finding ways to recruit workers. 
“We say childcare begins at conception,” he said. “I think it’s something we all need to focus on. There’s a lot more work to do.” 
Beyond raising the subsidy rates, Brooks said she hopes future state investments will make subsidies available to more families, provide more benefits for childcare workers, and make additional resources available to children with special needs.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: US senators consider Gov. McMaster’s chief attorney for federal judgeship
description: The former top legal counsel for the South Carolina governor is being considered for a lifetime federal court appointment, amid a rush to confirm nominees before the new Senate is sworn in.
text:
Elizabeth Crum, an attorney for the South Carolina Election Commission, left, and Grayson Lambert, the attorney representing Gov. Henry McMaster, huddle during a district court hearing Friday, Sept. 26, 2025, at the Richland County Courthouse in a case regarding the possible release of state voter information to the U.S. Department of Justice. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)The attorney who has represented Gov. Henry McMaster in court for the last five years is being considered for a lifetime appointment to the federal bench amid a rush to confirm nominees ahead of Democrats taking control of the U.S. Senate. 
Grayson Lambert, McMaster’s former chief attorney, was nominated this week to be a U.S. District Court judge for South Carolina. 
The Senate confirmation process of President Donald Trump’s pick began with a hearing Wednesday in the Judiciary Committee, where outgoing South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham introduced Lambert. 
“To fill this vacancy, President Trump could not have made a better choice than Grayson Lambert,” Graham told committee members. 
If confirmed, Lambert would replace Timothy Cain, the former chief judge of the U.S. District Court for South Carolina. Nominated by President Barack Obama in 2011, Cain stepped down as semi-retired on Oct. 1.
Lambert has argued for McMaster in state and federal courts since May 2021. Recent cases include questions about state law keeping the execution process secret, the constitutionality of South Carolina’s six-week abortion ban, and McMaster’s decision to send National Guard troops to Washington, D.C.
In a letter of support, McMaster said that he recommended Lambert “in the strongest possible terms.” 
“To be sure, a Governor’s lawyer must be an advocate. A judge, however, must be a neutral arbiter. I have complete confidence that Grayson recognizes and respects the difference, and his temperament and judgment are well suited to the judicial role,” McMaster wrote in the letter posted on the committee’s website.
Before working with McMaster, Lambert worked for law firms in Columbia. He holds a bachelor’s degree from the University of Virginia and a law degree from Duke University in North Carolina. He clerked for Judge Dennis Shedd on the 4th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals from 2012 to 2013. 

Grayson Lambert, attorney for Gov. Henry MaMaster, testifies Monday Nov. 6, 2023, before the Judicial Merit Selection Commission in Columbia, S.C., as a candidate for a seat on the state Court of Appeals. (Photo by Mary Ann Chastain/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

In 2023, he was among five candidates for an opening on the South Carolina Court of Appeals.
The Legislature’s judicial screening panel found him qualified but didn’t forward his name to the General Assembly for election.
During Wednesday’s hearing in Washington, Lambert said it’s been a “privilege to represent South Carolina’s efforts to legislate within its constitutional sphere and to ensure that federal courts don’t overreach and preclude the state from doing what the Constitution allows.” 
The clock is ticking for the Republican nominees, as the swearing in of new senators Jan. 3 will flip control to Democrats. Lambert is among about 20 judicial nominees awaiting a Senate vote in the lame-duck session. 
Booker and Cruz weigh in
Democrat New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said the committee should wait to vote on nominees until the new Senate is sworn in. 
Noting that South Carolina, Texas and North Carolina will each soon be represented by a Democrat and a Republican, Booker argued they could make bipartisan decisions together on who should be the judges on their state’s bench. 
“They would have affirmed the integrity of the judiciary. They would have affirmed the spirit of our democracy,” Booker said during the hearing. 
Democrat Annie Andrews‘ defeat of Graham in the midterm election was among nine flips for Senate Democrats nationwide.
Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz pushed back on Booker’s argument, pointing to when Democrats voted to appoint more than 20 federal judges following the presidential election two years ago before Republicans took control of the chamber in January 2025. 
“He cannot believe that a Republican Senate would be confirming judges nominated by a Republican president in the lame duck after an election. You know, you don’t need a particularly long memory to recognize the hypocrisy in what Sen. Booker said,” Cruz said. 
Booker, a potential 2028 presidential contender, is among Democrats already crisscrossing the state.
He is back in South Carolina, the first state on Democrats’ nominating calendar, this weekend. He is the keynote speaker at Friday night’s fundraising gala on James Island for the NAACP’s Charleston branch. And he’s set to speak at the Legislative Black Caucus’ gala Saturday night in Columbia.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT orders recounts in five towns with error in ballot tabulators
description: Recounts have been ordered in Andover, East Hartford, New Hartford, Norwalk and Scotland because of a programming error caused by a vendor.
text:
Five Connecticut communities have been ordered to recount votes cast in the 2026 midterm election after the discovery of a programming error that could have resulted in the double-counting of votes for cross-endorsed candidates.
Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas said in a press release that the error could have resulted in double-counting of votes in cases where a person marked more than one line for a candidate who was endorsed by more than one party.
The five communities are Andover, East Hartford, New Hartford, Norwalk and Scotland. The error was caused by the vendor who programs the ballot tabulators, not by the communities, the secretary of the state said.
Cross endorsements are common in Connecticut. For example, Gov. Ned Lamont appeared on the ballot on the Democratic and Working Families lines, and his challenger, Ryan Fazio, appeared on the Republican and Independent lines.
Two other statewide candidates, Thomas and Comptroller Sean Scanlon, appeared on three ballot lines: Both are Democrats cross-endorsed by the Working Families and Independent parties.
Connecticut uses paper ballots that are counted by digital tabulators programmed to catch double voting. If someone votes for more than one candidate — say, both Lamont and Fazio for governor — the tabulator rejects that ballot.
In cases where someone votes for a cross-endorsed candidate on more than one line, the tabulators are programmed to count only one of the votes. But that creates a secondary problem: In the returns, which of the extra votes should be discarded — ones cast on the major or minor party lines?

The returns for cross-endorsed candidates show on which ballot line the votes were cast. The governor and his challenger each appeared on two lines. Credit: CTMIRROR.ORG

The answer is that those votes initially are listed as being cast on “unknown” ballot lines, then assigned a party affiliation in the returns based on the proportion of the overall vote. 
Officials at the University of Connecticut, who oversee and test the accuracy of the tabulators, noticed that five communities had no votes listed as an “unknown” party line. 
Thomas said UConn, state election officials and the equipment vendor reviewed results from all 169 municipalities and found that no additional towns were affected.
“Our system is designed to get to the root of any issue that might come up, and when one does, we do something about it,” Thomas said.
A hand count known as a recanvass was ordered in all five towns.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma to consider special education textbooks for the 1st time
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma for the first time will review and potentially approve textbooks for children with severe and profound disabilities, a decision state officials say could improve instruction of vulnerable learners. The Oklahoma State Department of Education was unable to find any other state that separately evaluates and approves learning materials d[...]
text:
The Oklahoma State Textbook Committee listens to a presentation from Carolynn Bristow, project manager of educational materials for the Oklahoma State Department of Education, during a meeting Friday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma for the first time will review and potentially approve textbooks for children with severe and profound disabilities, a decision state officials say could improve instruction of vulnerable learners.
The Oklahoma State Department of Education was unable to find any other state that separately evaluates and approves learning materials designed for this student population, said Sherri Coats, the agency’s program director of special education.
Without an approved list of special education textbooks, most school districts lack a curriculum and high-quality classroom materials designated for students with significant cognitive disabilities, she said. Special education teachers often have to put together instructional materials on their own.
The State Textbook Committee on Friday took its first step toward changing that.
The committee, which approves textbooks for all school subjects, voted to include “special education alternate” as a new subject area in its 2027-28 adoption cycle.
Sherri Coats, program director of special education for the Oklahoma State Department of Education, speaks at a State Textbook Committee meeting Friday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
That means Oklahoma next year will begin reviewing instructional materials designed for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities and could consider adding these textbooks to a state-approved list, which would permit public schools to use textbook funds to purchase them.
“The fact that we don’t have high quality instructional materials for our most vulnerable students — I don’t understand the why,” Coats told the committee. “Why haven’t we done this? And I don’t know why other states haven’t done it either.”
Oklahoma designed alternate assessments and achievement standards for these students.
State records show just under 2,000 students in fourth, eighth and 11th grade took the alternate assessments in the 2024-25 school year, the most recent data available. An average of 25% made a proficient score in reading and 28.67% did so in math, state data shows.
This spring, between 12% and 38% made a proficient score, Coats said. Those levels are unacceptable and “indicate that instruction for this population is inadequate,” she said.
“Across the state, we’ve identified that most districts lack curriculum for this group of students, and we believe that is a contributing factor to the poor performance and the poor outcomes,” Coats said during the committee meeting. “It’s reported that districts do not have funding to purchase these materials, so teachers often construct fragmented curricula that lack standards alignment, and they lack rigor.”
Special education teachers use the same textbooks available to students without disabilities, said Cecilia Robinson-Woods, superintendent of Millwood Public Schools in Oklahoma City.
Millwood Public Schools Superintendent Cecilia Robinson-Woods speaks to the Statewide Charter School Board on Jan. 21, 2025, at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
That’s because special education students are legally entitled to have access to the same learning materials as other children, she said. Which specific textbook a teacher uses, though, corresponds to the learning level of an individual student.
A high school student with severe cognitive delays, for example, still must be taught civics like all students of that age, but the student might need a first-grade textbook for the lesson, she said.
A classroom of students with severe and profound disabilities often contains a wide variety of learning levels, so a special education textbook would have to account for that range, Robinson-Woods said. 
Still, she said having these books available could be a positive step.
“Anytime you can have prepared materials for teachers to use and they don’t have to figure out how to find it or compile it themselves, I think that is a good thing,” she said.
