name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Maui Water Supply Board To Planning Director: Where Are You?
description: For months, the Maui County Board of Water Supply has struggled to effectively review proposed developments, advise local officials on matters related to resource management and fulfill other legally prescribed responsibilities. That’s what board’s chair Nichole Inouye-Nohara maintains, blaming it on the planning director’s repeated refusal to participate in[...]
text:
For months, the Maui County Board of Water Supply has struggled to effectively review proposed developments, advise local officials on matters related to resource management and fulfill other legally prescribed responsibilities.
That’s what board’s chair Nichole Inouye-Nohara maintains, blaming it on the planning director’s repeated refusal to participate in board proceedings.
“This is more than a matter of attendance. It directly impairs the Board’s ability to discharge its responsibilities under the Maui County Charter,” Inouye-Nohara wrote in a draft Oct. 17 letter to Mayor Richard Bissen. “There is a rather remarkable mis-apprehension of the kuleana of the Board of Water Supply within the administration.”
On Thursday, the board unanimously voted to approve the letter, in which Inouye-Nohara formally requested that Bissen direct the planning director, Jacky Takakura, to publicly appear before the board and provide a written explanation of the Planning Department’s responsibilities to confirm the availability of water resources when reviewing subdivision and land-use proposals. 
Maui Mayor Richard Bissen appointed Jacky Takakura to lead the Maui County Planning Department shortly after former Planning Director Kate Blystone resigned in January, citing personal reasons. (Erin Nolan/Civil Beat/2026)
“The Board is not seeking to interfere with the Planning Department’s lawful administrative authority. Rather, it seeks the cooperation necessary to perform its own Charter-mandated advisory function,” Inouye-Nohara wrote in the letter.
Takakura’s insufficient participation perpetuates ambiguity regarding Planning Department procedures and responsibilities, impairs the board’s ability to advise the mayor and County Council, and undermines cooperation among county departments, according to an attachment to the letter.
The letter was drafted after months of attempts by the board to engage Takakura in discussions to answer questions about department responsibilities, streamlining coordination among the departments of Planning and Water Supply and reviewing legislation being considered by the County Council. 
Water Is At Center Of Dispute
Takakura has provided written responses to questions provided by the board, according to a statement from a county spokesperson Wednesday. She also appeared at an Oct. 15 meeting, but the board declined to hear from her and deferred their scheduled discussion about the department’s responsibilities related to securing water supply for subdivision applications.
“Director Takakura has made every effort to appear when requested at BWS meetings, declining only when she has had conflicts with her schedule,” according to the statement.
Responding to the board’s letter requesting Takakura’s presence at the 1:30 p.m. meeting on Oct. 15, a planning department secretary said in an email that the director was already scheduled to attend an in-person meeting at 2 p.m. on the same day.
Takakura did attend the meeting, though, and the board shuffled the agenda around so that they took up their discussion with her immediately after public testimony concluded at 1:41 p.m. However, members chose to reschedule the item so they would have more time to speak with Takakura, according to the meeting minutes.
Inouye-Nohara first reached out to Takakura on April 3, soon after Takakura assumed the helm of the Planning Department following the resignation of former planning director Kate Blystone.
“We would appreciate your perspective on how water supply is evaluated for commercial and private development, how the Planning Department tracks overall water supply conditions across Maui, and how these considerations are addressed at various stages of planning,” Inouye-Nohara wrote to Takakura in an email inviting her to attend the board’s meeting on May 21.
In her response, Takakura told Inouye-Nohara that some of those topics had previously been addressed by Blystone when the former director met with the board. “That might have been a year ago,” she wrote, then sharing excerpts from the Maui County Charter specifying the duties of  the departments of Planning and Water Supply.
Director Participation ‘Integral’
After Takakura did not attend the meeting on May 21, the board invited her to participate in another meeting over the summer.
“Our goal is to improve water resource planning for Maui’s future and streamline coordination between the Planning Department and the Department of Water Supply in the development of infrastructure improvements for a reliable water supply and emergency response,” Inouye-Nohara wrote in the draft letter to Takakura. “Through previous discussions with past-Director Blystone and staff members from the Department of Water Supply, we have identified what appear to be important gaps in the planning process regarding to countywide water supply.”
At the end of the letter, Inouye-Nohara attached document explaining why the board felt that it was imperative to meet with Takakura and outlining several questions requesting information about who specifically in the department can evaluate water use and supply, Takakura’s assessment of Maui’s water supply and resource planning process, and how the department tracks cumulative water usage and supply throughout the county.
In her response, Takakura declined to address most of the board’s questions, instead sharing a department organization chart and referring members to the charter.
The Maui County Charter expressly establishes the planning director as a “non-voting ex-officio member” of the Board of Water Supply, and therefore Takakura’s participation “is not merely an optional courtesy between departments” but an integral part of the board’s institutional structure, according to an attachment to Inouye-Nohara’s letter. Additionally, the board relies on access to information about planning decisions and administrative procedures to advise on issues like water-resource availability, system capacity and future water demand, according to the attachment.
Takakura previously told Civil Beat that she had only agreed to take on the role of planning director for the remainder of Bissen’s current term, which runs through the end of this year. 
Shay Chan-Hodges, the former water board chair whose term ended in 2021, said she couldn’t speak to the current situation or the current administration. However, the importance of departmental collaboration is clear, she said.
“Obviously the use of water is crucial to any kind of development and housing, which has come up over and over again,” Chan-Hodges said. “Communication overall, I think generally has not historically been great at the county. ”

description: Gov. The July 27 storms that affected Forest, Outagamie, Vilas and Winnebago counties also produced a strong tornado and damaged more than 2,000 homes as well […]
text:
Damage from a powerful tornado that hit Menasha July 27, 2026. Gov. Tony Evers has written to officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency urging them to reverse a decision denying federal disaster aid requested in the aftermath of the July storms in northeastern Wisconsin. (Photo by Appleton Police Department)Gov. Tony Evers has filed an appeal with the federal government to reverse its denial of emergency hazard mitigation funds following disastrous storms that hit northeastern Wisconsin in late July.
The July 27 storms that affected Forest, Outagamie, Vilas and Winnebago counties also produced a strong tornado and damaged more than 2,000 homes as well as businesses, utilities and public infrastructure, Evers wrote officials this week at the Federal Emergency Management Agency in Chicago and Washington. Many homes still need repair more than three months later, Evers wrote.
The federal government denied the state’s request in August for a federal disaster declaration after a joint state-federal assessment found more than $8 million in damage to private homes and more than $13 million in damage to public facilities and infrastructure, according to the governor’s office.
The requested funds are necessary to ensure that properties needing repair are also brought into compliance with local floodplain ordinances, possibly requiring buildings to be elevated or demolished, Evers wrote.
The funds are also needed so homeowners can make dwellings safe from flooding, such as by eliminating living spaces and basements that are below ground, and to build tornado-safe shelters.
FEMA chief, US House members push for emergency management changes

“In less than one year’s time, the residents of the State of Wisconsin have recently been impacted by three significant events that have received Presidential major disaster declarations: severe storms and flooding in August 2025, severe storms, tornadoes and flooding in April 2026, and severe storms and tornadoes in July 2026,” Evers wrote.
Hazard mitigation grant funding “has been denied for all three of these disasters,” he wrote, even as a number of communities have been hit twice this year alone, by the April flooding and the July storms.
Ensuring that the communities receive the requested hazard mitigation funds “is imperative,” he added, “so the communities in our state are able to recover and prevent similar impacts from future disaster events while saving local, state, and federal taxpayer dollars.”

name: VTDigger
title: PFAS contamination from capped landfill impacting Shaftsbury residents and officials
description:
Wells at 19 homes on Grove Road eyed for testing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  PFAS contamination from capped landfill impacting Shaftsbury residents and officials.
text:
The Select Board has voted in favor of $13,440 for testing of 19 wells on Grove Road. Mark Rondeau/Bennington Banner

This story by Mark Rondeau was first published in the Bennington Banner on Nov. 19, 2026. 
SHAFTSBURY – The town is dealing with a burgeoning, and expensive, problem with PFAS contamination of residents’ wells, apparently originating from the capped landfill near the Department of Public Works building on North Road.
“The town of Shaftsbury was found liable for a situation in which there had been contamination of waters from the landfill, which have led to … contaminated wells in the area,” said Select Board Chair Zoe Contros Kearl at Monday’s Select Board meeting.
“And the town is liable for the maintenance of those wells,” she said. “So, any well that tests above four parts per trillion that’s in the area affected by this situation, the town is responsible for remediating that issue.”
At Monday’s meeting, the board approved the testing of wells at 19 homes in proximity to the landfill on Grove Road for PFAS at a cost of $13,440. The proposal was put together at the request of the state Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) and the town has to pay for it, Contros Kearl said.
In addition, the board approved point-of-entry-water treatments systems (POETs) for four houses found to have contaminated wells. The cost to install the POET systems is $36,987, plus a $1,600 added-on cost per home if a UV water purification system is also needed.
Six homes previously had point of entry water treatment systems installed at the expense of the town because of the contamination.
Background
In June, 2016, the state’s Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) asked the town to test the capped landfill, which operated from 1967 to 2006. The test sample showed that PFOA was present in the landfill at a concentration of 25 parts per trillion, just above the then state limit of 20 ppt., according to a Banner article.

The edge of the landfill behind the Shaftsbury Department of Public Works building on North Road. Photo by Mark Rondeau/Bennington Banner

The state limit has since been lowered to 4 parts per trillion.
PFOA contamination has been an ongoing issue in this area, the state and in the nation. PFAS, of which PFOA is part, are man-made compounds that have been used in a wide range of industries since the 1950s, are persistent in the environment, and are harmful to human health.
Two former Chemfab facilities, owned by Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics, were located on Northside Drive and Water Street and operated in Bennington from 1969 to 2002. Lawyers filed a second class-action suit, representing Shaftsbury and Bennington residents over the contamination in August.
The Shaftsbury landfill contamination is a separate matter and links to the Chemfab plant have not been established.
“I am trying to get in touch with the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation and kind of understand the scope of this,” Contros Kearl said. “This is all coming up right now. It’s been ongoing but it has been manageable and now I have questions and concerns about how far does it go? How many more wells?”
Impact on budget
The expense for the testing and water treatment systems, which need to be maintained, in the fiscal 2028 town budget would range from $130,000 to $150,000, Contros Kearl said.
“One of the things to think about is whether (to) finance this cost. What to do? This isn’t something we’ll solve tonight,” she added. “This is the beginning of a big conversation about something that is so significant in cost and scope that it honestly feels very daunting to me.”

Town Administrator Carlyn Mickle, left, and Select Board Chair Zoe Contros Kearl at Monday’s Shaftsbury Select Board meeting. Screenshot from CAT-TV video

“This is an enormous amount of money going forward,” Board Vice Chair Naomi Miller said during the discussion.
“If these 19 wells were to come up (PFOA positive), this would be a tremendous cost to the town,” Contros Kearl said. “It’s already a tremendous cost to the town.”
Origin of the PFOA
Contros Kearl raised questions about the origins of the PFOA in the landfill. Those present in the audience at the meeting said that testing could indicate the contamination source.
“We’ve had conversations in which we’ve started to talk about how this came about, right? How these substances got into the landfill, whether there was any dumping on behalf of Chemfab, now Saint-Gobain,” she said. “But we don’t currently have any evidence of that being the case. But that was a question that we have asked and are trying to get a little bit more information on.”
She added, “So that’s a question that I have as just a person who understands where these wells lie and the nature of the work done at that facility. And I’m not suggesting that they did anything improper. But I am certainly curious because … we see these forever chemicals appear in water systems and water sources across the United States from a large host of types of industrial activity. It is interesting to consider who did the polluting and who is liable, and I think that that’s something for us to certainly look into.”

name: VTDigger
title: Fired Shelburne police sergeant stripped of police certification for role in deadly crash
description:
A state panel did leave open the possibility that the ex-officer could reapply for certification after a year. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fired Shelburne police sergeant stripped of police certification for role in deadly crash.
text:
Former Shelburne police officer Kyle Kapitanski pleads guilty to negligent operation in the 2024 death of cyclist Sean Hayes in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, September 4, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A former Shelburne police sergeant who pleaded guilty last year to striking and killing a cyclist  with his cruiser while on duty has been stripped of his law enforcement certification for at least a year. 
The Vermont Criminal Justice Council, a panel that oversees police conduct in the state, voted this week to approve an agreement reached with Kyle Kapitanski to revoke his law enforcement certification with the option of recertification at the discretion of the council after one year.
The agreement avoided a contested hearing on the matter. Kapitanski could not be reached for comment. 
Kapitanski had entered a plea deal in September 2025 in a criminal case against him stemming from the incident. He pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge of negligent operation of a motor vehicle with death resulting in the November 2024 crash that killed 38-year-old Sean Hayes of Burlington.
Kapitanski was sentenced as part of the plea agreement to six to 12 months in jail, all suspended, and he was placed on probation for two years. 
Kapitanski was driving his cruiser 40 to 45 mph in a 35-mph zone early in the morning of Nov. 11, 2024, on Shelburne Road in South Burlington when the crash took place, according to prosecutors.
Hayes appeared to be adjusting his bicycle and a trailer attached to it before starting to walk with the bicycle when Kapitanski’s cruiser struck him, court records stated.
According to the charging affidavit, leading up to the crash, Kapitanski had YouTube videos playing on a computer tablet mounted in his cruiser. 
Shortly after reaching a plea deal on the criminal charge, the town of Shelburne fired Kapitanski, who had been on paid leave since the crash. 
This week, Christopher Perkett, the criminal justice council’s associate general counsel, outlined the process Kapitanski would need to go through to get recertified as a police officer. 

READ MORE

“First, he would have to get an agreement from the council to be permitted to recertify because it’s at our discretion,” Perkett told council members. “Then he would have to recertify, which likely would mean he would have to go through full training again.”
Asked by a council member if a waiver of that training could be requested, Perkett replied, “We’ve never had this happen before. Our rules would permit him, I think, to ask for a waiver, but it would be a waiver that would have to be granted by the council.”
After the Vermont Criminal Justice Council voted this week to approve the stipulation, Donna Hayes, Sean Hayes’ mother, addressed the panel. 
“I want everybody to know he had a family,” Donna Hayes said of her son. “He has people who love and care about him.”
She described the devastating impact her son’s death has had on his family members. 
“Sean was in college,” Donna Hayes told the council, adding, “He wanted to be a police officer.”
As for Kapitanski, Donna Hayes said, “I don’t think he should ever be certified in law enforcement again.”

title: Olin Lagon: The Story Behind A Hawaiʻi-Born Dish As Big As Big Macs
description: This story weaves through a British warship, saimin dinners with Ray Kroc and a mall built on Kālias fishponds. In January 1987, a chef flew into Honolulu to help a California restaurant chain open its first store outside the state. The company picked the food court at Ala Moana. Our food culture inspired him. He […]
text:
This story weaves through a British warship, saimin dinners with Ray Kroc and a mall built on Kālias fishponds.
In January 1987, a chef flew into Honolulu to help a California restaurant chain open its first store outside the state. The company picked the food court at Ala Moana. Our food culture inspired him. He borrowed local flavors, and likely a local favorite. He created a dish that grew so big, last year the company sold nearly as much of it, by weight, as all the beef in every Big Mac sold worldwide.
There is a lot to unpack here. I think we should start in 1792.
That year, a British warship arrived in Kona with a curious Scottish surgeon named Archibald Menzies on board. Along the voyage he had collected orange seeds and sprouted them on board. By the time they landed here, they were seedlings. He gave them to aliʻi to plant, likely our first citrus trees.
Though rare, descendants of those original trees are still around today. Hawaii Tropical Fruit Growers describes the flavor as sweet and low in acid, with a taste similar to pineapple. An orange low in acid means your tongue tastes more of the sugars. Local fruit guru Ken Love calls it “sweet and juicy, it’s the perfect citrus for Hawaiʻi.”
With fruit this good, it is not surprising that the oranges were among Kona’s leading exports for decades. During the gold rush years of California, for instance, ships carried them to San Francisco.
The orange’s run didn’t last. Exports peaked around 1850. Sugar, coffee and cattle paid more, and growers shifted to them.


Ripe Kona oranges grown in a Brazilian variety trial. (Adenir Vieira Teodoro et al./ Wikimedia Commons)


A Mediterranean fruit fly. The pest reached Hawaiʻi in 1907, and California banned the state’s fruit four years later. (Scott Bauer/ Wikimedia Commons)


Then an invasive arrived. The Mediterranean fruit fly reached Hawaiʻi in 1907. These flies poke holes in the fruit to lay their eggs, and the fruits fall before they are ripe. California didnʻt want the fly and banned our fruit and vegetables in 1911. The federal government followed right behind in 1912 with strict quarantine rules. More than a century later, federal rules still keep lots of our fresh fruit off the continent.
Skip ahead to the 1960s, the formative years of American fast food. Back then, fast food meant you got the exact same food everywhere. But that is not what we did here. We have been mixing foods from all of our cultures for generations.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

The plate lunch is an iconic way of thinking about our food culture. As the world knows it, a plate lunch is two scoops rice, mac salad, a heaping of something from any of the cultures here, and maybe a side of something pickled or fermented. It goes back to plantation life in the late 1800s and likely took its current form on Honolulu’s waterfront in the late 1920s and 1930s. We had the OG fusion lunch wagons decades before fusion food trucks became trendy on the continent. So of course our restaurants here wanted to plate-lunchify a standardized menu.
That started to happen in 1968. Foodland’s founder, Maurice “Sully” Sullivan, opened Hawaiʻi’s first McDonald’s in ʻĀina Haina. Sully wanted saimin on the menu, and McDonald’s had never added a local dish anywhere. The story goes that he took Ray Kroc to dinner at Washington Saimin and Boulevard Saimin, and by the end of the night Kroc agreed, or maybe was cajoled, to do something the company had never done. Saimin became the first local dish McDonald’s ever put on its menu. McDonald’s got plate-lunchified.

Classic saimin at Jane’s Fountain on Oʻahu, topped with Spam, char siu, fishcake and green onion. (Honolulu Noodz/Wikimedia Commons)

Saimin itself is a plate lunch in a bowl. As Images of Old Hawaiʻi describes, “The Filipino family might have some extra green onions growing in their yard, the Portuguese family might have leftover sausage, the Hawaiian family’s chickens might have laid a couple extra eggs, the Korean family might have won bok unused from making kimchee.” Today, you can dump almost anything you have in the fridge into a bowl. My favorite addition is taegu. The one I steer clear of is natto – fermented soybeans.
Fast forward a couple of decades, back to that California chain from the opening. It picked a pioneering mall. Ala Moana opened in 1959 as the largest shopping center in the country. I remember from small-kid time that it had a revolving restaurant. I later learned it was Americaʻs first. Today, Ala Moana is still the worldʻs largest open-air mall and one of the most valuable in the U.S. I have way too many Ala Moana facts because the first tech company I co-founded built websites, and I led the design of the first Ala Moana site back in 1996.
The fast food company was Panda Express. On January 23, 1987, it opened in the new Makai Market food court.
The chef from the opening was Andy Kao, Panda’s executive chef. Maybe because of our spirit of food freedom, he leaned into local inspiration. Some accounts say one was mochiko chicken, a sweet and crispy fried chicken marinated in shoyu, sugar and garlic. It is similar to Japanese karaage, but the rice flour and the sweetness were added locally. The other was local citrus.
He created a bone-in, skin-on fried chicken coated in a thick, sweet, tangy and spicy orange sauce. Mochiko chicken layers the flavor in the batter. Kao put his flavor in the sauce.

A side of Panda Express orange chicken. (Willis Lam/Wikimedia Commons)

The dish sold well, but customers asked for a boneless version. Panda co-founder Andrew Cherng remembered some of that early feedback, “same flavor, do it without the bone.”
By now you probably figured out the dish – Orange Chicken.
Let me circle back to that food court one more time. Before there was Ala Moana Center, this was Kālia, a wetland of fishponds and loʻi that fed ʻohana living along this shore. In 1912 Walter Dillingham bought about 50 acres of it for $25,000 and filled it with coral dredged from projects such as the Ala Wai. Decades later his son Lowell built Ala Moana Center on it.
That ground once fed the people of Kālia. Today the city assesses the land alone at around $670 million, value built over a century of filling, building and growth. The land stayed in local hands until 1982, when it was sold off-island for the first time. Today most of the rent from Ala Moana’s stores flows to Brookfield, a Canadian company, and the profits from orange chicken flow to California. 
Hawaiʻi creates tons of value that ends up owned somewhere else. I know it is really hard, but keeping more of that value here is important work.
I am sure the next “orange chicken” is being dreamed up here right now. When it hits, I hope it stays home.

title: Attorney general loses suit against pornographic websites
description: A Marion County judge has dismissed a case filed by Attorney General Todd Rokita against sexually explicit websites he claimed were violating Indiana’s age-verification law. The office alleged that the content made available to children by the defendants — all of whom are associated with a multinational pornographic conglomerate known as Aylo — includes sexu[...]
text:
Pornhub, other sites, win dismissal of case brought by Attorney General Todd Rokita. (Getty Images)A Marion County judge has dismissed a case filed by Attorney General Todd Rokita against sexually explicit websites he claimed were violating Indiana’s age-verification law.
The office alleged that the content made available to children by the defendants — all of whom are associated with a multinational pornographic conglomerate known as Aylo — includes sexual violence, choking, rape fantasies, sex slavery and sex with teen girls.
Rokita in December claimed that the defendants violated the state’s Deceptive Consumer Sales Act in several ways by making false and misleading statements regarding the accessibility of the pornographic websites by Indiana residents, and by misleading consumers about their alleged hosting of child sexual abuse material and nonconsensual material.
Marion County Superior Judge Patrick Dietrick issued a ruling on Wednesday regarding the 42 challenged websites. He noted that the attorney general’s only evidence came from an investigator in Indiana who accessed the sites through a Chicago-based VPN.
Those with an Indiana IP address receive a blocking message.
“Since then, (Aylo) has received no income attributable to Indiana residents, has not offered advertisers the ability to target them, and has no record of any Indiana IP address reaching Freesite content other than the Passive Homepage,” the ruling said.
The dismissal was based on multiple factors for different defendants, including lack of personal jurisdiction and failure to state a claim.
Rokita’s office can appeal the ruling and also refile a case in the future with new evidence.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Complaint stays alive against dark money group over $60K donation to Engling campaign
description: An election law dispute between the top candidates for the Republican secretary of state nomination over an improper $60,000 contribution has been dropped, while action is still possible against the dark money group affiliated with U.S. Jim Banks that gave the money.
text:
Republican secretary of state candidate Max Engling, left, stands to shake hands with Knox County Clerk David Shelton during an Indiana Election Commission meeting on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)An election law dispute between the top candidates for the Republican secretary of state nomination over an improper $60,000 contribution has been dropped, while action is still possible against the dark money group affiliated with U.S. Jim Banks that gave the money.
At issue is a June contribution to Republican Max Engling’s campaign from Hoosier Leadership for America Inc. A complaint filed by Knox County Clerk David Shelton, who finished second to Engling at this year’s state GOP convention, alleged the group and Engling’s campaign violated state law limiting corporations and labor organizations to a maximum of $5,000 a year in contributions to statewide office candidates.
Shelton asked the Indiana Election Commission on Friday to dismiss the complaint against Engling, saying he was satisfied with evidence that his campaign had refunded the improper donation within a couple weeks.
The commission granted that dismissal along with Shelton’s request to keep active the complaint against Hoosier Leadership for America.
That organization is registered with state and federal agencies as a nonprofit corporation with a Fort Wayne address, which allows it to keep the sources of its money secret — the reason why such entities are commonly referred to as dark-money groups.
The ad-tracking firm AdImpact reported Hoosier Leadership for America spent $5.2 million on broadcast advertising during this year’s primary campaign against Republican state senators who opposed President Donald Trump’s demands for Indiana congressional redistricting.
Shelton said after Friday’s commission meeting that he believed the group should face fines for violating state campaign finance laws.
“I still think they are liable,” Shelton told the Capital Chronicle. “They should know better than that. They’ve been in the game long enough.”
Law makes corporations abide limits
The commission on Friday did not take up the complaint against Hoosier Leadership for America as a state Election Division staff oversight meant it had not received sufficient notice. No date was set for when the commission would consider action.
Engling campaign says it returned $60K donation from dark money group

The Capital Chronicle sent an email seeking comment to the person identified in TV advertising purchases as the organization’s treasurer, Charles Gantt of the Massachusetts-based political advisory group Bulldog Compliance.
Prominent conservative attorney Jim Bopp, who is representing Engling’s campaign, said the burden is on the corporation making political contributions to make sure they are abiding by the state’s limits.
An example given during Friday’s meeting would be a corporation giving $2,000 each to 10 candidates would exceed the $5,000 total limit without the individual candidates being aware.
“The statute is clear that the committee that received (the contribution) is not responsible, but the corporation,” Bopp said.
Dispute over delay in hearing complaints
The Election Commission — made up of two Republicans and two Democrats — faced controversy for not taking up before Election Day the complaint against Engling and two filed against Democratic Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh.
Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard unsuccessfully sought a court order forcing a pre-Election Day meeting, arguing the commission was abdicating its duty to enforce election laws. A Marion County judge this week dismissed Ballard’s lawsuit upon his request, according to court records.
The decision to wait until Friday for any commission action rested with commission Chair Beth Boyce, who is the Johnson County Republican chair. She declined to comment Friday to the Capital Chronicle about her reasoning.
Commission members voted unanimously to dismiss complaints against Bayh’s campaign alleging it received unreported in-kind contributions in connection with events hosted by Democratic Party organization and that printed materials promoting Bayh lacked required disclaimers. 
A Republican activist who filed one of the Bayh complaints requested it be dropped, while the other person lodging a complaint did not attend Friday’s meeting to pursue the matter.
Shelton filed legal arguments in support of Ballard’s lawsuit and said Friday that the commission needed to step up and enforce the campaign finance laws.
“Hoosiers deserve to know who the funding comes from for their candidates,” he said. “We’ve got to do what we can to maintain the integrity of our election processes here in Indiana, including campaign finances and dark money is coming in from who knows where.”

title: MT Capitol Christmas tree harvested near Wise River
description: Each year, the tallest Christmas tree harvested in Montana, as far as the Daily Montanan is aware, takes up residence under the Capitol rotunda in Helena for the holiday season, towering nearly three stories tall and adorned with more than 3,500 lights. On Thursday Gov. Greg Gianforte joined foresters to fell this year’s Capitol Christmas […]
text:
Gov. Gianforte joining partners to harvest the 2026 State Capitol Christmas Tree on BLM land near Wise River. (Courtesy photo)Each year, the tallest Christmas tree harvested in Montana, as far as the Daily Montanan is aware, takes up residence under the Capitol rotunda in Helena for the holiday season, towering nearly three stories tall and adorned with more than 3,500 lights.
On Thursday Gov. Greg Gianforte joined foresters to fell this year’s Capitol Christmas tree — a Douglas Fir — on Bureau of Land Management land near Wise River.
Near Seeley Lake, a Good Neighbor Authority project between the state Department of Natural Resources and Conservation and the U.S. Forest Service provided an active forest management site to harvest the Douglas Fir that will serve as the state’s Christmas tree, all while contributing to the health of the forest.
The tree was harvested in coordination with The Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) and KLM Contracting, along with the Montana Logging Association. Earlier this month, the governor, the BLM, and DNRC signed a memorandum of understanding to expand their Good Neighbor Authority partnership, which has supported projects from timber sale administration to fuels reduction since 2019.
“Each year, it’s a privilege to harvest a Montana tree from our public lands and display it in the State Capitol for all to enjoy,” Gianforte said in a statement. “It’s fitting that this year’s tree is from a BLM timber harvest given the recent expansion of our shared partnership to improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk. This year’s tree is an example of that commitment, and we’re proud to share it with Montanans this Christmas.”
The Capitol Christmas tree is selected from a different parcel of public land around the state each year. Similarly, the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., displays a Christmas tree harvested from a different National Forest each year. The last tree from Montana — a 79-foot tall Engelmann Spruce from the Kootenai National Forest — was selected in 2017.
This year the “People’s Tree,” a 76-foot Engelmann spruce, came from the Nez Perce-Clearwater National Forest in northern Idaho arrived in D.C. on Friday to become the nation’s Capitol Christmas Tree.
Following the governor’s lead, Montanans are able to harvest trees from the state’s vast public lands — data that is not available from state or federal agencies — creating a tradition for many Montana families.
The 2026 State Capitol Christmas tree will displayed in the Capitol rotunda throughout the holiday season. The governor and first lady invite Montanans to join them at the Capitol for a tree lighting ceremony on Monday, Nov. 30, at 5 p.m.
The governor encourages Montanans to participate in the unique tradition of harvesting Christmas trees from public lands to benefit forest health and resiliency as well as improve wildlife habitat.
Cutting any trees on state trust land requires a permit from the local DNRC field office. The cost is $10 per tree. To find a local DNRC field office to secure a permit in person to harvest a Christmas tree, see the map here.
Montanans can also harvest trees from National Forest land with a $5 permit, though some restrictions on height and species apply to trees from federal land.
Forest Service permits can be obtained online by visiting recreation.gov and searching “Christmas tree” and the forest you plan to cut it from, i.e. “Flathead National Forest, Lolo National Forest.”
Trees can also be cut from Bureau of Land Management land.

name: VTDigger
title: Tax every dollar the same, however it’s earned
description:
An increasingly automated economy needs a tax code that puts human beings first.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tax every dollar the same, however it’s earned.
text:
This commentary is by Justin Neuman, a professor of literary studies at Eugene Lang College, The New School, and a developer of philosophical software. 
As a parent, teacher, builder and endurance athlete, I’ve spent much of my life doing — and encouraging others to do — hard things. I believe in the value of work. So why, in Montpelier and in Washington, do we have a tax code that penalizes it?
According to the Congressional Budget Office, individual income and payroll taxes supplied more than 80% of federal revenue in 2026. In Vermont, personal income tax provides more than half of general fund revenue. In the most capital-rich society the world has ever seen, the government runs largely by leeching off human paychecks.
Here’s a vivid example. SpaceX advertised salaries of $90,000 to $160,000 for an executive assistant. Every paycheck is taxable income. Elon Musk, meanwhile, like any equity billionaire, can finance his lifestyle on loans by pledging shares as collateral. A loan isn’t taxed as income, so he can legally get cash without selling stock or paying tax on the gains for as long as he likes. “Buy, borrow, die,” as the estate planners tell their richest clients. His assistant, however, has to pay taxes on every check.
The asymmetry between owners and earners is about to get even more consequential, at least according to the stock market. The high share prices of global tech firms and historic valuations of SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic are, in part, wagers on replacement: that computers and robots will perform an ever-expanding range of the work once done by people, at margins no payroll can match. If companies produce more with fewer employees, returns grow while workers’ share of production shrinks. Anthropic and Nvidia are cases in point, with both companies generating more than $5 million in revenue per employee. I propose turning the current system on its head.
I call my plan a humanist tax code because it puts people and work first. Work, at its best, confers competence, builds responsibility and weaves people into the fabric of a community; it’s where many people find dignity and purpose. A check, on its own, gives a person none of that. A tax code can’t give life meaning, but it can stop charging people extra for pursuing meaning in their lives.
My proposal only asks one thing of the government: Count income consistently, whether it comes from people, companies or computers, and regardless of whether it arrives by paycheck, brokerage account or bequest.
One tax for all, and for all a fair tax.

READ MORE

Here’s how it would work.
First, eliminate federal income tax on the first $64,000 of income, from any source, for everyone. A hedge fund manager in New York and a carpenter in Vermont both work. The fund manager shouldn’t be taxed differently from the carpenter just because their pay arrives as a share of client gains rather than as a wage for working hours. A humanist tax code shouldn’t be focused on the rich or the poor; the goal is to make work more rewarding across the income spectrum.
Second, above that exemption, wages, capital gains, dividends and business income should face the same progressive schedule, without a discount for capital gains, but also without double jeopardy on corporate income. Gains should be taxed when they’re realized, the same way we tax a paycheck. That’s less radical than it sounds; the Tax Reform Act of 1986, signed by President Ronald Reagan, taxed gains and wages at the same top rate of 28%.
Third, treat inheritances as income to the people who receive them, above a large lifetime exemption. Today, by one estimate, inherited income is taxed at less than one-seventh the average rate on income from work. I have nothing against parents’ leaving their home, farm or savings to their children, but inherited wealth beyond that is a gain to the recipient and should be taxed as such.
Finally, there are two things a humanist tax code shouldn’t touch. First, Social Security and Medicare, including the payroll taxes that support them: These are withholdings paid by the people who will use the services, and that bargain is worth keeping visible rather than folding into the general fund. Second, the safety net: Rewarding work is not the same as punishing joblessness, and the people who can’t work, or whose labor isn’t paid, would lose nothing under my plan.
Could this replace the $3.2 trillion the federal income taxes raise today? That’s the essential question. With a taxable base of around $10 trillion, my proposal would need an effective rate of around a third. Under one model of this progressive schedule, anyone earning $50,000, like a carpenter or first-year teacher in a Vermont public school, would owe no federal income tax, instead of the roughly $4,000 they pay today. A school principal earning $100,000 would owe around $5,000, less than half the roughly $13,000 they pay under the current system. At the top end, however, a hedge fund manager earning $5 million a year with a second home in Vermont would owe more than $2 million in taxes, almost double what they likely pay under the current system.
I teach literary studies, so I’m a humanist by profession. I’m also a capitalist. I believe in the ingenuity and ambition of people. Actual humans. A market economy should encourage people to build things, solve problems, take risks and improve their circumstances, rather than concentrating capital among an ever-smaller group of owners. At the state and national level, a humanist tax code would stop treating work as something to tax and start treating it as something worth rewarding.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Tax every dollar the same, however it’s earned.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Federal judge blocks CT law that sought to regulate ICE agents
description: The ruling blocks CT officials from enforcing a 2026 law that sought to regulate ICE agents and stop them from wearing masks.
text:
A federal judge issued a ruling on Friday blocking Connecticut officials from enforcing a 2026 law that sought to regulate the actions of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and to stop federal agents from wearing masks and other face coverings.
U.S. District Judge Vernon Oliver determined that several sections of S.B. 397, which was passed by state Democratic lawmakers earlier this year, is likely to violate the U.S. Constitution.
As a result, Oliver, a former state Superior Court judge who was appointed to the federal bench by President Joe Biden in 2023, issued an injunction blocking four separate sections of the law from being enforced as the lawsuit continues to play out in court.
Three of those sections sought to empower Connecticut’s Inspector General, which is responsible for investigating state and local police shootings, to also examine and criminally prosecute federal agents who are operating in the state. 
And the fourth section sought to prevent ICE agents from wearing face coverings by making it misdemeanor for officers to wear a mask “while interacting with the public” while performing their official duties. 
In his written order, Oliver said that those portions of the law likely violate the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution. And he said President Donald Trump’s U.S. Department of Justice was likely to win the lawsuit that the federal government filed in May.
The state law, Oliver wrote, “plainly imposes conditions on how federal officers must conduct and present themselves during the course of their federal duties, and it subjects them to criminal and civil penalties if they do not abide by those state-imposed conditions.” 
“But the Supremacy Clause ensures that federal operations are not chilled by state prosecution and that federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority,” he added. 
The court injunction is a significant setback for Connecticut Democrats who sought to rein in ICE agents, who have drastically stepped up their enforcement practices across the country during Trump’s second term.
Masked ICE agents made an arrest at a courthouse in Meriden in September, raising questions about the law and whether ICE agents acted beyond their authority.
Gov. Ned Lamont, who signed the bill into law in May, urged the new Congress to protect immigrants.
[RELATED: ICE agents appear to be wearing masks in CT. Is that legal?]
“We are disappointed by today’s ruling and condemn ICE’s treatment of Connecticut residents,” Cathryn Vaulman, Lamont’s communications director, wrote on Friday. “Masked, armed agents without visible badges have surrounded cars in traffic and stormed homes and workplaces, rounded up parents dropping kids off at school and picked up a Cheshire high school student whose father aided troops in Afghanistan. ICE has terrorized and traumatized our communities. [The law] was meant to hold federal law enforcement officers to the same standards of accountability as local and state police. Gov. Lamont urges the new Democratic majorities in Congress to strengthen oversight of DHS and help us protect our immigrant communities from abuses of power.” 
The office of Attorney General William Tong reacted tersely: “We are reviewing the decision and evaluating next steps.”
Meanwhile, state Republican lawmakers in Connecticut celebrated the ruling. In a statement, several members of the state’s Republican caucus noted that they warned their Democratic colleagues that the law was likely to face opposition.
“We warned that the law violates the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause by attempting to regulate federal officers while they carry out their official duties. Lo and behold, a federal judge right here in CT agrees with what we had warned about,” they said. 
The statement, which was issued by Sen. Rob Sampson of Wolcott, Sen. Eric Berthel of Watertown and outgoing Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding of Brookfield, blamed Democrats for passing unconstitutional laws for the sake of “scoring political points.”
“When one party controls nearly every lever of power in Hartford, the temptation to ignore constitutional constraints in pursuit of political theater becomes far too common,” the Republicans wrote. 
Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, a key backer of the law as co-chair of the Judiciary Committee, said he did not believe the judge adequately weighed the Supremacy Clause against the inherent police powers of the states. 
“There was very robust debate over where Supremacy Clause begins and ends and where inherent police power begins and ends,” Stafstrom said.
“I respect the court, but I fear today’s ruling leaves Connecticut less safe, because it blocks the tools S.B. 397 gave us to investigate deaths involving federal officers and to make sure people know who is exercising police power in their communities,” said Stafstrom, a practicing attorney.
“The court did not find that any act of Congress overrides our law, and whether an officer acted within federal authority is a question that belongs in a real case with real facts, not one that should be decided before any case exists. This ruling is preliminary, and I will work with my colleagues and the attorney general’s office on next steps, because accountability is how we keep our communities safe,” he added.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: After license revocation and prison, Iowa attorney faces more sanctions
description: The only Iowa attorney to ever face disciplinary charges after having their license revoked and then reinstated is now facing sanctions from the Iowa Supreme Court. According to court records, attorney Sandra E. Suarez, a solo practitioner with a law office in Windsor Heights, is one of only four Iowa attorneys whose license was reinstated […]
text:
The Iowa Judicial Building. (Photo and seal courtesy of the Iowa Judicial Branch)  The only Iowa attorney to ever face disciplinary charges after having their license revoked and then reinstated is now facing sanctions from the Iowa Supreme Court.
According to court records, attorney Sandra E. Suarez, a solo practitioner with a law office in Windsor Heights, is one of only four Iowa attorneys whose license was reinstated after being revoked, and she is now the first and only Iowa lawyer to have faced new disciplinary charges following that reinstatement.
Court records indicate Suarez was admitted to the Iowa bar in 2000 and spent much of her early career in healthcare law, government relations and lobbying. In 2008, she began working as a multiclient lobbyist and, the Iowa Supreme Court stated in a recent filing, “as her lobbying career flourished, her social drinking morphed into problem drinking.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Suarez was convicted of drunken driving in 2009 and 2013, the court noted. In 2015, she was twice charged with third-offense drunken driving, pleaded guilty to both counts, and was sentenced to five years in prison.
In 2018, the Grievance Commission of the Iowa Supreme Court alleged that prior to being sent to prison, Suarez had committed 30 ethics-rule violations, including depositing $630 of client funds into her law firm’s operating account and then misappropriating the money for personal use. Her law license was then revoked by the Iowa Supreme Court.
Five years later, in 2023, Suarez applied for reinstatement of her license. After a public hearing, the court concluded Suarez had “demonstrated that she is of good moral character and worthy of readmission,” and reinstated her license to practice of law in Iowa.
A few weeks later, an individual retained Suarez to represent him on an immigration matter. At the time, however, Suarez remained disbarred from practicing federal immigration law before the Board of Immigration Appeals, the immigration courts, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Suarez was subsequently charged by the Iowa Attorney Disciplinary Board with engaging in the unauthorized practice of law in an immigration forum. She was also accused of violating multiple ethics rules in her representation of a divorce-case client by failing to prepare for a hearing, failing to inform her client of the date of the hearing, failing to attend the hearing, and failing to promptly inform her client of what transpired in the case.
In recommending a 30-day suspension of Suarez’s license, the commission alleged she “did more than fail to communicate” with her client and had also “provided information that was misleading and created a false impression regarding the status of the matter… (Suarez) intentionally misled her client.”
The Iowa Supreme Court recently agreed with the commission’s recommendation, finding that in the divorce case, Suarez had failed to file her client’s “crucial affidavit, despite his persistent inquiries. She missed the court hearing that had been scheduled a month earlier. She then flunked damage control by failing to promptly move to reopen and supplement the record with Joseph’s affidavit well before the court issued its adverse ruling another month later.”
While the court credited Suarez’s volunteer work for the Iowa Lawyers Assistance Program, noting that she has devoted significant time and effort to assisting lawyers with substance-abuse issues, it indicated it was concerned her more recent ethical violations “so quickly followed her reinstatement.”
“Suarez fumbled the fresh start we gave her,” the court said while imposing a 30-day suspension of her license.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Suarez for comment.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Fewer students, rising expenses and AI: UNC leaders focus on growing headwinds
description: UNC System President Peter Hans says the University of North Carolina system needs to operate more like Amazon and less like Sears. “At its peak in the 1970s, Sears accounted for 1% of the entire American economy with 3,400 stores,” Hans said. “Today, there are five stores nationwide.” Hans offered the retail history lesson at […]
text:
Students walk to class on the University of North Carolina Chapel Hill campus. The UNC Board of Governors discussed this week that the pipeline of incoming college students may remain flat through 2041. (Photo by Sean Rayford/Getty Images)UNC System President Peter Hans says the University of North Carolina system needs to operate more like Amazon and less like Sears.
“At its peak in the 1970s, Sears accounted for 1% of the entire American economy with 3,400 stores,” Hans said. “Today, there are five stores nationwide.”
Hans offered the retail history lesson at Thursday’s UNC Board of Governors meeting. He told board members higher education exists in a competitive marketplace and unlike Sears, the system cannot afford to become complacent or lose focus.
UNC System President Peter Hans at a Board of Governors meeting earlier this year. (Photo: PBS NC/UNC Board of Governors)
Hans said one bright spot for the system in recent months was a new strategic partnership between UNC-Chapel Hill and the University of North Carolina School of the Arts in Winston-Salem.
“This is about two universities sitting down together and asking a simple question, ‘What could be better done together than either of us can do alone?'” Hans said.
Hans said the 17 schools that make up the UNC system all have their unique identities, but to honor their missions, they need to find ways to operate more efficiently.
“There are multiple small, similar opportunities within our system where visionary leaders can vault their schools forward by forging closer ties,” said Hans. “That is my subtle hint to the chancellors. Hopefully they’re listening.”
Attracting new students, containing costs
Hans’ remarks came one day after a lengthy presentation by Dr. Mark Becker, the former president of the Association of Public and Land-Grant Universities and the president emeritus for Georgia State University. Becker, a nationally recognized leader in higher education, told UNC board members that “tectonic forces” are reshaping higher ed.
Source: Mark P. Becker, presentation to the UNC Board of Governors
Becker said North Carolina faces a flat pipeline of incoming high school graduates through 2041. Nationwide, higher education is facing a demographic challenge caused by falling birth rates in the United States. Research funding and international enrollment have both fallen since 2025.
Universities are also finding that public confidence in higher education has stalled, Becker said. Thirty percent of adults who expressed low confidence cited the cost, and 31% cited politics as a reason, according to a recent Lumina Foundation-Gallup survey.
Becker said while degree-holders earn more over their lifetime, 42% of recent graduates are underemployed in fields that don’t require a degree. For the millions of Americans who began college but left before ever earning a degree, they never saw the payoff, Becker said. And nearly half of borrowers (49%) who did not finish their degree owed more than they borrowed after seven years.
Entry-level job postings are down about 35% since 2023. But Becker said there are opportunities to offset that loss with experiential learning, internships and other types of work-based learning.
Becker told members of the board’s Committee on Strategic Initiatives that three-year degrees could help lower costs, speed entry into the workforce, and regain public trust in higher education.
New year, new budget pressures
The changing landscape comes as the board of governors is beginning to look at its budget priorities for 2027. During a presentation of the funding committee, board member Kirk Bradley noted that utility costs have risen 11% over the last three years and will be rising again after another rate increase.
“I think the key thing here is just efficiency, efficiency, efficiency, and all of our campuses are going to have to be looking at this,” Kirk said. “There’s a lot of headwinds facing us.”
UNC Board of Governors poised to increase tuition despite pushback from prominent conservative

Sonja Phillips Nichols, a board member representing Charlotte, said after hearing a presentation on UNC’s various funding models, it was clear that the UNC system needs to adopt a “both and” strategy.
“There’s going to have to be some cost-cutting measures on the campuses,” Nichols acknowledged. “At the same time, we as a board will have to support our campuses in their request for more money.”
After nine years of holding tuition flat, the UNC Board of Governors allowed most system universities to increase tuition up to 3% last year. N.C. State, UNC-Chapel Hill, and East Carolina University are among schools in the system requesting an additional 3% increase in undergraduate tuition next year to cover growing campus expenses. The UNC Board of Governors is expected to review tuition and student fee increases for the upcoming academic year at its February 2027 meeting.
Hans said the system must continue to improve not only course offerings, but how it handles admissions, financial aid, and the transferring of credits to keep pace with a rapidly changing world.
“Students aren’t going to pick the higher education equivalent of Sears. They won’t indulge in unresponsive bureaucracies,” said Hans. “They’ll just move on quickly. It’s among the reasons I consistently emphasize the word simplify, simplify, simplify.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Port MacKenzie rail construction could come as soon as summer, Alaska Railroad CEO says
description: Construction on the long-awaited Port MacKenzie railroad line may start in summer, the CEO of the Alaska Railroad said by phone Thursday evening. The line, which will connect Port MacKenzie to the railroad’s main line, has been expected for almost 35 years and promises to generate an industrial boom for the Matanuska-Susitna Borough by unlocking […]
text:
An Alaska Railroad train is in motion through the Chugach National Forest near Portage. (Photo by A&J Fotos/Getty Images)Construction on the long-awaited Port MacKenzie railroad line may start in summer, the CEO of the Alaska Railroad said by phone Thursday evening.
The line, which will connect Port MacKenzie to the railroad’s main line, has been expected for almost 35 years and promises to generate an industrial boom for the Matanuska-Susitna Borough by unlocking an alternative to the Port of Alaska in Anchorage and the port of Seward. 
The developers of an antimony mine and a coal-fired computing data center have already announced construction projects at the port in anticipation of the rail line.
This week, the board of directors for the state-owned railroad gave final approval for the $311 million rail line, which will be principally funded by a grant from the federal government. The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority is expected to provide $33 million in matching funds to unlock the grant, the railroad will pay additional costs from savings, and the Matanuska-Sustina Borough will provide cash, land and gravel to fulfill the remainder of the required match.
CEO Bill O’Leary said the exact timing of construction will depend on how quickly the federal government approves the railroad’s plans.
“Our goal is to really break ground this summer, but that is dependent upon a number of things that are going to involve the grantor agency, and how fast they can move in getting the grant in place and getting through any of the just formalities or required approvals that need to be there,” O’Leary said. “To that end, we’ve been already engaged with them. We’re working with them on what our timeline could be, and we’ll know more, I think, in the next — probably — month to six weeks about their stance on all that.”
As planned, the 32-mile rail line will stretch from Cook Inlet northward, along the western fringe of the Mat-Su’s built-up area, to the railroad’s main line near Houston.
Proposed as far back as 1992, before Port MacKenzie was even built, the railroad spur didn’t begin moving forward until 2002, when proponents started clearing a 30-foot-wide right-of-way.
The project was poised to move forward in 2007, but local opposition and a lack of funding stopped it again. Incremental progress followed in subsequent years — land was cleared and roadbed laid along much of the route, but no tracks followed.
Last year, the Alaska Railroad explored a public-private partnership with AIDEA and a group called Alaska Industrial Partners, but the railroad’s board had concerns with that arrangement and applied for a large federal grant, which was approved in October.
“This is a major win for the Mat-Su Borough and our entire state, and another important step toward unlocking Alaska’s extraordinary resource potential,” said Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, in a statement announcing the grant. 
The announcement was one of several high-profile funding announcements made by the Trump administration in Alaska before the November election, which included Sullivan’s re-election campaign. Sullivan, who lost re-election, is a close ally of the administration.
The grant was paid for with money approved for a rail program under the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted by Congress during President Joe Biden’s administration.
“This is exactly what we envisioned when we included the … program in our bipartisan infrastructure law, and it’s why I continue to push for additional funding through our annual appropriations process,” said Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, in a statement announcing the grant. “Good things happen in Alaska when we help fund infrastructure investments at the federal level.”
AIDEA has not yet voted to approve its $33 million match; that approval had been scheduled for a vote Thursday, but after five hours of closed-door discussions the corporation’s board adjourned its meeting until Nov. 24.
Gov.-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has asked AIDEA to pause spending actions until he takes office in early December, but O’Leary said he doesn’t think the incoming governor will oppose the railroad project.
This year, the Alaska Legislature voted 58-1 in favor of a resolution backing the railroad line, indicating it has broad, bipartisan support.
“It’s something we’ve been working on for a long time. We’re really excited to finally see a path forward to get tracks in the ground,” O’Leary said. “A lot of folks have been waiting a long time to see this get done. So we’re excited to be able to move forward on that.”

name: National
title: Democrats see missed opportunities after Black turnout surge across the South
description: As new details emerge about a Black midterm voting surge in Southern states, missed opportunities for Democrats are coming under more scrutiny, such as close U.S. Senate races in Florida and Louisiana that might have added to the party’s advantage in Washington, D.C.   Democrats in both states nominated Black candidates for U.S. Senate and turnout […]
text:
Florida U.S. Senate Democratic candidate Angie Nixon talks to reporters following her concession speech earlier this month. Some experts point to her narrow loss, and another in Louisiana, as evidence that more funding could produce even better Senate results in 2028. (Photo by Christine Sexton/ Florida Phoenix)As new details emerge about a Black midterm voting surge in Southern states, missed opportunities for Democrats are coming under more scrutiny, such as close U.S. Senate races in Florida and Louisiana that might have added to the party’s advantage in Washington, D.C.  
Democrats in both states nominated Black candidates for U.S. Senate and turnout among Black voters was high. Looking back, some political analysts see lessons for Democrats looking ahead to 2028, noting that more money from national party committees could have notched them at least two more wins.
In Mississippi,  of Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom saw an unexpected and historic success and will become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Similar bumps from Black voters in Florida and Louisiana that might have helped Democrats had there been more help, observers say. 
Midterm wins, near-misses could signal political change in the Deep South

“Louisiana is definitely the one the Democrats let slip away,” said Robert Collins, a political analyst and professor at Dillard University in New Orleans. In Louisiana, Republican Julia Letlow, an incumbent U.S. House member, won a narrow victory of about 25,000 votes over Democrat Jamie Davis, a farmer in the rural Delta region, for an open U.S. Senate seat. 
Democratic strategist Matt McDermott said that in Florida, Democrat Angie Nixon was “underfunded” in a 2.9-point loss to Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody. 
Immediately after the election, Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried called out her national party for not sending money earlier to her state’s candidates.
“Florida Democrats are looking at the results across the country and can only imagine what kind of a day we would be having if we had sustained national support and the investment this state deserves,” Fried said in a conference call with reporters after Election Day. “It is not about spending in Florida. It is about investing early in Florida the infrastructure that is necessary to win the third-largest state.”
Louisiana was not on McDermott’s list of states most vulnerable to Senate flips in 2028, but he told Stateline it’s “certainly a state where Democrats could play” even though incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. John Kennedy would be a formidable foe. 
In Louisiana, Letlow had a huge fundraising advantage, including almost $3 million in super PAC money compared with only a little less than $130,000 in such funds for Davis, Collins said.  
Davis also had little statewide name recognition as a municipal official in rural Tensas Parish, unlike Mississippi’s Colom, who was a well-known sitting district attorney with competitive fundraising and super PAC support. 
“Despite all those disadvantages, Davis came within 1.8 points,” Collins noted. “If the Democratic National Committee had put a couple million dollars into the race, on television ads and get-out-the-vote efforts, Davis wins this race, and I think he wins easily.” 
The DNC referred comment to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which sets spending priorities for U.S. Senate races. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Louisiana Democrats’ near-miss on Senate seat gives party hope for governor’s race

Data scientist Lenny Bronner pointed out the Louisiana near miss in an analysis this month of Black turnout in Southern states for states that had released detailed results. The South has most of the nation’s Black population, 59% as of last year, according to U.S. Census Bureau estimates reviewed by Stateline. 
“Worth wondering, for Democrats, what could have happened in Louisiana if they had had Mississippi style turnout among Black voters,” Bronner wrote in an X post. 
Bronner’s analysis for Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Virginia showed that precincts with large Black populations had higher turnout, compared with 2024, than areas with less Black population. The difference was especially stark for both Louisiana and Mississippi, indicating that Black voters were particularly motivated to vote this year compared to other groups.
However, Louisiana’s most heavily Black precincts only reached about 80% of 2024 turnout, when Donald Trump faced off against then-Vice President Kamala Harris, while similar precincts in Mississippi were near 100% of 2024 turnout.  
Democrat Colom’s Senate victory in Mississippi was historic, the first for a popularly elected Black senator from the state (there were previous Black senators after the Civil War when the legislature elected senators) and the first Democrat since 1982.  
Keneshia Grant, an associate professor at Howard University who wrote a 2020 book on Black Americans’ effect on the Democratic party in the South, said Black voters have long had power in Mississippi even if they were voting for Republicans willing to seek their vote. This may have been the first time they saw a realistic chance for a Democrat. 
Moody defeats Nixon in US Senate race

“Black voter turnout could have increased because they believed it would truly matter this go-round,” Grant said. “They are very clear about what is and isn’t possible in their state.” 
In Florida, NBC exit polling found strong support for Nixon, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, among Black voters: 94% of Black women and 77% of Black men voted for Nixon.  
“As a Black woman, I will stand for my vote,” Saretta Weston, a 35-year-old accountant, said after casting her ballot in Leon County, Florida. “There’s been a lot of oppression in (the) past. As of right now we have the opportunity to do that, what many before us could not do.” 
North Carolina elected Democrats to 11 of 14 U.S. House seats, including seven flips. There was a U.S. Senate flip in South Carolina, and Georgia elected its first Black and first woman governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms. 
Even in Arkansas, where Republicans swept statewide races, Democrats flipped 10 state House seats, enough to break a Republican supermajority and give Democrats a voice in budget votes. 
The narrow defeat for a Democratic challenger in Louisiana’s U.S. Senate race gave Democrats hope for statewide races next year, with a chance that Davis might run for governor next year. Davis did not return an e-mail requesting comment. 
He told The Guardian in an interview published Thursday that it “stings to come close” — he lost by less than 2 percentage points — and said that he did not have enough money to fight damaging attack ads from Republicans. 
And in an interview before the election, Democratic consultant James Carville noted the lack of national party funding support and told the Louisiana Illuminator, “If Jamie loses by two points, we are going to get up Wednesday morning, and we are going to wonder where the hell were you (national Democrats)?” 
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein contributed to this report.
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

title: State health department launches online survey on rural mobile health clinics
description: State health officials want to hear from rural Rhode Islanders about the kinds of healthcare services they’d like to see brought to their communities by mobile health clinics, an initiative funded by the sweeping federal tax and spending law enacted in July 2025. Mobile health clinics are vans outfitted with medical equipment and staffed by […]
text:
A staff member welcomes a parent and child to the Chickasaw Nation’s mobile Women, Infants and Children clinic in Ada, Oklahoma, in August 2023. Rhode Island is seeking residents’ input on plans for mobile health clinics in its rural communities. (Photo by U.S. Department of Agriculture)State health officials want to hear from rural Rhode Islanders about the kinds of healthcare services they’d like to see brought to their communities by mobile health clinics, an initiative funded by the sweeping federal tax and spending law enacted in July 2025. 
Mobile health clinics are vans outfitted with medical equipment and staffed by health care personnel to bring services directly to rural towns. Rhode Island’s mobile clinics are one major initiative supported by the state’s $156.17 million initial federal award as part of the Rural Health Transformation Program under H.R. 1, passed last summer. 
The Rhode Island Department of Health wants residents of the state’s 18 rural communities to share their thoughts via an online survey about how the state’s mobile health clinics should be developed as part of a federal grant program. The survey closes Tuesday Nov. 24.
Feedback will be used by the state to figure out where and when the mobile clinics might operate, as well as what services should be offered and how the mobile clinicians can add to and synchronize with existing health care infrastructure in the area.
The confidential, 10-minute survey is open to adult residents of the 18 communities. It asks questions like “How long does it usually take you to get to a healthcare appointment?” and “What is the best way for healthcare services to be provided in your community?” 
Survey respondents can also enter a raffle for gift cards. 
The survey comes as a sequel to another big infusion of federal healthcare money, announced Tuesday by the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services. The state has secured an additional $158 million for the second year of the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program, bringing Rhode Island’s total award to more than $314 million.
There are approximately 196,000 people living in Rhode Island’s 18 rural communities, accounting for nearly 18% of the state’s population, according to EOHHS data.
Rhode Island rural health projects take shape with $156M federal award

Federal definitions of “rural” are applied differently in different states but largely based on census data. They’re also stricter than the state-level designation, and the federal government considers only Westerly and New Shoreham as rural. 
Rhode Island defines rural communities as those with 25,000 residents and fewer than 1,000 people per square mile. 
The mobile health clinics are one of 13 initiatives outlined in the state’s rural health transformation program, which also includes investments in workforce development, behavioral health services and health information technology. 
EOHHS spokesperson Kerri White said in September that $7.2 million had been allocated to mobile health programming in the first year’s budget, with plans to support mobile dental services, family medicine, nutrition programs and school-based mental health services.
 



  What’s ‘rural’ in Rhode Island?
