title: Bill to reduce regulations on building energy infrastructure passes US Senate
description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects.The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.  The bill would shorten env[...]
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects.The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.  The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA. The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects.Opponents voiced concern that NEPA, a bedrock federal statute for environmental protection, would be too severely weakened and that tribes would lose power over the consultation process.Just two Republicans — Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley and South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds — voted against the bill. On the flip side, only 15 members of the Democratic caucus voted in favor.The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee’s leaders — GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — along with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chair, GOP Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and ranking Democrat, Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, negotiated the measure. In a statement celebrating the bill’s passage, Capito said the upper chamber “took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people.” Capito said she has “spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building,” adding that the bill “is the culmination of those efforts.” In his own statement, Heinrich said the measure would bring down electricity costs while preserving environmental standards. The bill “will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” the New Mexico Democrat said. President Donald Trump has backed the measure, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. In a statement of administration policy this month, the administration said the bill would “deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and economic growth across the United States.”  ‘Deeply disappointing’ But the bill has drawn sharp criticism from many environmental organizations, including the Center for Western Priorities, a public lands group.The Center’s executive director, Aaron Weiss, described the vote as “deeply disappointing,” adding that senators “who promised Westerners they would stand up for our public lands just voted for a bill that sells them out to Big Oil and Big Tech.” Weiss urged the House to reject the bill and allow the next Congress beginning in early January to craft “a permitting bill that builds clean energy without sacrificing America’s public lands.”In the lower chamber, House Natural Resources Committee Chair Bruce Westerman said the Senate vote marked “a strong step forward in fixing our nation’s permitting challenges,” in a statement Friday.The Arkansas Republican said he looks forward “to working with my colleagues in the House to swiftly pass this bipartisan bill that will unleash the full force of American innovation.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: About 15 months later, UK finishes investigation on law professor with mixed findings
description: The University of Kentucky has notified courts it finished an independent investigation into the conduct of a law professor that began last year after UK learned of an online petition he circulated that called for military action against Israel. The 137-page report has been filed with federal and state courts reviewing cases from Professor Ramsi […]
text:
UK has finished an investigation into a professor at the UK Rosenberg College of Law. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)The University of Kentucky has notified courts it finished an independent investigation into the conduct of a law professor that began last year after UK learned of an online petition he circulated that called for military action against Israel.
The 137-page report has been filed with federal and state courts reviewing cases from Professor Ramsi Woodcock where he is seeking to be restored to his teaching duties. In August, the U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the U.S. Eastern District Court of Kentucky should reconsider Woodcock’s case. A case is also pending in Franklin Circuit Court. The Kentucky Lantern also obtained a copy of the investigation report via an open records request to the university. 
Ramsi Woodcock has been reassigned from teaching and banned from entering the University of Kentucky College of Law, where he is an assistant professor.
The report prepared by McGuireWoods, a law firm based in Richmond, Virginia, includes portions of interviews from students and witnesses about allegations that had been previously discussed during a December 2025 hearing in the federal case, such as comments Woodcock made during academic panels and use of listservs. Woodcock also had a list of questions for interviewees, but some declined to answer those. McGuireWoods was also retained to prepare a “confidential attorney-client privileged report with robust legal analysis in anticipation of litigation.”
UK spokesperson Jay Blanton told the Lantern the public “report reflects an extensive independent review of serious concerns involving” Woodcock and “the complexity of this matter.” 
“The evidence raises significant concerns about conduct in professional settings, such as conferences and professional discussion groups, connected to his role as a University of Kentucky faculty member. At the same time, while there are some students who are reluctant to take him for class,  the review did not establish inappropriate conduct toward students in his regular classroom teaching,” Blanton said. “The university takes both findings seriously. We remain committed to protecting academic freedom, as defined by our Governing Regulations, and First Amendment rights, while also holding employees to appropriate standards of professional conduct. With the factual review complete, university leadership is evaluating the full record, our applicable policies, and previous judicial decisions, as we determine appropriate next steps.”
The report also addresses questions about the impartiality of the investigation, as an attorney for Woodcock previously noted that one of investigators, Farnaz Farkish Thompson, is listed as a contributor to Project 2025, which was created as a guiding document for the Trump administration leading up to the 2024 presidential election. Among its goals for the U.S. presidency, the document calls for supporting Israel. The report says Thompson’s contribution to Project 2025 was to restore Title IX regulations regarding campus sexual harassment, which she worked on while at the U.S. Department of Education. 
Woodcock provided a 57-page response as part of the investigation, which is also part of court filings. In that, he noted that his former students interviewed “described a classroom without politics in which students were treated equally.” Unnamed student reporters also said they learned of Woodcock’s petition after UK President Eli Capilouto shared a public message in July 2025 regarding the decision to reassign Woodcock and saying the petition “can be interpreted as antisemitic in accordance with state and federal guidance” and called Woodcock’s views “repugnant.” 
“The evidence shows a professor who expressed his views on a matter of intense public concern, as a scholar or a citizen, in brief remarks at academic conferences, in voluntary professional discussion forums, and on his own websites and social media, and who, by the consistent account of his students, taught his classes without politics and treated every student equally,” Woodcock wrote in his 57-page response. “None of the noticed allegations is supported. I have not violated any University policy or rule.”
Woodcock later told the Lantern in a statement that UK’s concerns about “conduct in professional settings and discussion groups” as a professor “means is that it wants to tell a law professor what he can and cannot say to his colleagues at academic conferences and in discussion groups for law professors about Israel’s genocide of Palestinians.”
“President Capilouto, who called my views ‘repugnant’ before any investigation began, is the designated decision-maker. The next step is for this obviously biased decision-maker to decide whether the report — which provides only the investigator’s version of the facts and no law —justifies discipline.”
Lawsuits pending
As the matter moves in federal court, Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman cited the federal case in a Supreme Court brief regarding academic freedom of professors along with a coalition of Republican attorneys general. The group is asking the high court to review a challenge to a Florida law and find that professors do not have special First Amendment rights beyond other public employees. Pointing to Woodcock’s case, the brief said, “under Sixth Circuit precedent, off-campus speech by a professor can qualify as protected official speech.” 
However, Woodcock previously told the Lantern that the brief uses “my case to make a point about classroom teaching, but my case involves no classroom speech.”
Woodcock is also challenging the appointment of now-Dean Gregory Van Tatenhove, a former federal judge, in Franklin Circuit Court. Van Tatenhove has been criticized for not having enough legal scholarship, and Woodcock’s case argues the action is a violation of his employment contract with UK. 
The Louisville Courier Journal reported UK spent more than $1.1 million in legal fees on the investigation and to defend itself in lawsuits. Most of that, about $848,000 was for the investigation and report. Another $38,000 related to an investigation UK did regarding a complaint Woodcock made about the university’s equal opportunity office.
Woodcock also questioned if UK “bypassed procurement law” by not running a contract with McGuireWoods through he state’s Contract Review Committee, but Blanton said UK “routinely asks its outside law firms to engage consultants or other law firms with specialized knowledge for one-time projects.” The contract with those firms and then costs are passed on to the university through normal invoices, he said.
The actual contract was between a law firm that regularly works for UK, Sturgill Turner of Lexington, and McGuire Woods, Blanton said.
“In this instance, the University needed a law firm that could handle a complex investigation involving information technology and witnesses on three different continents,” Blanton added. “None of the firms under regular contract had that specific expertise or capacity.”
As UK faces challenges from Woodcock over his political speech, the university is considering a policy to prevent users of university technology, including wifi, for political activity. The proposal has drawn concern from across the political spectrum. Rep. TJ Roberts, R-Burlington, and Lexington Councilwoman Emma Curtis are among critics of the policy. UK officials extended the comment period on the proposal to Nov. 30, according to a campus email. UK Provost Robert DiPaola told the Lexington Herald-Leader the proposed policy did not have to do with Woodcock’s lawsuits.

title: Disney maintenance workers to vote on new contract as allegation of intimidation surfaces
description: Skilled maintenance and trades workers at Walt Disney World’s parks are voting on a new contract Friday and Saturday, amid allegations by at least one union member that management has threatened to replace workers if they vote to strike. Disney has been negotiating a five-year contract over the past few months with the Craft Maintenance […]
text:
The Epcot theme part at Walt Disney World Resort. Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Skilled maintenance and trades workers at Walt Disney World’s parks are voting on a new contract Friday and Saturday, amid allegations by at least one union member that management has threatened to replace workers if they vote to strike.
Disney has been negotiating a five-year contract over the past few months with the Craft Maintenance Council, which represents eight unions: bricklayers, carpenters, electricians, laborers, operating engineers, painters, plumbers/pipefitters, and Teamsters.
The contract between the union and Disney expired Sept. 28 and has been extended month to month.
Kavin Griffin is executive secretary treasurer and CEO of the Southern Regional Counsel of Carpenters, which represents Carpenters Local 1820 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners. Members are concerned that the wages and benefits Disney has presented do not consider inflation, rising health care costs, and the high cost of living in Central Florida, he said.
“We’re the skilled workforce that basically puts the magic in the Magic Kingdom,” he said. “We’re just looking for a fair agreement at the end of the day and, especially when you’re looking at something that’s going to be in the five-year range, there’s a lot of forecasting. And today the company just hasn’t done a good job, in our opinion, of making something that’s palatable for that length of time. So, we’re representing our workforce, making sure that they get the best deal that’s possible.”
Negotiations have become so intense that the Southern Regional Council of Carpenters filed an unfair labor practice complaint against Disney with the National Labor Relations Board last week, alleging several workers had reported being told they are “replaceable” if they go out on strike.
“We experienced it firsthand just in my area alone, where leadership was basically reading their PowerPoint that came from corporate,” Zac Anderson, who works as an overnight attractions mechanic at Disney World and is a steward with Local 1820, told the Phoenix. The threat came on a section of management’s “Frequently Asked Question” page, regarding whether the carpenters have the right to strike, he said.
 “It was, ‘If a strike were to occur, we have a contingency plan in place, and if those who don’t show up to work are replaceable.’”
“We just want a solid contract,” Anderson added. “Nobody wants a strike to happen. We want to just have a fair deal. At the end of the day, Disney pays us to be thorough with our jobs to make sure that it’s the safest place we can be. We don’t have the accidents that you see going around just like you saw in Georgia a couple of weeks ago. That thing just doesn’t happen here. We’re very specifically high-trained, [make] constant upgrades, making sure that nothing’s going to happen.
“And now they’re talking about replacing us with anybody off the street, which they already have a hard time filling positions that they have now. This is the first time ever — people who have been here 20-30 years have said I have never seen management walk in on all shifts and say, ‘This is a good deal. You should go vote for it,’ and go over their sheet but then also threaten us with, ‘You’ll be replaced if you don’t come into work,’ basically.”
For most private-sector workers covered by federal law, it is an unfair labor practice for an employer to threaten employees for saying they will strike. Under Section 8(a)(1) of the National Labor Relations Act, employers cannot “interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees” exercising their right to engage in concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining.
The Walt Disney World Co. declined to comment on this story.

title: Delaware blockchain panel discusses digital IDs and a digital coin
description: A state task force is studying how digital credentials and payments could be used in public services. Its report is due July 1, 2027. By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE DOVER, Del. — Delaware residents can already carry a version of their driver’s license on a phone. At a Nov. 20 meeting of Delaware’s Blockchain and Digital Innovation Task Force, ... Read Mo[...]
text:

A state task force is studying how digital credentials and payments could be used in public services. Its report is due July 1, 2027.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
DOVER, Del. — Delaware residents can already carry a version of their driver’s license on a phone. At a Nov. 20 meeting of Delaware’s Blockchain and Digital Innovation Task Force, the discussion turned to how state government could use digital credentials and a digital coin, and what changes might require legislation.
Anastasia Dellaccio of The Digital Chamber’s State Network told the panel that states are learning from one another as they develop policy. She described them as “laboratories of innovation” and said the network helps bring people working on those issues together. The group publishes model legislation on digital identity, including privacy protections and use by government agencies, and on how states can align stablecoin rules with federal law. www.state.digitalchamber.org
How state-issued and state-endorsed digital IDs work
Delaware’s Division of Motor Vehicles launched its voluntary Mobile ID app in 2021. It gives residents a digital version of their state-issued driver’s license or ID card that they can use to verify their identity or age where it is accepted. The DMV says drivers must still present a physical license when required. new.dmv.de.gov
A slide presented to the task force outlined another model called State-Endorsed Digital Identity, or SEDI. Under that model, the state vouches for verified facts such as age or residency, and residents choose what to share and with whom. Someone could prove to a website that they are 21 or older while keeping their full birth date and address private. sedi.utah.gov
The presentation described a framework designed to prevent routine government tracking of when and where people use their credentials and to work across technologies and providers. Utah enacted a state-endorsed digital identity framework in 2026 and plans limited testing in early 2027. Delaware’s task force heard about the model as part of its policy discussion. sedi.utah.gov
What digital IDs could be used for
Someone applying for public benefits online could use a digital credential to prove who they are or where they live. Schools could use similar checks to flag enrollment or financial aid applications filed under fictitious identities, sometimes called “ghost students.” A slide presented to the task force also pointed to online age checks as a potential child safety measure.
Other examples included stronger identity checks when people open or recover accounts, where stolen or fabricated identities can be used to commit fraud. Verifiable credentials could help people confirm who is behind a message that claims to come from a government agency or business. The slide cited AI-generated impersonation and deepfakes and raised the question of how to tell whether an automated tool has permission to act for a person or organization.
Anastasia Dellaccio of The Digital Chamber’s State Network told the panel that a state-issued digital ID would address many problems that a State Government must address every day.  This slide was used to make that point.
Who could see where you use a digital ID?
An age check could reveal only that a person is 21 or older. If an agency, vendor or website records when and where the credential is used, those records could reveal more when combined over time. Any Delaware proposal would raise questions about who could keep those records, how long they could retain them, and under what conditions police could get access. Another question is whether residents could get the same public services with a physical ID.
The Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 6 of the Delaware Constitution protect against unreasonable searches and seizures. In Carpenter v. United States, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the government’s acquisition of detailed historical cellphone location records was a search that generally requires a warrant. Whether that reasoning would apply to digital ID records would depend on what the records reveal and how the government obtains them. www.supremecourt.gov
Utah’s law preserves the right to use physical ID and protects against state tracking of digital ID use “except as authorized by law.” How Delaware might write and enforce comparable protections remains an open question. le.utah.gov
What Delaware could gain from regulating stablecoins
In July, Gov. Matt Meyer signed the Delaware Payment Stablecoins Act, which creates a licensing and oversight framework for issuers of payment stablecoins. A payment stablecoin is a digital asset designed to maintain a steady value against a currency such as the U.S. dollar. legis.delaware.gov
Dellaccio said states could build on existing rules for money transmitters, trust companies and digital asset businesses. The federal GENIUS Act gives eligible issuers the option of state oversight under rules that are substantially similar to federal standards and go through a federal certification process. www.govinfo.gov
A state charter aligned with federal requirements could help attract stablecoin issuers, financial technology investment and jobs, Dellaccio said. Smaller issuers serving local markets or offering limited services could see lower compliance costs if oversight is tailored to their size and risk. State supervision could also let some issuers continue working with regulators they already know.
In Wyoming, the state’s Stable Token Commission launched the Frontier Stable Token, which is backed by reserves and redeemable for $1. The materials available from the Nov. 20 meeting leave open who would issue or operate a Delaware coin and what residents could use it for. content.govdelivery.com
Where Delaware’s blockchain work stands
Delaware’s work dates to 2016, when Gov. Jack Markell launched the Delaware Blockchain Initiative. In 2017, lawmakers gave Delaware corporations the option to use blockchain, a shared digital ledger, to track share ownership and keep other corporate records. The state later worked with IBM on a prototype for business lien filings and stock records. The Division of Corporations currently directs businesses to its e-UCC system for lien filings. www.prnewswire.com
What lawmakers asked the task force to study
The General Assembly created the task force in April to look for ways to attract and retain digital asset businesses, give companies clearer rules and protect consumers. Lawmakers asked the panel to review Delaware’s corporate recordkeeping laws, compare approaches in other states and examine how federal law affects what Delaware can regulate. The panel is also studying potential state and local government uses and their privacy risks. The resolution calls for input from industry participants, consumer advocates and academic experts. www.legis.delaware.gov
The panel, led by Sen. Darius J. Brown and Rep. Madinah Wilson-Anton, must send its findings and any recommendations to the General Assembly and the governor by July 1, 2027. For each recommendation, it must identify who would carry it out and whether it would require legislation, a regulatory change or additional resources. legis.delaware.gov
To Go Box

The task force’s next virtual meetings are scheduled for 10 a.m. Dec. 4 and Dec. 18. Check the General Assembly calendar and look for livestreams and recordings on Watch & Listen. legis.delaware.gov
For questions about joining a meeting or providing input, contact task force staffer Brandon Williams at 302-744-4039 or brandonf.williams@delaware.gov. Read the panel’s mandate in Senate Concurrent Resolution 143. legis.delaware.gov

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Woburn transit hub to sprout 595 apartments by 2031
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: Massport's board unanimously approved Cabot, Cabot & Forbes as the developer of the project spanning six acres of the 26-acre transportation facility.
text:
THE MASSACHUSETTS PORT AUTHORITY has selected a developer to build a mixed-use project to include 595 rental housing units at the Anderson Regional Transportation Center in Woburn.
Massport’s board unanimously approved Cabot, Cabot & Forbes as the developer of the project spanning six acres of the 26-acre transportation facility. The developer’s proposal includes 10,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space, 595 parking spaces and affordable housing options, Andrew Hargens, Massport’s chief development officer, said during Thursday’s board meeting. The development will include five residential floors over a two-level podium that houses parking as well as amenities and retail space, he said. 
The transportation center is home to Massport’s Woburn Logan Express, which offers bus service to and from Logan International Airport. It also sits along both the Lowell Line of the MBTA Commuter Rail and Amtrak’s Downeaster line. 
CC&F was the only developer to respond to an RFP seeking mixed-use development on the site, Hargens said. He added that the agency was looking for proposals that “capitalize on the transit-oriented development potential of the property.” 
The transit center sits within the 245-acre Industri-Plex Superfund site that was once home to a chemical and glue manufacturing facility, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Hargens said it was “paramount” the chosen developer had experience and ability to work with the EPA and address protection measures for the site. He said that CC&F is “extremely experienced” in the local market, has worked with Woburn officials and on projects of a similar scale within the same Superfund site. 
MassDOT and the MBTA co-own the transportation center with Massport. MassDOT and the T are expected to approve CC&F as the site’s developer soon, Massport said in a press release. After that, the agencies and developer will work on finalizing a term sheet and development agreement, Hargens said.
Massport said the project is expected to be finished in 2031.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Fort Martin gas plant could have hidden costs for West Virginians
description: The recently approved Fort Martin gas plant could lead to larger power bill increases for West Virginians if data center construction doesn’t materialize.
text:
Aerial view of Fort Martin, a coal-powered electricity power station  in Maidsville, West Virginia. (Getty Images)The recently approved Fort Martin gas plant could lead to larger power bill increases for West Virginians if data center construction doesn’t materialize. 
The West Virginia Public Service Commission announced this week that initial surcharges — additional cost tacked onto electric bills to pay for infrastructure like plants and power lines — would be $1.18 a month for homeowners and renters in the Mon Power/Potomac Edison territory. 
But if anticipated data centers don’t come to pay for the $2.48 billion Fort Martin gas plant in Maidsville, West Virginia, those charges could reach up to $25 a month by 2033. The plant could cost customers an anticipated total of $508 before electricity starts churning out in 2031. 
Lisa Chamberlain, a spokesperson for Mon Power’s parent company First Energy, said the company doesn’t anticipate that happening because a “large load customer” — namely a data center as described in the PSC filings — is very close to inking a deal and taking on the costs. 
“In all reality, the existing customers will not pay anything,” she said.
Chamberlain also noted that the surcharge will be reviewed on a six-month basis and works similar to a home construction loan — customers will only pay for what’s been spent. Even if the large load customer doesn’t sign prior to the first filing for a surcharge in January 2027, Chamberlain said residential customers will be made whole. 
“If they pay for three months, they will be made whole,” she said. 
Emmett Pepper, policy director for Energy Efficient West Virginia, said there’s no doubt that a high use customer like a data center would offset the cost for construction. But he’s skeptical if the pay back arrangement could work that way. 
“There is no state law that requires data centers to pay back ratepayers in the way FirstEnergy was describing,” Pepper said. 
The PSC, in its order approving the projects, recognized the danger that residential customers could be on the hook for the costs. But it also noted that Mon Power/Potomac Edison anticipates avoiding this through the data centers. 
“The Commission will hold the Companies to that commitment,” the commission wrote,“We will not, however, prescribe a fixed and static requirement on how that is accomplished.” 
The project has also raised other concerns. On Thursday, the United Mine Workers of America sent out a statement questioning if the existing coal fired Fort Martin Plant will still be used or idled once the gas plant is up and running. 
“The governor and political leaders love to talk up West Virginia coal when the cameras are rolling, but then they go behind closed doors to fast track and subsidize data centers and utility projects that wipe out mining jobs, gut county schools and ship profits out of state,” said Brian Sanson, president of the United Mine Workers of America.

text:
Louisiana received $1.6 million from the federal government to combat human trafficking from 2026 through June 2030. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Illuminator)The U.S. Department of Justice awarded Louisiana $1.6 million to set up a human trafficking task force. 
The Governor’s Office of Human Trafficking Prevention will oversee the creation of the group and expects to spend $400,000 of the federal funding before July 1, according to legislative budget documents released this week. The grant expires in June 2030.
The money will be used to help law enforcement address human trafficking with additional training, technical assistance, better coordination among agencies and collaboration with victim advocates, according to a writeup from the Louisiana Legislative Fiscal Office. 
The federal grant requires a 25% match of state funds, meaning Louisiana must put up $400,000 of its own money to get the federal dollars. A summary provided to lawmakers indicates the state will use funding in the existing budget of the governor’s office to meet that requirement. 
The state Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget approved the use of the money Thursday.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Midwest is ‘less red than maybe we assumed,’ Politico columnist tells South Dakotans
description: SIOUX FALLS — The blue wave was a ripple in South Dakota during the midterm elections this month, but the results nationwide and elsewhere in the Midwest show the red-and-blue map is less fixed than it once seemed, Politico’s Jonathan Martin said Thursday. Martin, Politico’s politics bureau chief and senior political columnist, spoke to reporters […]
text:
Jonathan Martin, Politico’s politics bureau chief and senior political columnist, speaks to reporters ahead of the opening lecture of the Lost Region Recovery Project Conference in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on Nov. 20, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — The blue wave was a ripple in South Dakota during the midterm elections this month, but the results nationwide and elsewhere in the Midwest show the red-and-blue map is less fixed than it once seemed, Politico’s Jonathan Martin said Thursday.
Martin, Politico’s politics bureau chief and senior political columnist, spoke to reporters before a lecture at Augustana University’s Center for Western Studies. The talk, with a standing-room-only crowd, opened the Lost Region Recovery Project Conference, which is devoted to Midwestern studies and continues through Saturday.
Democrats won major victories across much of the Midwest, including in Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Iowa and Kansas.
“What we’re looking at now is a Midwest that is less red than maybe we assumed,” Martin said.
In South Dakota, Democrats gained four seats in the Legislature, increasing from eight to 12 — with all the gains occurring in the Sioux Falls area. 
Podcast: What South Dakota’s blue ‘ripple’ means for the state Democratic Party

Democrats see hope in the results, but the problem for the party in South Dakota, Martin told reporters, is that “the Democratic bench is thin here.”
The Democratic Party hasn’t held a statewide office in South Dakota since U.S. Sen. Tim Johnson’s career ended when he did not seek reelection in 2014. The share of voters registered as Democrats has dropped from 34% in November 2014 to 22% in this year’s midterm elections.
“You just lost a lot of institutional memory and then the down ballot losses get worse every two years because it’s a self-reinforcing problem, right? It’s a vicious cycle,” Martin told reporters. “You lose down the ballot, you lose your bench — and so there’s nobody to even run of any stature, statewide.”
That cycle feeds on itself until it’s disrupted, Martin said, and it will take the party recruiting business people and non-politicians willing to “put their neck out there” in addition to nominating candidates who’ll challenge the national party “orthodoxy” to fit South Dakotans’ needs.
“And then guess what?” Martin said. “Luck and timing.”
Martin said some Democrats hurt themselves by deferring to independent U.S. Senate candidates in Idaho, South Dakota, Montana and Nebraska. All four of those independents lost to Republicans. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs ran as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds this year after running unsuccessfully as a Democrat against Republican Sen. John Thune in 2022. Voters saw through that, Martin said.
Martin added that past Democrats from the Dakotas, such as South Dakota’s former U.S. Sen. Tom Daschle, won for so many years by emphasizing local issues, especially agriculture. Politics, he said, has since become more nationalized.
Martin said the election wasn’t a “vote of confidence in Democrats,” but rather a “vote of no confidence” in Republican President Donald Trump and a cry for relief from higher prices caused by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran.
“Democrats were the vehicle,” Martin said.
Democrats “have got to be at least caught trying” to lower costs if they want to continue the wave into 2028 and beyond, Martin said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Longtime GOP consultant: Mississippi ‘you did good’ with Scott Colom Senate victory
description: U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom waves to his supporters during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

Like Scott Colom, I’m a seventh-generation Mississippian. Like Scott Colom, our dads are lawyers. His mom was a judge. My grandfather was a judge. Scott’s mom and dad met at Antioch Law School in Washington, D.C., where they were students of my Uncle Francis Stevens. Scott’s grandmother was a civil rights activist. My grandmother was president of the Mississippi chapter of the Association of Southern Women for the Prevention of Lynching. Yes, there was such a thing.
Scott’s dad, Wil Colom, was the Republican nominee for Mississippi state treasurer. I worked in Mississippi Republican politics. Wil Colom and I both worked with the late Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi. Scott went to Millsaps College in Jackson. I grew up walking distance from Millsaps.
Watching the Scott Colom campaign unfold often felt like waking from a dream and struggling to sort out what is real. Was this really happening? I have helped elect Republican governors, congressmen and senators from Mississippi. It has always been more difficult to elect a Republican than commonly assumed. Depending on the African American turnout and assuming a Republican gets 7% to 8% of that vote, a Republican needs near 70% of the white vote and, as my former client Haley Barbour says, “I have trouble getting 70% at Thanksgiving dinner.”
As the race started to get attention in October, I was often asked if Scott Colom could win. My standard response was that it was like taking two tires swinging from a tree limb and throwing a football through them from 20 yards. Can you do it? Absolutely. Is it easy? Hell no.
Politics is all about probability. Electing a Democrat the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction would require a favorable alignment of pretty much every variable in a race.
Wilbur Colom, a former Republican candidate turned Democratic Party supporter, attends a campaign event  for his son, Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom, in downtown Jackson on Aug. 1, 2026.   Credit: Taylor Vance/Mississippi Today
You needed the rarest of qualities in politics: a candidate graced with natural skills, grace and confidence that no consultant could manufacture. Call it a once-in-a-generation talent; only in Mississippi, it was more like once in many generations.
The opponent had to be a horrible candidate who generated no passion and sleepwalked through the campaign. That was Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who managed to combine the arrogance of an assumed victory with indifference. The total impression was someone who knew they would win but didn’t really care.
The national political climate had to be historically favorable to Democrats. Compared to the 2024 results, Mississippi shifted 23.5% more Democratic. Pause on that number. The last time Mississippi voted for a Democratic presidential candidate was Jimmy Carter in 1976.
The last Democrat elected to the US Senate was John Stennis in 1982. Haley Barbour ran against him. I made the ads. Stennis turned 80 in 1982, and Haley was 32. We used the slogan “A Senator for the 80s” with the unsaid comparison of not in his 80s. We assembled a talented campaign team of young Mississippi-born political operatives who later went on to great success in national politics. We thought we were the best and the brightest and would crush John Stennis, who first ran for office in 1927.
Stennis beat us like a rented mule, 64% to 34%.
How bad was it? Stennis held a yearly press conference — yes, yearly — that he called “the hour of accountability.” Not surprisingly, he refused to debate Haley, so I took footage of the Stennis press conference and staged a mock press conference with Haley that made it look like they were standing at matching podiums. Haley answered the same questions asked of Stennis, and then I cut it together with the Stennis footage into a 30-minute video.
When we tested it in focus groups, the general consensus was that Haley was a lot smarter, more energetic and knew the issues better. But most still voted for Stennis. That should have told us everything we needed to know. I said to Haley, “We can’t even stage a fake debate and win.”
Haley went on to win the governorship in 2003 and 2007, defeating the last Democratic governor of Mississippi, Ronnie Musgrove, who won largely because Republicans nominated a funeral home owner who seemed most comfortable around the embalmed.
A 23.5% Democratic shift is not the most startling statistic of the Colom Senate victory. Hyde-Smith won 61% of the over-65 vote, and Colom won 62% of the under-45 vote. As a political operative, that’s a shocking number. As a Mississippian, it seems inevitable.
Hyde-Smith was the Last Hope of the Confederate Lost Cause, posing with a gun and wearing a Confederate army hat at Jefferson Davis’ home in Biloxi. That’s also the official presidential library of the Confederate president, in case your bucket list of presidential libraries is incomplete.
I grew up in a Mississippi where the 4th of July was a muted holiday, more remembered for the day the siege of Vicksburg ended and the battle of Gettysburg was lost.
A cousin of mine recently came across a photo of me dressed in a Confederate cavalry general’s uniform, taken at a Junior League Old South Ball at the Jackson Country Club. I think I was 13. She is demanding a fortune not to post it online. Negotiations are ongoing.
My parents were what was known as “good on race,” always opposed to any segregationist candidates. But the Old South Ball was still a good theme for a charity event. Today, the Jackson Junior League has a yearly day of service on the MLK holiday.
At a time when our national politics has felt like a going-out-of-business sale on hope, Mississippi stepped forward to shock the nation and make history. For once, Nina Simone’s “Mississippi Goddam” was a victory chant. Yes, Mississippi Goddam. You did good.

Stuart Stevens, a Jackson native, is  a veteran political consultant, working on multiple high-profile Republican campaigns, including presidential and senatorial campaigns. He is now the senior adviser for the Lincoln Project, composed mainly of longtime Republicans who oppose Donald Trump. Stevens has spoken out on what he views as the country’s shift toward authoritarianism and is the author of multiple books, including the 2020, “It Was All a Lie: How the Republican Party Became Donald Trump.”

title: Des Moines University, UnityPoint Health partner for rural health collaborative
description: Health sciences higher education and a healthcare business are working together through a new partnership to target rural health needs and develop solutions for patients. Des Moines University Medicine and Health Sciences announced in a news release this week it has partnered with UnityPoint Health to establish the Rural Health Collaborative, starting in Web[...]
text:
Des Moines University and UnityPoint Health are launching a rural health collaborative with a focus on Webster County. (Photo courtesy of the University of Iowa Holden Comprehensive Cancer Center)Health sciences higher education and a healthcare business are working together through a new partnership to target rural health needs and develop solutions for patients.
Des Moines University Medicine and Health Sciences announced in a news release this week it has partnered with UnityPoint Health to establish the Rural Health Collaborative, starting in Webster County with a focus on targeted screening, cancer information and radon risk reduction.
“The data tells us there is a real opportunity to improve health outcomes in Webster County,” said Pravin Mishra, Des Moines University chief research officer, in the release. “Research can help identify where challenges exist, but meaningful change happens when communities help shape the solutions. By combining local perspectives with data-driven insights, we can better understand barriers to screening and follow-up care and work together to improve access, detect cancer earlier and support better outcomes for residents.”

According to the release, local data shows that one in five eligible Webster County residents receive lung cancer screenings, close to three-fourths of which catch the lung cancer diagnosis at a late stage. Six out of 10 colorectal cancer cases, which Webster County sees at a higher rate than the state and national averages, are also diagnosed at a later stage.
Webster County was estimated in the 2026 Cancer in Iowa report to see 250 new cancer cases among residents this year, falling within the state’s rate of 498.8 new cancer cases per 100,000 people. Expected cancer deaths, however, sit above the state’s rate, with the county projected to have 85 cancer deaths in 2026. There are 2,150 cancer survivors in the county this year, the report stated, out of an estimated 175,290 in the state.
Perspectives from Webster County residents were taken into account alongside data when crafting the initiative, the release stated, gathered from community cancer events and forums where people emphasized their need for screening information, guidance in navigating care and support in dealing with transportation and costs.
The program will focus on three initiatives in Webster County, the release stated. Targeted screening outreach will seek out those with a risk of developing cancer, connecting those who are eligible with recommended screenings and support them in their care journey. With the help of community partners, the initiative will also bring more awareness of radon and its risks and connect residents with resources.
The university and healthcare system will also create an online hub with county-specific resources for cancer prevention, screening and supports. All of these efforts aim to increase access to care, reduce health disparities and improve health outcomes, the release stated.
UnityPoint Health – Fort Dodge Market President Leah Glasgo said in the release the initiative will bolster healthcare access “close to home” for Webster County residents and improve their health.
“This work reflects a long-term commitment to partnership, listening and continuous learning,” said Jenn Crimmins, executive director of rural health for UnityPoint Health, in the release. “UnityPoint Health and Des Moines University will continue educating and engaging community members, reviewing local data and measuring progress to ensure the effort reflects the needs of Webster County while helping inform future rural health initiatives across Iowa.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Commentary: The Trump administration is pro-extinction
description: “Save the Whales” used to be one of the few slogans everyone could get behind, right up there with “Do unto others” and “Peace on Earth.” Over the past year, the Trump administration has proven that even this feel-good, common-sense maxim is too much to ask. A string of recent policies implemented or backed by […]
text:
In 2023, a North Atlantic right whale was spotted off the coast of Georgia with rope lodged in its mouth. (Photo courtesy of Georgia DNR/NOAA Fisheries)“Save the Whales” used to be one of the few slogans everyone could get behind, right up there with “Do unto others” and “Peace on Earth.” Over the past year, the Trump administration has proven that even this feel-good, common-sense maxim is too much to ask. A string of recent policies implemented or backed by the Trump administration threatens to drive North Atlantic right whales and countless other endangered species to extinction.
The administration has released a series of rules decimating the Endangered Species Act. The consequences are not theoretical. They concern whether we will allow preventable human activity to keep killing species that have no way to protect themselves.
Most recently, the administration has decided that destroying an endangered species’ habitat or otherwise killing an endangered animal by “accident” — no matter how predictable and preventable the “accident” — is no longer banned by the Act.
That distinction is dangerously divorced from reality. These days, endangered species do not generally disappear because someone sets out to kill them. They disappear because people build roads, clear forests, develop open waters, deploy fishing gear, and do other economic activities that make survival impossible. If foreseeable harm can simply be dismissed as an accident, the Endangered Species Act becomes far less capable of doing the job Congress created it to do.
This terrible decision puts North Atlantic right whales at especially high risk. Collisions with boats and ships, the highly avoidable “accidents” that the government could allow, are a leading cause of death for right whales. The whales are currently protected from these collisions by dynamic vessel speed limits that kick in at times and places where right whales are likely present. That would be more reassuring if the Trump administration hadn’t pledged to roll back those speed limits as well.
The permitting bill making its way through the Senate and supported by the Trump administration would put endangered species at even greater risk, by weakening science-backed safeguards and making it easier for development projects that threaten wildlife and their habitats to move forward. It would also fast track data centers, one of which has been proposed as an undersea facility in Eastport, further jeopardizing right whales.
To round out their anti-whale agenda, the Trump administration is also actively stripping away safeguards against the other primary killer of right whales: entanglements in fishing gear. They supported a bill — recently passed by the House and currently in the Senate — that would extend an existing moratorium on new policies around fishing gear until 2035. The moratorium would exempt the lobster industry from requirements of the Endangered Species Act and the Marine Mammal Protection Act for another seven years beyond the six years Congress already gave them.
Outgoing Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden of Maine claimed that he co-sponsored the bill because it “will protect our heritage lobster industry from unnecessary and costly new regulations related to the protection of the North Atlantic right whale.” Let’s be very clear: The lobster industry is an important part of Maine’s heritage, but the 382 critically endangered whales need additional protection during times of high risk from the strangling ropes used in a slew of commercial fisheries, including the lobster fishery. Even Maine’s own Department of Marine Resources has told senators that it and groups representing lobstermen believe the bill is not essential.
This bill would take us in exactly the wrong direction when solutions to fishing gear entanglements are at our fingertips. Scientists and partners have spent years developing and refining “on-demand” gear, which has far fewer dangerous vertical lines for marine life to get ensnarled in.
Right whales were named because whalers considered them the “right whale” to hunt, due to their slow speed and tendency to float near the water’s surface. We may have stopped killing these gentle giants with harpoons, but we never stopped wiping them out. Human activity is the only known cause of death for adult North Atlantic right whales in the modern day — not one has been documented living long enough to die from old age.
With funding and some political will, right whales, boaters, and the fishing industry can co-exist and even thrive. But instead of embracing this brighter future, our government wants to actively undermine right whales’ survival for short-term, questionable benefits.
“Save the Whales” was never really just about whales. It was about whether, when we have the power to stop something precious from disappearing forever, we choose to use that power.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan advocates launch coalition to push paid leave, universal childcare and higher wages
description: A new coalition of advocacy organizations, pushing for policies that enable a living wage, universal childcare and paid family and medical leave, launched this week as affordability takes center stage in political conversations around Michigan and nationwide.  Jayme Vosovic, the community engagement director at the Michigan League for Public Policy, explaine[...]
text:
Getty ImagesA new coalition of advocacy organizations, pushing for policies that enable a living wage, universal childcare and paid family and medical leave, launched this week as affordability takes center stage in political conversations around Michigan and nationwide. 
Jayme Vosovic, the community engagement director at the Michigan League for Public Policy, explained that the coalition, called Families Rising, stemmed from a series of listening sessions hosted around the state by the Michigan League for Public Policy and Michigan United in which participants were asked what makes it hard for their families to get by.
“No matter where we went, the three main issues that kept coming up were jobs with no paid leave, so getting sick or having a baby means losing a paycheck, childcare that costs as much as rent, if you can even find it at all, and wages that haven’t kept up with the price of groceries or rent,” Vosovic said. “We know these are not separate problems. They hit the same families at the same time, and we know that no single organization can fix them alone. So we knew we had to find strength in numbers.”
Leaders from various coalition members spoke about the importance of each of the three policy priorities.
Christina Hayes, a community organizer at Mothering Justice, said that, when talking with mothers and caregivers, they often find themselves “sandwiched” between caring for sick or elderly loved ones and raising their own children, all while employed, demonstrating the need for paid family leave policies.
McDonald Rivet speaks to Saginaw parents about childcare costs, highlights tax credit bill

“Paid leave protects financial security,” she said. “Families should never have to lose their income or risk falling behind on rent, utilities, groceries, while dealing with the family emergency.”
Hayes added that paid leave also acknowledges how many Michigan families serve as caregivers.
“Many residents are caring for aging parents, children with disabilities, or people that are facing serious illnesses,” she said.
Mori Anderson, a mother who said that she lives with kidney failure, explained exactly how important paid leave is for her to be able to survive.
“For me, paid leave is about more than time away from work. It’s about having the freedom to take care of myself, show up for my children, and maintain my livelihood without being penalized for circumstances beyond my control,” she said. “Healthcare equity must include workplace policies that allow for people to actually have access to the care that they need. Navigating a job with a disability should not require sacrificing your health.”
Wende Randall, the director of the Kent County Essential Needs Task Force, said universal childcare has positive impacts for early childhood development by exposing children to environments and social settings outside of their home, as well as in economic stability for families by reducing the pressures that limit the ability of parents to work.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kermit Williams, the political director of Oakland Forward, added that he hopes to see legislation with a floor of $25 per hour by 2028 — a wage that half of Americans do not make, he said.
“We have people that are working two or three jobs and still qualify for government benefits and assistance right now,” he said. “If we were to put a living wage in Michigan, we would be able not only to raise the economy that we need, but we would be able to make sure that people have time to spend with their families, their loved ones, their kids, pay for sick individuals, and other things that they need in order to survive and thrive.”
Many of the organizations involved with Families Rising have spoken at length since the midterm elections, in which Michigan Democrats won their trifecta on a largely affordability-focused platform, about the need to enact the policies on which officials campaigned on, focused on lowering costs for Michiganders. 
Hayes and Randall both noted that the coalition has been in conversations with returning and incoming legislators to find those who are willing to sponsor and champion legislation with these policies, as Democrats prepare to take a trifecta in Michigan’s state government.  
“We stay ready, so we don’t have to get ready. So even before the elections were going on, we were watching who was even running, and we already have our elected official champions lined up,” Hayes said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Number of flu cases in CT is up sharply this year
description: Flu season got an early start in Connecticut and across the country, with more than 2,500 reported cases in the state so far this season.
text:
Flu season got an early start in Connecticut and across the country, with more than 2,500 reported cases in the state so far this season. 
In the first two weeks of November, more than 1,040 residents were diagnosed with the flu, according to the Department of Public Health. Last year, around 335 people were diagnosed in the first two weeks of November and around 190 in October. This year, more than 1,300 people were diagnosed.
Manisha Juthani, the commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Public Health, said the state will not know the full impact of the flu this year until the end of the season.
“What we can say is that the flu season definitely started earlier, probably about a month earlier, than it did last year. As a consequence of that, we have nine deaths, all in people who were 50 and older, since late September,” Juthani said. “That’s higher than we usually have for this point in the year.”
The state-reported flu counts are “by far underestimated” since they only include lab tests, Juthani said. At-home tests or suspected cases are not reported to the state.
Across the country, the flu is hitting states early. While Connecticut’s early-season numbers are some of the highest in years, the state’s flu activity falls below many other states, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control.
There’s “no clear reason” why flu season began early this year, Juthani said. The early spread could be caused by anything from humidity levels — lower humidity allows for viruses to transmit more easily — to the strain of the virus that’s spreading. 
Slightly fewer Connecticut residents received the flu shot this year compared to 2025. Since the end of July, more than 940,000 people in Connecticut received a flu shot.
Juthani said more people 50 and older got a flu shots.
“The good news is that vaccination rates in people who are 50 and older is about 3% higher than we were at this time last year,” Juthani said. “We’re up to 37% already for people who are 50 and older. Now, would we like it to be higher than that? Of course.”
The best way to avoid the flu, especially as the holidays approach, is to get vaccinated, Juthani said. 
“So what I would really encourage people is if you are traveling, if you’re going to be seeing older relatives, gathering in big gatherings for the holidays, this is a great time to get up to date on all your vaccines,” Juthani said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Cybersecurity incident hits West Virginia Legislature
description: The West Virginia Legislature’s information technology system was the subject of a cybersecurity incident Thursday afternoon.
text:
The West Virginia state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Legislature’s information technology system was the subject of a cybersecurity incident Thursday afternoon. 
When the incident was discovered, outside cybersecurity specialists helped workers contain and investigate it, Ann Ali, communications director for the House of Delegates, said in a statement Friday. 
The Legislature’s webpage is down Friday as officials assess what’s been compromised, she said. 
Ali said so far it appears the incident was limited to the Legislature’s IT system. 
“We have no evidence showing that other state agencies or offices are affected,” she said. 
The situation is developing, and the investigation is ongoing, she said. 
“Any relevant findings will be shared as soon as it is appropriate to do so,” she said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lockdown lifted at Quinnipiac University, Friday classes canceled
authors: Ryan Caron King and Eric Aasen | Connecticut Public
description: A lockdown at Quinnipiac University was lifted early Friday morning amid reports of a possible gunman on campus.
text:
A lockdown at Quinnipiac University was lifted early Friday morning amid reports of a possible gunman on campus.
The university canceled classes Friday. Other university events may continue as scheduled, according to the university.
Hamden Police received a call Thursday evening about a person with a gun on the Mount Carmel campus, a call that’s now being investigated as an apparent hoax, officials said.
The university activated its emergency alert system and issued a shelter-in-place order. There was a heavy police presence on campus as officers were searching buildings.
The FBI assisted several agencies, including Quinnipiac’s public safety team, Hamden Police, and the Connecticut Special Weapons and Tactics team.
Law enforcement also investigated claims and images posted on social media, school officials said.
“We understand that there are questions about whether this was a swatting incident — a false report designed to create the kind of police response we experienced,” Marie Hardin, the university president, said in a statement. “The police will investigate that possibility. In the meantime, we are grateful that no one was physically harmed.”
Jayvon Norman and Tayvion Simmons, Quinnipiac freshmen, were playing basketball on campus Thursday evening when they got a text about a lockdown.
“We kind of didn’t take it serious at first,” Simmons said. “We kept playing, but then we kind of locked in and stopped playing.”
Then they barricaded the door and hid in a corner.
“We were really scared,” Norman said.
The university, located about 10 miles north of downtown New Haven, said counselors will be available to meet with students in person and via Zoom.
Classes were already not in session next week for the Thanksgiving holiday.
This story was first published Nov. 19, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida carries out record-breaking 20th execution this year
description: Florida executed Thomas Mitchell Overton Thursday night at the Florida State Prison in Bradford County. Overton, 71, was convicted of murdering a Monroe County couple during a home invasion in 1991. He was also convicted in the death of their unborn child. It was the 20th execution in Florida this year, the most in a […]
text:
The execution chamber at Florida State Prison. (Via Florida Department of Corrections)Florida executed Thomas Mitchell Overton Thursday night at the Florida State Prison in Bradford County.
Overton, 71, was convicted of murdering a Monroe County couple during a home invasion in 1991. He was also convicted in the death of their unborn child.
It was the 20th execution in Florida this year, the most in a single year in state history, and represents more than half of the executions (39) in the United States in 2026. It followed the 19 executions that Florida conducted last year, which to that point was the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976.
The state has two more executions planned for December.
“I never killed anyone,” Overton said shortly before he was administered the three-drug lethal injection protocol on Thursday night, according to the Associated Press.
Overton had insisted during his decades as a death row inmate that he was innocent.
The husband’s sister, two brothers, and cousin witnessed the execution, according to the AP. The man’s sister said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.
“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”
The execution took place shortly after a new survey reported that public approval for the death penalty for convicted murderers in the United States has dropped to 49%, the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971. That’s according to a Gallup Poll conducted last month.
DeSantis said earlier this summer on the day two executions took place in Florida that he didn’t “take any joy” in signing death warrants.
“I think we’ll probably end up having done more [executions] than any administration in the history of the state of Florida,” DeSantis said on July 28. “And I’m not like taking any pride in that, because it’s a weighty thing, but to me as we move through those and bring justice, that makes a big difference for a lot of people out there who suffered really, really serious tragedies. So, we’ll continue to do that.”
A group that opposes the death penalty said Thursday that DeSantis will get his wish to be remembered as the governor who carried out more executions than any in Florida history.
“But his legacy will be measured by what he was willing to overlook to claim that record,” said Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty in a statement released immediately after Overton’s death was announced. “As more of the country leaves the death penalty behind, he has used the final years of his governorship to desperately keep Florida clinging to it.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas secretary of state says payment for partial U.S. Senate recount ‘raises serious concerns’
description: Kansas secretary of state raises questions about funding source for $47,500 partial recount of U.S. Senate votes in Shawnee, Johnson and Wyandotte counties.
text:
Kansas Secretary of State Scott Schwab, a Republican, says he'll report to federal officials details of a Libertarian Party candidate's request and Show Me the Votes Foundation's funding of U.S. Senate vote recounts in 60 precincts in three counties. This is a May 19, 2026, image of Schwab in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Secretary of State Scott Schwab sounded an alarm about the source of funding for a partial recount of U.S. Senate votes for a Wichita activist who previously made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud in Kansas.
Schwab said in a statement Thursday the source of $47,500 to pay for the hand counts in three urban counties “raises serious concerns about potential violations of federal campaign finance restrictions.” His statement indicated misconduct could involve contributions from impermissible sources or an attempt to bypass federal campaign donation limits.
Schwab, who leaves office in January, said he would refer information to the Federal Election Commission and the U.S. Department of Justice “for review and any appropriate action.” He said the Kansas Secretary of State’s Office has no authority to enforce federal campaign law.
The request for a targeted recount of ballots in 60 precincts was submitted by David Graham, the Libertarian Party candidate for U.S. Senate. In the Nov. 3 election, Graham received 3% of the vote in an contest won by Democrat Adam Hamilton, who was the first Democrat from Kansas elected to the U.S. Senate since the 1930s.  Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall was defeated.
Schwab said Graham made the request Tuesday for tabulation of 23 precincts in Johnson County, 21 in Shawnee County and 16 in Wyandotte County.
The secretary of state’s office said Graham sought the recount for the “sole purpose” of assisting “Beth Clarkson with her academic research.” Graham didn’t cast doubt on accuracy of precinct vote totals, Schwab said.
Clarkson has championed election fraud conspiracies in Kansas for more than a decade. She leads a state-registered corporation, Show Me the Votes Foundation, that was founded in 2015.
On Thursday, a $47,548 cashier’s check drawn on the Show Me the Votes Foundation’s bank account — not Graham’s campaign account — was submitted to the Secretary of State’s Office to pay for the recounts. The source of the funds provided to the foundation hasn’t been disclosed, Schwab said.
Schwab authorized the three counties to begin the recounts, which could extend into the weekend. The secretary of state has repeatedly said over the years that Kansas has fair and accurate elections.
Under state law, the recount bond payment had to be made upfront because the U.S. Senate margin of victory for Hamilton exceeded 0.5%. He received 51% of the vote to Marshall’s 46%.
Neither Clarkson nor Graham could be reached for comment about the controversy Friday morning.
Clarkson, who earned a doctorate in mathematics, has worked as a statistician for Wichita State University’s National Institute for Aviation Research. She was responsible for claims under the Kansas Open Records Act from 2013 to 2018 that sought audit tapes of Sedgwick County voting machines.
She sought the information to investigate what she described as statistical anomalies in election returns. Kansas courts rejected Clarkson’s approach and ruled private citizens couldn’t have access to election records for independent auditing of results.
In an online column posted in October 2017, Clarkson wrote about her growing concern with the accuracy of voting machines. She explained how she joined volunteers to conduct an election audit through exit polling at five south-central Kansas locations in the November 2016 election.
“I’m afraid that the evidence from those exit polls point overwhelmingly to our voting machines being manipulated,” she said. “Not by enough to alter any outcomes in the races studied — the maximum deviation between our exit polls and the official results was less than 5% in suspect races. But still extremely troubling to me as a voting citizen of Kansas.”
Clarkson said “scattered anomalies” were likely related to process flaws rather than malicious intent, but comparing exit polling with published results “indicate that the election results might have been compromised.”
In the 2016 presidential race won by Republican Donald Trump against Democrat Hillary Clinton, Clarkson said votes appeared to have shifted from Clinton to Trump in four of the five exit polling locations. In Wellington, the fifth site, she said “substantial errors” pushed the vote in Clinton’s favor.
“This looks like malicious tampering of the results by at least two different parties with opposite intentions,” she said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Federal judge stands by ruling in Oklahoma poultry pollution lawsuit
description: The twenty-year legal saga between Oklahoma and several Arkansas-based poultry companies will continue after a federal judge again refused to vacate his order to make way for a settlement agreement. Nearly a year ago, Oklahoma Northern District Court Judge Gregory K. Frizzell ordered the poultry companies to pay millions and change their practices to reduce [...]
text:
A federal building in downtown Tulsa, pictured July 26, 2026, houses various agency offices and courtrooms. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)The twenty-year legal saga between Oklahoma and several Arkansas-based poultry companies will continue after a federal judge again refused to vacate his order to make way for a settlement agreement.


Nearly a year ago, Oklahoma Northern District Court Judge Gregory K. Frizzell ordered the poultry companies to pay millions and change their practices to reduce the effects of poultry waste in eastern Oklahoma’s Illinois River Watershed.
After that order, the companies agreed on a less stringent cleanup plan with the state. But for that plan to kick in, Frizzell would need to vacate his order. He declined, saying the settlement wouldn’t be sufficient to right the wrongs in the watershed.
The poultry companies and the state reached a new agreement incorporating some of Frizzell’s feedback and presented it to the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Circuit bounced it back to Frizzell.
On Wednesday, he issued an opinion again declining to vacate his order.
Frizzell cited case law that requires “an extraordinary remedy” and “exceptional circumstances” to vacate a judge’s decision.
He also said switching to the settlement terms would not be in the public interest. He pointed to:

“Nebulous oversight” and lack of guardrails on the settlement payments
Failure to limit the total amount of poultry waste that can be applied to land in the Illinois River Watershed
Too short a term for the agreement (seven years)

The poultry companies also dragged their feet as long as possible before reaching an agreement with the state, Frizell said.
“Defendants have litigated this case in such a protracted manner as to monopolize the judicial resources of this court for years, often for the sole purpose of delay,” he wrote.
Even after Frizzell issued a conclusion holding the companies responsible for the effects of poultry waste in the Illinois River Watershed, the defendants did not agree to clean-up solutions until nearly three years later, when Frizzell ordered a stringent clean-up plan.
“The parties’ failure to negotiate a settlement in the period between the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law and the Judgment suggests they ‘roll[ed] the dice’ and now seek to erase the result of that gamble through vacatur,” Frizzell wrote.
Frizzell’s December 2025 cleanup order still stands, although appeals are pending in the Tenth Circuit Court.
