name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: EPA Fines At Site Preceded Incinerator Fuel Leak As Questions Mount
description: Reworld, previously known as Covanta, has long managed Honolulu's H-Power plant with limited oversight thanks to no-bid contracts, a 2015 city audit found.
text:
As Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi vowed on Thursday to be transparent about a massive fuel spill at Oʻahu’s incinerator H-Power, there remain significant unanswered questions about how the spill occurred, why it went undetected and undisclosed for months and where government oversight may have failed. 
More than 400,000 gallons of fuel leaked from a hole in an underground pipeline at the facility from January through May of this year, officials disclosed at a Thursday press conference. Blangiardi said he had only learned the full scope of the incident on Tuesday, which he called a major communications failure.
Officials assured the public that drinking water would be safe from the contamination. 
But many questions remain about a city’s contractor, which manages H-Power. The company has occupied a unique role as a longtime no-bid contractor with extraordinary latitude to operate without much city oversight, according to a 2015 city audit. And it has been cited with multiple violations related to pollution and worker safety in recent years. 
It is not known what caused the hole in the pipeline, nor exactly how far the fuel plume has spread, how long it will take to fully remediate and why the issue was kept quiet from the public for so long. Blangiardi said impacts to the shoreline are not expected, but officials on Thursday did not provide any details about how they know that.  

Civil Beat: 
400K-Gallon Fuel Leak In Hawaiʻi Kept From Public For Months

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is in charge of regulating aboveground fuel tanks like the ones at H-Power. The last recorded inspection of the facility by the EPA was on July 30, according to the agency’s online enforcement data, which doesn’t list any fuel storage-related violations. 
The EPA has yet to answer questions from Civil Beat about when it became aware of the spill and whether it is conducting its own investigation into the H-Power leak.
Latest From Civil Beat
Honolulu City Councilwoman Andria Tupola, who represents the Westside, vowed to push for answers, including “a complete timeline of who knew what and when” and information about when workers were notified and how they will be protected. 
Tupola said she would advocate for independent, public testing of the soil, groundwater and air in the area, and she is calling for “full accountability” from Reworld, H-Power’s contractor, including coverage of long-term cleanup costs and payment of any penalties under its contract. 
There should also be a requirement that the public be notified of these kinds of events, she said. 
“Westside families learned today about a fuel leak roughly 20 times the volume of the 2021 Red Hill spill, six months after it was discovered,” she said. “That is unacceptable.” 
Councilman Tyler Dos Santos-Tam, who was recently voted by his peers to be the next chair, said he will be asking the Department of Environmental Services to brief the council and the public in the coming weeks.
In a statement on Thursday evening, Dos Santos-Tam said he wants to ensure that claims about the water being safe are backed up by independent environmental testing, results of which should be made public. And communication problems need to be addressed, he said.
“Fixing this one leak is not enough,” he said. “We need to make sure problems like this reach the Mayor, the Council and the public in days, not months, so we can address them head on.”
Violations Of Pollution And Safety Rules
Reworld has a history of violation notices in recent years. 
There have been three formal enforcement actions against the H-Power facility since 2019 for breaches of the Clean Air Act, according to the EPA database. The violations, which are not outlined in detail online, resulted in $23,900 in fines. 
The largest fine of $19,700 was for air pollution that contained particulate matter. The plant also was cited seven times for air pollution violations in 2017, but no fines were issued. 
Rework was cited by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration in March of this year for two violations — both deemed by OSHA as “serious” — resulting in fines totaling $29,790. 
The H-Power facility at Campbell Industrial Park on Thursday. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
One violation was for failure to “provide safe work places and practices by elimination or reduction of existing or potential hazards.” 
The other found Reworld in violation of a rule requiring that supervisors and managers be trained to recognize potential hazards, maintain safety and health protection in the workplace and reinforce employee safety training. 
The agency’s website doesn’t disclose the specific circumstances that led to the violation notices. An inquiry sent to the Hawaiʻi Department of Labor and Industrial Relations did not receive a response as of Thursday afternoon. 
Long-Term Control, No Bid Contract
Reworld has been the city’s H-Power contractor since the early 1990s, when the facility opened, and the contractor and the city’s management have faced some scrutiny in that time. The city said Thursday that the current contract extends through 2032.
A 2015 city audit found the city was failing to provide proper oversight of the contractor, which was then called Covanta. The city did not assign the needed resources to monitor the contractor, instead relying on consultants to do that work, the auditor found. 
As a result, the audit said, the city used no-bid contracts to give the company a monopoly on H-Power operations “without realizing” they were extending its right to run the facility for decades.
Reworld has been the city’s H-Power contractor since the early 1990s, but a 2015 city audit found the city was failing to provide proper oversight. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Most localities only do contract extensions of five to 10 years, the audit found.  
Covanta’s contract terms also obstructed the city’s ability to oversee it, the audit said. Its contract limited the city’s access to the company’s records, restricted its ability to do audits and allowed for the destruction of records in violation of state law. 
“Based on the unfavorable contract terms, the lack of staff in the energy recovery branch, ENV’s failure to assign the resources, needed to administer the complex H-POWER contracts, and other factors,” the audit said, “we believe contract administration problems will recur.” 
The auditor, Edwin Young, made several recommendations, including not letting the company “write one-sided contracts that favor the contractor.” 
Then-Mayor Kirk Caldwell’s administration, via then-Managing Director Roy Amemiya, disputed the audit findings, as Civil Beat reported at the time. Still, the administration agreed to most of the audit recommendations, according to the audit report.  
City managers claimed the contracts were justified and in the best interests of the city and said the existing contract is a good contract, according to the audit. 
“We respectfully disagree,” the auditor wrote. 
Civil Beat asked Blangiardi’s office on Thursday which of the audit recommendations, if any, have been followed in the last decade. The office was unable to provide an accounting of that on Thursday. 
In a statement, Blangiardi’s communications director Scott Humber said the mayor’s office recognizes the importance of the findings and recommendations in the audit, which was conducted more than five years before the current mayor took office.
“Our administration is reviewing the historical record to better understand what corrective actions were taken in response to the audit and whether any of those findings remain relevant to current operations,” Humber said. 
“We are not going to speculate about actions taken under a previous administration or characterize the current status of those findings without first verifying the facts.” 
Humber continued: “Mayor Blangiardi has made it clear that he expects accountability, transparency and effective oversight of all City operations and contracts, including H-POWER. Those expectations remain unchanged.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Thirty Meter Telescope Gets New Life With Hawaiʻi Regents’ Vote
description: The vote creates a fresh path for TMT but could also kick off more protests and acrimony. Funding is another hurdle.
text:
After a decade of delays and protests, the Thirty Meter Telescope is at a pivot point — either move forward or completely languish. On Thursday, the state took a small step that suggests the project is on the move again.
The state Board of Regents voted Thursday to allow construction of new telescopes on Mauna Kea on land where old telescopes have been decommissioned and removed. It’s a step that may help clear the way for TMT but possibly trigger more controversy and protests.
E. Kalani Flores, a cultural practitioner who has been deeply involved in the opposition to TMT, predicted it will never be built despite the Thursday vote by the regents.
“It’s a waste of effort and time on everybody’s part,” Flores said in an interview after the regents’ vote, “but it’s a last ditch effort by UH and whoever else is supporting the TMT to try to make it look as though they have a chance to build on Mauna Kea.”
A standoff between protesters and law enforcement in 2019 halted construction of TMT on Mauna Kea.  Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2019
“What they’re really trying to do is they’re trying to give some hope to the TMT project, that they still have an opportunity to build on Mauna Kea,” Flores said.
Many astronomers view the TMT project as essential by for unraveling mysteries of the universe. It has been stalled since 2019 after thousands of Native Hawaiians and their supporters protested and blocked construction on Mauna Kea, but officials with the TMT International Observatory have been quite clear they still want to build the telescope there.
Conflict Between State Law And Master Plan 
The regents’ vote this week amended what is officially known as the Master Plan for The University of Hawaiʻi Maunakea Lands E Ō I Nā Leo (Listen to the Voices), which applies to an area at the summit that is controlled by the university. That area is generally acknowledged to be the best site in the world for conducting astronomy, because of little water vapor at its 13,803-foot-high summit.
The problem was the university’s master plan specified that five of the 14 telescope sites on Mauna Kea would be “ineligible for future astronomy use” after the telescopes were removed.
That language conflicted with a 2022 state law known as Act 255 that specified decommissioned sites on Mauna Kea are to be prioritized over undisturbed sites for new telescope construction.
The amendment that was unanimously approved in the vote by the regents on Thursday removed the reference in the master plan that made decommissioned sites “ineligible for future astronomy use.”
The master plan still acknowledges the UH has “committed to reducing the number of operating astronomy facilities” in the area of the mountain the university controls, which has slowly been happening. The UH’s Hōkū Keʻa telescope has also been removed, and the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope (UKIRT) has begun the decommissioning process.
Kumella Aiu urged the regents to vote against the amendment, saying “I think our community has been very clear on where we stand on the issue of Mauna Kea, and I don’t think it changes just because we decide to do it differently.”
Fengchuan Liu, TMT’s project manager, has told the regents “we believe we can” construct the huge new telescope on the former site of a decommissioned telescope site, and TMT has studied the former Caltech Submillimeter Observatory site as a possible site. The Caltech facility was removed from the mountain in 2024.
TMT has also inquired with both the regents and the Mauna Kea Stewardship and Oversight Authority (MKSOA) about the possibility of building on a site where a previous telescope has been removed.
Mauna Kea supporters hold their line in June of 2015 as, at left, DLNR law enforcement officers tell them to clear the road so their vehicles can drive to the summit.  Cory Lum/Civil Beat
Liu said in an interview Mauna Kea continues to be TMT’s preferred site and is “the site we are focusing our effort on, but we understand respecting the community and getting the community’s support is paramount.”
Many people have asked why the telescope cannot be built on a decommissioned site, he said, and TMT is looking at that possibility even though it has a permit to build at another location on the mountain. The TMT board last October inquired about the permitting process that would be involved in shifting the project to the site of a decommissioned observatory.
“We don’t want to rush this, we want to do what’s right, and this is why looking at a decommissioned site is part of it,” Liu said.
Costs Have Escalated
Flores predicted TMT will not be built because it will face an outpouring of opposition from Native Hawaiians and other opponents, and because the project lacks the funding it needs for construction.
The mountain is considered sacred land to many Hawaiians, and the 2019 protests that blocked construction of TMT attracted participants from across the state. The issue became a focus of Hawaiian activism, cultural revival and the sovereignty movement.
The cost of the project has escalated as TMT has been delayed for the last 10 years, and it is unclear where the backers of the project will get the money necessary to finally build the telescope.
A report for the National Science Foundation in late 2024 calculated the total cost of the TMT project would be $3.9 billion, and indicated $700 million had already been spent by that point.
At the time the five partners in the project had committed $1.7 billion, and were expected to contribute a total of $2 billion in cash and in-kind contributions. Additional partners were being sought, and the project sponsors hoped to convince the NSF to provide another $1.6 billion. 
That has not yet happened. The NSF in 2025 instead announced plans to fund the Giant Magellan Telescope in Chile, leaving TMT in a kind of funding limbo. 
Operating the telescope is expected to cost about $60 million per year, a figure that sponsors expected would increase during the project’s 50-year lifetime, according to the report.
The Thirty Meter Telescope International Observatory is a partnership of institutions in Japan, Canada, India and the U.S., including both the California Institute of Technology and the University of California.
An artist’s rendering of the Thirty Meter Telescope, which has been delayed for a decade by protests and other setbacks.  Thirty Meter Telescope
TMT’s primary mirror would be 30 meters in diameter, and would gather between nine and 16 times more light than the largest existing optical and infrared telescopes. Liu said the project will allow astronomers to explore some of the most profound mysteries of the universe.
The plan is to use the telescope to explore mysteries such as the relationship between black holes and galaxies and how stars and planets form. It is ideally suited for finding planets outside of our solar system, an ability that could contribute to the search for life elsewhere in the universe.
“We have some fundamental questions we just don’t understand,” he said, including the nature of the mysterious “dark matter” and “dark energy” that make up some 95% of the mass-energy in the universe.
The TMT would help astronomers to see farther and in more detail to try to answer “all of these questions, what is the universe made of, are we alone, how did the universe and galaxies evolve over the years,” he said.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Feds Auctioned Off Deep-Sea Mining Permits In American Samoa. It Wasn’t Legal
description: The National Marine Fisheries Service went forward with the auction Thursday despite a court ruling.
text:
The Trump administration auctioned off millions of dollars’ worth of leases for deep-sea mining exploration in federal waters off American Samoa, despite a judge ruling the auction was unlawful earlier this week.
The auction has given two unnamed deep-sea mining prospectors the right to conduct exploratory activities in 31 million acres of federal waters off the coast of American Samoa, where they hope to harvest metals and minerals from the seafloor. That material is prized for use in renewable energy technology and batteries, among other things.
The auction came just days after Hawaiʻi District Judge Jill Otake’s Monday ruling that the National Marine Fisheries Service “did not even consider” the potential effects of mining exploration activities on marine wildlife in the lease zones. Environmental groups fear the administration’s decision to ignore Otake’s ruling is a preview of its intent to flout the law in its bid to mine tracts of international and U.S. territorial waters in the Pacific Ocean.
Numerous countries and environmental organizations have opposed the administration’s stance on deep-sea mining, for fear of its many unknown environmental impacts. The Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi and Fa’asao Amerika Samoa are among them — Earthjustice filed a lawsuit on their behalf in August in an effort to halt Thursday’s auction.
The suit alleged that the National Marine Fisheries Service failed to adhere to the Endangered Species Act, ignoring the risk mining activities pose to several endangered migratory species of whales, turtles and sharks. Otake ultimately agreed in her Monday ruling.
“I would say I’m surprised. But I feel with this administration, it’s not surprising to see them disregard a court ruling and proceed as if nothing happened,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton told Civil Beat.
The two lease areas for deep-sea mining prospectors cover 31 million acres and run over 20,000 feet deep. (Courtesy: Department of Interior)
The lease sales, worth $3 million each, are a national first and “a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security,” U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”
Mining companies want to essentially comb the seafloor for polymetallic nodules, grapefruit-sized orbs comprising nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese, among other elements that are especially important for modern technologies.
But the process of harvesting those nodules is seen as destructive, with the potential of stirring up sediment and disrupting the fine balance of oceanic ecosystems. The long-term effects of deep-sea mining can persist for decades, according to recent research.
Fa’asao Amerika Samoa, part of the first lawsuit, has a long list of concerns about mining of the seabed around the U.S. territory. The organization said in a 2025 letter to the Department of Interior that the islands stand to gain nothing from the mining, which will “endanger livelihoods, destroy traditions, and erode the cultural foundations that define the Samoan people.”
Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi Executive Director Jonee Peters is concerned that the largely untested mining practice will have negative effects on marine life in American Samoa and beyond, as animals migrate far beyond the territory and reach Hawaiʻi.
“We all rely on our ocean for subsistence,” Peters said. “If that is threatened, what happens to our food sources and our cultural identity, which all starts with the oceans?”
The lease areas sit between 150 and 240 miles east of Pago Pago, the capital of American Samoa, with waters up to 20,100 feet deep. The leases cover a term of 20 years but do not allow for mapping mineral or metals deposits, testing or actual mining, which is how it justified its decision to overlook the effects of mining in the lease zones. Otake disagreed.
Otake’s determination was seen as a litmus test for other mining lawsuits, of which Earthjustice has at least four, in partnership with local environmental groups. One opposes a similar exploration lease auction for U.S. territorial waters off the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, scheduled for Dec. 16. Otake will preside over that case.
Eaton is concerned the administration’s willful disregard of the ruling is setting a precedent.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Landry’s new rules for nonprofits to get state funds rankle some legislators
description: New rules Gov. Jeff Landry put in place held up tens of millions of dollars for local governments and civic organizations for three weeks this fall.
text:
State money that lawmakers approved for various nonprofit organizations and local government use was delayed for weeks earlier this fall under new rules Gov. Jeff Landry put in place to vet each recipient. Some lawmakers have said the governor is overstepping his powers. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)New rules Gov. Jeff Landry put in place held up tens of millions of dollars for local governments and civic organizations for three weeks this fall, and state Treasurer John Fleming said his office is still working to make sure everyone owed funding gets paid. 

“We have a backlog. It’s just going to take a little time to get through that,” Fleming told lawmakers Thursday at a meeting of the Joint Legislative Committee on the Budget at the Capitol.

The holdup has left legislators from across the political spectrum disgruntled. Several lawmakers said they have received calls from nonprofit and local government leaders who depend on the money. 
“Of course, if there’s fraud, waste and abuse, we want y’all to stop it. But why stop the entire process?” Rep. Denise Marcelle, D-Baton Rouge, said. 
Fleming froze disbursements to hundreds of entities — such as local parks departments, senior citizen organizations and food banks — from Oct. 21 until Nov. 13. The pause was in response to new public contract requirements the Landry administration issued to more thoroughly vet nonprofits that receive state money.

As a compromise with lawmakers, Landry’s staff and Fleming agreed not to impose the new rules on nonprofit contracts executed before Dec. 15. 
But Senate President Cameron Henry, R-Metairie, suggested the Landry administration might be overstepping its authority with the stricter requirements for these nongovernmental organizations, or NGOs. By law, the legislature is supposed to have more power than the governor over state spending decisions.  

“I thought we got to appropriate the money, and then other people get to execute it,” Henry said. “We’re kind of blending those two right now, and it’s not making a whole bunch of people real happy. Because if we do it here, we can do it for other things unrelated to NGOs, and we don’t want that either.” 
Henry also said it was disruptive to adopt stricter rules for nonprofits in the middle of the annual state budget cycle, which started July 1. Had the new rules gone into effect before lawmakers approved the budget in May, they could have avoided giving money to any nonprofit that couldn’t meet the new standards, he said.  
Nonprofits are a popular target for legislators’ pet projects. Unlike most other elements in the state budget, they are inserted with no public discussion or transparency about which legislator has asked for them. 
Landry’s office declined to answer a question about why the governor didn’t veto nonprofit funding from the budget that concerned him. If he had removed more of it himself, there would be less need to use the new rules he imposed a few weeks ago. 

It was a tactic former Gov. Bobby Jindal used to crack down on nonprofit spending in the state budget, vetoing hundreds of legislators’ earmarks during his first two years in office. 
Angele Davis, Landry’s inspector general and chief integrity officer, is leading his effort to scrutinize nonprofit allocations. She was also Jindal’s budget chief.

The new rules require nonprofits receiving state funding to provide more detailed lists of vendors or subcontractors they use and to cap their administrative expenses at 10% of the state allocation they receive. They must also take standard anti-fraud measures when using the public dollars and submit their bank statements to the state, among other changes. 
Some, but not all, of the new rules are required under a 2025 state law that hasn’t been enforced, Davis said. Landry also placed more scrutiny on nonprofits with an executive order in late July he called the Louisiana Taxpayer Protection Initiative. 
In October, the governor’s office announced the inspector general and treasurer had uncovered four instances since 2023 in which state appropriations to nonprofits had been misspent.  

They include a $400,000 payment to the National Association for African American Economic Development and $37,500 for Divine Kingdom Ministries in the 2024-25 fiscal year. 
The two other suspect allocations, totalling $50,000 and $250,000, were made to organizations that haven’t been publicly identified. In an interview Thursday, Davis said more information about the transactions couldn’t be shared because investigations are still ongoing. 
The four infractions, totaling less than $750,000, make up a very small amount of hundreds of millions of state dollars spent with nonprofits in the past three years. In the 2026-27 fiscal year alone, the state has allocated $113 million to 272 different nonprofit organizations, according to Davis.

The inspector general said her office has not finished its review of nonprofit state spending. 

“We know that it’s very difficult once you pay the funds out to go back and chase and try to recoup those funds. Restitution is pennies on the dollar,” she told lawmakers. 
Legislators are particularly concerned about one new rule they said might prevent smaller nonprofits from getting their state funding. The Landry administration has reduced the funding a nonprofit can obtain upfront from 50% to 25%. Davis wants most of their state funding paid through reimbursements. 
Sen. Gerald Boudreaux, D-Lafayette, said some organizations don’t have enough reserves on hand to spend money ahead of time and wait on a state reimbursement. They need the money in advance of spending it to run state-funded programs, he said. 

Commissioner of Administration Taylor Barras, who oversees budgeting for the governor, told lawmakers Thursday that exceptions could be made for nonprofits that need more flexibility.

title: One Book, One Child, One Conversation at a Time Across Delaware
description: One Book, One Child, One Conversation at a Time Across Delaware By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE A picture of a bear can stop a story in its tracks. A preschooler might want to know where the bear sleeps, what it eats or why it looks so grumpy. For a Read Aloud Delaware volunteer, that’s a good place to ... Read More
text:
Photo Courtesy of Read Aound Delaware, Inc
One Book, One Child, One Conversation at a Time Across Delaware
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
A picture of a bear can stop a story in its tracks. A preschooler might want to know where the bear sleeps, what it eats or why it looks so grumpy. For a Read Aloud Delaware volunteer, that’s a good place to pause. The question gives the child a chance to steer the conversation before the two turn the page.
Read Aloud Delaware brings volunteers into local preschools, childcare centers and kindergartens to read with children ages 1 to 5. The visits happen one child at a time, so a curious reader can linger over an illustration, point out a familiar animal or ask to hear a favorite part again.
“Your role is to read and talk with the child about the pictures and story,” the organization explains on its website.
A book can give a child a reason to try out a new word or describe something they recognize. A story about a trip to the park might lead to counting ducks on a pond or talking about the colors of the leaves. A question as simple as “What do you think happens next?” gives a child room to put an idea into words. The volunteer can follow the child’s lead, whether that means finishing the story or spending a little more time on the ducks.
Each reading session usually lasts five to 15 minutes, giving volunteers time to share books with several children during a visit. Most readers spend about 90 minutes to two hours at their assigned site once a week. Over time, they get to know the children and learn which books draw them in. For a child, a familiar face who remembers a favorite story can be one more reason to look forward to the next visit.
“No teaching experience is needed, and there is no lesson to prepare,” the organization says on its website. Staff explain what to expect before a volunteer begins. Readers share age-appropriate books and make time for the questions, observations and stories children bring to the page.
Families can start building that routine at home from the day a child is born, the organization says. For a newborn, being held and hearing a familiar voice are part of the experience, whether an adult reads a picture book or repeats a nursery rhyme. As children grow, they can take a more active part by pointing at pictures, choosing books or asking for another reading of a story they already know.
Read Aloud Delaware also offers LENA Start for families with children from birth through age 3. The free program brings families together for 10 weekly, guided sessions focused on finding more chances to talk with young children during everyday routines. A parent might name the clothes going into the laundry basket or pause during a meal to let a toddler answer with a sound, a gesture or a word. The organization says it has served more than 150 families through sessions in English and Spanish.
There are other ways to help, too. Volunteers can assist with office work, special events and other projects, and the organization accepts donations of children’s books. Someone who enjoys being in costume can dress up as a storybook character at a special event. Businesses can ask about arranging a group volunteer visit or supporting the program through sponsorship. Read Aloud Delaware directs prospective volunteers and businesses to their county office for details.
For anyone considering a weekly reading visit, the work can begin with a book, a seat beside a child and a few minutes to see what catches their eye. Sometimes the best part of the visit is the conversation nobody could have planned.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri faces nearly $3 billion gap between spending requests and tax revenue
description: Missouri faces a gap of almost $3 billion between the cost of keeping state government agencies open in the coming fiscal year and available tax revenue, according to a review of department budget requests. That gap is equivalent to nearly one-fifth of the requested spending from the state’s general revenue fund, which relies primarily on […]
text:
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe delivering his 2025 budget message to lawmakers. Kehoe will present a new budget in January and must find $3 billion to cover the difference between likely revenue and requested spending (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).Missouri faces a gap of almost $3 billion between the cost of keeping state government agencies open in the coming fiscal year and available tax revenue, according to a review of department budget requests.
That gap is equivalent to nearly one-fifth of the requested spending from the state’s general revenue fund, which relies primarily on income and sales taxes to pay for public schools, healthcare, prisons and other programs. 
For five years, the state has appropriated more general revenue than it received. Over that period, a fund balance that stood at $5.7 billion on June 30, 2023, is expected, under the most recent official estimate, to be about $265 million by June 30, 2027.
Officials in Gov. Mike Kehoe’s administration are meeting this week with legislators and budget staff to forecast the likely tax receipts over the coming 18 months, an estimate due to be released next month. State Budget Director Trevor Foley declined a request for an interview, citing commitments to the ongoing discussions.
Missouri surplus peaking at $8 billion as governor prepares to act on state budget

“The development of the governor’s budget recommendation is still in progress,” he stated in an email to The Independent.
The early outlook is pessimistic, according to lawmakers interviewed by The Independent and a presentation Monday to an education task force.
“I do what I can to really keep a pulse on what’s happening in terms of our state finances, and things aren’t looking great,” state Sen. Maggie Nurrenbern, a Kansas City Democrat who serves on the Senate appropriations committee, said in an interview.
State departments are requesting $16.5 billion in general revenue for the fiscal year beginning July 1, up from the $15.5 billion appropriated for the current fiscal year ending June 30. The requests include more than $640 million in additional funding for mandatory Medicaid costs and $182 million more to maintain current funding levels for public schools.
State revenue fell in the fiscal year that ended June 30 and it has struggled to reach growth targets for the current year. The estimate issued in December 2025 was for $13.65 billion, with the gap between revenue and spending paid from accumulated surpluses.
“We’re going to revise the (general revenue) estimate, and it’s probably going to go down, in my opinion,” Adam Koenigsfeld, director of the state Senate Appropriations Committee staff, told a task force studying the state’s public school funding formula. “So then, your resources go down, and your bottom line goes down.”
The gap could grow even larger.
Two items, both costing approximately $300 million, aren’t included in the department requests. 
The first is the extra money the state public school foundation formula law indicates is needed to fully fund education. The State Board of Education voted in September not to include the money in its request.
The other is an increase in the state’s share of most Medicaid costs. In mid-October, the federal government issued new reimbursement rates that will require Missouri to pay an additional 1.5 percentage points of those costs. The new state share for traditional Medicaid will be about 36.5%, Koenigsfeld said during his presentation.
The change does not apply to adults covered by the Medicaid expansion constitutional amendment passed by voters in 2022. Missouri will continue to pay 10% of the cost of that coverage.
Of the $450 million in additional general revenue included in the request to maintain Medicaid program at current levels, $27 million is for adults in the expansion group. Along with the change in federal reimbursement rates, the traditional Medicaid program will cost Missouri as much as $900 million more.
One way to reduce those costs is to eliminate services that are optional under federal law. In 2005, Koenigsfeld recalled for the education task force, that meant targeting services like eyeglasses, dental care, wheelchairs and durable medical equipment.
House Minority Leader Ashley Aune, a Democrat from Kansas City, speaks to reporters in May following the House’s passage of the state budget (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
“I’m fearful about what kind of cuts we are going to be forced to make,” said House Minority Leader Ashley Aune, a Kansas City Democrat.
There are more than 60 new members entering the 163-member Missouri House. State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick met with incoming members and warned them that deep cuts were coming, Aune said.
Lawmakers are also being warned that funding for local projects will be difficult to secure, she said.
“Part of that is just setting expectations in the Legislature that the highway facade in your district is not a priority when we’re trying to get kids on buses every day,” Aune said.
The House will have a new Budget Committee chairman, state Rep. Bill Owen, a Springfield Republican. He said he will ask subcommittees to scrutinize agency budgets seeking savings and justification for long-standing programs.
Not every dollar appropriated by lawmakers is spent. Construction projects can take years to complete, leaving money unspent in a given fiscal year.
For money appropriated for state operations, unfilled positions are a common reason. In fiscal year 2025, $1 billion appropriated for operations was unspent.
“The subcommittees are going to focus on getting into the core budget and asking, on every line item, ‘why is this money still here? What are we doing?’” Owen said.
Kehoe will put his imprint on the budget when he makes his recommendations in January. Programs targeted for cuts will organize to protect funding, and any area shielded from reductions will work to prevent cuts elsewhere from being shifted onto their budgets.
“You can’t get it if you don’t ask for it,” Owen said. “Though the answer is probably ‘no’ anyway.”
 Revenue outlook

The decline in state revenue in fiscal 2026 was the first such decline this century that occurred outside an economic recession.
Democrats blame falling tax revenue on the tax cuts Republicans have pushed through since 2015. Since the surplus began growing in 2022, lawmakers have enacted tax cuts estimated to reduce annual revenue by more than $1.5 billion. 
In a special session before the 2022 election, Republicans pushed through income tax cuts with an estimated revenue reduction of $764 million. In 2023, another Republican-sponsored bill eliminated state income taxes on Social Security and public pension payments.
In 2025, the GOP enacted a law eliminating the tax on capital gains — profits from the sale of investments — that reduced revenue by more than $500 million.
Missouri faces budget crunch as capital gains tax cut hits harder than expected 

There are two more revenue-triggered cuts in state tax law, which would, once both take effect, also trigger a capital gains tax exemption on corporate income tax returns. The triggers are based on revenue growth exceeding inflation over a five-year period and are unlikely to occur in the coming fiscal years.
“My take is that two decades of Republican leadership have led us in the wrong direction,” Nurrenbern said. “Two decades of Republican leadership have bankrupted the state and have caused regular working Missourians to really face the brunt of these consequences, while we have seen the rich get richer.”
Through Wednesday, Missouri revenues were growing compared with the same period in fiscal 2026, but at half the rate needed to meet the target. If revenues rebound to the target, then match inflation in the coming year, the treasury would take in about $14.1 billion. 
That would still leave lawmakers more than $2 billion short of meeting the agency requests.
Owen, who spent his career in the private sector in banking, said members of his party have been too focused on tax cuts.
“I tell them ‘you guys love to play on the income side of the income statement, and you just totally ignore the expense side of the income statement’,” he said. “Well, now we’re going to have to play on the expense side.”
 Cash stash

The general revenue fund isn’t the only place to find money for state programs. Lawmakers began looking for other sources of cash during this year’s legislative session.
The first target was the $600 million set aside in 2022 and 2023 for renovation and expansion of the Capitol Building.
To support public schools, lawmakers took $89 million from the fund. The budget also includes $104 million for the Missouri State Capitol Commission to make accessibility and other improvements. 
Kehoe allowed the funding for schools but restricted the use of the money for building improvements.
In the next session, all the money should be returned to the general revenue fund, Nurrenbern said.
“It would be very poor to continue with any sort of conversations on the capitol renovations when we are failing to pay our bills to our local public schools,” she said. “We cannot talk about building what I would say would be a ballroom next to the White House.”
Then-House Budget Chair Cody Smith, R-Carthage, highlighted money set aside for Interstate 44 during a March 2024 news conference. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
There are two other substantial pots of money set aside for major highway projects.
In 2023, lawmakers set aside $1.4 billion of general revenue to pay for the Interstate 70 reconstruction project. As of Oct. 31, $1.1 billion remained in the fund.
In 2024, the legislature allocated $204 million for improvements on Interstate 44. On Oct. 31, that fund held $109.5 million.
During meetings this week, Owen said, he heard a suggestion that some, or all, of the cash financing should be replaced with bonds.
“My comment was, look where interest rates are today,” Owen said. “If the 10-year treasury was down under (4%), then I’d be a little more excited than having it over five.”
He’s reluctant, but more willing, to use the Capitol renovation funds. 
“When are you ever going to get your hands on that money again?” he said. “But again, at some point we’ve just got to say, we’ve got to fill the gaps and say let’s prioritize.”
While the money has been waiting to be spent on I-70 and I-44, the balance of the State Road Fund — which receives state fuel taxes and federal highway reimbursements — has grown. 
The end-of-year balance was just under $1 billion in June 2021, a few months before a state fuel tax increase took effect. On Oct. 31, the balance stood at $2.1 billion. 
The highway projects are important for state economic health, Nurrenbern said. That doesn’t mean they have to be paid for with money saved from 2023.
“I certainly wouldn’t support doing anything that would stall those,” she said. “I would support looking at any sort of creative proposals that come forward in terms of how we can fund those.”
 New dynamic

In May, when the House was holding final votes on spending bills, 22 Republicans joined Democrats to oppose the bill that allocates money to public schools. The foundation formula appropriation was $190 million less than state law indicates is needed for full funding, and a portion of the funding that was appropriated came from an uncertain source.
The bill passed, but with just one vote to spare.
In April 2024, when the budget was on the House floor for debate and amendment, then-state Rep. Deb Lavender, a Manchester Democrat, found 27 Republicans willing to support her against the powerful Budget Committee chairman on a proposal to add $97 million for services for people with developmental disabilities. 
Democrats held only 52 seats when those votes were held. In the new General Assembly, they will hold 68 seats. The difference will be felt in committee meetings as well as floor debate.
Instead of 10 seats on the 30-member Budget Committee, the 42% of House seats held by Democrats would entitle them to 13. That would mean a Democrat would have to persuade only three Republicans to alter a budget item instead of six.
Owen said he’s not sure what will change about the dynamic, either in floor debate or committee work. There will be more than 60 new members in the 163-member House.
“I don’t know if they’re a bunch of screaming banshees or if they’re a bunch of love hounds,” Owen said. “Probably more the previous than the latter, but you don’t know.”
The difference will be a louder voice and the specter of Republican incumbents facing more competitive elections, Aune said.
The problem, she said, is that Democrats will be trying to mitigate cuts instead of showing where the state should make greater investments.
“So many people are going to get cut that we actually do want to fund and we do want to send resources to, but we just won’t be able to,” Aune said.
Republicans will have to listen, she said.
State Rep.-elect Tracey Steele, right, speaks with Sonya Mosier while campaigning Oct. 10 for the 12th District Missouri House. Steele is one of 16 Democrats who won a seat previously held by Republicans. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)
Democrats flipped 16 seats in the election and came within 10 percentage points in 17 more, enough potential pickups to take the majority in 2028.
“It is my intention to build a program over the next two years that will both defend and work to flip additional seats,” Aune said.
The budget debate could become more contentious as Democrats seek to use their new numbers. The party also gained two seats in the state Senate.
“We’re going to literally be forced to fight over every nickel and dime in the state budget next year,” Nurrenbern said. “That puts a lot of Missourians, especially those who are most vulnerable, in a terrible bind.”
With the large number of new members, Nurrenbern said, it is important to assert the Legislature’s authority over spending.
“It’s really important for legislators to recognize that we are the ones that hold the purse strings,” she said. “If we appropriate the money for the foundation formula, the governor cannot line-item veto that.”
Owen said he wants to build a budget process that recognizes, on both sides of the aisle, the responsibility of the Legislature.
“We are the board of directors for a $50 billion statewide social service not-for-profit. It’s a business,” Owen said. “We’ve got to run it like a business.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Supreme Court considers a limit on governor’s power to restructure state government
description: The Alaska Supreme Court heard oral arguments Thursday on a year-old dispute between Gov. Mike Dunleavy and the Alaska Legislature over a basic question: If the governor issues an executive order during a special session and the Legislature disapproves, do lawmakers need to vote it down during the special session, or can they wait until […]
text:
In this screenshot from Gavel Alaska, Alaska Supreme Court Justice Jude Pate listens to oral arguments on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in a lawsuit between the Alaska Legislature and Gov. Mike Dunleavy. (Screenshot)The Alaska Supreme Court heard oral arguments Thursday on a year-old dispute between Gov. Mike Dunleavy and the Alaska Legislature over a basic question: If the governor issues an executive order during a special session and the Legislature disapproves, do lawmakers need to vote it down during the special session, or can they wait until the next regular session?
“We agree with the governor that this issue is not squarely addressed by precedent,” legislative attorney Kevin Cuddy told the court Thursday, “and the reason for that, we submit, is because no governor in the history of the state has ever attempted to … shoehorn 40 changes of Alaska statutory law into a special session that is constitutionally limited to just 30 days.”
During a special session in August 2025, Dunleavy issued an executive order that would have created a cabinet-level Alaska Department of Agriculture. Alaska and Rhode Island are the only states without one, and a special task force on food security had recommended its creation in 2022. 
Lawmakers had voted down a previous executive order on the issue and disagreed with the governor’s repeat attempt, saying they preferred to create the agency via legislation. Despite that preference, the Legislature failed to pass an enabling bill in 2025, prompting Dunleavy to reissue the executive order in August.
Alaska Legislature halts Dunleavy effort to create agriculture department

The Alaska Constitution permits legislators to halt executive orders with a joint vote of the state House and Senate, but if an executive order is issued during a special session, the Constitution is vague about whether that vote must take place during the special session or if it can wait until the Legislature’s next regular session.
Article III, Section 23 of the Alaska Constitution says in part, “The legislature shall have sixty days of a regular session, or a full session if of shorter duration, to disapprove these executive orders.”
In August 2025, legislators declined to vote on the agriculture order, and the governor said the failure to vote meant the department could go forward. 
Legislators disagreed with that interpretation of the constitution and sued Dunleavy to block the move. At the end of 2025, Juneau Superior Court Judge Mariana Carpeneti ruled that the Legislature was correct, blocking the department’s creation.
The Dunleavy administration appealed to the Alaska Supreme Court, which received written arguments through the year before taking oral argument Thursday in Anchorage.
Alaska Department of Law attorney Laura Fox, representing the governor, said justices should stick to the plain language of the constitution when interpreting the dispute.
“A special session is a session,” she said. “The court does not add missing words to the constitution, and you’d need to add missing words in order to limit the governor’s executive reorganization power … to only regular sessions of the Legislature.”
Cuddy, an attorney hired on contract to represent the Legislature, said justices should look at the history of the state’s constitutional convention. Three preliminary drafts of Article 23 all said “that executive orders requiring the force of law shall become effective at the close of the next regular session of the legislature, unless there is a legislative veto,” Cuddy explained.
That changed in the final version of the constitution because its authors envisioned having no end date for the regular session, he said.
“There is simply no mention of special sessions anywhere. It’s not in the drafts. It’s not in the committee reports. Not even mentioned once in all of the debates. That silence matters,” Cuddy said.
Four of the court’s five members were appointed by Dunleavy. The lone member who was not, Chief Justice Susan Carney, was traveling and absent from Thursday’s oral argument. Staff for the Supreme Court said she could participate in the case if needed to break a tie. 
Justice Dario Borghesan, presiding over Thursday’s arguments, said the court will issue a written decision at a future date.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Utility regulators order up audit of Xcel’s billing, customer service issues
description: Minnesota utility regulators on Thursday ordered Xcel Energy to undergo an outside audit amid mounting scrutiny of the Minneapolis-based company’s billing and customer service issues. The Minnesota Department of Commerce will oversee the audit, which will be paid for by Xcel and completed by the end of 2027, according to a verbal order from the […]
text:
Xcel Energy headquarters in Minneapolis. (Photo by Getty Images)Minnesota utility regulators on Thursday ordered Xcel Energy to undergo an outside audit amid mounting scrutiny of the Minneapolis-based company’s billing and customer service issues.
The Minnesota Department of Commerce will oversee the audit, which will be paid for by Xcel and completed by the end of 2027, according to a verbal order from the five-member Public Utilities Commission at Thursday’s public hearing. A post-audit report will be made public, commissioners said. 
A ratepayer advocate welcomed the audit and said they were hopeful it marked a turning point in the Public Utilities Commission’s more than year-long investigation into an electric utility that serves more than 1.5 million customers across the state.
“The PUC proceeding demonstrates what we have been hearing from Xcel customers for years — customers are not receiving the service that Xcel promises, and that is guaranteed under Minnesota law,” said Annie Levenson-Falk, executive director of the Citizens Utility Board of Minnesota.
Xcel spokesperson Medgan Boldt said in an email to the Reformer that the company takes the situation seriously and has already made progress on “improving our billing processes, reducing backlogs and addressing the underlying issues affecting customer billing.” 
Dozens of Xcel customers, including the cities of St. Paul, St. Cloud and St. Louis Park, complained to the commission this year about billing errors that have resulted in mounting late fees or missing credits for onsite solar energy production.
At Thursday’s hearing, commissioners also raised concerns about Xcel’s customer service. 
At one point, they played a recorded phone call between an Xcel customer in arrears and a Public Utilities Commission mediator on one end and two Xcel representatives on the other. The company representatives appeared dismissive of the customer’s predicament, questioned the mediator’s identity and appeared unaware of basic facts about Minnesota’s Energy Assistance Program or state law governing utility bill payment plans. 
Xcel is taking “additional action” on customer service quality, Boldt said.
“Our customer service representatives are receiving additional training and tools to deliver more timely, empathetic service to customers when they call for help. That includes additional information on energy assistance programs,” she said. 
Other Xcel customers’ complaints hint at more widespread billing and accounting issues.
A September complaint from St. Paul Mayor Kaohly Her detailed seven separate billing issues over the past two years, including changes to service period cutoff dates that in one case resulted in 12 billing statements coming in a single month; misapplication of payments resulting in late fees; and delayed credit refunds, to the tune of $20,000 at one city facility. 
Her said city staff have had to contact Xcel representatives “hundreds of times” about the issues.
“Xcel representatives have generally been responsive and appear to be making good-faith efforts, but even they have often been unable to fully explain the root causes of these errors, which suggests the issues may lie deeper within Xcel’s billing systems and processes than individual staff are equipped to address,” she wrote.
Commissioner Hwikwon Ham suggested Thursday that he and his colleagues would seek to hold Xcel executives accountable for the lapses.
Xcel gave CEO Bob Frenzel a $3 million bonus in 2025, up from $1.2 million in 2024, according to the Star Tribune — in part because the company exceeded customer satisfaction targets tied to executive pay after falling short the three years prior. But the improvement came after Xcel switched from the widely used JD Power residential customer survey to an “internal customer experience index” that gave the company a “much larger sample size of surveys [and] a much more granular look at results,” a spokesperson told the Star Tribune.
Xcel critics say it’s a bad look for the company to boost pay for top executives amid an extraordinary investigation into how it treats customers.
“Regulators were right to send a clear message that Xcel needs to actually provide quality service and customer satisfaction, not just pay its CEO a bonus for it,” Karlee Weinmann, research and communications manager for the Energy and Policy Institute, told the Reformer. 
The Energy and Policy Institute has been sharply critical of Xcel and other for-profit utility companies for earning what it says are excessive profits at ratepayer expense. The group released a report in March that showed Xcel with a higher profit margin than most other U.S. utilities.
Boldt cited a nearly 90% reduction in “outstanding residential billing referrals and rate change requests” and significant reductions in canceled invoices and “aged billing issues” as evidence Xcel is moving in the right direction. But she said the company “has more work to do.”
“Despite these improvements, too many customers are still experiencing billing and customer service issues. We heard the Commission and will collaborate closely with the third-party auditor on ways to improve,” she said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Indigenous land stewards at Haskell embrace cultural and ecological benefit of controlled burns
description: LAWRENCE — The leader of a group of Indigenous land stewards at Haskell Indian Nations University says colonization stole the tradition of cultural fire from her, and she wants to reignite it.  Courtney King, a Haskell masters student, is one of five members of the Advisory Fire Council, a team of academics reintroducing fire to […]
text:
Courtney King stands July 26, 2026, on Haskell Indian Nations University land in south Lawrence. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — The leader of a group of Indigenous land stewards at Haskell Indian Nations University says colonization stole the tradition of cultural fire from her, and she wants to reignite it. 
Courtney King, a Haskell masters student, is one of five members of the Advisory Fire Council, a team of academics reintroducing fire to Haskell’s land for the community’s cultural, ecological and educational benefit.
The council planned a six-years-long series of controlled cultural burns in parts of the 143 acres of woodland, wetland and prairie on campus south of Lawrence. They held the first burn on Nov. 13.
 
Reviving a tradition
Native Americans tended to land with controlled fire thousands of years ago. The practice became cultural knowledge and tradition passed down through generations across North America, King said. She is a citizen of the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma and her ancestors originally lived in the Great Lakes region.
But colonial settlers suppressed, removed, forcefully assimilated and terminated Native Americans, extinguishing cultural fire practices King might have otherwise inherited.
She said working on the burn plan has brought her closer to her family roots. 
“Most of all these knowledges have been stripped away from my people through colonization,” she said. “So reconnecting in that way is really healing.”
The members of the council — King, Nana Allison-Brewer, Melinda Adams, Joseph Brewer II and Daniel Wildcat — work together to restore cultural fire as a tradition. 
But they are not the only ones. Nations in other states and in Kansas continue the practice, including the Iowa (or Ioway) Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska and the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation.
However, the council doesn’t know how long it has been since Haskell’s land has burned, apart from two areas 16 years ago.
Daniel Wildcat looks at Haskell Indian Nations University from a prairie on campus on July 26, 2026. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)
The burn won’t look like the agricultural burns many Kansans are familiar with. Unlike a rancher burning a pasture, the council is not concerned with working efficiently.
Rather, they plan to avoid machines and backpack water sprayers. Instead, they will spread the flames with natural materials such as cattail tufts or native grasses. But they will have drip torches, a handheld canister of liquid fuel and a spout with a burning wick on the end, in case they need them.
The council has included nearby nations and Indigenous communities to participate. King anticipates a ceremony and prayers to occur.
The council will notify the city, but will not allow the public to join them. They plan to invite indigenous communities including original nations of the region and the four federally recognized nations in Kansas. 
Wildcat, a Haskell professor of 40 years and a scholar in environment and Indigenous knowledge, said the practice is based on a mutual relationship between people and nature.
“When Indigenous people look at a forest, they see relatives. We see ourselves as literally kin with the land, with the trees, with the plants, with the animals,” he said. “That’s not Indigenous romanticism, that’s kind of modern science, isn’t it? And doesn’t evolutionary theory now for over 200 years teach that all life on this planet is related?”
King said her work encourages such harmony. 
“Every day I go out on the land. It just reminds me why I’m doing what I’m doing,” she said. “And that’s to care for the many various species we still share these lands with. And they want to be here, and they want to thrive with us.”
 
Healing the environment 
Over time and with great effort, cultural fire can revitalize native Kansas ecosystems, restore bat and other animal populations and improve public health, King said. 
The fire on Haskell’s land can heal damage done by the lack of fire by slowing invasive species encroachment and opening up canopies of trees blocking sunlight from the floor of prairies and woodlands. After the burn, they will plant seeds of native species.
Still, the land will take decades to respond, King said, and become “who she’s meant to be. Who she has been for thousands of years.”
While the council’s initial impact on the land will be small, Wildcat hopes the burn will inspire others.
“So, that’s really, I think, what a lot of the work now is about, is just trying to embody ancient knowledge, ancient wisdom,” Wildcat said. “And then people will see that, and they’ll go like, oh, wow, maybe we ought to all be trying those kinds of things.”
 
Courtney King works on the land outside of the Haskell Greenhouse on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)
Creating research opportunities
Haskell students will study the results of the burns, said Nana Allison-Brewer, a Haskell mathematics faculty member and the director of the federal grant that funds Haskell’s land stewardship program. She is a citizen of the Navajo Nation and a descendant of the Colorado River Indian Tribes. 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture funds the greenhouse through a grant program for tribal colleges and universities. The grant supports four kinds of opportunities: research, leadership, community partnership and land stewardship.
The land stewardship opportunity is the Haskell Greenhouse. King manages the on-campus land, plant nursery and a small group of student researchers and Allison-Brewer manages the federal funding.
Greenhouse student researchers will collect data from current species, the burns, soil samples and new growth, Allison-Brewer said.
She hopes their efforts will reach students elsewhere.
“We’ve been having discussions with other tribal colleges and universities, TCUs, who are also trying to bring back their traditional burning practices and cultural practices,” she said. “This could be that model to help them.”
She also said this research will help future Haskell students as the land slowly responds to their stewardship over many years.
“It’s really exciting,” she said, “to know that these practices will continue to carry on for more generations to come.”

name: WyoFile
title: Jury awards $6 million to former Wyoming Boys’ School resident for punitive isolation
description:
Verdict follows eight-day trial that scrutinized practices at state-run juvenile facility in Worland.
The post Jury awards $6 million to former Wyoming Boys’ School resident for punitive isolation appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—A jury late Thursday awarded a former resident of the Wyoming Boys’ School $6 million after concluding staff there subjected him to punitive isolation and denied him due process to challenge his confinement.
Jurors in the U.S. District Court in Casper took about seven hours to reach their unanimous decisions, which concerned several periods Blaise Chivers-King spent locked in 7-by-10-foot cinderblock detention rooms at the state facility in 2020 and 2021. Chivers-King brought his claims against Wyoming Boys’ School Superintendent Dale Weber and Dorm Supervisor Mike Nelson. 
The jury did not rule in favor of Chivers-King’s claim of excessive force against Thad Shaffer, a security manager at the boys’ school. 
“We are so proud of our client,” Allison Mahoney, an attorney for Chivers-King, told WyoFile. “This was not easy for him to sit in court and listen to testimony.” 
Ciara Boerman, who also represented the former boys’ school resident during the eight-day trial, told WyoFile that the jury’s verdict “sent a strong message in recognizing that this is wrong.” 
The jury’s decisions come more than two years after six former residents sued the school for alleged abuse. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. Chivers-King’s case was the first to go to trial. 
The complaints and trial shed light on allegations of troubling conditions that have been difficult for the public to investigate. Citing juvenile privacy laws, the Department of Family Services has shared little insight into conditions at the facility. “A big piece of this was the lack of oversight,” Boerman told WyoFile. “This is a problem that needs to come to light.” 
Chivers-King alleged Weber and Nelson violated his 14th Amendment rights by subjecting him to punitive isolation in detention rooms on multiple occasions. One of the stints Chivers-King sued Weber for lasted 15 days. 
Attorneys showed images of the school’s detention facilities throughout the trial. The white cinderblock rooms are barren besides a toilet and a mattress that staff provided at night. The rooms don’t have windows that look outside, and staff at times covered the window in the door with a magnet.
Chivers-King testified during the trial that his confinement felt arbitrary. He described feeling confused when staff kept him isolated even after he had become calm. He was also on occasion locked in a detention room for a predetermined amount of time. “Even when he did what he was supposed to do, they kept him in there,” Boerman told jurors during closing arguments. 
Whether Chivers-King’s confinement served a legitimate purpose was central to determining if boys’ school staff violated the 14th Amendment, which protects detained people from arbitrary punishment.
Images and video footage presented to the jury showed Chivers-King self harming while in detention, including banging his head against the wall and at multiple points trying to strangle himself. “The vast majority of that time he spent with his own thoughts, thinking about how to end his life,” Boerman said during closing arguments. 
“I hope this sends a message that legislation needs to be enacted in Wyoming to address solitary confinement,” Mahoney said after the jury delivered its verdicts. 
Lawyers for the state argued school staff were responding to safety concerns and did their best under difficult circumstances to keep everyone, including Chivers-King, safe. In closing arguments Thursday morning, defense attorney Scott Ortiz emphasized that Chivers-King’s time at the school coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic, which created additional challenges for staff. “I cannot think about a more difficult task than having to fulfill their legitimate governmental objectives under those circumstances,” Ortiz told jurors. 
The defense attorneys’ questions and evidence throughout the trial also focused on Chivers-King’s behavioral and mental health difficulties before his time at the boys’ school and moments at the facility when he suddenly became violent — including punching, kicking, head-butting and biting staff — after appearing to be calm. Even employees who liked Chivers-King, Ortiz told jurors, “still characterized him in these very dangerous terms,” telling the jury that he would at times act out aggressively.
Dale Weber, superintendent of the Wyoming Boys’ School, sits for a portrait on April 19, 2022 in Worland. He took over in January. Prior to that, he’d been the school’s clinical director for several years. (Victoria Eavis/Casper Star-Tribune)
They also attempted to shift responsibility from Weber and Nelson to the former superintendent, Gary Gilmore, whom they said gave the final word over when and how long Chivers-King would be confined. Weber became superintendent of the school in March 2022 after Gilmore, who has since died, retired. Prior to that, Weber was the school’s deputy superintendent, but took over as interim superintendent for a stretch of time when Gilmore was on medical leave. Gilmore was the subject of a human resources investigation when he returned.
Weber described Gilmore as “very authoritarian.” “I don’t believe I had any authority to challenge his decisions,” he testified. But in closing arguments, Boerman noted that Nelson and Weber signed documents related to Chivers-King’s time in detention rooms. “That’s convenient, but that’s not accountability,” the attorney said, referring to the defendants’ assertion that Gilmore was responsible. 
The trial is the first of several concerning former residents’ accusations of abuse against the school. The next is scheduled to start Dec. 7.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Commuter rail contract could reignite debate about MBTA’s eternal budget gap
description: The T’s financial headache could be exacerbated by a massive new commuter rail deal, but for many advocates, the system’s importance leaves no choice but to absorb the costs.
text:
LAWMAKERS HAVE VIRTUALLY no say over which outside company the MBTA will hire to run its sprawling commuter rail network when the current massive contract expires next year.
They will, however, quickly be called into action to help foot the bill.
The MBTA’s current deal with commuter rail operator Keolis became the largest operating contract in state history when it was awarded in 2014. Since then, its value has swelled to nearly $6 billion — more than $1 billion above initial estimates — and roughly 20 percent of the T’s annual operating budget now goes toward paying for the commuter rail.
The price tag is expected to be quite a bit higher in the next iteration, which will land as the MBTA continues to grapple with a sizable gap between its revenues and spending every year despite a series of one-time investments from Beacon Hill.
To many of those eagerly awaiting word on who will win, there’s no choice but for the state to grin and bear it.
“These are not investments that we can afford not to make,” said Kate Dineen, president of the business-backed group A Better City. “This is likely to be a very sizable contract, but think about what we’re getting for that contract. Think about the benefits that the commuter rail of today and the commuter rail of five to 10 years from now are going to deliver for our region.”
There’s a lot riding on the deal: The commuter rail network transports more than 115,000 passengers per weekday on average, and unlike the buses and subways, its 700 miles of track across 12 lines stretch well beyond the Boston metropolitan area, serving as a key conduit for housing and job centers.
MBTA higher-ups plan to make a recommendation of who should win the contract when the agency’s board of directors meets publicly in December. Board members could vote then and there to seal the deal, which would give the winner a bit more than six months to prepare before the July 1, 2027, start date.
Three consortiums submitted bids: Keolis, in a partnership with British firm Amey Ltd.; Mass Regional Rail, which includes the firm that ran the commuter rail for more than a decade until it was replaced by Keolis in 2014; and Transdev North America, part of the same multinational company in charge of the controversial Boston Public Schools bus contract.
The T operates its own buses and subways, but it has long contracted outthe commuter rail system. MBTA officials originally expected their agreement with Keolis — which 12 years ago underbid the incumbent — would top out at a cost of around $355 million per year. In fiscal year 2026, the T in fact spent $621 million on commuter rail, about one-fifth of its entire operating expenses, according to a budget update presented last month.
Brian Kane, executive director of the watchdog MBTA Advisory Board, said officials have learned by now that many bids involve “a certain amount of blue smoke and mirrors.” He’s estimated the new deal could surpass $10 billion.
“When Keolis underbid last time, I think there was a sense that was a number that could actually be achieved. The MBTA was very quickly relieved of that knowledge,” Kane said. “Frankly, coming into this new bid, I think that experience has been frontloaded, so I hope that whatever number comes out is a more realistic number.”
This time around, the procurement baked in one mechanism in particular that could alter the math: After one year, the winning operator will have a chance to update what it charges to account for any unforeseen developments. Whatever the deal is starting in July 2027, that price might change.
On top of that, the costs of running the commuter rail will continue to rise as pay raises guaranteed in union contracts take effect and as the price of diesel — which powers all of the T’s current commuter rail trains — skyrockets amid the US war in Iran.
All of that will inevitably collide with a stark fiscal reality: For a generation, the MBTA has struggled to bring in more moneyin revenue than it spends. Beacon Hill has directed significantly more funding toward the agency in recent years, but policymakers continue to lean on one-time injections with no guarantee they will maintain the level of aid from one year to the next.
A significantly bigger line item to pay for commuter rail could widen the gap at a time when state government is already struggling to offset federal funding losses elsewhere.
“It’s going to put continued pressure on the Legislature to come up with additional funds for the MBTA on an annual basis, which they’re just going to have to do,” said Stephen Silveira, a senior vice president at ML Strategies who chaired the Massachusetts Transportation Finance Commission in the mid-2000s. “If the contracts come in more expensive — quite frankly, even if they came in at the current rate — the pressure’s going to be on the Legislature and the governor to come up with that money, because right now, I don’t feel confident that the money’s there.”
Some worry locking in higher costs for the commuter rail system could come at the expense of improvements to the T’s core bus and subway services, especially with a persistent budget gap. Arguably, the commuter rail is already subsidized at a disproportionate rate: It carries about 12 percent of the T’s riders yet receives 20 percent of its operating dollars.
“Every penny that goes to the new operator is not going to making the buses better, is not going to hiring more bus operators so they can run more service, is not going to the Better Bus Network, which to me is as important as commuter rail,” added Stephanie Pollack, a former state transportation secretary and now a senior fellow at the MIT Mobility Institute. (Pollack is also a Greg Torres senior fellow at MassINC, the nonprofit that publishes CommonWealth Beacon.)
For skeptics of the T’s ballooning budget, the forthcoming commuter rail decision underlines structural problems that need attention. The Pioneer Institute, a free market-oriented think tank, last year published a report criticizing how quickly MBTA operating expenses rose in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic began and suggested the agency was paying far more than its peers on areas such as buses.
“It all costs too much,” said Charlie Chieppo, one of the report’s authors, in an interview. “I have no problem with paying 10 percent more or 20 percent more to make the T work better. I have a problem paying 50 percent more than people do in other places for reasons that are easily solved,” he said, citing as an example a strained retirement system.
Even if the T’s budget continues to run in the red, state policymakers are less wary of giving the agency more money than they were a decade ago. Gov. Maura Healey and her deputies have made a point to criticize their predecessors for “underinvestment” in transit after the early-2020s nadir of slow zones and federal safety investigations.
That could set the stage for officials to pick a costlier commuter rail bid if they feel there are strong enough upsides for service, especially with an eye toward efforts to electrify and modernize the system that will unfold in the coming years.
“I think what’s top of mind for the deciding folks on this contract is not necessarily getting the cheapest or the lowest,” said Kane, whose group represents cities and towns who help fund the T. “It’s getting the best value, and I think that’s a different approach at the highest level.”

title: It’s raining money for Anthropic, and just plain old water on the rest of us
description: Nothing gets you thinking about flood insurance like an extended atmospheric river pummeling your neighborhood.
