We’re all happy for you; now please don’t train your AI […]
text:
A repaired section of the levee near Isleton on the Sacramento River on April 1, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Nothing gets you thinking about flood insurance like an extended atmospheric river pummeling your neighborhood. We got you covered with a couple stories today on new efforts to prepare for El Niño. 
If you work for Anthropic, you might feel like it’s raining money. We’re all happy for you; now please don’t train your AI to take our jobs. Perhaps you’d like to donate to CalMatters. 😬
And we have new stories on California’s most diverse class of lawmakers. Believe it or not, the people in the Capitol next year will be almost as diverse as the state they represent.
El Niño is here, and the expected deluge is going to test California’s latest efforts to prepare for flooding. 
In the Central Valley, communities are banking on floodplain restoration projects as a way to minimize risk. The practice allows floodwater to spill out — reconnecting rivers to land where water can safely spread out and sink into aquifers. 
That’s the plan at Dos Rios State Park — located near Modesto where the Tuolumne and San Joaquin rivers meet.
In 2023, winter storms caused floodwater to spread across Dos Rios, reducing flooding as far as four miles downstream with no infrastructure damage or significant erosion. River Partners, the nonprofit helping restore the floodplains, spent 14 years on the project, from buying the land to finishing the last pieces this year. 
Julie Rentner, its president, estimates the state needs about 50 more projects like Dos Rios, or about 100,000 more acres of floodplain restoration.
Another Central Valley community, meanwhile, tried a new approach to prepare for the financial consequences of a climate disaster. It didn’t work out. 
Two years ago, the city of Isleton on the banks of the Sacramento River launched a special insurance policy for floods. Instead of paying for actual damage, so-called parametric insurance pays out a set amount when a disaster crosses a certain threshold; for a flood, that’s when the water reaches a certain height. 
Isleton’s flood insurance program offered recovery funds up to $2.5 million if a levee failed. But roughly a year after it launched, the pilot stalled.
Isleton’s parametric policy ended on July 20 and wasn’t renewed. 

Iva Walton, a former Isleton city councilmember: “It’s so sad because it is such a great idea. … If ever it would be nice to have extra support in case of a flood, the time would be this year.”

Read more about Dos Rios’ floodplains and Isleton’s flood insurance from CalMatters’ Katie Rodriguez and Rachel Becker, respectively.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


Newly minted Anthropic billionaires


Anthropic’s logo displayed on the Nasdaq MarketSite tower in New York on Nov. 19, 2026. Photo by Andres Kudacki, AP Photo




After months of anticipation, artificial intelligence giant Anthropic went public Thursday, making the largest stock market debut in history. The stock was initially priced at $83 per share, opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17. 
With its initial public offering, the valuation of the San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI chatbot is estimated to range from nearly $1.5 trillion to a little over $2 trillion. The company’s IPO is expected to create billionaires and millionaires overnight: Its seven co-founders would each be worth more than $18 billion and the average Anthropic employee owns at least $72 million in shares.
The staggering influx of wealth is anticipated to drastically change San Francisco, further squeezing the already pricey Bay Area housing market. To protest the company’s IPO and what they view as harms wrought by AI technology and companies, demonstrators rallied outside Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco, as well as the entrance of the Nasdaq exchange in New York, where police arrested some protesters.



A kids’ dental health law with no teeth 🦷


A dentist checks the teeth of a kindergartner at De Vargas Elementary School in San Jose on Feb. 8, 2018. Photo by Karl Mondon, Bay Area News Group




A state initiative to prevent rotting teeth in young students is in its own state of decay, reports CalMatters’ Rebecca Plevin.
Because untreated dental problems can lead to missed school days, California created the Kindergarten Oral Health Assessment in 2006, which requires students to be screened for cavities and tooth decay before they enter public school. The program is also supposed to help families connect with dentists and identify students’ dental needs.
But the program is falling short, according to a recent state audit report, which focused on six school districts and the California Department of Public Health. Districts did not maintain reliable data about all aspects of the program, reported incorrect information to the state and lacked formalized procedures for following up with families that didn’t return oral health assessment forms.
Meanwhile, the state health department hasn’t verified the districts’ data and isn’t using the data to analyze whether the state is making progress on improving kids’ oral health, according to the audit. The program’s source of funding — a 2016 tax on tobacco products — is also dwindling.
Read more.



And lastly: CA’s most diverse Legislature


From left to right: Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra and Senate President Pro Tem Monique Limón at a news conference at the state Capitol on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




The California Legislature is poised to be the most diverse Legislature in state history in terms of race and gender. For the first time, it is set to achieve gender parity, with 60 women lawmakers. More Latino, Black and LGBTQ state legislators than ever will also take office in January. Read more from CalMatters’ Nadia Lathan.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: We need more housing, but Question 7 was a blunt instrument
description: The question failed because it was a poorly designed solution applied to a complex problem, and voters saw through the clever marketing to recognize its flaws.
text:
GIVEN THE SCALE of the housing problem in Massachusetts, a well-crafted remedy should win in a landslide. And yet, Question 7 failed at the polls, despite being pitched as a “starter homes” accelerant. 
Question 7 would have set the statewide minimum lot size requirement for new single-family homes at 5,000 square feet for parcels with adequate street frontage and access to public water and sewer services.  
Its rejection on November 3 wasn’t due to “ballot fatigue,” as some proponents have dismissively claimed. It failed because it was a poorly designed blunt instrument applied to a complex problem, and voters saw through the clever marketing to recognize its flaws. 
Question 7 presumed that starter home construction has slowed to a trickle solely due to land use policy — the lots are too damn big! — while disregarding all other factors that impact home construction in today’s economy. In short, blame local government, and bring down the hammer of a statewide, one-size-fits-all solution. The voters of Massachusetts deserve better, and they said so. 
It’s true that local zoning changes were happening at the same time that home prices were taking off in Massachusetts, but claiming that one caused the other ignores the myriad factors that affect the marketplace. A lot has changed since the starter home heyday of the 1960s, when a gallon of gas cost 30 cents and a modest new home cost $15,000. 
With this in mind, let’s review the shortcomings of approaches like Question 7: 
• Construction costs: The cost of materials for building a new home has climbed by 50 percent since 2019, according to industry experts. The prices of concrete for foundations, lumber for framing, and appliances for kitchens spiked after the COVID pandemic and spiked again due to recent tariff policies. On top of this, the labor market is particularly tight in the building trades, forcing developers to increase wages, which again adds to costs. The demands of ever-tightening building codes drive prices even higher. 
“The cheapest house that you could possibly build is still not a starter, what somebody would call a starter house,” Chris Lyons, a 48-year-old developer from East Bridgewater, told MassLive for a Question 7 postmortem. “The actual economy of it is that you’re going to build $800,000 houses. This isn’t the 1960s. … That’s not how it works.” 
Question 7 brushed aside this reality and omitted affordability guardrails, leaving it to for-profit developers to determine the size and price point of homes that would have been built. In a high-demand market, this would simply mean more high-end housing. If we want to get serious about creating entry-level homes, construction costs are the elephant in the room. 
• Asking voters to vote against themselves: The voters who were asked to support Question 7 are the very same voters who make zoning decisions in their communities — at town meetings in 292 towns and through their representative councils in 59 cities. Asking them to support a proposal that removes their input from the equation is a fool’s errand. 
The grounding principle of the state’s approach to zoning is that local leaders and residents are best positioned to make decisions about the future of their communities. Municipal leaders are more accountable to the public than any other level of government. Their constituents bend their ear at the grocery store, the local coffee shop, and the soccer field. Municipal leaders are intimately familiar with what their schools, environment, infrastructure, and public services can handle. Bypassing this local expertise and input is a recipe for adverse outcomes. 
• Inequitable application: Question 7 claimed to be a statewide remedy, but it required a forensics expert to determine where it would have applied and where it would not. One community would be impacted, but its neighbor would not. In many towns, the law would apply only to portions of the community. The application analysis had to drill down to individual lots.  
The irony here is that any attempt to impose a one-size-fits-all rule on all communities is upended by the reality that our 351 cities and towns are indeed different. Worcester has little in common with Worthington, and efforts to treat them the same are irrational. 
• Infrastructure: Question 7 was contingent on access to public water and sewer, but shrugged off the issue of capacity limits in local systems. A consequence would have been costs borne by taxpayers for costly infrastructure upgrades. For a housing solution to be effective, infrastructure must be a consideration. 
• Market conditions: Massachusetts is a desirable place to live, which has driven demand, and prices, over the past half-century. More recently, private equity and institutional investors have gained a significant presence in the residential marketplace, which further increases demand for limited housing stock, driving prices higher still. Worthwhile housing solutions cannot ignore this reality. 
• Effective alternatives: There are productive ways to go about kickstarting home construction. One great example is the federal 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which focuses on increasing housing supply, streamlining federal regulations, modernizing federal housing programs, and placing limits on large, institutional investors buying single-family homes — all without top-down mandates.  
Another example is the new Move-In Mass program, which provides development financing to help build more affordable starter homes using modular, manufactured, and other cost-effective construction methods. Municipal leaders stand ready to partner on practical solutions like these. 
Election Day has now come and gone, and we face the same housing crisis that we did before November 3. If we’re serious about moving the needle, we’ll need a clear-eyed assessment of why Question 7 failed. Rather than scapegoating cities and towns, let’s roll up our sleeves and dig in on solutions that can really make a difference. 
Adam Chapdelaine is executive director and CEO of the Massachusetts Municipal Association.

name: Nevada Current
title: NV would join growing push for plug-in solar power under proposed legislation
description: Nevada may soon join nearly a dozen other states in giving renters, apartment dwellers, and those who cannot afford rooftop solar a low-cost way to generate their own electricity. Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch (D-Washoe) is proposing a bill that would allow residents to plug solar systems directly into residential outlets to generate electricity, bypass[...]
text:
Balcony solar is popular in parts of Europe and is becoming more common in the U.S. (Photo: Getty Images)Nevada may soon join nearly a dozen other states in giving renters, apartment dwellers, and those who cannot afford rooftop solar a low-cost way to generate their own electricity.
Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch (D-Washoe) is proposing a bill that would allow residents to plug solar systems directly into residential outlets to generate electricity, bypassing the need for costly rooftop installations.
Plug-in solar panels work by converting solar energy into usable electricity that is then fed through a plug into a standard wall outlet and pushed to other outlets, reducing the amount of electricity that a household draws from the grid. 
Plug-in solar panels — also called “balcony solar” — are not illegal, but power providers often require formal interconnection agreements for systems connected to the grid, including smaller portable solar energy systems that can fit on balconies and porches.
If passed, the legislation could bring solar within reach for people who have been shut out of the market, from renters and apartment dwellers to homeowners that cannot afford a full solar installation.
Interest in plug-in solar has quickly spread across the U.S. since Utah became the first state to pass legislation allowing residents to plug panels directly into their wall outlets in the spring of 2025. 
Since Utah’s bill passed last year, 11 states have adopted similar legislation, while 23 more states plus the District of Columbia have introduced similar bills, according to information tracked by the plug-in solar lobbying group Bright Saver.
New York lawmakers also approved a plug-in solar bill this year that is awaiting the governor’s signature, and a bill in Massachusetts has passed in one chamber so far.
“Pretty much every state on our border has either already approved these units or is in the process of approving them,” said La Rue Hatch. “If you can buy this in every other state around us, then you should be able to buy it in Nevada too.”
Nevada’s plug-in solar bill is still in the drafting phase, said La Rue Hatch, who submitted her bill draft request in April. Bill draft requests are not official bills, they are requests by lawmakers for a draft of the proposed bill they can further amend and discuss during the legislative session.
“I’m hoping to be able to pre-file it. So hopefully, sometime in December or January, the language will be public to everyone,” La Rue Hatch said. 
Chauntille Roberts, a regional director for Vote Solar who is helping draft the legislation, said that while the legislation is still in the early stages, the language would be similar to plug-in solar bills in other states.
That would mean Nevada’s proposed bill would allow the installation of safety certified plug-in solar systems up to perhaps 1,200 watts, without approval from a local utility, following a screening by an electrician. The bill would also specifically exempt smaller systems, such as those under 390 watts, from safety certification and building-wiring requirements that would apply to the larger systems.
“Traditional rooftop solar doesn’t work for everyone,” Roberts said. “This gives us an opportunity to close some of the gaps that we’re seeing.”
The low-cost technology has taken off in parts of Europe, but is relatively new to U.S. markets. Underwriters Laboratories (UL), a private company that develops safety certification standards for consumer products, didn’t even have certification standards for plug-in solar until December 2025. 
Nevada’s state-regulated electricity monopoly, NV Energy, noted “plug-in solar is still an emerging technology in the U.S.” 
“While these systems are still evolving in the U.S. market, we are monitoring developments to better understand their potential benefits, safety and operational considerations, and any impacts on the electric grid,” said a spokesperson for NV Energy in a statement on the proposed plug-in solar bill.
Bright Saver, a nonprofit group that promotes and sells plug-in solar panels, contends that plug-in solar is as safe as other common household appliances when used in compliance with safety standards.
Plug-in solar is not meant to replace a rooftop solar system, which produces significantly more power, but can help cut down energy costs at a fraction of the price when compared to their rooftop counterparts, said Cora Stryker, the co-founder and CEO of Bright Saver.
Stryker said state legislation could accelerate clean energy adoption by opening an entirely new market for clean energy and signaling growing demand to manufacturers.
“We really saw it and still see it as an extremely powerful way to bring more people into clean energy generation while making life more affordable,” Stryker said. “Once people see that clean energy is cheaper and more reliable, they will want to adopt it in mass and fight for clean energy policies and legislation.”

name: California
title: California just elected its most diverse group of lawmakers yet
description: From Congress to the governor’s office, this election was a year of many firsts. That includes the California statehouse where, for the first time, women will hold an equal number of seats as men. Black, Latino and LGBTQ members were also elected in record numbers.
text:
In summary
From Congress to the governor’s office, this election was a year of many firsts. That includes the California statehouse where, for the first time, women will hold an equal number of seats as men. Black, Latino and LGBTQ members were also elected in record numbers.


From Alaska to Georgia, historic firsts abounded this November as newly-elected candidates for federal and state offices broke through racial and gender barriers nationwide.
California was no different: more women, Latino, Black and LGBTQ lawmakers are set to take office in January than at any other point in state history, and its top three leaders will all be of Latino descent.
At least 70 out of the 120 legislators, or 58%, will be people of color, up from a record 67 in 2025, according to the California State Library. While that is still behind the 68% Californians who are nonwhite, the Legislature did achieve gender parity for the first time with 60 women lawmakers. The gains are big wins for gender equity and racial, ethnic and sexual diversity in the chambers and signify a shift in the electoral power of minorities in California.
Women and Latinos make up the two biggest caucuses, giving them sway over the legislative agenda, USC political scientist Christian Grose said.
“On issues where the Latino Caucus might agree, the Latino Caucus is going to flex more power,” he said, adding that the same will hold true for women. “Certain issues are going to dominate the agenda in ways that 10 years ago, or even 20 years ago, especially, that wouldn’t be the case.”
The increases coincide with Democratic gains in California and across the country with the liberal party cultivating voters and candidates from diverse backgrounds. The incoming Democrats will boost the party’s supermajority in the Legislature next year to historic levels, which will likely be 100 out of 120 members.
Record numbers
Currently, 59 women hold office in the Legislature, with 20 in the Senate and 39 in the Assembly. Next year’s class will add one more woman in the Assembly. 
Close the Gap California Executive Director Susannah Delano said this month’s election results surprised her. Close the Gap advocates for electing progressive women in state government. Nine of the candidates it recruited in California won their races. 
More women and people of color were on the ballot than any ever, many of whom emphasized affordability, which contributed to their successes this year, Delano said.
“It really is the culmination of more than a decade of hard work and investment,” she said.
Six of the group’s 14 recruits this cycle flipped their seats in what amounted to a bloodbath for Republicans in the statehouse. GOP Assemblymembers Jeff Gonzalez and Leticia Castillo were among the casualties.
Latinos will make up 42 of all members, up from the 2025 record of 40, according to the state library. Black lawmakers will see their presence grow to 14 from 12 members. LGBTQ legislators will increase from 14 to 15 representatives.
These gains allow the majority party identity-based coalitions to exert more influence and accomplish their policy goals. For the Black delegation, that means continuing to push for criminal justice reform and, more controversially, cash reparations for slavery.
“It gives us more opportunities to build the alliances and coalitions that we need, and to send a message that the Black Caucus will never stop trying to deliver on reparations,” said Assemblymember Corey Jackson, a Democrat and incoming chair of the Legislative Black Caucus.
The big 3
The Latino Caucus is likely to benefit from the fact that the state’s top three leaders, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President Monique Limón, are all Hispanic. 
And electoral wins for LGBTQ candidates outside of San Francisco, such as Annalisa Perea in the Central Valley and Clarissa Cervantes in the Inland Empire, hold symbolic meaning, Equality California spokesperson Jorge Reyes Salinas said.
The group, which backs LGTBQ candidates, spent at least $25,000 in independent expenditures to support Cervantes this election. 
“It challenges the assumption that a candidate’s sexual orientation is a barrier to winning elected office in these communities,” he said.

name: California
title: Artificial intelligence flourished in California election advertising — and divided voters
description: Political campaigns nationwide spent over $137 million on computer-generated images of fake events. Some ads were comical, others were polarizing.
text:
This election year Californians saw political candidates battle massive robots, wax heroic as caped crusaders and kowtow to bloodthirsty crowds and rich fat cats. 
These were all fake images, generated via artificial intelligence to help political campaigns stand out online and on air. Election campaigns across the country spent more than $137 million on AI-generated ads by mid-October, according to researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project, with Republican groups accounting for about 80% of those messages.
Many of the spots featured humor and exaggeration — such as former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt’s depictions of himself as Batman, and failed gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton’s turn as a gladiator wowing a crowded coliseum that included rival Xavier Becerra and Gov. Gavin Newsom. 
Other campaign ads weren’t exaggerations and seemed more realistic, such as a mailer circulating in a San Diego suburb showing a male school board candidate behind a desk and his female opponent working a fake bake sale. She said it was a sexist image.
Are AI-generated images effective in political ads? We asked Ramesh Srinivasan, a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast. We edited his comments for length and clarity.
More campaigns seem to be using AI-generated images or deepfakes — or am I just just noticing it?

Ramesh Srinivasan is a UCLA professor of information studies who also hosts the Utopias podcast. 

Absolutely, that’s true. The president has put out plenty of AI-generated content. Yes, there’s no lack of what we call “AI slop” that’s almost everywhere. But I think the issue is less the AI slop and more the way in which AI is being used to promote and create — we could almost say — propaganda-type targeting. 
In the last 10 years, we had a lot of buzz about the Cambridge Analytica story, which was the way a third-party organization was advising many right-wing and other candidates, using people’s data to create content to target them based on predictions of their psychology. Everybody was pretty worried because, in theory, you could use data that you gathered about people, possibly through purchasing their credit card records from data brokers, and you can target someone and influence them — not around who to vote for but even the desire to vote at all.
Now we are seeing not just that concern — which never got resolved — but the likelihood that AI systems can, in real time, create content that targets you based on your psychology, without going through the entire multi-step process of buying one’s data, gathering the data and creating content based on the data. 
So the days of third-party propagandists using data to psychologically target people is something of the past because AI can do that automatically. 
Are you saying that’s because the algorithm automatically delivers to an individual voter an ad that’s going to be tailored to them?
Exactly. Because if I’m able to gather and access a bunch of data about you — not just data you put online on Instagram, but actually data about your credit card records —  I can use all of that data to essentially influence what you see and what you don’t see, which is already happening with social media. 
But in this case, AI can create content that directly targets you based on data about you. So that  is why this is very pernicious, because people don’t have disclosure around when something is or is not AI-generated, which is why I’ve been working with some folks in the U.S. Congress and folks in our state Senate to try to, at a minimum, force these third parties to watermark anything that is created by AI.
What do you mean by watermark and why? 
Watermarking is where an image says where it comes from. It’s something that’s put on an image that can never be written over. It would say “AI generated.” It’s like a way of flagging something. A lot of the content we were seeing prior to the election was AI-generated on social media platforms, on TikTok, Instagram, etc., and none of that was flagged. 
A  recent ad posted on Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton’s YouTube account portrays him as a gladiator.
The Steve Hilton AI ads often had a line saying they were AI-generated.
A lot of them are doing it. The bigger picture is that people need to know what is or is not “real” or human-created when they encounter content online, because many of us are experiencing the wider world through online platforms.
Are voters being fooled by deepfakes? Are they confused? 
It’s impossible in many cases to be able to tell the difference. And that is not really our fault as voters or as citizens. 
Of course, there’s AI slop, where you’re not trying to hide that it’s being created with AI. For example, the president when he tweeted out that picture of him, like Jesus or something like that, healing the sick. The patient in the bed looked like Jon Stewart (host of “The Daily Show”). Everyone knew that that was AI. The president wasn’t trying to hide that.  
We experience a lot of stuff that is sort of just odd, weird and surreal looking. But the goal in those cases isn’t to fool people.
What ends up being effective though? Does AI convince people to vote for a candidate? 
It has to do with believability and trust. Based on initial research, we don’t see significant evidence that people are able to tell between AI-generated content that’s designed to look exactly like human-created content versus not. 
So, insofar as anything we see or read influences how we vote or whether we vote, this would influence it. So that’s not good for a democracy to function. 
It’s not just about everybody voting. It’s about people being able to see the world from some similar reference point. That has been a huge problem when it comes to the ways in which social media micro-targets people. 
An ad posted on Steve Hilton’s YouTube account features Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra as a puppet, hidden in a Trojan horse.
You may be seeing a whole different vision or perspective on any given issue. AI just is an add-on to a much bigger problem, which is that for a democracy to function, people have to have some common basis of reality —  let alone a common basis of what is or is not true.
Data is being used about us to influence what we see, what we believe and what we feel. And all of that micro-targeting creates a huge issue, because you can’t have a collective form of governance — or even agreement on anything — unless you’re all exposed to something that you (all) believe is true.
Are people on both sides of the political spectrum doubting everything they see online?
I think it’s widely shared. During the Biden administration, there were many claims — valid or not — made by the president that those big tech companies were censoring what people were seeing or not seeing. I think there is no question now that we’ve seen many of the Big Tech companies bend the knee to the president. At least we saw that at the inauguration. Let’s see what happens now after these midterms.
Technologies have long stood for direct ways in which they can expand what we do, rather than replace who we are. You can imagine the use of large language model technologies to give us ways to explore different themes, different ideas. But they shouldn’t be the start and end of it.
If people’s jobs and lives are being replaced by machines that are collecting data about us to essentially replace us, we no longer matter. So political questions, democratic questions will no longer have us as part of it. 
Are we going to be replaced by machines that use propaganda to influence how we behave, what we think, how we feel? Are we going to actually see the wider world in ways other people also see it? 
All of those questions are now on the chopping block, meaning they can be answered in a pro-democracy, pro-economic-security way. But to do that, we need to do a lot of work to rein the platforms in and the AI companies in, to make sure they adhere to some basic standards of disclosing to people when their data is being collected, paying people for their data and watermarking content.
Regulation is not a buzzkill. Regulation doesn’t mean stopping innovation. It means directing innovation so we have human innovation, social innovation, economic innovation accompanying technological innovation. 
Technologies never exist in a vacuum. They are built upon human values. 
What role might AI play in the 2028 elections?
The big question is will a leader emerge that recognizes that these AI technologies are here to stay? They can serve very useful and productive purposes for us. They can actually expose us to the wider world, not as replacements of us, but as tools to help us explore and understand,  to actually make them work and protect our democracy.

name: California
title: Letting rivers flood on purpose worked at Dos Rios. Can California do it 50 more times?
description: This story is part of a partnership between CalMatters and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. With a very strong El Niño underway this winter, and questions growing about whether California levee systems can handle the potential surge of floodwater across the Central Valley, the state may soon see how well one of its oldest […]
text:
This story is part of a partnership between CalMatters and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
With a very strong El Niño underway this winter, and questions growing about whether California levee systems can handle the potential surge of floodwater across the Central Valley, the state may soon see how well one of its oldest flood-management strategies holds up in a new form.
Floodplain restoration, which reconnects rivers to land where floodwater can safely spread, slow down and sink into aquifers, has become a growing bet for the state. California has invested $40 million in floodplain restoration for the San Joaquin Valley since 2023 and set aside an additional $21.5 million to kickstart floodplain and habitat restoration projects along rivers in Kern, Kings and Tulare counties.
The idea of giving rivers room to overflow isn’t new. More than a century ago, after floods in 1907 and 1909 that extended down the Sacramento River, California turned away from relying on levees alone and began building the Sutter and Yolo bypasses, broad floodplains that let the river spill out rather than break through.
Projects like Dos Rios State Park, which opened to the public in 2024 near Modesto, bring that same principle to the San Joaquin Valley, which never got such a system. What they lack is scale: Julie Rentner, president of River Partners, the nonprofit helping restore these floodplains, estimates the state needs about 50 more projects like Dos Rios. With El Niño approaching and much of the $10 billion climate bond voters approved in 2024 still unspent, there may be an opening. 
Advocates say the projects can lower downstream water levels and can reduce flood risk for vulnerable communities, from Stockton and Grayson in the San Joaquin Valley to Hamilton City in the Sacramento Valley. But expanding them means pushing against what Rentner calls a deep inertia: a habit of funding maintenance of existing flood infrastructure instead of rethinking how rivers can flow to benefit the public.
A century-old idea
Six large concrete structures line the Sacramento River between Mount Shasta and the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, all with one primary purpose: to divert excess water over the banks and into an adjacent basin or bypass. Some of that water rejoins the river; some spreads across low-lying wetlands or agricultural lands, where it can recharge groundwater.
The largest of these bypasses, the Yolo, can carry roughly four times the Sacramento River’s flow. The Army Corps of Engineers now calls it “a 100-year-old nature-based solution,” and researchers have held it up as a national model for flood control that coexists with fish, wetlands and farming.
The Sacramento Weir on the western bank of the Sacramento River between the Yolo Causeway and the Garden Highway on Jan. 9, 2023. The Sacramento Valley has experienced a series of strong rainstorms that have inundated the region. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
The state is still investing in that system. Preparing for El Niño, Gov. Gavin Newsom celebrated the completion of the nearly $31 million Tisdale Weir Rehabilitation project, an upgrade to an old flood-control structure in Sutter County. 
The San Joaquin Valley has nothing on that scale. The proposed Paradise Cut Bypass Expansion project would provide similar protection for at-risk areas in Stockton. But that project has been mired in planning for a generation.
“The magnitude of the water that needs to move through a flood bypass there in the South Delta is much much bigger than what the Paradise Cut project can advance,” Rentner said, adding that floodplain restoration is needed too. “It’s a very good flood expansion project. We still need a couple more big bypasses like that, if Stockton’s going to be as protected as Sacramento is.”
Dos Rios: A test case
“There was a time when I was 7 or 8 years old, where we couldn’t get to Modesto because the only road that led to Modesto would get flooded,” said Lilia Lomeli-Gil, a resident of Grayson, a small agricultural town downstream from the rivers.
Just upstream, on land that flooded just as routinely, the state and its partners have tried something different: letting it flood on purpose.
Dos Rios State Park, located roughly eight miles west of Modesto where the Tuolumne and San Joaquin River meet, used to be home to two dairy farms before River Partners acquired the land in 2012. Once flood-prone farmland, those farms struggled with staying profitable, according to Rentner, experiencing routine floodwater seepage and salt inundation that damaged the soils.
River Partners aims to seek out similar kinds of land, working with farmers and landowners in flood-prone regions to convert it back to a floodplain with public benefit. 
The 2,100 acre restoration is the state’s largest public-private floodplain project. Newsom’s 2026-27 budget summary heralds Dos Rios as a major accomplishment: the state’s first new state park in a decade, restoring former agricultural lands to provide floodplain habitat and boost climate resilience. The state counts it toward its nature-based climate targets, and advocates see it as a blueprint.
An aerial view of Dos Rios Ranch in June of 2023. Photo courtesy of River Partners
The 2023 winter storms put it to the test. Rentner said there is no way to isolate the performance of a “sponge” or “shock absorber” in the flood system, since the hydrology is too large and complex. But the floodplain performed as designed, she said, reducing flooding as far as 4 miles downstream with no infrastructure damage or significant erosion. 
In 2023, the floodwater spread wide across the restored land.
“The extent of floodplain inundation was huge,” Rentner said. “Just 10 years ago, in the 2017 high-water event, the river in this location was about a quarter mile wide in flood stage, and almost 2 feet deeper – meaning much more pressure on downstream levees.”
What’s holding the floodplain solution back
Rentner remembers the Dos Rios area roughly 25 years ago, when she first moved to the valley. River Partners spent 14 years on the project, from buying the land to finishing the last pieces this year. Rentner said that California needs about 100,000 more acres of floodplain restoration, and that the state should invest more in expanding flood-system capacity, rather than maintaining existing systems. 
Some of that money could come from Proposition 4, the 2024 initiative that set aside $3.8 billion for drought, flood and water supply.
Expanding the approach takes more than money, said Jane Dolan, president of the Central Valley Flood Protection Board. 
“It’s all tight budgets, huge demands,” she said.  “And it takes some analysis and field work and some cooperation from property owners and civic leaders as to where to start.”
The coming winter may test recent restoration efforts and bring renewed attention to the San Joaquin Valley, where communities around Stockton, Manteca and Lathrop lack the kind of bypasses that protect the Sacramento Valley, and floodplain restoration efforts there have been stuck in planning for years.
“The next step is: How do we get to implementation of the shovel-ready projects, and how do we get to the next chunk of land acquisition and restoration that we know we need to do,” Rentner said.

name: California
title: El Niño is here. This flood-prone town’s insurance pilot was a state model — then it fell apart
description: Two years ago, the tiny city of Isleton on the banks of the Sacramento River became the testing ground for something no California town had tried: a state-funded, community-based flood insurance policy, paying out automatically when the water rose past certain heights. State officials lauded it as an innovative strategy for communities facing climate-fueled [...]
text:
Two years ago, the tiny city of Isleton on the banks of the Sacramento River became the testing ground for something no California town had tried: a state-funded, community-based flood insurance policy, paying out automatically when the water rose past certain heights.
State officials lauded it as an innovative strategy for communities facing climate-fueled disasters.
“We need to think creatively about how new insurance pilots like this Delta community project can be tested and scaled to help our most vulnerable communities,” California Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara said in a statement at the time. 
But as an El Niño winter approaches and the Trump administration pulls back on disaster aid, the pilot is stalled — robbed of momentum by the same factors that keep communities across the state desperately underinsured for floods. 
It wasn’t the concept that doomed it, but the cost and messy local politics in a region where communities are already overburdened and underresourced. Even so, this kind of insurance, parametric insurance, is gaining ground as a complement to traditional insurance to quickly cover costs that extend beyond property losses. 
Last week, the Department of Insurance’s general counsel issued an opinion letter describing when parametric products count as insurance. The city of Santa Cruz and the Tahoe Donner homeowners association have already bought parametric policies. 
California has begun spelling out how to regulate these policies, describing them as a way to help “avoid downward economic spirals” for communities in crisis.  
“Which has long been something that people would like to see happen, but is just very, very difficult in practice,” said Carolyn Kousky, executive director of Insurance for Good. “Like how do you pay that premium all the time? Then the next (question) is, how do you distribute that money?”
Kousky added, “It’s an important nut to try to crack.”
Lifeblood and flood
Isleton, a city of fewer than 800 people, sits in an extremely high-risk flood zone where the poverty rate is roughly double the state average. Miles upon miles of aging levees hold back water that’s both a draw and a threat to the historic town. 
The levees have failed before — drowning Isleton under eight feet of water on a summer day in 1972 and forcing every single resident to evacuate for months, if not longer. Pam Bulahan, still an Isleton resident, was 9 years old at the time. She remembers someone knocking at the door before dawn, telling her family to get to higher ground.  
She still remembers how the floodwaters smelled. “It was scary because you know, the water stinks. We don’t know what’s under there.” 
A repaired section of the levee near Isleton on the Sacramento River on April 1, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Despite the risk, roughly half of Isleton’s residential properties carry flood insurance policies, according to an analysis of FEMA data by Jeanine Foster, a hazard mitigation and emergency management consultant. 
That’s higher than the state average. But it’s far less than flooding experts think is wise. 
A first for California
The idea for narrowing the gap between disaster and recovery in Isleton came from UC Davis graduate student Kathleen Schaefer, who worked for the Federal Emergency Management Agency for nearly a decade before starting graduate school.
Schaefer launched a first-in-California community-based parametric flood insurance program, which offered quick recovery funds up to $2.5 million if a levee failed. 
Parametric insurance is more flexible than the traditional kind. It pays out a predetermined amount triggered by the severity of a disaster — a temperature, an earthquake magnitude, a water level — rather than the amount of damage. 
The payout may not match someone’s actual loss, or may not come at all if the trigger isn’t hit. But its flexibility means it can cover things traditional insurance typically doesn’t, such as evacuation costs, lost business or tax revenue. 
The prospect of direct cash payments without a lengthy claims process, Lara said at a hearing two years ago, makes it especially exciting. 
“No questions asked, no claim process. The money is given if it meets the scale,” Lara said. “Parametric insurance can improve resilience in communities.” 
Iva Walton, a former city councilmember who owns the Mei Wah Beer Room in the historic downtown, said that in the beginning, the parametric insurance plan made a lot of sense. 
“Living in this little independent city, I thought it was such a great fit for us to be able to take some control of a disaster somehow,” Walton said. 
Schaefer spearheaded the creation of a special Delta Region Geologic Hazard Abatement District. It was an entity separate from the city government that could accept state funding and assess local fees to eventually pay the premium on its own. The state funded one year of the premium with $100,000, and set aside funding for the next. 
By that measure, Schaefer said, the program was a success. 
“We implemented it. We proved we can do it,” Schaefer said. “So then the challenge is: well, how do you keep it going?” 
That’s where it ran aground. 
Isleton in crisis
As Schaefer’s program launched, the City of Isleton plunged into a different kind of crisis — a financial one so severe it prompted a Sacramento County Grand Jury investigation into the city’s governance. It was the 10th grand jury investigation into Isleton in 35 years. 
In the disarray, the flood insurance pilot stalled before its second year. The special district — though distinct from the city government — couldn’t retain enough board members to reach a quorum needed to administer the program. 
“We’re a little small town, and what tends to happen is the same people try to help the city, and they either get burned out or they get kicked out,” said Walton, who left the city council after what Walton described as increasingly challenging relationships with city staff. “It’s a tough place to try to make change.”  
Now, only Walton and Bulahan remain on the dormant board. And everyone points the finger at someone else — at city staff, at the special district, at a financial crisis consuming local bandwidth and destroying goodwill.  
Ultimately, Walton said the prospect of a local tax to pay the premiums long-term sapped public appeal, especially after rates for traditional flood insurance dropped. “It was a hard sell for our broke-ass community,” Walton said. 



The town of Isleton on April 1, 2025. Photos by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Interim City Manager Jon Kennedy told CalMatters in an email that it wasn’t the concept that was the problem for him — it was the details he wasn’t clear on. 
“It’s concerning that a program of this nature was launched without an established process for distributing potential insurance proceeds or an apparent long-term sustainability plan,” Kennedy said in an email. 
Though the special district purchased a one-year parametric policy that went into effect July, 2025, the board hadn’t yet worked out who exactly would have been eligible for a payout in a flood. The policy ended on July 20, and wasn’t renewed. 
Now, the rains are here. 
“It’s so sad because it is such a great idea, and could have been such a benefit to pretty much everyone in town. And it just fell by the wayside,” Walton said. “Here we are in El Niño year … If ever it would be nice to have extra support in case of a flood, the time would be this year.”
California isn’t ready 
More than 7 million people and roughly $900 billion worth of homes and buildings are at risk of flooding — numbers that could balloon to $1 trillion in property damage and 1.5 million people displaced in a megaflood. 
Standard homeowners policies exclude flood damage — yet only 1.4% of households in California have purchased additional flood insurance. Less than a third carry it in areas the federal government deems at highest risk, where government-backed mortgages require it. 
As Kousky put it, “We don’t like buying things we hope to never use. We don’t like thinking about disasters when it’s sunny outside. We have a very poor understanding of risk.”
That’s a problem, Kousky said. “There are no other good sources of dollars for recovery.”
Federal disaster aid is shrinking. The Trump administration has cut staff, withheld resilience grants and denied recovery funds. Nearly two years after the Los Angeles wildfires, Gov. Gavin Newsom traveled to Washington D.C., pressing Congress for $13 billion in disaster aid that still hasn’t come. 
FEMA has said it intends to shift more responsibility to states, POLITICO reported. But a federal survey recently reported that emergency managers in state, local and tribal governments are understaffed and underfunded. 
“There’s something of a perfect storm story here,” said Nicholas Pinter, a professor and associate director of the UC Davis Center for Watershed Sciences. “If there is large flooding this winter, we could be on the hook for it in ways that we never would have been, under previous administrations.”
An important tool, with a catch 
Despite the infighting and disarray, the Department of Water Resources sees a silver lining — that the pilot “successfully generated private-sector interest in partnering with special districts to develop community-specific, risk-based flood insurance options,” said spokesperson Jason Ince.
River Road, also known as State Route 160, runs along the levee of the Sacramento River on April 1, 2025. The levee system protects adjoining communities from flood risk from the river. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Ince said that the Department of Water Resources is preparing a report on the Isleton project. And Michael Soller, a spokesperson for the insurance department, said that the small pilot opens the door for others to try. 
“It cannot happen fast enough. The challenges facing California communities from climate change are immense and require innovation at all levels,” Soller said in an email. “No party can do this alone, and we will continue pushing for new answers to the largest problems facing local communities.”
The catch is that those seeking parametric insurance must be able to show some insurable interest and proof of loss, the state’s general counsel letter said last week. 
These logistics, and others, are already complicating some organizations’ efforts to purchase such policies for vulnerable communities, according to Carly Finkle, a senior policy manager with the nonprofit Canal Alliance. 
Others have had success. The city of Santa Cruz purchased parametric policies triggered by earthquake and flooding, according to Ross Brandon, the city’s risk and safety manager. Unlike Isleton’s, Santa Cruz’s policies pay out to the city, rather than residents, to help cover costs like business interruption and damage to coastal roads and other infrastructure.
“(People) look to us to help them when something happens,” Brandon said. “To make sure we’re up and running is probably one of the most important things.”
Schaefer said she is heartbroken about the results in Isleton, but optimistic that parametric insurance may yet help California communities prepare for a future of more costly, climate-fueled disasters. 
“I think we’re kind of collectively trying to figure it out, trying to see if it works,” Schaefer said. “Nobody is saying, ‘This is a really stupid idea.’”
This story was made possible in part by support from The James Irvine Foundation.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Analyzing Utah’s blue wave: Many Republicans didn’t turn out; others crossed over to vote blue
description: A new report is shedding light on how Utahns’ voting patterns contributed to this year’s blue wave election, even in typically ruby red Utah.  The biggest factors are twofold: First, many Republicans — especially MAGA supporters loyal to President Donald Trump — simply didn’t turn out. And second, more Republican leaners and independents crossed over […]
text:
Ben McAdams hugs family members after talking to supporters during an election night party for Democrats at the Hilton in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A new report is shedding light on how Utahns’ voting patterns contributed to this year’s blue wave election, even in typically ruby red Utah. 
The biggest factors are twofold: First, many Republicans — especially MAGA supporters loyal to President Donald Trump — simply didn’t turn out. And second, more Republican leaners and independents crossed over to vote for Democrats.

That’s according to an analysis written by Brigham Young University political science professor Quin Monson for the university’s Center for the Study of Elections and Democracy. 
“The biggest cause, as far as I can tell from the data between the results for U.S. House in Utah (from) 2024 to 2026, is a drop off in turnout among the Trump Republicans,” Monson told Utah News Dispatch on Thursday. “The next biggest cause is some crossover voting.” 
Monson analyzed Utah’s 2024 and 2026 U.S. House election results and compared surveys of Utah voters conducted by BYU’s Center for the Study of Elections and Democracy in both election years. In 2024, 6,513 Utah voters participated, while 5,230 participated in this year’s survey. 
Monson stressed that the data doesn’t show a trend indicating voters switching political parties or identities — but rather they changed who they voted for. 
“Somebody voting for a Democrat does not mean that they’ve become a Democrat,” he said. “They’re very different. Crossover voting does not mean Republicans are becoming Democrats. It means that they’re fed up with Republican voting and they voted Democratic for a number of potential reasons.” 
‘Blue tsunami’ hits Utah: House Republicans on pace to lose 17 seats, breaking supermajority

But the bigger difference between 2024 and 2026 in Utah, he said, “is some of the most loyal MAGA Republicans just didn’t show up” this year. 
Three takeaways stand out from Monson’s analysis: 

The Republican share of the electorate got smaller in 2026: Counting independents who identify as leaning GOP, Republicans fell from 63% of congressional voters in 2024 to 52% in 2026. Meanwhile, Democrats rose from 29% in 2024 to 38% in 2026, and those who identify as pure independents rose from 7% to 10%. And the biggest single drop in participation was among those who identify as “strong” Republicans, from 35% to 28%.


The middle moved: Independents went from a near tie (43% voting Democratic, and 39% voting Republican) in 2024 to clearly favoring Democrats (57% to 22%) in 2026. The share of those who identify as “lean” and “weak” Republicans voting Democratic roughly doubled, from under 1 in 10 in 2024 to about 1 in 6 in 2026.
The strongest partisans didn’t move: Those who identify as “strong” Republicans gave their party’s candidates 96% in 2024 and 94% in 2026. “Strong” Democrats stayed at 97% in 2024 and 98% in 2026.

“Most of the Democratic gain came from a different mix of voters, not from Republicans switching sides,” Monson wrote in the report. 
While Democrats won 33% of the statewide congressional vote in 2024, that jumped to 47% in 2026. Meanwhile, Republican candidates fell from 62% in 2024 to 47% in 2026, “leaving the two parties essentially tied,” the report says. 
Utah Gov. Cox: Republicans ‘suffered a historic defeat.’ Now, he says they have to ‘listen’

Monson concluded that voting behavior changed “mostly in the middle.”
“Independents and Republicans with looser party ties moved toward Democrats in their voting behavior,” he wrote. “Strong Republicans and strong Democrats voted for their own party at almost exactly the same rates as in 2024.”
Republicans who crossed over, he wrote, were “traditional” Republicans, not MAGA supporters, with virtually no Republicans who identified with the MAGA movement voting for a Democrat for Congress. 
Notably, Monson also found that voters who identified as active members of Utah’s predominant faith, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, “moved toward voting for Democrats as much or more than other voters.” 
“The religious makeup of the electorate barely changed, but active Latter-day Saints more than doubled their Democratic vote, from 13% to 28%,” Monson wrote. “This shift is likely a result of 2024 Trump voters turning out at a lower rate in 2026, though some Latter-day Saint Republicans also crossed over to vote for Democrats.”
What caused MAGA voters to stay home, and why did some in the middle cross over?
Monson said the “why” behind Utah’s blue wave could have many reasons: maybe middle-ground voters were turned off by Trump politics or they weren’t energized to go to the polls because it was a fairly “boring” election with no statewide races.
Utah, he said, is “just part of the national story,” with a blue tsunami that washed over the entire country. 
Utah House Democrats shake up leadership after the blue wave doubled their caucus

“We’re not the only place that saw the tidal wave hit,” he said. 
But for the state, it was a “relatively sleepy year,” he said. “And I think the Trump Republicans, some of them at least, are a little discouraged. The president’s got us in a war, the economy’s not great, gas prices are high … I mean there’s a lot of reasons played out nationally that this isn’t the most exciting time.” 
“Another reason, potentially, is that these Trump Republicans, the ones that didn’t show up, are probably also the segment of the Trump Republicans that are just kind of less engaged in politics generally,” he said. “So a sleepy midterm election just doesn’t get their attention.”
To Monson, Utah’s blue wave boils down to low turnout for Republicans and “slightly more defection than you would normally see.” 
“Then you mix that in with, you know, the Democrats in Utah did a pretty good job of recruiting candidates to run for the state legislature in targeted races,” he said. “I don’t think anyone realized in advance just how big of a deal it would be. But you’ve got to give the Democrats credit for having competent opponents on the ballot, ready to capitalize and take the votes.” 
He said an opposing minority party has to have candidates on the ballot poised to strike if “the majority party stumbles.” 
“And the Republicans in Utah got caught a little bit complacent and just a little bit in the vortex of a Trump meltdown, basically,” he said. 
Why did some Latter-day Saints cross over?
Monson said it appears active Latter-day Saints that were willing to vote for Democrats are “for whatever reason, the ones that haven’t been captured by the Trump identity.” 
“So I think that makes them more open to crossing over,” he said. “They’re more easily able to see the problems with the Trump administration and the problems with candidates that are too closely aligned with Trump, and maybe also just have sort of reached the end of their patience with the politics that comes out of that wing of the Republican party.” 
In a closed-door vote, Republicans pick Sen. Evan Vickers to be next Senate president

But Monson said the data shouldn’t be interpreted to assume that most “Latter-day Saints are ready to vote Democratic.” 
“Maybe over the next 20 to 30 years we’ll see an incremental shift, because that’s how it would happen,” he said. 
But it’s too soon to say whether this year’s election is part of a larger trend. 
“It’s not something that happens in a single election, ever,” he said. “It’s going to happen over time.”
“The gains are small and incremental, and they’re also contingent upon things continuing along the lines that they have for the last 10 years,” he said. “If the Republican party continues to be dominated by Donald Trump or Donald Trump-like politicians … and the Democrats are able to nominate, in Utah and nationally, left to center (or) closer to center than the far left. That would, I think, bode well for a continued shift.” 
So does all this mean Utah is turning blue? 
“I say maybe,” he said. “But let’s wait a decade or two to be sure. … You can’t be sure about that from one election result. You’ve got to wait, and you’ve got to see consistent change in the same direction over several elections.”

Utah House Vote Survey Analysis 2024_2026 Nov 18
