title: Ranchers are the last holdout against industrial animal agriculture. Is their future at risk?
description: This is the second part in a three-part series originally published by Investigate Midwest. Read the first story here.  In western Nebraska, where cattle outnumber humans, years of drought have battered the shortgrass prairie and Sandhills so relentlessly that the land is struggling to feed all of its cattle. The seemingly unending dry spell, which […]
text:
One of the largest feedlots in the country is located in Nebraska near the Colorado and Kansas border. photo by Zach Lucero, for Investigate MidwestThis is the second part in a three-part series originally published by Investigate Midwest. Read the first story here. 
In western Nebraska, where cattle outnumber humans, years of drought have battered the shortgrass prairie and Sandhills so relentlessly that the land is struggling to feed all of its cattle.
The seemingly unending dry spell, which has plagued much of the Midwest, is contributing to a historic cattle shortage that is pushing beef prices to record highs. A developing El Niño is currently bringing some relief, but drought persists in parts of the region.
And yet, in the same parched landscape, hidden behind hills near Nebraska’s border with Colorado and Kansas, the country’s largest cattle feedlot — Blackshirt Feeders — is under construction.
A feedlot is where many cattle go after grazing on pasture and nursing from their mothers at the ranch. It’s where they spend the final months of their lives, eating grain-based feed to put on weight before they are slaughtered.
Blackshirt Feeders, founded by three veterinarians and other investors, began operating in 2024 and continues to expand. Once completed, the facility could house up to 200,000 cattle from anywhere in the country. Annually, it would draw more than 1.5 billion gallons of water from the Ogallala Aquifer, which is currently facing record-low levels, and generate manure equivalent in weight to approximately 1 million pickup trucks. The project’s scale has galvanized local residents, who have tried unsuccessfully to stop its development.
But there is another, less discussed feature of the operation: almost all of Blackshirt’s cattle are born on dairy farms, not ranches.
A breeding practice that once played a limited role in beef production is gaining momentum. Known as “beef-on-dairy,” the practice involves breeding dairy cows, typically Holstein, with beef bulls such as Angus. Rather than breeding all their cows for milk production, dairy farmers can inseminate selected cows with semen from beef bulls, producing calves raised for beef. While this practice is not new, genetic selection has significantly improved the quantity and quality of beef these crossbred calves can yield.
For now, beef-on-dairy is helping ease the cattle shortage. But its explosive growth in recent years has some ranchers worried that beef production will increasingly shift toward industrial dairy farms and away from ranches.
“This is a tremendous danger to the industry,” said Bill Bullard, CEO of Ranchers-Cattlemen Action Legal Fund United Stockgrowers of America (R-CALF USA), an organization of independent ranchers. “It threatens the independence of U.S. producers, and it is going to further erode rural areas that are dependent on a vibrant and widely dispersed cow-calf sector.”
In just a decade, beef-on-dairy calf production grew from 50,000 head in 2014 to 3.22 million in 2024, according to industry estimates. Beef-on-dairy cattle now make up an estimated 26% of the feedlot population. For consumers, this means that more steaks on store shelves may come from beef-on-dairy cattle, though there is usually no way of knowing from the label.
Despite this rapid growth, experts in the field insist that beef-on-dairy production will never replace traditional ranching, since there aren’t enough dairy cows to meet demand. But projects like Blackshirt and other developments reveal that the industry is increasingly betting on the beef-on-dairy model — a model that also comes with animal health and welfare concerns. Beef-on-dairy cattle typically live in confinement instead of grazing on pasture, while research shows that these animals are more prone to certain health problems.
“It’s a confinement model from birth to plate,” Bullard said. “It is going to facilitate the vertical integration of the industry by the largest beef packers and companies like Walmart.”
The beef industry’s vertical integration
In the U.S., ranchers own their cattle. Calves at the ranch graze on pasture and nurse from cows until weaning, typically at three to seven months old. Ranchers then sell their weaned calves, usually at live auctions scattered across rural America.
Some calves go to “stockers,” who raise them for several more months on pasture or forage-based diets before sending them to feedlots. Others go directly to feedlots, where “feeders” put the animals on grain-heavy diets designed to fatten them up. Once the cattle reach the desired market weight, feeders sell them to meatpacking companies, or “packers,” which slaughter the animals.
Ranchers, stockers, feeders, packers. The many ways these factions buy, sell and negotiate with one another — and with retailers, distributors and other players in the industry — has been described by economists as one of the most complex supply chains in the world.
For meatpackers, the system leaves much of the supply chain beyond their control, making it difficult to secure a consistent, uniform supply of cattle at stable prices.
Beef-on-dairy is changing that.
“The beef-on-dairy model closely resembles the vertical integration of the pork and poultry industries,” said Mike Callicrate, a prominent Kansas rancher and business owner whose ranch is about 35 miles south from the Blackshirt feedlot. “This is exactly what the meatpackers want. They want to be able to control it all.”
Mike Callicrate driving through his ranch in St. Francis, Kansas, in September 2026. (Photo by Zach Lucero/Investigate Midwest)
By removing ranchers from the equation, the beef-on-dairy model could open the door to the vertical integration of the beef industry — or as ranchers often call it, the “chickenization” of the beef industry.
It is a system of control over the entire supply chain that Tyson Foods pioneered in the chicken industry in the 1950s and 1960s, and the pork industry adopted more widely in the 1990s. It gave meatpackers control over how animals are raised, transforming animal agriculture into a highly industrialized, standardized system in which companies coordinate production and animals typically live in confinement from birth.
The model is simple: The meat company usually owns the animals and controls every stage of production, from breeding and feed production to processing and distribution. The farmer owns the farm and equipment, assumes substantial debt and bears the financial risk. Companies can produce as many animals as the market demands and rely on farmers, bound by strict contracts, to raise them. By keeping the animals in confinement, companies eliminate the impact of unpredictable weather that is part of raising animals outdoors.
“The cattle industry remains the last frontier in terms of vertically integrating the industry,” Bullard, from R-CALF, said. “It takes vast areas of forage to raise the mother cows and the calves.”
The four largest meatpackers — Tyson Foods, JBS, Cargill and National Beef — wield enormous power in the beef industry, controlling about 85% of beef processing, shaping policy and influencing prices. But, so far, they cannot directly dictate when or how ranchers raise their cattle, or how much they are paid for them.
The open cash market of live auctions gives ranchers the opportunity to receive the highest possible price for their calves, a degree of leverage that commercial poultry and pork farmers do not have. That independence from meatpacking giants makes ranchers one of the last bastions of traditional American agriculture.
“There’s barely any or basically no independent hog feeders currently,” said Corbitt Wall, a well-known cattle market analyst who has built a following among American ranchers through his daily commentary on the cattle market. “I’m afraid that’s going to be the way of the cattle, too.”
The dairy industry offers meatpackers a way to bypass ranchers, live auctions and open pastures.
Most dairy farms already keep cattle in confinement from birth, and beef-on-dairy allows them to use the same infrastructure and supply chain to raise crossbreed animals for meat. The scale of modern dairy farms makes them a natural fit for the beef industry’s growing demand.
Many of today’s dairy farms are large industrial operations that use sophisticated technology and genetic breeding programs. The average dairy farm is now more than eight times larger than it was in 1978, according to the latest available Census of Agriculture data. Farms with 2,500 cows or more are increasingly common, as smaller farms continue to disappear.
Graphic courtesy of Investigate Midwest.
Speaking on a radio talk show in January, Iowa cattle producer and market analyst Brad Kooima referred to beef-on-dairy as “the gorilla in the room,” warning that it could have serious consequences for the beef industry.
“I watched them wreck the hog market. I lived it. I see what’s happened in poultry. This scares me to death,” said Kooima.
He also called beef-on-dairy a meatpacker’s “dream.” Callicrate, the Kansas rancher, agrees.
“If they can get those calves locked into their supply chains the day they’re born, they know exactly when they’re gonna hit the slaughterhouse,” Callicrate said.
The end of the American rancher?
Vertical integration can happen in different ways. Major players further up the supply chain — meatpackers, retailers, or large feedlots like Blackshirt — can gain greater control of the supply chain through ownership or contracts.
Tara Felix, a leading beef-on-dairy expert and professor at Penn State’s College of Agriculture, told Investigate Midwest that a model in which meatpackers own beef-on-dairy calves from birth through slaughter is “a possibility.”
But she says that it is not how the industry operates today. Currently, most dairy farmers sell their newborn beef-on-dairy calves on the open cash market, much like ranchers sell their cattle.
Speaking on a podcast earlier this year, however, Felix said that arrangement may not last. She expects beef-on-dairy production to move toward “a more integrated model.”
“There are already parts of the beef-on-dairy industry that are becoming what I would call ‘vertically integrated,’” said Felix on The Beef Podcast Show.
Blackshirt is one example of this shift. The feedlot owns all of its cattle and has contracts with dairy farms to secure a steady supply of beef-on-dairy calves. A different example is a Wisconsin dairy farm that owns its beef-on-dairy cattle until slaughter. This arrangement could allow the farm to contract directly with a meatpacker and supply beef-on-dairy cattle that meet the packer’s requirements.
Walmart has also become a powerful player. The retail company opened its own beef processing plant in Kansas last year and said this move would strengthen its supply chain’s “resiliency and control.”
Regardless of how the beef-on-dairy model evolves, Felix rejects the idea that beef-on-dairy is a threat to independent ranching. Speaking with Investigate Midwest, she described the small independent rancher as “the backbone of the beef cattle industry” and argued that the beef-on-dairy sector could never replace traditional ranching.
“For several decades now, our dairy population in the United States has remained nearly stagnant at nearly 9 million mama cows,” Felix said. “Those cows can only produce one calf per year. At most, they could produce nearly 9 million calves if biology were perfect.”
That number is far below the roughly 25 million calves for beef the U.S. harvests each year, Felix noted.
The nation’s dairy cow herd has, as Felix noted, hovered around 9 million for decades. But last year it shifted from the lower to the upper end of that range — reaching its largest size in more than 30 years.
Agricultural economist Brian Earnest said that dairy farmers, many of whom are currently under financial strain, are increasingly seeing beef-on-dairy calves as a valuable source of profit.
“The big reason why we have a larger dairy cow herd or not retiring as many of those is beef-on-dairy,” said Earnest, speaking at this year’s Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Midwest Agriculture Conference in October.
The life of a beef-on-dairy calf
A beef-on-dairy calf experiences a very different life from a traditional beef calf. While not all farms adopt the same practices, the following is a typical scenario.
Within the first 24 hours after birth, dairy farmers separate the calf from its mother and ship it by truck to a “calf grower,” also called a “calf ranch,” often in a faraway state. There, workers house the newborn calf in a confined, individual hutch measuring less than 15 square feet and feed it grain and milk replacer. In some facilities, the newborn calf may also receive growth-promoting antibiotics.
At around 80 to 100 days of age, the calf moves into a pen with other calves, where it continues eating a grain-based diet until it reaches 500 to 700 pounds. Workers then transport the calf by truck to a feedlot, where it gains additional weight before heading to a meatpacking plant. At a feedlot like Blackshirt, calves stay for more than a year — roughly twice as long as traditional beef calves spend in feedlots.
Dairy farmers from as far away as Florida send newborn calves to Kansas Dairy Development (KDD) in Deerfield, Kansas, allowing them to focus on milk production while the calves grow. Known as “calf growers” or “calf ranches,” these facilities house calves in individual hutches, where workers feed them grain and milk replacer. An increasing share of KDD’s calves are beef-on-dairy. Calves destined for milk production eventually return to dairy farms, while beef-on-dairy calves are sent to feedlots. (Photo by Zach Lucero/Investigate Midwest)
“Those beef-on-dairy cattle never get a chance to enjoy their best life,” Wall, the cattle market analyst, said. “They really never get to enjoy anything. They’re stolen from their mothers the day they’re born.”
The industry is aware that these cattle-raising practices are far removed from the idyllic image of ranchers in cowboy hats tending herds across open pastures.
Ruth Woiwode, a cattle welfare specialist and professor at Oklahoma State University, wrote in April about how the dairy industry’s growing role in beef production could affect the beef industry’s public image.
She pointed to a viral video of a calf grower operation. “Recent publicly circulated video footage illustrates how quickly attention can focus on these systems,” Woiwode wrote.
Woiwode warned that the scale of these operations — some which have 80,000 newborn calves in individual hutches — makes them vulnerable to public scrutiny. High employee turnover increases the likelihood that footage from inside these facilities will be recorded and shared, according to Woiwode.
“In systems where employees perform hundreds of repetitive care tasks per shift… individual interactions are more likely to be captured on video,” Woiwode wrote.
In California, home to one of the largest calf growers in the country, these operations may violate state animal cruelty laws, according to farm animal advocates. But state officials have shown little interest in enforcing the law.
There are also concerns about animal health.
A 2024 research paper by Temple Grandin, the world-renowned cattle expert and Colorado State University professor, warns that genetic selection may be having a serious impact on animals’ health.
Grandin wrote that intensive genetic selection for “economically attractive meat traits,” such as rapid growth and oversized ribeyes, may be contributing to alarming increases in congestive heart failure and lameness — problems particularly evident in beef-on-dairy cattle.
She has observed widespread physical abnormalities among these crossbreds, noting that many Angus-on-Holstein steers develop twisted, corkscrew-shaped claws, leading to lameness and mobility problems.
Grandin urges the industry not to accept these conditions as normal. “Dairy producers became so accustomed to looking at lame cows that they no longer perceived it as a problem,” she wrote.
Liver abscesses are another major problem in beef-on-dairy cattle.
Liver abscesses are infected pockets in the liver, usually caused by digestive problems linked to high-grain diets. While traditional feedlot cattle typically have abscess rates of around 1-in-5, beef-on-dairy cattle can see rates of 1-in-2 or higher, with some groups reaching more than 80%.
Felix, the Penn State beef-on-dairy expert, noted that liver abscess rates can vary significantly from one region to another. While breed differences exist, geography is also an important factor, although scientists don’t yet understand why.
“Whether it’s beef-on-dairy or whether it’s beef-on-beef, liver abscesses are a regional challenge,” Felix said.
The industry’s big bet
Besides Blackshirt, other recent developments suggest that the beef-on-dairy model is appealing to the industry.
In 2021, Cargill partnered with Nestlé and Texas Tech University on the “Beef Dairy Accelerator” program, a three-year initiative to accelerate producer adoption of beef-on-dairy crossbreeding.
Land O’Lakes, one of the country’s largest dairy businesses, promotes beef-on-dairy through its subsidiary, Purina Mills. The animal nutrition company sells a milk replacer for beef-on-dairy calves that, according to the company, can “help reduce animal size variability.” The promise of uniformity is central to the appeal of the beef-on-dairy model: producing calves with predictable growth and traits suited to standardized production systems and meatpacker demands.

ABS Global, an artificial insemination company owned by the British company Genus plc, is particularly benefiting from the rise of beef-on-dairy.
Dairy farmers are increasingly relying on artificial insemination to breed dairy cows with beef genetics, rather than using beef bulls. For milk production, they are also adopting “sexed” semen to increase the likelihood of producing female offspring.
The company reported that the share of its sales to U.S. dairy farms consisting of sexed and beef genetics grew from 16% in 2016 to 78% in 2023. Genus’s 2025 annual report showed ABS is seeking to “drive increased adoption” of beef-on-dairy.
Cargill and ABS Global have also supported research into beef-on-dairy at public universities. At a 2024 industry conference, Texas Tech University professor Dale Woerner, whose position is endowed by Cargill, encouraged the industry to continue producing beef-on-dairy cattle.
“Beef-on-dairy crossbreds have added enough value to the beef supply chain that we should never change what we’re doing. We should continue creating these crossbred cattle for the future,” said Woerner.
Historic cattle shortage
The U.S. total cattle inventory is as low as it was in the early 1950s, when the country’s human population was less than half of what it is today. While drought is accelerating the shortage, the issue has been building for decades.
Since 1978, the U.S. has lost roughly 4 in 10 ranches. More than 1 million operations raised beef cows in 1978, compared with roughly 622,000 in 2022, according to the most recent data available from the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Groups like R-CALF, which represents independent ranchers, point to free trade agreements like NAFTA and decades of industry consolidation as key factors that have pushed ranchers out of business.
Beginning in the 1980s, a lack of federal enforcement of antitrust laws fueled a wave of mergers and acquisitions as the industry began favoring larger operations and economies of scale. In the beef industry, this consolidation left four companies controlling more than 80% of cattle processing. Today, those companies — known as the Big Four — are Tyson Foods, Cargill, and the Brazilian-owned National Beef and JBS.
Only 10 meatpacking plants currently process nearly half of all U.S. beef. Feedlots have grown larger, while smaller operations have shut down. For ranchers, fewer feedlots mean fewer buyers for their cattle.
“Our industry is already contracting and contracting at an alarming rate,” Bullard, from R-CALF, said. “[Beef-on-dairy] will make it even less economical for independent beef cattle operations to continue.”
Meatpackers are confronting a cattle shortage that may be, in part, a consequence of their own making. Beef-on-dairy is just one way the beef industry is responding to a shrinking cattle supply.
The industry is also feeding cattle for longer periods and adopting a new controversial growth-promoting drug, two practices that are pushing cattle to extreme weights. Bigger cattle allow meatpackers to squeeze more beef out of each animal.
The Trump administration has tried to address the cattle shortage by bringing in more foreign beef, claiming it would lower prices for consumers. But strong demand continues to keep beef prices high, and the imports have done little to change that.
The move angered ranchers across the country, while groups like R-CALF and Farm Action believe meatpackers benefit from the increased imports. Others speculate that JBS influenced Trump’s policy decisions.
Joesley Batista, the scandal-plagued co-owner of Brazilian meatpacking giant JBS, met with Trump shortly before the president announced plans to expand beef imports from Argentina. Batista met with Trump again before the administration eased import restrictions on other countries, particularly Brazil.

Cutting out the middlemen
In the heart of the Great Plains, about 35 miles south of the Blackshirt feedlot, Mike Callicrate runs a ranch, feedlot, and meatpacking plant side by side.
About a dozen calves, all black-coated but for a few reddish-brown ones, nibble on grass alongside a mother cow. They are in one of the few parts of the ranch where grass is still lush in September.
The rest of the herd, about 1,200 cattle, is in the feedyard. There, Callicrate feeds his own cattle and those of nearby ranchers. Once they have put on enough weight, the cattle will travel about 400 feet to the small packing plant that Callicrate built with the help of his son. The plant has a small office for the USDA inspector, who comes by every time animals are slaughtered.
In the 1990s, Callicrate joined nine other cattle producers in an antitrust lawsuit against meatpacking giant IBP, which Tyson Foods later acquired. They accused the company of manipulating cattle prices and pushing independent ranchers out of the market.
The lawsuit came with consequences. Major meatpackers refused to buy Callicrate’s cattle and he eventually had to shut down his feeding operation. Instead of leaving the cattle business altogether, he decided to do things differently: Callicrate scaled back his operation and began selling beef rather than cattle.
“We have completely screwed ourselves in this industry. This is why people like me have said ‘enough,’” said Callicrate. “Twenty-six years ago, I said ‘I’m not doing this anymore.’”
Callicrate sees his operation as a blueprint for what a fair and competitive beef industry could look like in the U.S.
He gives his cattle antibiotics only when they need them, and never uses hormones or growth-promoting drugs, he said. After slaughter, Callicrate ships the carcasses by truck to a Colorado facility, where butchers cut and package the meat for sale at his Colorado Springs store. It’s a regional, direct-to-consumer business.
Callicrate acknowledges that he is able to keep the operation afloat because of the income from his more prosperous business, a humane castration device that he invented in the 1990s and that is now sold internationally. He believes ranchers across the country could have similar success if meatpackers, retailers, and food distributors did not have so much control over the market.
“This is very simple, affordable, but you can’t do it unless you have a market,” Callicrate said. “It’s a completely broken and corrupted system.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Future docs: Get rid of Medicaid middlemen
description: We are second year medical students at the University of Minnesota, just beginning our journey into medicine, looking forward to the incredible privilege of being physicians.  We have already seen the power that medicine has to improve people’s lives. We have also seen shortcomings in the medical system that can prevent patients from receiving care. […]
text:
(Photo by Ariel Skelley/Getty Images)We are second year medical students at the University of Minnesota, just beginning our journey into medicine, looking forward to the incredible privilege of being physicians. 
We have already seen the power that medicine has to improve people’s lives. We have also seen shortcomings in the medical system that can prevent patients from receiving care. Chief among them is the role of insurance companies, whose tactics interfere with patient care by forcing doctors into a constant struggle to gain approval for treatments that they prescribe. Health insurance companies claim that they must micromanage doctors because overuse of medical services is the primary cause of high healthcare costs, and doctors are the main cause of the alleged overutilization. This is despite patients in the U.S. utilizing the healthcare system less and paying more for those services than comparable high income countries1,2. 
Removing these health insurance middlemen from our public healthcare programs — such as MinnesotaCare and Minnesota’s version of Medicaid, known as Medical Assistance — would reduce healthcare costs and improve the quality of care. Private insurance companies are taking our hard-earned premiums, and rerouting the money directly into their pockets. The full extent of the money that is not used for healthcare by insurance companies is opaque, although current statute says that 15% of money paid to private insurers may go to non-healthcare related costs, which includes paying armies of administrators and loosely defined “quality improvement activities” that can be spent on marketing, travel and entertainment due to how loosely they are defined. 
In contrast, state-run Medicaid programs, whose only non-healthcare spending goes to administrative cost, have a steeply reduced overhead. Indeed, Medicaid overhead is roughly 4%, allowing for more spending more on actual healthcare. The main argument for why we in the United States need insurance companies rests on the assumption that doctors and patients can’t decide what care is best for them and will order unnecessary tests and appointments. Our healthcare system allows administrators hired by your health insurer to determine if you qualify for the surgery that your doctor recommends or the medication that decreases your risk of having a heart attack. 
Additionally, there is little evidence supporting this assumption that without the supervision of health insurers, Americans would vastly over-utilize healthcare. 
A 2025 study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research found that patients in the privatized version of Medicaid use healthcare a similar amount when compared to the public versions of the programs but are significantly less satisfied. When private health insurance companies try to reduce wasteful spending in the medical system, their blunt tactics of prior authorizations and denials of care often deprive patients of access to necessary care. More than a quarter of physicians surveyed by the American Medical Association found that insurance denials led directly to life-threatening events for a patient. 
A study by Physicians for a National Health Program found that removing health insurance middlemen would cut 10-17% in Medicaid total spending. This is calculated by taking into account the money saved by deprivatizing Medicaid and adding in the potential of a modest increase in healthcare usage, which results in cost savings. So why don’t we just ditch these private health insurance companies?
There is currently a bill in the Minnesota Legislature poised to do just this: the Patient Centered Care bill. This bill, which will get a fresh airing with a new Legislature next year, establishes a system in which the state of Minnesota directly pays healthcare providers for the services that they provide for Medicaid patients. Instead of allowing insurance companies to gamify the healthcare system to maximize profits, the bill moves the destination of healthcare dollars back into the hands of Medicaid patients and their doctors. 
As future physicians, we support the removal of private insurance from Medicaid as a step towards fixing our broken healthcare system. We encourage you to check out the PCC bill, and you can contact your state representatives to ask them about it, too.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA slated to get another $177M in rural health funding
description: For the first time, the Olympic Area Agency on Aging since September has offered free dementia screenings to roughly 90 locals who live in Washington’s coastal counties. Otherwise, residents don’t have much access to this opportunity; there isn’t a geriatric psychiatrist in the region, which has some of Washington’s oldest counties, said Laura Cepoi, the […]
text:
Doctors behind sunblind caring for patient in emergency care unit of a hospital with respiratory equipment. (Getty Images)For the first time, the Olympic Area Agency on Aging since September has offered free dementia screenings to roughly 90 locals who live in Washington’s coastal counties.
Otherwise, residents don’t have much access to this opportunity; there isn’t a geriatric psychiatrist in the region, which has some of Washington’s oldest counties, said Laura Cepoi, the agency’s executive director. Screenings allow people to detect the condition that leads to diminished brain function early, and work to stop it from getting worse. 
“You’re able then to have agency over your own life,” Cepoi said. “It is probably one of the kindest things you can do for yourself and the people you love, so that you’re all aware of what are the next steps in your journey.”
The work is funded by a small slice of the $181 million pie that Washington state got this year from the Trump administration to spend on improving rural healthcare. 
Next year, Washington is set to receive $177 million, though that figure is still subject to change, federal officials announced this month. A budget for how the 2027 dollars will be spent is expected by the end of the year.
The $177 million award is for the second year of the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program, which is set to provide $50 billion across all 50 states in that period, or $10 billion per year. If apportioned equally to each state, all would get $200 million per year, or $1 billion across the program’s five-year span. 
If the pace continues, Washington would fall short of that number and get a total of roughly $896 million over the half-decade.
Republicans in Congress established the initiative last year. They intended to make up for hundreds of billions of dollars in losses rural hospitals and others are set to face due to less federal funding and the addition of work requirements to continue qualifying for Medicaid, the federal low-income health insurance program.
Washington alone is expecting at least 200,000 residents to lose coverage, not necessarily because they don’t meet the new mandates but because of the barriers to showing eligibility.
The enrollment losses will force hospitals to shoulder more of their costs for care, since they won’t be getting reimbursed by insurance. Rural providers, where the healthcare system is already fragile, will likely take the hardest hits. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Local health officials agree that the federal rural health dollars won’t come close to making up the money they’ll lose.
Providers currently sit in the calm before the storm with those cuts. Some have already hit, with around 10,000 immigrants losing Medicaid coverage in October and the expiration of subsidies for insurance through the state’s Affordable Care Act exchange. 
But the work requirements don’t take effect until next year. Initially, they were slated to start Jan. 1, 2027, but the Trump administration recently offered states a six-month delay in enforcing them. Washington has opted in, so the requirements won’t apply until July 1.
The Rural Collaborative is doling out $5.4 million to rural hospitals, mostly for administrative efficiencies.
“If we’re successful, not a single one of our hospitals will close,” said Elya Prystowsky, the collaborative’s executive director. “That’s the most obvious litmus test.”
“Right now, it feels like we’re in an apartment, and we could hear somebody coming up the stairs, but we can’t see who it is, and we’re all just scared it’s the boogeyman,” Prystowsky added. “But it may just be the pizza delivery man. It may not be as bad as we all think it will be.”
Where Washington stands
Washington’s $177 million for 2027 ranks ninth lowest in the nation, above states like New Jersey ($142 million), Connecticut ($154 million) and Rhode Island ($158 million).  Larger states  — California, Alaska, Montana and Texas — have been at the top of the list each of the past two years. Texas, next year, is slated to receive $282 million. Only three states saw their second-year totals drop more from this year than Washington, according to an analysis by the health research firm KFF.
“Rural hospitals are so resourceful and can do so much with so little that it’s still a lot of money,” Prystowsky said. “It just has to get to the right place. It can’t get absorbed in places where it won’t make an impact.”
Washington has about 1.1 million rural residents. That pencils out to about $159 for each of them, slightly more than the national average, but below neighbors like Oregon, Idaho and Montana, KFF found.
Half of the $50 billion fund is evenly distributed to all states with approved applications. But doling out the rest factors in the number of rural residents and medical facilities in each state, along with state policies, a downside for Washington, since it’s often at odds with the Trump administration.
Where the money is going
Washington has pushed out all of its $181 million for the first year. The money can’t be used to backfill lost revenue from federal cuts, and aims to go far beyond boosting hospital finances and instead reshape the healthcare system in these communities.
Over $33 million went toward growing the rural health workforce. Tribes got $19.4 million, $669,000 to each that is federally recognized in Washington. Nearly $24 million paid for technology and data solutions, like the University of Washington’s Project ECHO, which mentors and educates clinicians in rural areas virtually. Almost $22 million went toward improving rural behavioral health, including money for schools. In Pacific County, people can wait 18 months for mental health services, for example, Cepoi said.
The biggest slice of Washington’s funding, more than $59 million, targeted improving hospital infrastructure, technology and services. 
The Washington State Hospital Association spearheaded much of that work, which could include everything from artificial intelligence technology for notetaking to updated stretchers, telehealth tools and CT scanners.
“One of the bigger challenges for rural hospitals is that because they operate with such slim margins, it’s very hard to make the kind of capital investments that they want to make,” said Jacqueline Barton True, the association’s senior vice president of advocacy and rural health. 
Cepoi’s area agency on aging has also mobilized vans to bring health services to rural communities west of Puget Sound. The first four of those served about 300 people, each of them getting about three screenings on average, like testing to measure blood sugar, vision or blood pressure. In Ocean Shores, over 100 people turned out. 
In South Bend, 33 people turned out for a mobile clinic. Of those, 30 didn’t have health insurance. Otherwise, they may have ended up in emergency rooms for care, Cepoi said.
She hopes the organization can continue providing these services through the five years of the rural health program.
“We’re doing this because people in our rural communities deserve access to care,” Cepoi said. “They shouldn’t have to drive hours, wait months, or go without services simply because they live in a more remote part of Washington. We have an opportunity to make a difference.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Missouri voters rejected more than an abortion ban
description: Missourians have now twice confronted efforts to restrict reproductive freedom. But this latest vote also brought forward transgender rights to bodily autonomy. In 2024, Missourians did something remarkable. At the time, the state enforced an aggressive abortion ban that had no exceptions for rape, incest, and no protections when the patient’s life was at ri[...]
text:
Reproductive rights supporters gather around the stage at a Stop the Ban watch party in opposition to a proposed abortion ban amendment on Nov. 3, in St. Louis (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).Missourians have now twice confronted efforts to restrict reproductive freedom. But this latest vote also brought forward transgender rights to bodily autonomy.
In 2024, Missourians did something remarkable. At the time, the state enforced an aggressive abortion ban that had no exceptions for rape, incest, and no protections when the patient’s life was at risk. Voters chose freedom instead. They enshrined reproductive freedom in the state constitution with 51.6% of the vote, overturning the state’s abortion ban.
This was a huge, but narrow win, one earned through organizing, door knocking and the hard work of convincing our neighbors that decisions about their bodies should be made by them. I was part of that effort. I knocked on doors because I believed Missourians deserved the opportunity to make their own healthcare decisions.
This year, Missouri voters were asked to revisit that decision. A repeal of the reproductive rights amendment was the ballot. Once again, Missourians voted for freedom, protecting access to care and their private decisions. And the ranks of supporters expanding, with approximately 55% voted no to reinstating an abortion ban.
The margin was wider and the message this time around is worth examining. The effort to strip reproductive care was combined with a ban on best practice healthcare for transgender youth. A calculated campaign against transgender Missourians that anti-abortion activists felt would help them win where they had failed just two years ago.
Missouri was among five states this year where voters decided on the rights of their transgender neighbors via ballot measure, marking one of the first nationally coordinated attacks against transgender Americans via the ballot initiative process.
Instead of proposing measures that expand freedom, proponents demanded that the majority decide whether to restrict freedom including of a small group of people. Yet in two states, voters chose to protect trans youth.
Voters in Missouri who know what it’s like to have their freedoms taken away spoke up for each other, including for trans people. Voters in Washington rejected a measure that would out LGBTQ youth against their will. Anti-trans policies aren’t the political slam dunks their supporters expect. Even where anti-trans measures succeeded, results show they are far from universally embraced.
There are also signs that voters are weary of politicians making transgender people a political football.
A GLAAD poll of registered voters showed rejection of anti-trans campaign ads. Voters accurately saw them as cynical tactics to distract from their priority issue: cost of living and affordability. Anti-LGBTQ politicians and special interest groups simply refused to face facts and listen to voters, resulting in historic rejection of candidates spreading disinformation and fear about transgender people in the midterm elections.
Transphobia lost far more than it won at the ballot box.
Missourians rejected an abortion ban by an even wider margin than their 2024 vote, proving we cannot be reduced to political stereotypes. We are not a monolith, and we live in communities with people affected by the policies being debated.
Sadly, anti-abortion, anti-LGBTQ politicians have said they are not finished with this fight. But the results from November deserve to be taken seriously. You cannot keep asking Missourians to surrender personal freedoms and assume we will eventually say yes.
We will keep saying no.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lawmakers detail what they want in next speaker of Nebraska Legislature
description: LINCOLN — Most returning Nebraska lawmakers say they’re looking for someone who can bring people together and work across the aisle as they consider who will be the next speaker of the Nebraska Legislature. State Sens. Teresa Ibach of Sumner and Kathleen Kauth of Omaha so far have said they’ll seek the top role for […]
text:
State lawmakers gather on the final day of Nebraska's 2026 legislative session. Not pictured: State Sens. Jana Hughes of Seward and Dan Quick of Grand Island. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Most returning Nebraska lawmakers say they’re looking for someone who can bring people together and work across the aisle as they consider who will be the next speaker of the Nebraska Legislature.
State Sens. Teresa Ibach of Sumner and Kathleen Kauth of Omaha so far have said they’ll seek the top role for the 2027-28 legislative cycle. Any of the Legislature’s 49 members could run by Jan. 6. Speaker John Arch of La Vista, who has held the role since 2023, is exiting the Legislature after eight years due to term limits. 
Leadership votes are decided by secret ballot on the first day of each legislative biennium for speaker, the chair and vice chair of the internal Executive Board and 16 committee chairs.
State Sens. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, and Teresa Ibach of Sumner, right, are vying for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature in the 2027-28 legislative cycle. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Gov. Jim Pillen was reelected to another four years to lead the executive branch. The next speaker and new chair of the Legislature’s Exec Board will lead the legislative branch.
The Nebraska Examiner asked all 34 returning state lawmakers whether they were running for leadership in 2027 and asked two dozen of them what qualities they want in the next speaker.
Fourteen freshman lawmakers will also join the Legislature in 2027, as will former state Sen. Patty Pansing Brooks, who sat out four years due to term limits. The class finished training, or “senator school,” on Nov. 10.
Some returning senators declined to take a position on Ibach or Kauth, some noting the possibility that other candidates might jump into the race or their concern of possible retaliation if they picked a side. Others explained why one of the pair has their support or opposition.
Here’s what lawmakers had to say about what they’re looking for in their next speaker.
‘Managing 48 cats’
State Sen. Barry DeKay of Niobrara, Agriculture Committee chair, said the chamber will need to “figure out how to play well together and get some bipartisan stuff done.” He said he’s waiting to hear specifically from Ibach and Kauth on their proposed paths toward getting 25 votes on legislation or, in the face of a filibuster, how to get to 33 votes to end debate.
State Sen. Barry DeKay of Niobrara, chair of the Legislature’s Agriculture Committee, center, meets with Speaker John Arch of La Vista. March 31, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“I think there’s some opportunity to work very well together and get some bipartisan legislation passed without having to go to 33,” DeKay said.
DeKay and others noted that the Legislature will no longer have 33 Republicans. That supermajority had allowed conservatives, when united, to pass legislation despite filibusters.
In 2027, the Legislature will have 30 Republicans, 18 Democrats and one registered nonpartisan.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward said the Legislature will need someone who has a “good temperament,” is very calm and fair-minded, and is willing to work with all sides on an issue, not just Republican-Democrat divides but also geographic rural-urban separations and other considerations.
“That, to me, is No. 1 on who should be speaker,” Hughes said
“You’re managing 48 cats,” Hughes added. “You’ve got to have somebody that has the patience to be able to do that.”
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward meets with State Sens. Tom Brandt of Plymouth and Danielle Conrad of Lincoln during the first day of the Legislature’s special session on property taxes on July 25, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sens. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue, Stan Clouse of Kearney and Tony Sorrentino of Elkhorn were among a handful of lawmakers who said they feel both Ibach and Kauth would do the job well. Holdcroft noted Kauth will be term-limited after 2028 and Ibach after 2030.
Given the changing Legislature, Holdcroft also noted the minority can block everything with a filibuster, which was at times tough to overcome even with 33 Republicans.
‘Get along with everyone’
State Sen.-elect Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha, a registered nonpartisan, defeated state Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn this fall. He had been seen as a frontrunner for speaker, but state Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte had said he would run for speaker if von Gillern lost rather than try to succeed him as Revenue Committee chair.
Kauth had pledged to run no matter von Gillern’s fate.
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, center, meets with, from left, State Sens. Dave Murman of Glenvil, Barry DeKay of Niobrara, Steve Halloran of Hastings, Steve Erdman of Bayard and Brian Hardin of Gering. Feb. 23, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Jacobson, chair of the Legislature’s Banking, Commerce and Insurance Committee, said that when then-Gov. Pete Ricketts appointed him to the Legislature in 2022, it was in part because Jacobson wanted to make a difference for rural Nebraska and all Nebraskans. He said that he needs to be in a position where he can do that, and that the Revenue Committee will be “front and center” as the Legislature faces a projected $1.2 billion budget deficit through mid-2029 and as lawmakers again say they’ll focus on property taxes.
“I just feel like having a seat at the table, and potentially the seat at the head of the table of the Revenue Committee, is the best place that I can make a difference,” Jacobson said.
“Some have said we’d be removing a chess piece from the floor,” Jacobson added, if he became speaker. “I think that did resonate with me. I may be making the wrong decision, but I don’t think so. I think this is the right place for me at this time.”
State Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston gives a tribute to Speaker John Arch of La Vista on the final day of the 2026 legislative session, the end of the fourth regular session under Arch’s leadership. The frame includes signatures from all 48 of Arch’s colleagues and shows a man herding cats. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
When Jacobson bowed out of the speaker’s race, he endorsed Ibach. She jumped into the race Nov. 8, months after Kauth and after the election. Jacobson said Ibach has qualities to succeed.
“I don’t think we want a lightning rod to be the speaker. I don’t think we want someone who’s going to be divisive,” Jacobson said. “We need to bring someone who can bring people together and get along with everyone in the body.”
‘Truly listen to everyone’
State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha declined to comment on Ibach’s candidacy, but he did describe Kauth’s tenure as “laser-focused on fringe culture-war issues.”
“That’s not the leadership this body needs,” Fredrickson said in a text. “I wish her well.”
State Sens. Megan Hunt of Omaha, John Fredrickson of Omaha and George Dungan of Lincoln, from left, meet on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. Aug. 8, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
He criticized Kauth for creating the new Nebraska Conservative Leadership Fund political action committee, which waded into 16 of 25 legislative races this year, including Fredrickson’s reelection. The PAC spent more than $800,000, and Republicans won in 10 of those 16 races. 
Fredrickson, state Sen. George Dungan of Lincoln, Maxwell-Ostdiek and Omaha state Sens.-elect Cindy Johnson, Jess Goldoni and Christy Knorr won in the other six races.
Fredrickson noted there’s still a lot of time before the session begins Jan. 6 for people to run.
Dungan, who plans to challenge Jacobson for Revenue chair in 2027, said Arch, as speaker, “went out of his way at certain times to make sure he was at least doing his best to be fair.”
State Sen. Margo Juarez of Omaha. Jan. 8, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Certainly, I disagreed with certain decisions that were made, but at the end of the day, I think that he cared about the institution, and I think that that’s what we need in a future speaker,” Dungan said.
Dungan said a speaker shouldn’t “weaponize” the role to “achieve a very niche agenda.”
State Sen. Margo Juarez of Omaha said she was specifically glad Ibach put forward her name, and she thinks she’s approachable and listens, qualities she wants to see in the role.
‘Petty partisan power play’
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln said there’s a “fair amount of fluidity” in various races for leadership, given that some lawmakers are just coming off the campaign trail and the session is still weeks away.
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, left, talks with State Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue. Jan. 29, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“What I am seeing and hearing in the Legislature is, for the most part, a pretty strong, petty partisan power play that does not match the post-election rhetoric of seeking collaboration and collegiality and a more balanced approach, which is exactly what the voters of Nebraska asked the Legislature to do by sending a more balanced set of senators to the body,” Conrad said.
Of current speaker candidates, Conrad said Ibach has at least indicated a willingness to sit down and visit with lawmakers of different political leanings.
Conrad is heading into her 13th year as a lawmaker. She served under two speakers in her first two terms and three served while she was out of the Legislature.
State Sen. Tanya Storer of Whitman. Feb. 10, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The most effective speakers she’s observed, Conrad said, brought a certain level of humility and an “absolute” commitment to mutual respect and worked hard to be protective of the institution and fair-minded with every lawmaker.
“That doesn’t mean that I’ve always agreed with all of their decisions, but I think those are the ingredients that make for an effective speaker,” Conrad said.
Conrad said some have encouraged her to consider leadership, but she hasn’t decided yet.
‘A true leader quality’
State Sen. Tanya Storer of Whitman said she’s looking for a speaker who has experience managing groups of people and is well-versed on the rules. She said given the unicameral’s nature, it’s important to have a “real steady hand.”
“I think it’s just really important that the speaker elected, again, has exhibited the ability to be fair, to be firm, but also bring people together,” Storer said. “I don’t know that speaker is where you cut your teeth on leading a large body of folks.”
State Sens. Jana Hughes of Seward, Carolyn Bosn of Lincoln and George Dungan of Lincoln, from left, meet on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. April 2, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Carolyn Bosn of Lincoln, chair of the Legislature’s Judiciary Committee, said she’s looking for someone who can get good policy across the finish line in a way where everyone feels like they were given an opportunity to be heard.
Bosn said that with the budget and revenue bills, it will be important “having a speaker who recognizes the intricacies of everybody’s different perspectives, what perspectives people might be coming from … and being able to manage the floor with decorum and a true leader quality.”
“Sometimes the leader stands in the front, sometimes the leader stands in the back, and sometimes the leader stands next to you,” Bosn said. “And I want somebody who can do all three of those things.”



What qualities are desired in the next speaker of the Legislature?
State Sen. Eliot Bostar (Lincoln): “I am looking for a speaker who will prioritize the good order and function of the body and maintain the interests of the state and its residents as the top priority for all of us.”
State Sen. Danielle Conrad (Lincoln): “What I’m really going to be looking for is transparency, collegiality, a commitment to maintaining our strong nonpartisan unicameral legislature, a commitment to ensuring a fair-minded approach, commitment to ensuring that we the people’s branch is a co-equal, independent branch of government.”
State Sen. Stan Clouse (Kearney): “I think it will take a lot of discussion amongst the body to determine which person they feel is the right fit. Not necessarily the most qualified or the best person, but the right fit for where we want this body to go.”
State Sen. Rob Dover (Norfolk): “I would look for someone that would respect all of the various positions and be a good listener and work diplomatically to reach consensus on passing legislation.”
State Sen. Rick Holdcroft (Bellevue): “I think the new speaker needs to be able to hold the line on negotiating, be a tough negotiator and try to get some agreements to allow more legislation to pass on the floor. Otherwise, it’s going to be a very long session.”
State Sen. Mike Jacobson (North Platte): “As long as we have someone who, I believe, can bring people together, calm the waters and keep us moving forward, that’s going to be important.”
State Sen. Margo Juarez (Omaha): “I’m definitely going to think about what my experience has been the past two years, obviously. And, to me, if you didn’t display the skills then, I’m not quite confident that you’re going to have the skills going forward.”
State Sen.-elect Patty Pansing Brooks (Lincoln): “I’m looking for a good listener who is able to work across the aisle and bring people together. And I’m looking for a kind heart.”
State Sen. Dan Quick (Grand Island): “I think someone that’s going to listen to every senator and … who’s going to be able to work through all those issues and try to work with the senators who are opposing each other and then try to get it all worked out.”
State Sen. Dave Wordekemper (Fremont): “Somebody that’s open-minded to unite the body and have a common goal with both sides, because there’s not supposed to be sides, and just pass good legislation for our citizens in our state and grow our state with good legislation.”

name: WyoFile
title: Disease puts white-tailed deer on chopping block
authors: Christina MacIntosh, Jackson Hole News & Guide
description:
Wildlife managers would like to see fewer deer amid concern about chronic wasting disease
The post Disease puts white-tailed deer on chopping block appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
JACKSON—The Wyoming Game and Fish Department is in the process of shrinking the population of white-tailed deer in the Jackson region to “little to no” animals due to concern about a growing population and the spread of chronic wasting disease in northwest Wyoming.
That’s according to a departmental update on CWD delivered to the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission earlier this month.
The strategy came out of a 2020 plan from the department to manage CWD, an always-fatal, highly transmissible neurological disease in ungulates, said Sam Stephens, the department’s wildlife biologist for the South Jackson region. That plan called for trying to reduce concentrations of deer irrespective of species, but decreasing white-tailed deer populations in particular is “low-hanging fruit,” Stephens said.
“In large parts of the state, we surveyed the public about what they will tolerate in terms of CWD management actions, which are not often popular,” he said. “Aggressive white-tail harvest is one of the most supported management actions.”
In the Jackson region, wildlife managers are concerned about white-tailed deer on elk winter range, as CWD can be spread through environmental contamination from urine, feces, blood and saliva of infected animals. Wildlife managers first detected CWD in the Jackson Elk Herd in a hunter-harvested cow in 2020. The National Elk Refuge detected its first two cases last winter.
White-tailed deer abundance in northwest Wyoming has increased in recent years, Stephens said. That could be due to winters becoming more mild.
“A lot of their historic population swings have largely been governed by winter severity,” Stephens said. “Big winters knock them back.”
Game and Fish does not monitor white-tailed deer populations outside of “incidental observations” documented during other field work. Department staff collected 44 observations in the Jackson region between 2000 and 2010, which leapt to 300 between 2010 and 2020, Stephens said. Department staff have documented another 200 in the six years since.
The highest concentrations are along river bottoms, such as the Snake River between Wilson and South Park, the lower Gros Ventre River and parts of Star Valley along the Salt River, Stephens said.
“We’ve really seen that shift in population and abundance really post 2010,” he said.
Only two white-tailed deer in the Jackson region have tested positive in the past few years, Stephens said. Real prevalence could be higher as the department can only sample dead animals.
But statewide last year, white-tailed deer had the highest CWD prevalence of any big game species, with 25% testing positive, according to data presented to the commission. Twenty one percent of tested mule deer were positive and 4% of tested elk were infected.
That’s because white-tailed deer are non-migratory, occupying a 10-square-mile home range, Stephens said. Migrating buffers mule deer from disease transmission, as they use a larger landscape rather than staying concentrated in one area. Resident mule deer populations are as likely to have CWD as white-tailed deer, Stephens said.
Winning strategy?
The department has liberalized white-tailed deer in the Bighorn Basin, doubling or tripling quotas in some hunt areas and allowing the season to run all fall through December, Stephens said. It’s difficult to track the effect of those actions on CWD, as wildlife managers have to measure prevalence over a long period of time.
It’s not a bad idea to keep white-tailed populations low, said Kyle Richardson, an assistant professor of wildlife ecology at University of Montana Western. Richardson studies CWD in southwest Montana. It’s “simple disease ecology,” he said, that as populations decline, disease declines.
“Nobody wants to see white-tailed deer eradicated from an area, or elk, or anything else,” he said. “But at the moment we’re so in the dark about methods of control for this. There aren’t a whole lot of options.”
The approach is scientifically sound, but using it only on one species limits the efficacy, Richardson said. That’s particularly the case given that Game and Fish and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which manages the National Elk Refuge, continue to feed elk during the winter in northwest Wyoming. Continued feeding is strongly supported by outfitters and ranchers, though conservationists oppose the practice.
“I use your elk population in my disease ecology class to teach students what not to do,” Richardson said. “You’re inviting disease if you’re feeding wildlife.”
Changing seasons
The department started selling white-tailed deer-specific licenses, as opposed to those that can also be used for mule deer, south of Jackson in 2015 and north of Hoback in 2018.
Stephens does not anticipate a dramatic increase in licenses in the region in the immediate future. That’s because many white-tailed deer reside on private land along river bottoms, making access difficult. The department currently acts as a middleman between hunters and landowners, Stephens said. If there were more of both who were interested in decreasing white-tailed numbers, maybe the department would increase licenses.
“It wouldn’t make sense to really liberalize our harvest strategy if those licenses aren’t currently being used,” Stephens said.

name: WyoFile
title: Why did the porcupine cross the road?
description:
The persistent porky put up a fight, but a WyoFile reporter persevered in shooing the quilled rodent to safety. 
The post Why did the porcupine cross the road? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
SINKS CANYON—The shin-high rodent was seemingly unperturbed by my presence on Monday evening as I crouched down with my iPhone to snap a pic.
Quills ostensibly at the ready, the beady-eyed porcupine set his course. 
He was coming at me, advancing at perhaps a mile an hour. 
So I simply got up and moved.
Now crouching on a different part of the road near the Sinks Canyon State Park-Shoshone National Forest boundary, the porcupine pivoted. 
After the course correction, it was clear. This porcupine was the aggressor in this face-off. Little did it know, I was just hoping to get a photograph or two and then haze it from the road so it didn’t get smushed. 

After being temporarily hazed into the ditch, a porcupine circles back toward the road up Sinks Canyon. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

There’s no saying for sure it’s the same one, but social media chatter leads me to believe the bold porcupine has been hanging around Sinks Canyon for weeks. 
“We’ve also noticed similar behavior,” said Skylar Sargent, a maintenance technician at Sinks Canyon State Park. 
“It’s not what you would typically expect in a mammal,” he added. “What I’ve found in my own research is that it’s common for them to seem unafraid and unbothered by potential threats. They can’t run very fast, but their quills kind of just allow them to not care, for the most part.” 
At least on Monday night, the porcupine went beyond apathy. Some crazier behavior on my part temporarily convinced it to head for the ditch, but then it circled right back.
Eventually, after lofting some small stones its way, the animal decided it had better things to do. It scampered off the road surface and into the ditch — a safe haven with nightfall fast approaching — and that was that. 
So far, Sargent hasn’t fielded any reports from the public about the porcupine, but he shared some words of wisdom for those who do happen upon the bold animal. 
“Watch out for him on the road,” Sargent said. “And it’s a really good reason to leash your dogs. This is wildlife that your dog’s not going to know how to deal with.”

text:
Owosso residents held a vigil on Nov. 19, 2026, honoring two homeless people and a dog found dead in a tent. (Photo Erick Diaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)Tyler Beebe enjoyed taking walks around the homeless encampment in Owosso, located between South Cedar and Cass avenues, recalled 45-year-old Reanna Denter. “Are you looking for treasures? Because there are treasures everywhere,” she remembers him always saying before inviting her to go for a walk.
Denter is one of about 10 people living in the encampment where Tyler Beebe, Amy Hicks and her dog, Luna, were found dead in their tents on Nov. 16.
On Thursday afternoon, dozens gathered a short distance from the encampment for a candlelight vigil honoring Beebe, Hicks and Luna. The vigil brought together residents, volunteers, religious leaders and people who have experienced homelessness. 
Beyond remembering those who died, participants called attention to the difficulties of finding permanent housing, accessing mental health services and other social services, and surviving outdoors during Michigan’s cold months.
“There is no progress,” Nicole Bryant, 26, said. “Cities are trying to evict people who are homeless from their encampments. Lansing’s the same way. People just got removed from their campsite out there.  They’re basically putting a band-aid over a bullet hole. Some of these people just got kicked out of their house, or their house burned down, or something that they can’t even prevent.” 
“There’s a lot of hate on the homeless out here, a lot, and it’s not their fault for being homeless,” she finished.

Bryant, a friend of Beebe, who recently experienced homelessness herself, described the daily challenges of living without a permanent place to stay, including finding food, accessing showers, obtaining clean clothes, and securing a safe place to sleep. She also pointed to long waiting periods for housing assistance, estimating it could take about a year to access that support.
Bryant said Beebe had been trying to find housing but struggled to access available assistance.
The circumstances surrounding the deaths remain under investigation. Police said they found a heating source, including an unventilated propane tank, inside the tent.
In a statement shared with media outlets, City Manager Nathan Henne said the city is part of the Owosso Emergency Warming Center, participates in its organizational meetings and commits resources if necessary.
“The warming center’s most common challenge is a lack of volunteers to staff the nightly shifts,” he says. “Owosso officers routinely encourage people living outdoors to seek help from local resources, including the warming center, Homeless Angels and Jennifer’s Place. However, each provider has its own admission rules and resource limits that are difficult for some to abide by.”
And for people currently living in encampments, the need for assistance is immediate. Patty Bixby, a community volunteer with approximately 10 years of experience supporting people in need, said more resources and volunteers are necessary to address the situation.
“The needs are monetary funds and volunteering,” Bixby said. “It really takes a village to be able to help all these people. This is just one encampment. There are several in this community, and the city isn’t doing enough.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As winter approaches, the vigil served both as a memorial and a call for action.
Deanna Aldrich, 62, a community member who organized the vigil, said she wanted to bring residents together after learning about the deaths and recognizing the need for a broader community response to this issue.
“Homeless people need to have some programs in place,” Aldrich highlighted. “People say, ‘Okay, here’s where you can go get food,’ but we need some programs to help them. Maybe they don’t know how to read or write. Maybe they don’t know how to fill out an application. Maybe they don’t have a phone. Maybe they don’t have a physical address that they can use to get a job. Maybe they have a felony charge, and nobody’s going to hire them.”
“I just want people to be aware,” she added. “It’s going to start getting colder, and they’re working diligently to open the shelter and the churches overnight. But we need people. We need people to supervise that and to be willing to spend some time.”

title: After feds let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho officials unsure if they’ll take it
description: Nearly a week after federal regulators let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho health officials say they’re still deciding if they’ll take it. Last week, the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services extended the deadline for states to implement work requirements from Jan. 1 to June 30. The move came amid hurdles in several […]
text:
More than a fifth of Idahoans removed from Medicaid have since-re-enrolled, new data shows. (Getty Images)Nearly a week after federal regulators let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho health officials say they’re still deciding if they’ll take it.
Last week, the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services extended the deadline for states to implement work requirements from Jan. 1 to June 30. The move came amid hurdles in several states.
Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services

A spokesperson for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare on Wednesday said the agency is mulling its next steps.
“We just found this out on Friday and are still reviewing our options and readiness for further implementation,” agency spokesperson AJ McWhorter told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email.
The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare has been planning to implement the work requirements on Jan. 1. Under the federal “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” work requirements, also called community engagement requirements, require people enrolled in Medicaid expansion to prove that they are working, doing community service or educational or training activities for at least 80 hours each month. 
About 82,500 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicaid expansion, the state says. Medicaid work requirements and other changes in the “Big Beautiful Bill” could kick 20,000 to 34,000 Idahoans off Medicaid expansion by 2028, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. 
But in July, state health officials said their initial review found that 68,400 Idahoans on Medicaid expansion met the new work requirements. About 63% of people on Medicaid expansion across the country are working, according to KFF, a health policy research group.
If Idaho doesn’t take the six-month delay for work requirements, it wouldn’t be the first federal leniency the state passed up on this policy. The state health agency said this summer that it wouldn’t give Medicaid expansion patients who have disabilities a one-year grace period to not provide proof that their condition interferes with their ability to comply with work requirements.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Auburn University Board of Trustees to vote on new post-tenure review policy
description: The Auburn University Board of Trustees is scheduled Friday to consider new policies for post-tenure review that a faculty group calls “a fundamental restructuring of the relationship between the university and its faculty.” The change was authorized by a state law signed by Gov. Kay Ivey earlier this year that also authorized boards of trustees […]
text:
William J. Samford Hall at Auburn University in Auburn, Alabama. The Auburn University Board of Trustees is expected to consider a new post-tenure review policy during its meeting on Friday. (Photo by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Auburn University Board of Trustees is scheduled Friday to consider new policies for post-tenure review that a faculty group calls “a fundamental restructuring of the relationship between the university and its faculty.”
The change was authorized by a state law signed by Gov. Kay Ivey earlier this year that also authorized boards of trustees to disband faculty senates and drew protests at Auburn.
According to the board’s meeting materials, the university will use a four-category scale. The four categories are “exceeds expectations,” “meets expectations,” “does not meet expectations” and “unsatisfactory.” Under the policy, post-tenure review would occur at least once every six years. No faculty member could be reviewed more than once a year.
The policy states after the review is done, the dean of the college will make a recommendation to the provost who can “seek advice from an appropriate faculty advisory body or other peer review body before making a final performance rating determination.” 
After the provost assigns a performance rating, the university president “shall exercise such review, approval, or oversight of post-tenure review determinations as provided by university procedures.”
The Auburn Chapter of the American Association of University Professors said in a statement Thursday night it “unequivocally opposes” the tenure review policy.
“This policy represents a fundamental restructuring of the relationship between the university and its faculty,” the statement said. “At its core, it concentrates unprecedented authority in administrators while diminishing the role of faculty judgment and due process.”
Under the proposed policy change, professors who receive a rating of “does not meet expectations” will be referred to the provost to determine if a “Performance Improvement Plan” will be appropriate. Tenured professors who received a rating of “unsatisfactory” and can be dismissed without havinga a Performance Improvement Plan.
Previously, the University Senate conducted the post-tenure review process. The changes were authorized by HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka and signed by Gov. Kay Ivey, in April. The law led to Auburn and Jacksonville State University abolishing their faculty senates over protests from instructors at the schools. The University of Alabama and Troy University voted to maintain theirs. 
“This policy reflects a university that sees us as employees to be monitored and managed. It is what happens when trust is replaced by administrative control,” the AAUP statement said.
A petition from the United Campus Workers of Alabama, an organization that works to improve working conditions, wages and benefits for all higher education employees, exceeded its goal of 500 signatures to maintain the current post-tenure review process.

title: Tennessee campaign finance regulator to try to find the source behind $1.6M in ads over PBM bill
description: Tennessee’s campaign finance agency wants more information about the group that spent $1.6 million on ads opposing legislation that banned companies like CVS from owning both a pharmacy and a pharmacy benefit manager.  The Tennessee Registry of Election Finance will hold a show-cause hearing in January, where a representative from Shaping Health Initiative F[...]
text:
The Tennessee Registry of Election Finance is seeking information about a dark money group that ran ads during the last legislative session opposing a bill banning companies from owning both pharmacies and pharmacy benefits managers. (Photo for John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s campaign finance agency wants more information about the group that spent $1.6 million on ads opposing legislation that banned companies like CVS from owning both a pharmacy and a pharmacy benefit manager. 
The Tennessee Registry of Election Finance will hold a show-cause hearing in January, where a representative from Shaping Health Initiative For Tomorrow Inc., SHIFT, can argue why the organization shouldn’t have to disclose the donor behind its spending. 
“The idea is a representative from SHIFT can show up and make its case,” said Bill Young, the executive director of the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance.
The registry’s board made the decision following a complaint from former Tennessee Senate Republican Caucus Chair Ken Yager and an investigation by the state Attorney General’s Office that found the group had spent $1.6 million. 
The Lookout previously tracked about $500,000 of SHIFT’s spending by compiling records from the Federal Communications Commission public inspection files.
Dark money group running $500k in TV ads to oppose TN pharmacy benefit manager regulation bill

The question is whether SHIFT, by naming state senators during an election year, must appoint a treasurer, form a PAC and disclose its donors and spending under a state campaign finance reform law passed in 2022. 
SHIFT attacked state senators who supported SB 2040, a bill that banned pharmacy benefit managers from also owning pharmacies. The law effectively targets CVS Health, which is the only company in Tennessee to own both brick-and-mortar pharmacy locations and a PBM. 
CVS Health, UnitedHealth/Optum, and Cigna/Express Scripts are the three largest PBMs, controlling almost 80% of the market, according to KFF Health, an independent policy research organization.
CVS Health sued Tennessee lawmakers in May over the legislation in a case that is still pending. 
The Tennessee Registry of Election Finance has been battling several entities that have so far refused to register with the state for their election spending. 
The American Exceptionalism Institute, a nonprofit group that never registered with the campaign finance board, ran ads critical of now Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn during the 2026 campaign. A Blackburn campaign surrogate filed a separate complaint.
CVS sues Tennessee over pharmacy benefit manager monopoly law

Even when they register, dark money groups can still effectively hide their donors. 
For example. the Choose Freedom PAC, which boosted Blackburn, and another PAC called Best of Tennessee PAC, essentially hide their donors through an incorporated company.
Choose Freedom PAC is funded by Choose Freedom Inc., and Best of Tennessee PAC is funded by Best of Tennessee Inc. But registering makes it easier to track how the groups spend their money.
