title: NC school districts receive $311 million in grants as facility needs climb to $18 billion
description: Seven North Carolina school districts will receive nearly $311 million in state grants for school construction and renovation projects, the state Department of Public Instruction announced this week.  NCDPI said it received 77 applications from 46 districts, requesting nearly $2 billion in total. The money comes from a lottery-funded program created by the G[...]
text:
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)Seven North Carolina school districts will receive nearly $311 million in state grants for school construction and renovation projects, the state Department of Public Instruction announced this week. 
NCDPI said it received 77 applications from 46 districts, requesting nearly $2 billion in total. The money comes from a lottery-funded program created by the General Assembly in 2017. 
“These grants will help districts better serve students, educators and communities with healthy, safe and secure learning environments that enhance the overall quality of education across the state,” State Superintendent Maurice “Mo” Green said in a statement.
The largest award, $62 million, will go to Elizabeth City-Pasquotank Public Schools to renovate Northeastern High School, which serves students in grades six through 12. The project also includes a career and technical education center serving the district. 
Lee County Schools will receive $52 million to merge two existing campuses into a new middle school that includes a districtwide career and technical education center. 
Another four districts will each receive $42 million each to build new elementary school schools, the cap for elementary school projects. 
North Carolina school facility funding needs climb 37% to nearly $18 billion

The grants come as North Carolina school districts see a big jump in facility needs and face questions about how to pay for them, especially with a newly passed constitutional amendment on property tax limits that threatens a key way counties raise money for schools. Public schools have nearly $18 billion in projected facility needs over the next five years, a 37% increase from the 2020-21 assessment, according to a DPI survey released earlier this month. 
The report also estimates another $14.78 billion in needs for years six through 10, which brings the total projected needs over the coming decade to nearly $33 billion. Much of that spending, $9.8 billion, is for renovations, a 77% increase from the previous survey. About $6.2 billion will be needed to build new schools.
Among the seven districts receiving grants, Hoke County Schools reported the largest five-year facility needs, at about $283 million, but received a $42 million award which will go towards building a new elementary school. It’s a fraction of what’s needed, but a spokesperson said it’s a welcome relief in a district where four of the eight elementary schools were built between 1945 and 1957. 
“While this funding addresses a significant priority, substantial needs remain across the school system, including classroom additions, renovations, and improvements to mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and other building systems,” a district spokesperson said.
Bertie County Schools, which reported about $41 million in facility repair needs, received a $42 million grant for a new elementary school. A district spokesperson said it will not address needs at Bertie Early College, Bertie High School or Bertie Middle School.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Street gangs and mobsters want money — and social media stardom, panel says
description: Organized crime has embraced the technology age, with gang members and mobsters alike serving police up clues on social media.
text:
Organized crime has embraced the technology age, with gang members and mobsters alike serving up clues on social media to cops tracking and investigating them. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso / New Jersey Monitor)While some see public health perils in social media, crime investigators see clues.
Police have increasingly hopped online to mine social media to investigate, track, and contain organized crime in New Jersey, because even street gangs and mobsters want to be influencers, a panel of investigators testified in Trenton Thursday.
Gang members rap about their latest lawbreaking feats in reels posted to Instagram, TikTok, and other platforms, while a whole podcast genre has sprung up featuring street toughs dropping intel and aging mafiosos reminiscing about life in La Cosa Nostra, officers told the New Jersey State Commission of Investigation.
The watchdog agency convened the three-hour hearing at the Statehouse to hear how street and motorcycle gangs, the mob, and other organized crime groups have evolved in recent years. Technology was a recurring theme, as investigators recounted all the ways modern criminals have gone digital.
“Members of one of these neighborhood gangs will go and commit a crime, commit a shooting, and as crazy as this might sound, go and make a song about it and post it on social media, identifying themselves as the one who committed the crime, talk about individuals that they’ve shot at, mentioning individuals that they’re having these disagreements, or we would call it a beef, in the street,” said Capt. Erik Hoffman of the New Jersey State Police.
The videos and podcasts have helped keep crime investigators current on gang slang, like “drilling” (shooting someone) and “bipping” (breaking into or stealing cars), said Cheryl Annese, an intelligence agent with the Camden County Prosecutor’s Office.
They’ve also helped police track where gang members are, while the gangs have used social media to build clout, recruit new members, and warn off rivals, panelists said.
“In addition to being able to brag about the conquests that gang members have on the street, they’re also able to exploit these videos as tools to promote the gang,” said Joseph Procopio, a detective with the Atlantic County Prosecutor’s Office. “What we see in a lot of these videos are weapons, a lot of weapons. That not only is a factor that helps gain membership within the gang, but it’s also used to display their firearms against their rivals.”
Violence is down statewide, with Hoffman projecting shootings would fall below 500 this year. That would be a record low since statewide tracking of gun violence began in 2009. But gangs’ growing use of social media has implications there, because investigators have tied some gang violence directly to social media, Procopio said.
“When it’s displayed on social media, it is consumable by a much larger audience, and so it makes the disrespect factor that much greater,” Procopio said. “I’ve also personally investigated shootings that were precipitated by posts on social media.”
Thursday’s hearing came six months after the commission hosted a similar hearing in May. Testimony in the spring focused on organized crime in North Jersey, while panelists Thursday talked mostly about South Jersey.
But some trends persist no matter where in the state criminals operate — motorcycle gangs are expanding, youth who join gangs are getting younger, gang members who go to jail or prison strengthen gang ties and ideology there, and profit motives trump loyalty or anything else, panelists said.
South Jersey, with all the casinos crowded along the shore, has particular problems with organized crime relying on illegal gambling to build its illicit wealth, panelists said.
The mob historically focused on illegal gambling and loansharking. New Jersey’s legalization of sports betting in 2018 unintentionally renewed that opportunity for organized crime, said Brian Bruton, an investigative agent with the commission.
Legal betting sites like FanDuel and DraftKings require bettors to pay money up front, and they’re regulated, with rules requiring bettors to be 21 or older and declare winnings on tax filings, said Detective Sgt. Michael Gallant of the New Jersey State Police. Illegal bookies prey on people who don’t want to follow those rules or have run out of money, he added.
“You have casual bettors that are betting with the legal bookmaking operations, but then you have some serious addicts that are betting with the illegal bookmaking operations,” Bruton said.
Brian Bruton, a special agent and investigator with the State Commission of Investigation, speaks during a public hearing on organized crime in New Jersey on May 19, 2026, at the Statehouse in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Idaho nonprofit Envision provides the gift of sight and hearing
description: Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision, figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss. Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way. “I’ve […]
text:
Idaho nonprofit Envision helps provide eye exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. (Photo by Getty Images)Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision, figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss.
Jay Lugo is the executive director of Envision, an Idaho 501(c)(3) nonprofit that receives hundreds of inquires a month about help with vision care and eye exams. (Photo courtesy of Envision)
Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way.
“I’ve seen people break down and cry when they put on a pair of glasses and discover they are able to see,” Lugo says. “It fills my heart with joy being able to do that – and I sleep well at night knowing that we are making a difference. But it’s not just me. It’s the volunteers and office co-workers who see that happen, and the 1,400 Lions Club members throughout the state who get information about what’s being done. So, a lot of people are involved.”
And Lance Grady of Boise is glad for that. He didn’t break down in tears when he recently was fitted with glasses, but he did look across a street and see a squirrel climbing a tree. And he could see letters, numbers and names on buildings.
“I wouldn’t have been able to see any of that without my glasses,” he said. “This has been life changing. I can drive and do other things that I was unable to do.”
Grady’s story began by word of mouth.
“A family friend talked with me about reaching out to the Lions,” he said. “They were determined to help me find something – without spending $400 for a pair of glasses. “I’m so thankful … a lot of stress has been lifted from me.”
Lugo has seen similar stories play out many times.
“When people are able to see, they can get a driver’s license, fill out a job application and be productive,” Lugo says. “There is such a big gap with healthcare, and we’re only talking about eyesight and hearing. The state doesn’t provide aid with eyeglasses for those over the age of 18, so you are not going to get eyecare assistance if you are at the poverty level.”
Envision helps fill the void, providing exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and Lugo says demand is high.
“I get at least 20 applications in my email box every day, which is about 600 a month,” he says. “Every one of those are from people who need glasses and are at the poverty level. There are a lot of people who are hurting.”
Envision started in 1969 as Idaho’s only eye bank and arranging corneal transplants remain a big part of the nonprofit’s operation – along with the tradition of collecting and refurbishing used eyeglasses. People throughout the state can drop off glasses at the Division of Motor Vehicles, Walmart opticals and local optometry offices.
“It’s important to note that November is National Donate Eye Month,” Lugo says. “As I’ve seen first-hand, Idaho is a giving state with the nation’s largest registry per capita. Idaho is at 62 percent, and the national average is around 38 percent.”
Envision has opened a retail operation that is available to people throughout Idaho.
“This gives us a sustainable source of revenue, beyond grants,” he said. “People still will get glasses at a free or discounted rate, but we’ll be able to provide something else. All people need to do is download a prescription and we can ship directly to those living in Idaho, or the United States.”
Donations – large and small — will continue to be crucial to Envision’s success. The nonprofit receives no state or federal funding.
“Every $50 donated provides an eye exam with a pair of glasses,” Lugo says. “Every $200 donated provides a hearing aid. Every $100 donated restores eyesight to someone that suffers from corneal blindness.”
It doesn’t take much to make a big difference in someone’s quality of life.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Tennessee Senate speaker candidate flipped on his head
description: Tennessee Sen. Paul Bailey thought he had the votes lined up to capture the Senate speaker’s job in a head-to-head battle with Sen. Jack Johnson until people started flipping. Bailey needed 14 supporters to win the Senate Republican Caucus election, as a protest candidate of sorts in a fractured caucus to replace outgoing Speaker Randy […]
text:
Tennessee Republican state Sens. Paul Bailey, left,  and Jack Johnson, right, both thought they had the votes to be nominated as Senate Speaker by their GOP colleagues. Johnson won, but neither man was write about the votes they got. (Photos by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Sen. Paul Bailey thought he had the votes lined up to capture the Senate speaker’s job in a head-to-head battle with Sen. Jack Johnson until people started flipping.
Bailey needed 14 supporters to win the Senate Republican Caucus election, as a protest candidate of sorts in a fractured caucus to replace outgoing Speaker Randy McNally and become first in line to succeed the governor.
“I touched base with all 15 that had originally, verbally committed to me. I talked to every one of them Monday through Tuesday morning to make sure they were all sticking. I walked in there thinking I had 15,” Bailey said.
But alas, the outsiders would remain on the sidelines. 
Johnson might have thought he had more votes, too, as many as 17. But neither he nor Bailey garnered as many as they thought they would, though Johnson came out ahead with what is believed to be a 15-12 count in the 27-member caucus, according to multiple sources.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The caucus allowed Sen. Brent Taylor to vote by proxy and Sen. Kerry Roberts to vote absentee. Roberts, who told the Lookout he supported Johnson from the outset, was in his Cordell Hull office teaching an online accounting course. Taylor had to go to Washington, D.C. for organizational meetings after winning the 9th Congressional District race over Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson.
Initially, caucus leaders wanted to let Taylor vote by proxy without checking in with the rest of the Republican senators. Word has it they even tried a dry run to D.C. and back to see if Taylor could do both, but eventually they let the caucus decide whether to allow his attorney to vote for him, all in the name of transparency.
The caucus election is important because, with a supermajority, Republicans determine the speaker, who also serves as lieutenant governor, next in line if the governor is incapacitated or otherwise unable to serve.
The die is cast, but Bailey and Johnson are still trying to figure out who misled them and voted for the other.
Incoming Sen. Jimmy Matlock, a former Knoxville House member taking over McNally’s Senate seat, told the Lookout he talked to McNally every day during the caucus election time frame, so often that he couldn’t recall whether McNally encouraged him to vote for Johnson instead of Bailey.
“He liked both of them, and he and I hardly even mentioned that,” Matlock said. “No, he didn’t pressure me at all. He gave me some thoughts, of course, and I think he had good rapport with both men, and he certainly shared with me his excitement that either one of them could win.”
McNally was expected to stay out of the race after his favorite, Sen. Ferrell Haile of Gallatin, stepped out of the contest.
McNally told the Lookout last week that he didn’t try to influence the speaker’s race outcome. A spokesperson did not respond this week when asked to confirm again that McNally sat on the sidelines.
That’s not exactly what these walls are saying. Of course, this is what happens when you depend on politicians to keep their word.
Looking in the classifieds
Tennessee’s Bureau of Ethics and Campaign Finance is looking for a new chief following Bill Young’s decision to step down from the post at the end of the year.
Young notified the state’s Ethics Commission and Registry of Election Finance this week he is retiring Dec. 31 and recommended assistant director Lance Frizzell take his spot. 
After a great deal of groveling at a joint meeting of the two groups, including comments about Frizzell’s past job as chief of staff for former Republican Senate Speaker Ron Ramsey, they decided to advertise the job for the sake of “transparency.” Frizzell, who they said has shown no signs of party or political favoritism over seven years, will work as interim director following Young’s departure until the joint boards make a permanent hire.
As interim, Frizzell will receive a pay increase. But as Registry board members noted, based on the rate of inflation, Young is making less than he was seven years ago despite pay increases that have pushed his salary to about $205,000 annually. (Everyone feels his pain.)
Because of the holidays and length of time it will take to wade through an expected onslaught of applications, interviews and meetings, it could be mid-March before they make a hire.
Young, 70, a former judge and BlueCrossBlueShield executive who sought the state’s attorney general post, hinted that he has another opportunity in the offing. But while he couldn’t talk about it, he isn’t likely to go too far.
One more “copper cent” coming up
At the risk of sounding repetitive, this column has reported multiple times that former state Rep. Joe Towns once said he wouldn’t pay one more “copper cent” to the Registry for campaign finance report shortcomings.
Despite those words, Towns wound up forking over $22,000 in a settlement fee after the board reduced penalties totaling $66,000 in an email vote taken as the COVID pandemic struck in 2020.
Towns, who was elected criminal court clerk in Memphis this summer, had to eat those words six years ago. And it appears he might have to dole out some cash again.
Former state Rep. Joe Towns, who left the legislature after being elected Shelby County Court Clerk in August, racked up $10,500 in fines from the Tennessee Bureau of Ethics and Campaign Finance for errors in his campaign finance reports. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The Registry board has levied a total of $10,500 in penalties against Towns for failing to file a corrected campaign finance report and for two late reports. It also set hearings this week on two other reporting failures. 
Towns is clearly handcuffed when it comes to filling out computer reports, something every lawmaker has to do. But he also took the stance over the years that it made no sense for the Registry to penalize him heavily for raising money to run for a position that paid so little, an average of about $22,000 over the past 20 years.
Unfortunately for Towns, his discrepancies have become a tradition. But unlike his appearance before the Registry in 2020 when he referred to himself as the “prodigal son,” shortly after Young took the director’s post, Towns hasn’t shown up at any meetings to plead his case. Maybe he just doesn’t have one anymore. Yet he does have a decent-paying job with no shortage of clients in Memphis’ criminal court.
Recycled again
Blackburn made an interesting pick this week when she selected Josh Smith to run the Department of Correction. He stepped down in August from the Federal Bureau of Prisons, and he served a five-year prison term after pleading guilty to conspiring to possess and distribute cocaine and pot in 1998. 
Blackburn noted in her release that he had “firsthand experience” that would help him in the new role. We’re not sure whether that means he knows how inmates try to game the system or whether he knows how to run a prison.
Tennessee governor picks former fed prison official, inmate to lead Correction Department

Otherwise, Blackburn’s cabinet appointments have been somewhat mundane. 
Marie Williams will remain as commissioner of the Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services, and Stephen Smith will keep running TennCare, the state’s Medicaid program. Likewise, former state Rep. Andy Holt will continue as Agriculture Department commissioner, because everyone loves him, and Mark Ezell will keep serving as commissioner of Tourist Development. Gov. Bill Lee once said he wakes up every morning thinking about Tennessee tourism, so Ezell must be really popular. (This is not made up.)
Michael Hendrix, a policy director in Bill Lee’s administration, will be Blackburn’s chief of staff, possibly because he’s never heard a question he wouldn’t answer.
Todd Kaestner, a Tennessee Board of Regents member, will head up Finance and Administration, giving hope that he’ll add life to budget presentations, if they still hold them. We’ll find out in January.
“Don’t look back / A new day is breaking” *

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Group to ask West Virginia lawmakers for $16.5 million in anti-smoking efforts
description: An organization that advocates for anti-cancer policies says they’ll ask West Virginia lawmakers for an increase in funding anti-tobacco efforts during the 2027 legislative session.
text:
The American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network plans to ask for lawmakers to earmark $16.5 million for tobacco prevention for anti-smoking campaigns in 2027. (Photo by Douglas Sacha/Getty Images)An organization that advocates for anti-cancer policies says they’ll ask West Virginia lawmakers for an increase in funding anti-tobacco efforts during the 2027 legislative session. 
Doug Hogan, government relations director for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network in West Virginia, said the organization plans to ask for lawmakers and Gov. Patrick Morrisey to have $16.5 million earmarked for tobacco prevention. The funding would be used over several years on anti-smoking efforts. 
West Virginia has the highest smoking rate in the country, at 17.8% and the second highest rate of new lung cancer cases, according to a report released this week by the American Lung Association.  
West Virginia has among the highest rates of smoking-related cancers in the country, according to the state Department of Health. 
“We think that we can really make significant strides and lower those usage rates for West Virginians with an increase in the amount of allocations and investments that we have in those programs,” Hogan said. 
The $16.5 million amount comes from a recommendation made by a previous governor’s task force related to anti-smoking efforts, Hogan said. 
During the 2026 legislative session, the American Cancer Society advocated for legislation allocating a portion of the state’s settlement from the vape manufacturer Juul toward youth anti-smoking efforts.
Lawmakers passed and Morrisey signed House Bill 5691, which allocated $2.9 million from the state’s $7.9 million Juul settlement toward youth tobacco prevention and prevention programs. Juul settled with the state in 2023 over allegations it marketed products to underage users, according to reporting by the Associated Press.
Due to technical issues, the state has not legally committed the $2.9 million from the Juul settlement, and the funding is currently in a surplus budget account, Hogan said. 
“So, again, we’re calling on the governor to reauthorize, if you will, that Juul money, so that those Juul funds will be directed to tobacco control and can be used for youth tobacco prevention, that would go to combat the ill effects of Juul targeting youth with e-cigarettes and other products from years ago.”
Thursday marks the 50th anniversary of the American Cancer Society’s Great American Smoke Out, an annual event that aims to encourage smokers to take the step of starting to quit, bolstered by the moral support of many others across the country. 
“Basically we look at the Great American Smoke Out as a day for people to make a plan to quit, make that plan, and then follow through with that plan for tomorrow, the next week, next month, for the following year,” Hogan said. “But we’re very excited about it again because it is the 50th year. It’s a milestone that offers us the opportunity to celebrate five decades of progress against tobacco, while confronting growing concerns as well.”
A report released this week by the American Cancer Society indicates that smoking cigarettes is gaining appeal on social media platforms, with a particular focus on women and girls. 
“(The report) finds that the toxic smoking aesthetic is making cigarettes seem appealing to a new generation of young women and girls, primarily, while concealing the harm,” Hogan said. “This is a very troubling trend that we’re seeing, and one certainly that we ill be devoting additional resources to combating. 
“We want to get the word out that this is a negative trend that we’re seeing out there in the social media realm, especially when it comes to young women and girls,” he said. 
The legislative session starts Jan. 13, 2027.

title: Alabama Public Library Service Board installs new chair, seeks new director
description: The Alabama Public Library Service Board Thursday elected Amy Minton, a board member who helped lead efforts to restrict library materials for minors, as its new chair. Minton will replace John Wahl, who was elected Alabama lieutenant governor earlier this month. “I am thrilled, honored and humbled to be chair,” Minton said in an interview […]
text:
Former Alabama Public Library Service Board Chair John Wahl, left, and current APLS Chair Amy Minton, right, listen to a speaker at its meeting on Nov. 19, 2026 in Montgomery, Alabama. The board voted to make Minton the new chair of the board and seek a new director. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Public Library Service Board Thursday elected Amy Minton, a board member who helped lead efforts to restrict library materials for minors, as its new chair.
Minton will replace John Wahl, who was elected Alabama lieutenant governor earlier this month.
“I am thrilled, honored and humbled to be chair,” Minton said in an interview with the media following the meeting. “I look forward to working with all the public libraries. Reading has always been a passion of mine. As the parent of two grown children now, we lived in public libraries, so I look forward to helping the public libraries.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Minton has led efforts to restrict specific library materials from minors, particularly those with transgender characters or themes or so-called “gender ideology,” which the board has not defined. Board members said the moves were an attempt to remove what they considered obscene or sexually explicit books. Critics have said the moves are an attempt to censor literature with LGBTQ+ themes or characters.
In 2024, board members required libraries to adopt policies to prevent minors from having access to what they considered inappropriate books. In November 2025, the board approved a policy introduced by Minton banning materials with transgender and “gender ideology” from youth sections in libraries.
Three authors and Read Freely Alabama, a freedom of speech organization that opposes the APLS Board restrictions, filed a lawsuit earlier this month against the ban, alleging it violated the First Amendment.
Members also unanimously voted to post the library director’s position that Kelyn Ralya currently occupies after four of the seven members gave her an unsatisfactory rating. One abstained, another gave her a satisfactory review while another rated her as excellent.
Wahl and others declined to comment on the specific reasons for giving her an unsatisfactory rating. Rayla was not terminated, but board members said they wanted to find other potential applicants.
“The director’s job requires an extensive skill set, and it is a difficult position,” said APLS board member Kasandra Stevens, who led a subcommittee evaluating Ralya’s performance. “I think it would be important to put it out there for 30 days, get the listing within the next week, and put it out for 30 days and see if we can get applications.”
Rayla assumed the post after Minton led a board effort to remove former Director Nancy Pack in March 2025.
If APLS hires a new director, Rayla would return to her prior post as the assistant director of APLS and oversee the Library Services and Technology Act (LSTA) federal grants that APLS administers. The Board is looking to fill the post in January.
Rayla told the Board during Thursday’s meeting that “she appreciated the opportunity,” but that she did not imagine herself in the position long term.
She also told the Board Thursday that she delayed appointing an assistant to be a resource for local libraries to comply with the administrative code changes. The appointment power belongs to the director, and Rayla said during the meeting in August that she decided not to fill the position.
Minton and Wahl said they wanted that position filled to support libraries. During the meeting in August, Minton alleged that she found books in the children’s sections that should be prohibited by reviewing the catalog of libraries. She did not identify the specific libraries.
Several parents spoke during the public participation portion of the board meeting in September to urge the agency to hire someone to assist libraries with complying with changes to the administrative code.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Jasmyne Crimiel expresses excitement, outlines goals for upcoming legislative session
description: Jasmyne Crimiel says she’s not sure what to expect in her first session in the Alabama House of Representatives. But she’s looking forward to it.  “I do think that there is some uncertainty, but uncertainty is okay. I think that there’s a lot of power that we do have,” said Crimiel, a Democrat elected earlier […]
text:
Jasmyne Crimiel, D-Montgomery, won election to Alabama House District 74. (photo courtesy of candidate) 
 New members
This is part of an ongoing series profiling the Alabama Legislature’s freshman lawmakers.


Jasmyne Crimiel says she’s not sure what to expect in her first session in the Alabama House of Representatives. But she’s looking forward to it. 
“I do think that there is some uncertainty, but uncertainty is okay. I think that there’s a lot of power that we do have,” said Crimiel, a Democrat elected earlier this month to represent House District 74 in Montgomery. “There were a lot of seats that were flipped. I think that there were a lot of seats that you know we were able to maintain, just like mine. So I’m very excited about what’s to come.”
Crimiel, a lawyer and nonprofit owner, received 12,239 (73.9%) votes in unofficial returns, according to the Alabama Secretary of State’s office. Republican nominee Alva Lambert received 4,315 (26%) votes.
Crimiel said she wants to focus on supporting public education and mental health in schools. 
“I just want to make sure that our teachers are getting a pay increase, and I’m supporting that,” Crimiel said. “And also, mental health in our children has been something that has been talked about, and it has been something that has been spoken about and addressed during prior legislative sessions.”
The district, which covers east Montgomery, was held by Republicans until Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, flipped the seat in 2022, following redistricting that made it friendlier to Democrats. It was the first Democratic flip of a Republican-held seat in the Alabama Legislature since 2010.
Ensler, who left the seat to run for Alabama lieutenant governor, said in an interview Friday that he was “confident that (Crimiel) will do a great job.”
“She’s in touch with the issues that matter most to people in the district, and that’s everything from having access to affordable healthcare to good quality public schools to safe neighborhoods,” he said. “And I know she’s focused on helping continue to deliver solutions that address those issues, and she has a great attitude about going into it. And I’m excited about what she’s going to do.”
Crimiel said because of her background in law, she would like to serve on the Judiciary, Public Safety and Homeland Security and County and Municipal Government committees.
“(For a) majority of my legal career, I was a prosecutor, and I prosecuted cases involving sexual assault, the things that keep you up in like human trafficking, everything like that. And now I’ve switched a little bit in my legal career, and I do civil litigation,” she said. “But I say all that to say I want to go where my strengths are. I want to go where I know that I can be an asset and where I know that I will have great impact.”
The Alabama Legislature will convene on Feb. 2.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: Thurmond’s real fight is over money, not demolition
description: The arranged marriage between the National Park Service and the residents of Fayette County, West Virginia, still has plenty of issues to work out.
text:
The commercial district was where the majority of businesses operated in Thurmond, West Virginia. (Photo by Louise McLaughlin/National Park Service)Most marriages fail over fights involving money. While not the most common daily fight, arguments over money last longer, cause more damage, and become one of the leading indicators or relationship discord.
The arranged marriage between the National Park Service and the residents of Fayette County, West Virginia still has plenty of issues to work out. While “preservation” is the topic at hand between the feds and locals, money is the issue. Since there will be no divorce between the NPS and local residents of the New River Gorge National Park and Preserve and surrounding area, finding a way to make this relationship work is the only alternative to perpetual drama. And since the federal government is going to win just about every argument when it comes down to it, constant fighting is going to limit what little say local residents have. 
Case in point, and suddenly on the radar of influencers and social media accounts, is the current situation in Thurmond, West Virginia. Especially the train station and downtown store fronts of Commercial Row that have graced pictures, films and visitors for over a century. Part of the National Park Service since the New River Gorge was declared a National River, and now National Park and Preserve, Thurmond is mostly owned by the NPS. Two things happen in parallel when the federal government owns places like Thurmond: Nobody can do anything to preserve anything without the government’s say so and permission, and the government can only preserve what it has funding to preserve. 
Words like “preservation” and “historical” make lovely nomenclature, but are not magic spells. 
Back in 2009, funding was set aside and some restoration and preservation work was done in Thurmond. By 2022, the intervening years of wear and tear combined with some good, old-fashioned vandalism was really starting to show again. What any property manager, historic preservation folks, or anyone who has ever tried to maintain any kind of property knows was self-evident in Thurmond. Occupy and use is the most effective method of preserving a structure; if it isn’t used and occupied, time and nature is most effective in destroying it. The NPS suggested demolishing some of the outlying and more decayed structures so they could focus resources on and maintain the core of Thurmond — Commercial Row, and certain other structures. Locals pushed back, and the demolitions were pushed back.
The current cycle of decay, fund, restore, repeat involves a large splash of federal cash from the Great American Outdoors Act. The NPS has put out a detailed plan wanting to fix up Commercial Row “to preserve historic homes, modernize water and wastewater systems, and improve site features throughout the district.” Part of the plan is still the demolition of some structures, but quite a few have been given a reprieve, for now. 
Notable among the structures off the demo list is the Dun Glen Ark. The two story wooden structure that looks exactly like what it is called sits roughly on the site of the infamous Dunglen Hotel. Before a 1930 fire that burned it to ground and the ensuing years where the two word name of the place became one, the hotel had 100 rooms, a 24/7 bar and gambling hall and notorious stories of various partying and debauchery since it was across the river from dry and respectable Thurmond. The only partying the Ark sees these days is the recreational kind by rafters and boaters using the adjacent river, and by generations of area youths who know a good meet up, hook up and party up spot when they need one.
The NPS version of sparing the Dun Glen structures is offering leases for use. The ark is safe, but the boat rack and other structures are “lease or destroy.” There are still other structures in the area under NPS ownership slated for demolition. The locals are not happy. There are meetings, protests, social media posts, influencer involvement and threats of legal action. Screaming headlines like this one from Yahoo, “US National Park Bulldozes Historic Town Despite Local Protests,” are pretty misleading. While some of the structures in Thurmond proper are being removed, the part of Thurmond most people picture-and most pictures of Thurmond depict-Commercial Row is what will be restored with the refocused resources. 
While residents and everyone else have a right to voice their opinions as they see fit, the kerfuffle over the demolitions and attempts to stop them are the wrong fight to have if you are truly interested in the long term preservation of Thurmond and the New River Gorge. It costs nothing to show up on social media and meetings after the heavy equipment is allocated to get to work. It costs money, resources, and constant attention to maintain these structures in the years between outrages and funding pushes. 
Despite the rhetoric, both sides of the preservation fight have valid points. Locals who complain that it was the NPS who let the structures slated for demolition fall into disrepair in the first place aren’t wrong. The NPS pointing out funding is finite and focusing on the big ticket, Instagram ready parts of attractions like Thurmond and the water, retaining walls, and upgrades needed to please the increasing crowds of park visitors must be the priority are not wrong either. Plus, the NPS operating budget has faced flat budgeting and personnel cuts for the actual running of things separate from special legislation like the GAOA funding. 
Even the loudest voices against demolition should concede not every building everywhere can be a museum. The leasing program will give one argument or the other a strong data point: if there really is a need and want to preserve and use these structures, the application process is there ready and waiting. We will see if any of the loud voices online who demand usage put their names to paper and start using. 
Even with the more than $30 million in improvements, time is undefeated and at some point those improvements will need to be renovated again. Preservation and historic are too often used as magic words that folks think will mean whatever they are applied to stays that way forever. But preservation costs money. Places on the demolition lists like the Prince Brothers store 20 miles from Thurmond in Prince, West Virginia will pass into history. Commercial Row in Thurmond will be retained. The difference for good, bad or indifference is money. And twenty years from now, the metric of was it worth it to preserve it will be answered in attendance, operational budgets, lease agreements and funding for continued preservation. Money will tell the truth of the thing. The NPS and local resident relationship will greatly depend on how everyone handles not only this allocation of funding but the management between now and the next funding crisis. Marriages, arranged or otherwise, aren’t easy …or cheap.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Brown students take to the streets to help Rhode Islanders navigate Medicaid changes
description: The interior of Frog & Toad’s Westminster Street location is a busy piece of scenery, furnished with knickknacks, decorations, mementos and rows of blind box toys waiting to be revealed. Aidan Choi and Alexa Pupillo walked into the Providence gift shop Wednesday afternoon with a stack of flyers containing another kind of density: Information about […]
text:
Brown University public health graduate students Alexa Pupillo, left, and Aidan Choi approach Colombia Auto Service on Westminster Street in Providence on Nov. 18, 2026, to distribute information about upcoming changes to Medicaid. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The interior of Frog & Toad’s Westminster Street location is a busy piece of scenery, furnished with knickknacks, decorations, mementos and rows of blind box toys waiting to be revealed. 
Aidan Choi and Alexa Pupillo walked into the Providence gift shop Wednesday afternoon with a stack of flyers containing another kind of density: Information about the federal changes coming to Medicaid. Could they maybe add one more thing to the vista of merchandise? 
“I realize you guys have so much cool stuff going on already, or like hung up,” Choi told the shop’s co-owner Erin Schofield, “But we have some flyers it could be helpful for folks to have if there’s an area that you think would make sense…I think this is the most important one because it has all the timelines. It’s a little dense. I’m sorry.”
Schofield actually thought it was “awesome,” and agreed with a smile, pointing to an area where community flyers go up.
“Leave us one, and we’ll put it right on the wall,” Schofield said. 
Choi and Pupillo and seven other Brown University public health graduate students are participating in a two-year initiative to educate Rhode Islanders and help them navigate federal changes to Medicaid, the joint state and federal health insurance program for people with low incomes. 
Some of these changes already took effect on Oct. 1, including new restrictions on eligibility for noncitizens. Work requirements coming Jan. 1 are expected to impact more people, but Rhode Island is currently weighing whether it will take advantage of the six-month extension period the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Nov. 13. 
“For our work, we’d welcome that,” Choi said of the possible reprieve. “The process of even applying to Medicaid, even before changes, is very complex. … This delay period is nice for us to be able to help people understand it better.”
Regardless of when the work requirements ultimately take effect, Choi said that “people will have to adapt to this new system” at some point. 
The fellowship is a joint effort between Brown’s People, Place, and Health Collective and the state’s Medicaid program, with both parties announcing the partnership during an Oct. 14 event at Brown. 
The first part of the fellows’ work is canvassing. They trek neighborhoods across Providence twice weekly, equipped with stacks of educational flyers and handouts that relay — in nine languages, from English and Spanish to Creole and Khmer — the changes coming to Medicaid. 
On Wednesday afternoon, Choi and three other fellows stopped at nearly every business on a roughly half-mile stretch of Westminster Street, and found success at each of the half-dozen or so storefronts, leaving flyers hanging on bulletin boards, taped to windows, or at a busy eye doctor’s office, in the hands of a front desk clerk who said she would ask her boss. 
“People are pretty willing to put up information,” Choi said. “We’re not selling anything. We’re just trying to keep folks informed.”
The second part of their work consists of what they call “drop-ins” at established community organizations and health care facilities, where they serve as certified application counselors and can help people apply for or renew their insurance. 
“The goal is that people have a place to find us and that we become familiar faces rather than flyers,” Choi said at the kickoff event.
Charlie Merrick, a research assistant who helps coordinate the fellows’ activities, said in an email Thursday that the students have covered a lot of ground since they started in October. They’ve visited roughly 75 businesses, distributed more than 850 flyers and helped more than 120 people directly at drop-in sites, Merrick said.
The fellows are paid $23 an hour for 10 hours of work each week, according to Abdullah Shihipar, a research associate at Brown’s People, Place, and Health Collective. 
Choi has previously organized and canvassed on tenant and immigrant rights issues in Providence, and these experiences helped him to learn the uniqueness of each of the city’s neighborhoods. The fellows first sought out “areas with a high density of folks that may be impacted by those non-citizen changes,” and have since moved on to prioritize broader outreach over the work requirements.
This broader fieldwork calls for a level of comfort in talking to a wide variety of strangers, as demonstrated by their Wednesday outing. Only one of the four identified as a fluent Spanish speaker: Mikel Lacroix, also the only Rhode Island native in the group that day.
On their final stop, Lacroix and Kensie Fosko split from Choi and Pupillo to tackle two businesses at once. Choi and Pupillo, both who claim just working familiarity with Spanish, decided to canvass an auto shop, Colombia Auto Service. 
“If you need me, just yell across the street,” Lacroix joked.
Choi and Pupillo nevertheless engaged in a roughly 10-minute conversation with an auto shop owner that ranged from health insurance to her teenaged daughter’s own career aspirations in public health, as well as a question about where a customer might obtain health insurance. Before they left, the owner had moved aside a display of windshield wipers so Pupillo could tape the flyer to the window.
What the fellows don’t do while traversing across Providence, Choi noted, is ask people about their Medicaid status. 
“We want to walk the line of privacy well, while also being able to clarify with people if they do have questions that they can email us,” he said.
Brown University public health graduate students Kensie Fosko, left, and Mikel Lacroix share a laugh as Lacroix displays flyers detailing federal changes to Medicaid on Westminster Street in Providence on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Navigating new restrictions
Big changes to Medicaid eligibility first rolled in on Oct. 1, one of the lasting shockwaves from the sweeping federal tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed into law in July 2025. Those revisions affected eligibility for refugees, asylees and people with several other immigration statuses. 
An earlier estimate from state officials counted fewer than 3,500 noncitizens who would possibly be affected. Ultimately, there were fewer than 2,000 people in Rhode Island deemed ineligible for coverage, Kerri White, a spokesperson for the Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services, said in an email Thursday. 
Pupillo said that during drop-in duty at the refugee-focused nonprofit Dorcas International, she has helped people explore alternative insurance options on the state’s health insurance marketplace.
“But frankly, all the premiums are too expensive, so the next best option after that is trying to refer them to free care,” Pupillo said, adding that free clinics “are going to be very heavily impacted by the changes. 
“They’re already preparing for even longer wait times.” 
Pupillo said she’s also encountered Medicaid beneficiaries who have lost their insurance cards or are having difficulty accessing their accounts. And the street team occasionally encounters someone with lots of questions or interest, particularly around access to dental care, she said.
The changes scheduled for Jan. 1 dictate that certain adults ages 19 to 64 enrolled in Medicaid expansion programs will need to demonstrate that they work, volunteer or participate in other qualifying activities for at least 80 hours a month, attend school half-time, or meet an income threshold. There are exemptions for some groups, including the medically frail. Some beneficiaries will also be required to renew their coverage twice a year, instead of annually. 
There are about 66,000 adults enrolled through Rhode Island’s Medicaid expansion program, White said in her email, while noting that many of these recipients “may already be completing activities that meet the work requirement criteria or may qualify for one of several exemptions.” 
But these changes may still be delayed if the state opts to delay the work requirements through June 30, 2027. Beneficiaries’ compliance would still be evaluated during this time, but recipients’ coverage would not be terminated or denied.
White said that the state is assessing the temporary reprieve as well as a possible good faith waiver extension which derives from a recent court decision concerning the medical frailty exemption.
Brown University public health graduate student Alexa Pupillo posts a Spanish-language flyer detailing federal changes to Medicaid in the window of Colombia Auto Service on Westminster Street in Providence on Nov. 18, 2026. The university’s Medicaid fellows distribute educational materials in nine languages. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Closing the information gap
Nebraska can illustrate what work requirements look like in practice: The Cornhusker State gradually began instituting the work requirements in May, first applying them to new applicants that month.
A September analysis by KFF of the early Nebraska data showed that there were 533 Medicaid coverage losses in July and August tied to work requirements. Of these losses, 92% involved recipients who would have renewed their insurance but failed to verify requests for their work information. Only 8% were found to be affirmatively noncompliant. 
States have also been experimenting with the best ways to reach residents about impending changes to Medicaid, such as statewide informational tours in Montana and New Mexico, according to a July report from KFF.
But Shihipar at ​​Brown’s People, Place, and Health Collective said he was unaware of initiatives in other states that enlist students for Medicaid outreach like Brown does.
The fellows have also been learning from their fieldwork excursions. Pupillo said public health practitioners’ work is “often an unseen service,” and that the general populace doesn’t “see public health in their everyday life.”
“When you’re talking to people who are unaware of the Medicaid changes or confused by them, it reminds you the importance of having public health people out there actually helping people directly, and connecting this sometimes very nebulous field to their everyday lives,” Pupillo said. 
Choi, meanwhile, thought the fellowship underlined how important it is to understand how policymaking affects people in real life — knowledge especially important for students who may one day help write those policies, he thought. 
“If we want to be focused on improving people’s lives, we need to understand how they’re receiving and thinking about these public services,” Choi said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Has Kentucky’s legislative process gotten more transparent?
description: Our representative democracy rests on a fundamental principle: We, the people, have a right to participate in decisions that affect us. Since 2023, the League of Women Voters of Kentucky has published annual reports describing how Kentucky’s General Assembly weakens that principle by using fast-track maneuvers and undemocratic tactics that limit transparency[...]
text:
Kentucky Senate at work in March 2024 in the Kentucky Capitol, now closed for renovation. The legislature is meeting this year in temporary quarters.(Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)Our representative democracy rests on a fundamental principle: We, the people, have a right to participate in decisions that affect us.

Since 2023, the League of Women Voters of Kentucky has published annual reports describing how Kentucky’s General Assembly weakens that principle by using fast-track maneuvers and undemocratic tactics that limit transparency and public participation.

Has the legislative process improved since our first report? The answer is yes and no. In our latest report, “How Can They Do That? 2026 Challenges to Transparency and Citizen Participation in Kentucky’s Legislative Process,” our analysis shows improvement in two of the processes we monitor, and little or no change in other processes. We also note increased use of piggyback bills, reported for the first time this year. The report can be found at lwvky.org/how-can-they-do-that.

Improvements occurred in these areas:

● Use of scheduled committee meeting times: Our past reports have shown that
legislative committees often canceled scheduled meetings and then held “surprise”
meetings on short notice, making it hard for the public to observe and participate. This situation improved in 2026, when committees held 90% of meetings at scheduled times, compared to 79% in 2024. The number of “surprise” meetings declined from 47 in 2024 to 28 in 2026.
● Journal of Proceedings: In the past, publication of the Constitutionally-mandated journals of legislative proceedings have lagged by as many as five years. Currently, however, published journals are complete through 2025.

Unfortunately, we saw little improvement in other processes that we have been monitoring.

Both the Senate and the House used fast-track maneuvers like early bill readings and last-minute committee substitutes to pass about 20 percent of all bills that became law in 2026, compared to one percent in 1998. 

The legislature has also increased its use of shell bills and piggyback bills to dramatically alter the content of bills late in the session and rush them through the process too quickly for the public to understand and give input. In 2026, 145 shell bills were filed, compared to only 15 in 2010. Piggyback bills, which are prohibited by House and Senate Rules, had been declining for the past 10 years, but the number jumped back up to nearly 30 in 2026, reversing years of progress.

Going forward, we ask that the legislature ensure public participation by:

● Continuing to improve its use of scheduled committee meeting times to transact
business, and publishing records of legislative actions promptly–including minutes of
committee meetings (which are not consistently available during 60-day sessions).
● Limiting the use of fast-track maneuvers to emergency situations
● Filing genuine bills rather than adding substantive content at the last minute through
shell bills and piggyback bills.
● Bringing back a webpage for legislators to prefile bills before each session, giving the
public time to give input that might improve bills before they are filed.

The League of Women Voters of Kentucky supports informed and active citizen participation in government. But citizens can only participate if they are given time and opportunities to do so. We urge the General Assembly to take a hard look at the processes we describe in our report, and work toward expanding Kentuckian’s voices in the lawmaking process. Our interactive report can be found on our website at lwvky.org/how-can-they-do-that.

title: Loudoun County pauses new data center applications for a year
description: Loudoun County, home to Virginia’s data center alley, is putting a one-year pause on processing new data center applications.  The county board voted 7-1-1 to approve the pause after a monthslong push. The pause l gives county officials time to update siting standards “to identify and mitigate anticipated data center compatibility issues.” About 245 data […]
text:
A view of a data center in Loudoun County. (Photo courtesy of Karen Graham/Loudoun Times-Mirror)Loudoun County, home to Virginia’s data center alley, is putting a one-year pause on processing new data center applications. 
The county board voted 7-1-1 to approve the pause after a monthslong push. The pause l gives county officials time to update siting standards “to identify and mitigate anticipated data center compatibility issues.”
About 245 data center facilities are built or under construction in Loudoun, totaling 58 million square feet, according to the county. An additional 55 million square feet of proposed facilities have been approved or are under review. 
Board member Juli Briskman said county staff estimate the pause could affect 33 active applications for data centers and substations. Briskman led the push for the pause after hearing concerns from many of her constituents.
“For years, I have been pushing for Loudoun to take back control of unchecked data center development,” Briskman said in a statement. “With the pause now in place, the Board has an opportunity to hold this industry more accountable for its impacts and ensure that the interests of our residents come first.”
Loudoun sees some of the industry’s largest financial impacts, with more than $1 billion in tax revenue this year from data centers alone.
Nicole Riley of the Data Center Coalition testified against the pause at Tuesday’s meeting, saying that it could invite legal challenges and disrupt investments made under existing rules.
“While we recognize that growth can raise important questions that are worthy of public discussion, sweeping policies to impose a moratorium do not solve complex infrastructure challenges,” Riley said. “Instead, they risk stalling economic opportunity, reducing job opportunities and shrinking the workforce pipeline, and defunding essential local public services.” 
The pause marks the start of the second phase of Loudoun’s effort to revamp the siting and zoning regulations for data centers. 
In March, the county completed the first phase, which led the board to eliminate by-right development for data centers. That process had allowed projects to move forward without public hearings or a board vote. 
Some projects were grandfathered into the by-right permitting process. Briskman previously introduced a motion to end that exemption, but county attorneys found that doing so would invite legal challenges. Those projects are exempt from the current pause.
In the second phase, the county will consider restrictions on siting data centers near schools, residential communities and other sensitive areas. It will also consider height limits, noise levels, onsite power generation and other effects of the facilities.
The county expects to complete the second phase in July 2027. Applicants affected by the pause will have to update their proposals to meet any new requirements.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Will Virginia join other states in banning a pesticide linked to Parkinson’s disease?
description: Once in a while you are surprised to find out that a hazardous product you assumed had been long since banned is still available and in regular use. Toxic chemicals fall into this category with depressing frequency.  The U.S. regulatory system, often criticized for being slow to approve new projects and products, has never been […]
text:
A farm in Prince William County. A bill to ban pesticides containing paraquat in Virginia stalled in the General Assembly this year. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury)Once in a while you are surprised to find out that a hazardous product you assumed had been long since banned is still available and in regular use. Toxic chemicals fall into this category with depressing frequency. 
The U.S. regulatory system, often criticized for being slow to approve new projects and products, has never been good at removing dangerous chemicals from the marketplace once they are on the shelves. 
And so it is that herbicides containing the potent neurotoxin paraquat are still legal for use in Virginia, in spite of mounting evidence connecting paraquat to brain diseases including Parkinson’s. After a failed effort in the General Assembly to change that, health advocates hope this is the year Virginia bans paraquat.
Paraquat, sold under a number of brand names including Gramoxone, kills all the vegetation it touches with what the manufacturer describes as “lightning-fast burndown.”  This allows farmers to broadcast-spray it “before, during, or after planting, but before crop emergence.” It is also good for killing the foliage on potato plants to make the tubers easier to harvest. 
Not surprisingly, paraquat also poisons animals that ingest it, and it likewise poses a threat to any humans unfortunate enough to be around when it is being sprayed. This can include farmworkers who aren’t wearing protective equipment or downwind neighbors who inhale drifting aerosols. 
As a short video from the Environmental Working Group (EWG) describes, people who are exposed to paraquat often don’t know it until it’s too late. EWG is one of the advocates seeking a Virginia ban on paraquat, along with the Sierra Club, Parkinson’s Foundation and American Parkinson Disease Association.
 The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency classifies any product that contains paraquat as a restricted-use pesticide, keeping it out of the hands of zealous homeowners. Farmworkers who use it must undergo training from the manufacturer to become a certified applicator. However, compliance with pesticide safety requirements in general tends to be inconsistent.
The good news is that paraquat is used on less than 2% of Virginia farms. The bad news is, that still amounts to 200,000 acres. And Virginia does not require notification of neighboring landowners when pesticides are sprayed on farms, so nearby residents don’t know they are at risk.
Needless to say, paraquat is not used in organic farming.
Paraquat is banned in more than 70 countries, often going back decades. The list includes Canada, Europe, most Middle Eastern and West African countries and much of Asia. In the U.S., Vermont became the first state to prohibit its use, California has begun a phase-out, and bills to ban its use have been introduced in a dozen states. 
Ironically, most paraquat sold in the U.S. is manufactured in China, even though its use is prohibited there. The largest U.S. distributor, Sygenta, is owned by a Chinese state enterprise.
Paraquat’s value as an herbicide was discovered in 1955, quickly followed by discovery of its potential for neurological harm in humans. Indeed, the 50’s and 60’s were something of a heyday for finding terrific new chemicals that were also seriously problematic. DDT was popular, too, before it killed off most of our bald eagles. The first of thousands of PFAS chemicals began making Teflon a household name around the same time, driving a still-thriving industry linked to cancer, immune system diseases and birth defects. These join tens of thousands of other legacy chemicals that are known to be dangerous but remain legal to use; in most cases, the EPA has never tested them for safety. 
In the case of paraquat, the EPA knew of its toxicity from the time that it was approved in 1964. Ten years later, the agency considered canceling its registration, but didn’t, even as concerns about paraquat’s harms continued to mount. In 1978, EPA added paraquat to the list of restricted-use chemicals requiring training and protective equipment for those who used it. 
By the 1980s, scientists were documenting an association with Parkinson’s Disease. Over the years, evidence mounted showing that farm workers and nearby residents of farms where paraquat is applied develop Parkinson’s Disease at a rate much higher than the general public. 
A 2011 study funded by the National Institutes of Health found that farm workers who applied paraquat were 2.5 times more likely to develop Parkinson’s than non-users. In 2013, a study by paraquat manufacturer Sygenta confirmed the NIH finding. 
 EPA rejected calls for a ban but moved to tighten restrictions on paraquat in 2021, then reversed course in 2025, saying the matter needed further study. Following that decision, 20 former EPA officials and scientists signed a letter calling on the agency to ban paraquat. 
In Virginia’s last General Assembly session, Del. Nadarius Clark, D-Suffolk, and eight other Democrats introduced House Bill 1375, which would have banned the manufacture, sale and use of pesticides containing paraquat. The Farm Bureau and the Virginia Agribusiness Council opposed the bill, arguing that safer alternatives cost more. 
An Agriculture subcommittee narrowly recommended the bill after adopting amendments to allow existing inventory to be sold and used. However, the full committee continued the legislation to 2027, a polite way to kill it. The vote was unanimous – including Clark himself, who serves as the vice chair of the committee. 
From where I sit, the surprise decision to continue the bill suggests that the committee may have been acting on a request from the governor. Abigail Spanberger had only recently taken office, and her secretary of agriculture and forestry, Katie Frazier, was formerly executive director of the Virginia Agribusiness Council. 
My call to Clark’s office was not returned, however, and advocates say they believe the vote was intended to delay, but not to defeat, action on paraquat. 
Geoff Horsfield, legislative director for EWG, told me in a phone call that he thought the committee vote simply reflected members’ unfamiliarity with the issue. Clark has already agreed to put the bill in again, he said, and a Senate patron will be announced soon. The job of advocates now is to educate legislators – and the public – about the dangers of paraquat to Virginians.
Horsfield emphasized that “this is a public health issue, not a farm issue.”  Parkinson’s is the fastest-growing neurological disease in the country, he added. With EPA doing nothing, states have to act.

name: National
title: Midterm wins, near-misses could signal political change in the Deep South
description: The midterms are over but Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson is back on the road, visiting churches and community centers across the congressional district he narrowly lost. He wants to thank voters who supported him. And he’s determined not to lose the connections he built during a long-shot campaign that has come to exemplify Democrats’ […]
text:
Tennessee Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson turns to his wife, Oceana Pearson, during his election night party in Memphis. Pearson narrowly lost his race for Congress, and his defeat — and Democratic optimism — is part of a pattern that repeated across the Deep South up and down the midterm ballot. (Photo by Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)The midterms are over but Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson is back on the road, visiting churches and community centers across the congressional district he narrowly lost. He wants to thank voters who supported him. And he’s determined not to lose the connections he built during a long-shot campaign that has come to exemplify Democrats’ growing ambitions across the Republican-controlled South.
He came closer than most anyone expected to winning. Pearson’s Republican legislative colleagues redrew the U.S. House district earlier this year to break up a longtime Democratic stronghold around the majority-Black city of Memphis, diluting it with Republican-heavy areas to net the state an additional GOP seat in Congress.
And it worked. Barely. Pearson lost to Republican Brent Taylor by about 1 percentage point in the newly drawn district, which the nonpartisan Cook Political Report said President Donald Trump would have won by 21 points.
“I was campaigning in communities that were over 60% rural, white, Southern, and we came within one point,” said Pearson, who is Black.
“It is possible to win here.”
His narrow defeat — and Democratic optimism — is part of a pattern that has repeated across the Deep South up and down the midterm ballot, where the blue wave that engulfed other parts of the country only lapped at Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi and Tennessee. In these states, Republicans held onto power, for the most part.
But Democrats made significant inroads that would have seemed unthinkable a year ago: from a nail-biting Senate race in Mississippi where the Democrat squeaked out a win over the Republican incumbent to down-ballot races where Democrats flipped state legislative seats in areas where Trump won with wide margins just two years ago.
“You knock enough doors, you talk to enough people, you go to enough places, and you’re hearing the same stories,” said Pearson. “Republicans who say, ‘You’re the first Democrat I’ve ever voted for,’ and people who’ve never voted in their lives saying, ‘I’m registering to vote to vote for you because I want something different.’”
But how durable are those gains? In a region full of Republican legislative supermajorities, where Trump remains popular and where few Democrats have held statewide offices in more than a decade, do the midterm results signal a change in the South’s political future, or were  they an anomaly driven by a unique set of circumstances?
Many experts remain skeptical that states such as Alabama or Mississippi are on a path to become neighboring Georgia, which is now a solid battleground state where Democrats won every statewide seat on the ballot this year. They see midterm results as not an embrace of Democrats so much as a negative referendum on Trump.
“I know Democrats get excited in places like Alabama and Louisiana and Mississippi when Democrats win elections,” said David Hughes, a political science associate professor at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who studies the politics of the American South. Voters were primarily motivated by anger over issues including high costs, the Iran war and congressional redistricting, he said.
Black voting advocates in the South say the midterm surge was not just a ‘blue wave’

“It’s interesting, but it’s largely a fluke and there will be a reversion to the mean.”
But Southern Democrats see glimmers of opportunity for lasting, even generational change in wins such as Democrat Scott Colom’s in Mississippi, where he beat Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on a razor-thin margin to become the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. Or in U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, who defeated his Republican opponent in an Alabama congressional district that state legislators redrew this year to favor Republicans. 
And they see it in surprisingly close gubernatorial races in Tennessee and Florida, where Republicans eked out wins with one or two percentage points over their Democratic opponents.
None of that means the Deep South has suddenly become a different place politically, said Anneshia Hardy, a voting rights activist in Alabama who studies Southern politics.
“But it does mean that we need to pay closer attention to what’s happening beneath the statewide results,” she said. “The political landscape is not nearly as static as our electoral map suggests.”
On a national level, she said, Democrats could learn from the South about building coalitions and creating political opportunities where they don’t already hold power.
Quoting Andre 3000, the famed Atlanta rapper and half of hip-hop duo Outkast, she said, “‘The South got something to say,’ and I hope folks are listening.”
Voting rights and Black political power
In a region that was the epicenter of the fight for voting rights 60 years ago, the recent congressional redistricting ignited a fire among voters, and particularly among Black voters, who showed up to the polls in numbers rarely seen in a midterm election, activists and experts told Stateline.
The U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais earlier this year all but nullified a provision in the federal 1965 Voting Rights Act that required states to draw electoral maps to give racial minority voters the opportunity to elect their chosen candidates.
Republican state legislators  rushed to redraw their congressional maps to favor GOP candidates in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas. Democrats tried gerrymandering in California and Virginia.
That redistricting decision was pivotal for Southern voters, and for Black voters in particular, Pearson said.
“I think if that had not happened, we would not have seen a number of the victories we saw,” he said. “To have such an ignited and excited Black Democratic voting base, I think the attack on voting rights was the key issue that really awakened people’s attentiveness and conscientiousness.”
Black politicians win newfound power across state, federal governments

Midterm turnout is typically much lower than it is for presidential elections. But this year saw historic turnout, even in the South. Democrats saw their share of the vote increase in every county in states such as Alabama, where Democratic turnout nearly doubled over 2022 numbers while GOP votes declined slightly. Nearly 1 million Mississippians turned out to vote, rivaling presidential election years.
One-third of Mississippi and Louisiana ballots were cast by Black voters. In Georgia, turnout among Black voters increased more than 11% over the 2022 midterms while white turnout shrank.
Activists say the high turnout in the South was built on decades of voter outreach and community organizing, particularly in Black communities. It just needed a spark to ignite, they said.
Republicans lit the match when they began gerrymandering in earnest earlier this year.
The newly drawn maps provided a tangible example for casual voters to see how state and national leaders wield power, and how they can take it away from their constituents, Hardy said. Louisiana, the state at the center of the Supreme Court’s Callais case, saw voter turnout surge especially in parishes — the state’s equivalent of counties — where congressional lines were redrawn, said Louisiana political consultant Mary-Patricia Wray, who’s worked on statewide campaigns for both Republicans and Democrats.
“Voters are very much aware that when we elect our legislature, it will be in charge of redrawing our maps again,” Wray said. “I think that awareness truly did drive Black turnout in Louisiana specifically, and I think it did in any state where there was a potential to have an impact on congressional maps.”
Democrats nationally had their best performance with white voters in years, tying with Republicans for white voters after not having won white voters in a presidential election since 1964. In the growing urban center of Madison County, Alabama, a majority-white electorate flipped three state house seats from red to blue, and sent down-ballot Republican incumbents packing, including the incumbent sheriff. In suburban, majority-white Rutherford County south of Nashville, Tennessee, Democrats flipped three state House seats.
“One of the surprising things about Democrats doing well in the South was that many of these weren’t on the radar” of the national Democratic party, “and they won anyway, with little resources,” said Kent Syler, a political science professor at Middle Tennessee State University.
“Now they’ve demonstrated that there’s an opportunity here, you’re going to see more recruitment of top-quality candidates and you’re going to see more resources for those candidates, because this election proved you have a chance.”
Looking ahead
Louisiana and Mississippi are two of just three states — Kentucky is the other — that will hold elections for state offices and legislative seats in 2027.
And Democratic near-misses in those states are already fueling speculation over the next round of elections. Democrat Jamie Davis, who lost the Senate race in Louisiana to Republican U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow by about 25,000 votes, less than a two-point margin, is reportedly eyeing a run for governor.
Young, diverse voters showed up for midterms as older, Trump voters stayed home

But the political climate remains volatile.
“Neither party can take anything for granted. The electorate is just ticked off,” said Hughes, of the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. “If Democrats don’t find a way to deliver (on their promises), I have confidence that the voters will turn them out of office down the line.”
One thing the South showed national Democrats as well as Republicans, several experts told Stateline, was that more moderate candidates who avoided national disagreements over wedge issues tended to do better at the polls.
“I saw a preference for moderate incumbents over extreme incumbents at every level of the ballot,” for both parties, said Wray, the Louisiana political consultant.
Hughes thinks it will take a greater demographic shift — voters moving in from other states and bringing their politics with them, plus a continued rise in turnout from Black voters and other minority groups — to create the conditions in states such as Alabama that propelled Georgia or North Carolina to swing-state status.
Democrats across the South are hoping for more investment from national groups, now that the South has shown a win is possible. They’re looking at the tens of millions poured into races in Texas and Georgia, arguing even a fraction of that could make a difference in state houses and governor’s mansions across the region — and from there, influence political control of the nation’s highest offices.
Pearson said he’s working on creating a political action committee to continue building on the Democratic successes and near-successes of the midterms.
“I believe the litmus test for America’s democracy is what happens in the South,” he said. “We can perfect this American experiment if we invest in the South and I’m more hopeful and optimistic about us doing it than ever before.”
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.
