name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Here’s what to watch in the new-look General Assembly
description: I don’t think I can overstate the seismic shift we are going to see in the new Indiana General Assembly. Yes, Republicans are still in control, but the amount of change going into a crucial budget session is incredible. There are 37 new lawmakers in the House and Senate – meaning a full quarter of […]
text:
Indiana's House and Senate are virtually starting from scratch in 2027. Indiana Statehouse in September 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)I don’t think I can overstate the seismic shift we are going to see in the new Indiana General Assembly. Yes, Republicans are still in control, but the amount of change going into a crucial budget session is incredible.
There are 37 new lawmakers in the House and Senate – meaning a full quarter of the Legislature is new.
Indiana hasn’t seen that kind of shift since the early 1980s, according to Capitol & Washington’s casualty list.
Indiana Senate President Pro Tem Chris Garten speaks during a Senate session on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Generally, turnover in the General Assembly comes from retirements or resignations. But this year incumbent defeats took out 25 legislators over the primary and general elections.
With that goes hundreds of years of legislative experience — how to write a bill, build support, educate colleagues on complex issues, find solutions to thorny disagreements and help constituents.
The chambers also have new leaders in House Speaker Ben Smaltz, R-Auburn, and Senate President Pro Tem Chris Garten, R-Charlestown.
Garten’s ascension was expected as the Senate Republican caucus voted internally months ago to have him replace the outgoing leader. He is a passionate, smart former Marine who has been in the Senate since 2018.
In recent sessions, he has led a crackdown on food and healthcare assistance programs and pushed for lawmakers to have more authority over state agency rules and actions.
Rep. Ben Smaltz, R-Auburn, speaks with reporters after his selection as Indiana House speaker-elect on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Smaltz’ elevation was a surprise following the former speaker’s election night defeat. A few members sought the post but Smaltz — an even-keeled legislator with 14 years’ experience in the House — garnered the support of his fellow members.
His temperament is calm and unruffled compared to Garten’s fiery speeches.
Smaltz previously chaired the House Public Policy Committee, where many gaming, alcohol and abortion matters were sent. Recently he has handled rules matters for the chamber.
His recent legislation includes required expungement of certain “red flag” gun seizure law records and the unsuccessful congressional redistricting bill.
There are a shocking 29 new committee chairs in the House and Senate. Some have led other committees before, but many are new to the leadership role. And chairs are the first line that a bill must get pass. Even getting a hearing is sometimes a win.
Here are the key committees you should keep an eye on:

Rep. Jake Teshka, R-North Liberty, takes over the House Education Committee, which has been run by former Rep. Robert Behning for 15 years. Behning is largely responsible for education reform in the state. One item Teshka will push this year is limiting student screen time in school.
Rep. Martin Carbaugh, R-Fort Wayne, will lead the House Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications Committee after its longtime leader was defeated as well. It’s a new challenge for Carbaugh, who has been in the House since 2012. But he previously focused on insurance and healthcare issues. Utility costs have been a huge focus the last year and Hoosiers are looking for help. Legislation involving data centers would also go to this panel.
Rep. Craig Snow, R-Warsaw, is taking over the most powerful committee in the House — the budget-writing Ways and Means Committee. Former leader Rep. Jeff Thompson was reelected but Smaltz decided to go a different route. Snow has been groomed in recent years for the position and gets his chance earlier than expected. The budget touches every aspect of state government and Snow will have to deliver on the caucus’ key priorities.
Sen. Tyler Johnson, R-Leo, will lead the Senate Health Committee. It’s the first chairmanship for the emergency room physician, but he has been vocal on healthcare issues since he joined the chamber in 2020. He sometimes clashed with the former chair, who preferred a more measured approach to key issues.
Sen. Scott Baldwin, R-Noblesville, is heading up the Senate Tax and Fiscal Policy Committee. While the budget will go to the Appropriations Committee, other financial matters will head to Baldwin. He has served since 2020 and has been involved in fiscal topics for years. Property taxes will likely be on the front burner this session — a difficult topic to thread the needle.
Sen. Justin Busch, R-Fort Wayne, takes over Senate Public Policy. He has served in the Senate since 2018. He previously served on the committee but it’s his first chairmanship. In the past, he has authored bills on riverboat gaming, wine delivery, charity gaming and physician noncompete agreements. Issues such as license plate readers or prediction markets could be funneled here.

That is all a lot of change for a year in which lawmakers must pass a two-year budget spending around $46 billion. Almost half of that goes to K-12 and higher education with other large expenses being Medicaid and public safety.
Let the gauntlet begin.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: ‘A very nimble state’: Scanlan vows New Hampshire will keep first-in-the-nation status
description: The Democratic National Committee has again rebuffed New Hampshire and placed it third in its schedule for the 2028 presidential primary calendar, but Secretary of State David Scanlan, citing state law, plans to disregard the decision and go first anyway. It’s a saga that could set New Hampshire on the path for a repeat of […]
text:
Secretary of State David Scanlan speaks to reporters about his reelection bid during a Nov. 17, 2026, press conference at the Legislative Office Building in Concord. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)The Democratic National Committee has again rebuffed New Hampshire and placed it third in its schedule for the 2028 presidential primary calendar, but Secretary of State David Scanlan, citing state law, plans to disregard the decision and go first anyway. It’s a saga that could set New Hampshire on the path for a repeat of the contentious 2024 fight.
New Hampshire has, for decades, held the first primary election in the country each cycle (though Iowa has selected its nominee via caucus beforehand). However, the DNC has worked for years to change the schedule. 2028 is no different.
The DNC wants South Carolina to hold the first primary this cycle on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada on Feb 1, New Hampshire on Feb. 8, New Mexico on Feb. 15, Michigan on Feb. 22, and Virginia on Feb. 29.
Iowa and New Hampshire’s place in the calendar has long been criticized by those who believe their lack of racial diversity doesn’t reflect the nation as a whole. Some go as far as to say that staggering the primaries is unfair to voters in states at the end of the calendar, who don’t get to weigh in on the candidates who dropped out after poor showings in early states.
In return, Granite State politicos offer high-minded arguments about how New Hampshire’s small size forces candidates into the sort of retail politics that allows voters to get to know them intimately as opposed to just seeing them in campaign ads and national media. They also argue it allows candidates with little name recognition, campaign funds and connections a better shot at winning. President Jimmy Carter’s 1976 victory in the state is hailed as a prime example.
In 2024, the DNC also tried to move South Carolina, a state where President Joe Biden performed well in previous cycles, ahead of New Hampshire and Iowa, where Biden performed poorly. New Hampshire officials refused to accept being relegated and entered into a bitter showdown with national Democrats. In New Hampshire, state law requires the secretary of state to schedule the presidential primary at least one week before any other state’s. In 2024, Scanlan defied the DNC and scheduled it for Jan. 23. That year, the DNC refused to sanction the state’s primary and stripped it of its delegates.
However, Biden had little competition in the primary that year and ultimately dropped out of the race before the general election, and Vice President Kamala Harris took his place on the ballot without a primary election victory. In 2028, which will likely see a more open and competitive primary for the Democratic nomination, an unsanctioned primary could be more consequential.
Still, Scanlan is convinced the state can win the fight this time around.
“New Hampshire is a very nimble state,” he said. “We can pull off an election very quickly, and you have to be prepared to wait long enough until you know when other states are going to hold their primary, and then you pull the trigger.”
In South Carolina, the state political party sets the primary, per state law. In Nevada, state law allows the secretary of state to adjust the date of the primary, but only with permission from the state legislative commission’s approval. New Hampshire, on the other hand, gives the secretary of state sole discretion on when to hold the primary. Scanlan wants New Hampshire to use that to its advantage and simply outlast the other states. He contends other states don’t do elections as well as New Hampshire.
“I’ve been to Nevada, another state that the DNC has placed in front of New Hampshire,” Scanlan said at a recent press conference. “There is no way that Nevada can replicate what happens in this state. It just can’t happen.”
Scanlan is not guaranteed to be secretary of state when 2028 rolls around, however. The state Legislature selects the secretary of state in New Hampshire, and this year’s vote is scheduled for Dec. 2. A Republican, Scanlan is facing at least three challengers. After Democrats won massive majorities in both chambers earlier this month, the party may decide to go with a new candidate more aligned with the party, though historically both parties have sought continuity in the office. Carleigh Beriont, a Hampton Select Board member and 2026 congressional candidate; state Rep. Patrick Long; and former Democratic staffer James Butler are currently courting lawmakers for their support.

title: New Indiana scholarship targets students at risk of not completing degrees
description: A new scholarship in Indiana will assist financially strapped college students at risk of dropping out of school to finish their degrees. INvestEd, a nonprofit student loan and financial aid provider, will award up to $3 million each year to Hoosiers about to start their junior or senior year of college. The National Student Clearinghouse […]
text:
INvestEd CEO Joe Wood reveals a new scholarship for college juniors and seniors at the Indiana Commission for Higher Education office Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A new scholarship in Indiana will assist financially strapped college students at risk of dropping out of school to finish their degrees.
INvestEd, a nonprofit student loan and financial aid provider, will award up to $3 million each year to Hoosiers about to start their junior or senior year of college.
The National Student Clearinghouse estimates just shy of 270,000 Hoosiers have earned college credit but never finished their degree.
The Success Scholarship is designed to close the financial gap for students who may otherwise be forced to quit college early.
“For a student facing a remaining balance that they cannot cover, those dollars could make the difference between continuing towards graduation and putting their education on hold,” INvestEd CEO Joe Wood said. “They may not finish. Every penny of this scholarship reduces what Hoosiers have to borrow and have to pay out of pocket.”
INvestEd intends to distribute scholarships proportionately throughout Indiana’s 92 counties.
Scholarships will be applied after all other applicable financial aid, with up to $5,000 a year available for eligible students to use toward the cost of attendance at an accredited four-year college or university.
Applications are open for the 2027-28 school year now through Feb. 5, 2027. Wood said the organization will consider each applicant’s financial need and academic achievement.
Applicants must be Indiana residents and U.S. citizens to be considered for the award.
The program will be administered by the Central Indiana Community Foundation, which will notify recipients of their awards. A maximum of 600 scholarships will be given a year.
Gov. Mike Braun and Education Secretary Katie Jenner praised the scholarship for helping make college affordable for students who may not otherwise be able to graduate.
“We know that success is rarely a straight line,” Jenner said. “Life happens. For some, financial barriers may have gotten in the way. Others may have faced academic challenges, family responsibilities or unexpected life circumstances.”
“But whatever the reason,” she said, “we have a great opportunity to help more Hoosiers who dream of entering higher education and completing that degree to actually cross the finish line.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: JB Forbes, photojournalist from Kansas, publishes book that urges us to ‘Always Take The Shot’
description: When I was a photography intern at a daily newspaper in 1999, my first photo editor told me on my first day, “Working on a daily newspaper is a hoot. If we do great work, well, that’s nice. And if we screw things up, we can always do better tomorrow.” That same mercurial, swerving nature […]
text:
J.B. Forbes includes this photo in “Always Take the Shot” with this caption: “Me covering the Jayhawk Relays during my junior year at KU in 1971.” (Photo submitted by J.B. Forbes)When I was a photography intern at a daily newspaper in 1999, my first photo editor told me on my first day, “Working on a daily newspaper is a hoot. If we do great work, well, that’s nice. And if we screw things up, we can always do better tomorrow.”
That same mercurial, swerving nature of photojournalism at a daily newspaper comes through in “Always Take the Shot,” a hefty coffee table slab of a book, full of images by J.B. Forbes, a Kansas native and long-time staffer at the St. Louis Post-Dispatch.

The cover of “Always Take the Shot,” a photojournalism book by Kansas native J.B. Forbes, which showcases decades of working in American newspapers. (Photo by J.B. Forbes)

Roughly in chronological order, the book presents Forbes’ work as a parade of mini-chapters — alternately somber then silly, personal then political, children then celebrities. For instance, a series of photos from a St. Louis flood transitions to an NFL game and then to an international reporting trip to Bosnia. Later in the book, we follow Forbes on these wildly different assignments one after the other: photographing tornado disaster areas, drunken canoe trips and a local kidnapping. 
As the topics for the photos veer, Forbes’ accompanying words describe a profession that has rapidly faded in American journalism: the do-it-all photographer for a daily metropolitan newspaper. In that way, his book is a valuable slice of journalism history with its comprehensive account of decades spent lugging around a camera bag. 
Forbes’s personal history is rooted in Kansas. The opening pages of the book feature stories from his days at Shawnee Mission East High School, sharing training runs and the darkroom at the University of Kansas with track and field Olympian Jim Ryun, learning photojournalism in Topeka and chafing under the racist mandates of an editor in Parsons. 
In the prologue, Forbes recounts watching a first photographic image appear in a Polaroid while growing up in Prairie Village: “I watched my very first photo of a rose develop in 60 seconds before my eyes. I was hooked.”
Forbes and I spoke this week during a telephone interview before he visited Kansas to celebrate the induction of photographers who will join him in the Kansas Photojournalism Hall of Fame. On Friday, as part of the same road trip, he will hand-deliver a copy of his book to his alma mater, Shawnee Mission East. 
The interview has been edited for length and clarity. 
J.B. Forbes, author of “Always Take the Shot.” (Photo submitted by J.B. Forbes)
What is it about carrying a camera around for the purpose of photographing people for a newspaper that gets you such access and insight into what a community is like? 
Those cameras were my ticket into everywhere, and it was such wonderful access. It would allow me not only into places, but allow me to ask questions about the private things in people’s lives and get to know them. Because I was interested, I took my responsibility very seriously and always enjoyed just going up and asking people these private, intimate questions about their lives.
Talk a little bit about what drew you to photojournalism and what you remember about the Kansas beginnings of things.
I joined the camera club in junior high school, and learned how to put film in the back of a 35-millimeter camera … I also joined the art club because I thought that was really interesting. Something that has inspired me ever since then is art magazines, and in particular southwestern art. I look at those pictures, and I try to get into the artist’s head about why they did things the way they did. 
In high school, I applied to get on the high school newspaper, and they made me the sports editor. I was running at that time, and my cross country team won state. … I was the top runner, and I talked to (newspaper adviser) Mr. Robert Dillon about writing about that. I wouldn’t put quotes in there about me, but I would put my stats in there because I was leading the team. And our football team was losing every game, so I made that (story) real small. 
(Wayne State College in Nebraska) gave me a little scholarship, but I was homesick and I was running pretty well, so I decided to transfer back to KU. I did meet the famous runner Jim Ryun, who I wanted to run with, and I got to run with him in practice. I never got to really run with him in a race … but he and I ran the streets of Lawrence together, which I thought was just the most amazing thing.
I went to dinner at his apartment with him and his girlfriend. I saw pictures on the wall that he had won prizes for. … I thought, my gosh, I’m never going to beat this guy running, but I can take better pictures than this. And so, at the end of the year, I quit the KU track team in dramatic fashion … and I went right to the journalism department and said, “Remember me, Jim Ryun introduced me, and I’d like to get into the program.” And they let me.
J.B. Forbes poses with his dad during graduation festivities at the University of Kansas where Forbes graduated after studying photojournalism. (Photo submitted by J.B. Forbes)
What gave you a sense that you could take good storytelling pictures?
I liked the idea of recording events and people, and being out there in the world. Not being tied down to a desk job or some other work. … It was just a number of things. The art drew me in also, and just the idea of being out and about. The excitement of it also had a lot to do with it.
I need you to explain just what the atmosphere was like at the Topeka Capital-Journal in the 1970s — the buzzing throng of photographers who were defining what excellence in photojournalism was. What did it feel like?
I was in such awe of these guys, even though they were only slightly older than me. I was in awe of their talent, of their energy, of all the expertise, the imagination that they put into the work, and I had the wonderful chance to lean over their shoulders in the darkroom. I could just stand there and lean over the shoulder of Brian Lanker and watch him do his magic with pictures — and Jim Richardson.
Everybody there was in awe, but also scared of (director of photography) Rich Clarkson, because he had such a reputation and he demanded such excellence, but he had such a fiery temper, and it would just go off at different times. And everybody was scared of it.
That’s the kind of atmosphere it was back in that time. I learned so much from these guys, and they were so willing to teach me and to tell me why they were doing things the way they were.
Considering Kansas photojournalism, it seems exceptional the amount of talent for such a small state. Do you think about Kansas and photography in that way?
I think a lot of it had to do with Rich Clarkson. … He did a wonderful job of recruiting photographers to Topeka. I think it was through just sheer determination, drive and his managerial skills that the Topeka paper displayed the artwork of the photographers so well. That drew other people in. So, I was at the right place at the right time. … I think it’s just luck and timing.

In “Always Take the Shot,” J.B. Forbes explains how this photo of three children from Parsons, Kansas, eventually helped to change a policy prohibiting Black people from being published in most photographs in the local newspaper. (Photo by J.B. Forbes)

In your chapter about Parsons, you talk about photographing the small town, but you also talk about your conflict with the editor of the newspaper — his embargo on photographing Black people under certain conditions and how you pushed up against that. That’s not something that I have very often heard of a young photographer doing. I’m curious how you remember that period.
My editor, who really helped me with my book, said, “Are you sure you want to put this part in there?” And I said, “Well, it was my life. It’s what happened. This is how I remember it.” 
(The editor’s policy) was so obvious, and I even had reporters telling me, “No, we don’t put pictures of Black people in the paper unless there’s crime involved or they’ve been involved in a house fire or something like that.” There were … no uplifting stories about (Black people). It was little things like that that really got me. It was stuff that wasn’t taught to me in (journalism) school: the part about politics and how the influence of one man, one editor in a small town — how much he affected what was going on with his paper.
What was your approach to photographing sports? How did you try to do it differently from the hordes of other photographers surrounding you?
My goal in every sporting event that I covered was to get a picture that told a story of the game. And, boy, that didn’t happen all the time. I was always concerned about those lines underneath the picture (the caption), not just any old action shot. I wanted to have meaning and tell a story with it. I tried to anyway … trying to get that peak action of the decisive moment, if at all possible.
J.B. Forbes shows off his Jayhawk tie during the awards ceremony for the Pulitzer Prizes in 2015, where he and the photography staff of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch accepted the award for their coverage of the community reaction to the police killing of Michael Brown. (Photo submitted by J.B. Forbes)
Although I didn’t do a strict page count, I think the largest of your mini-chapters is dedicated to the community reaction to the 2014 shooting of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, and the coverage that earned the Pulitzer Prize for the Post-Dispatch staff. What was it like to be in the middle of the most important story in national news, if not international news, and covering it in your own community? 
The first day of coverage, I just thought, “It’s another shooting. It’s another terrible killing where people are protesting against the police.” It didn’t really dawn on me until it kept getting bigger and bigger.
Then you start to realize, “Man, this is a really big story.” And I started seeing so many (journalists) from out of town. I know that all of us on the staff were thinking, “We don’t want these other people from out of town to beat us in our own city.” 
So, I think it helped us really up our game and try to cover every aspect of it. For me, after a few days of sort of standing on the sidelines during these confrontations day after day, night after night, I thought, “I’m not seeing the kind of pictures that really make a difference. I can’t get them if I’m just standing on the sideline. So I have to get out there in the middle of these protesters and shoot from that angle,” which I did. And I think that made our coverage better.
This book documents the life of a daily newspaper photographer in a community — and the fact that daily metro newspapers would previously send photographers out of the country or out of the region to cover stories that were particularly important. We don’t have that same photography job as a mainstay in the media anymore. It’s becoming particularly rare. Do you see the same kind of history in the book?
Yes, I do. I was realizing at the time, as my career was starting to wind down, how much it was changing. The things that I like to cover were going away, and those were being designated now to specialists. If you want to cover a war, then you go off and cover a war. But you don’t come back home to cover sports, news and everything else. 
(In the book,) I wanted to show the pictures of how I lived it. I would go from big events to little bitty events. And then sports and then news. How I lived it — that’s how I wanted it to read. You just have to go through and see from day to day what I was doing.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Thanksgiving dinner costs drop 8% in Indiana, Farm Bureau survey finds
description: Indiana families can expect to pay about 8% less for Thanksgiving dinner this year, with cheaper turkeys and lower prices for nearly every holiday staple bringing the cost of a traditional meal for 10 people below $50. The Indiana Farm Bureau’s annual market basket survey found that Thanksgiving dinner will cost an average of $49.17, […]
text:
The average cost of a 16-pound turkey in Indiana fell to $19.38 this year, helping bring down the overall price of Thanksgiving dinner. (Getty Images)Indiana families can expect to pay about 8% less for Thanksgiving dinner this year, with cheaper turkeys and lower prices for nearly every holiday staple bringing the cost of a traditional meal for 10 people below $50.
The Indiana Farm Bureau’s annual market basket survey found that Thanksgiving dinner will cost an average of $49.17, or $4.92 per person. That’s down $4.45 from last year’s $53.62 total.
Indiana’s holiday meal costs are also nearly 16% below the national average of $58.63 — a difference of $9.46.
The latest estimate continues a decline from the $61 meal cost recorded in 2022, when inflation and supply chain disruptions drove up Thanksgiving grocery prices. Costs have fallen about 19% since then.
This year’s meal remains about 15% more expensive than the $42.66 recorded in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, however.
The biggest pocktbook saver is turkey, which accounts for roughly 40% of the meal’s total cost.

A 16-pound turkey costs an average of $19.38 in Indiana, down from $21.09 in 2025 and about 18% cheaper than the national average of $23.68.
“Our shoppers in Indiana found their turkeys to be about 8% cheaper on average than they were in 2025,” said Indiana Farm Bureau Chief Economist Todd Davis. “Which could be a result of a 6% increase in U.S. turkey production in 2026. Grocery stores could also be using a lower turkey price tag to get shoppers in the door to purchase the rest of their Thanksgiving items.”
Prices also declined for nearly every item included in the survey.
Pie shells saw the largest percentage decrease, falling 23% to $2.84, followed by frozen peas, down 20% to $1.44. Fresh cranberries dropped 16% to $2.06, while pumpkin pie filling fell 10% to $3.60.
Whole milk was the lone exception, increasing 11 cents to $3.16 per gallon.
The survey also includes stuffing, sweet potatoes, rolls, carrots, celery, whipping cream and miscellaneous baking ingredients.
Despite lower grocery prices, though, Davis said farmers continue to face higher production and labor expenses.
Farmers receive about 12.6 cents of every retail food dollar, putting their estimated share of this year’s Thanksgiving meal at $6.20, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates cited by Farm Bureau.
The Indiana survey was conducted in early November by volunteer shoppers who collected grocery prices before most holiday sales began. Shoppers were instructed to find the lowest available prices without using special coupons or promotional deals.

title: Advocate reports nonprofit hospitals gain more in tax breaks than they give
description: A new report argues that nearly three out of four Wisconsin nonprofit hospitals don’t give back community benefits in proportion to what they gain from their tax-exempt status. text:
A new report says nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks often exceed their contributions to community health, but hospitals dispute the methods used by the organization that conducted the research. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A new report argues that nearly three out of four Wisconsin nonprofit hospitals don’t give back community benefits in proportion to what they gain from their tax-exempt status.
Hospital representatives contend the report’s math paints a distorted picture, leaving out some costs that should be included.
The report’s publisher, the Lown Institute, defends its choices, limiting the benefits it includes in the calculations to “direct spending on the community,” in the words of an institute official.
Lown published its 2026 “Hospital Fair-Share Spending” report Tuesday, with data from across the country. The report is based on published information from fiscal year 2023.
According to the report, slightly more than half of nonprofit hospitals nationwide — 52% — gave back less than they received in their total tax exemptions that year.
In Wisconsin, the gap was wider, with 70% of hospitals getting more in tax breaks than they give in community benefits as Lown calculates them.
“Wisconsin families are footing the bill for massive tax breaks given to nonprofit hospitals, yet a handful of wealthy hospital systems guard resources while patients drown in preventable medical debt,” said Bobby Peterson, executive director of ABC for Health, citing the Lown report’s Wisconsin data. ABC for Health is a public interest law firm that assists low- and moderate-income people with medical debt and in navigating the healthcare system.
The Wisconsin Hospital Association pushed back on the findings, calling the report “a misleading and incomplete picture of the contributions Wisconsin’s nonprofit hospitals make to their communities.”
Lown’s definitions of community benefits omit “billions of dollars in very real costs hospitals absorb while caring for Wisconsin patients, particularly those covered by Medicare and Medicaid,” the WHA said.
Focus on healthcare social responsibility
The nonprofit Lown Institute was founded by cardiologist Dr. Bernard Lown in 1973 as the Lown Cardiovascular Health Research Foundation. It originally focused on research and education around heart disease and advocating for preventive medicine, non-invasive management and compassionate healing. 
It became the Lown Institute in 2012 and refocused its work on the overuse and underuse of medical treatment and a range of other health policy issues, many of them centered on healthcare social responsibility.
Lown’s hospital spending report draws data from hospitals’ filings with the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and their nonprofit 990 reports to the Internal Revenue Service.
In return for the federal, state and local tax exemptions that nonprofit hospitals receive, “they are expected to provide free and discounted care and invest in programs that improve community health,” the report states in its introduction.
The report finds a gap between some wealthy and well-known hospitals with community benefits that fall short of the value of their tax breaks and other facilities that “contribute well beyond what they receive,” according to the report.
“Some of America’s wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack,” said Dr. Vikas Saini, the Lown Institute president. “Tax exemptions aren’t a gift — they’re an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain.”
ABC for Health reviewed the Lown report and concluded that in 2023, Wisconsin hospitals collectively provided $633 million less in community benefits than they received in tax exemptions — “an amount the Lown Institute estimates could eliminate medical debt for 341,815 residents,” ABC for Health stated.
To calculate a hospital’s total tax break, the report adds up the hospital’s savings from not paying taxes and from paying lower interest on bonds because they’re tax exempt, and from tax-exempt charitable donations.
The report limits its definition of community investments — including expenses that, in Lown’s analysis, directly contribute to better community health and excluding expenses that do not.
One omission: a hospital’s Medicaid shortfall — the gap between what the hospital receives from Medicaid and the cost of care that it reports.
Judith Garber, a senior policy analyst at Lown, said hospitals use the shortfall numbers to justify higher prices for other payers; to qualify for bonus payments that hospitals can receive if they serve a large number of Medicaid patients and patients without insurance; and to support their case for federally required discounts on drugs from drug manufacturers.
“Then they want to count it a fourth time as a community benefit,” Garber said. “We exclude it for that reason and because it simply does not reflect direct spending on the community. If we were to include Medicaid shortfall, wouldn’t it need to be offset by the amount they collect above cost for private pay?”
ABC for Health singled out three hospitals associated with large Wisconsin hospital groups — emblematic, the organization said, of how the differences between tax breaks and community benefits were “concentrated in major systems.”
At  Froedtert West Bend Hospital the report calculated 2023 community benefits were $80.8 million less than tax exemptions. At Aurora St. Luke’s Medical Center in Milwaukee, it reported benefits $79 million less than tax exemptions and at Aurora BayCare Medical Center in Green Bay the report calculated benefits were $38.7 million less than tax exemptions.
ABC for Health noted that 37 Wisconsin hospitals provided community benefits that exceeded their tax breaks, and singled out St. Croix Regional Medical Center and Mile Bluff Medical Center, in Juneau County. Each reported total benefits that exceeded their tax breaks by more than $11 million.
Hospital systems find fault
Along with the Wisconsin Hospital Association, Froedtert and Aurora both criticized the report’s findings.
Because of how Lown calculates benefits, “the report does not capture the full scope of these investments and their impact,” an Aurora statement declared.
Citing its own 2025 report , Aurora — which operates hospitals in 18 locations in eastern Wisconsin, not just the two singled out by ABC for Health — said its community benefits totaled $1.93 billion in 2025. That figure includes activities “hospitals are required to report to the IRS and that health systems across the country regularly include when assessing their community benefit,” according to the statement.
A spokesperson for Froedtert ThedaCare issued a statement that said the Lown Institute “has used selective methodology and isolated data points to produce its report as appears to be the case here.” At the hospital system, “We continue to follow all appropriate processes regarding exemption status, as we work to advance the health of the communities we serve.”
A statement from the hospital association charged that Lown was “selectively defining what counts as a community benefit,” in the process omitting “billions of dollars in very real costs hospitals absorb while caring for Wisconsin patients, particularly those covered by Medicare and Medicaid.”
The result “is simply not a fair or accurate assessment,” the WHA statement asserted.
The hospital association argued that in 2023 — the year covered by the new report — $1.6 billion in Medicaid reimbursement shortfalls and $3.3 billion in Medicare shortfalls should be included as “real costs of caring for patients that are excluded from Lown’s definition of community investment.” 



How the Lown Institute calculates hospitals’ tax breaks, community benefits
The Lown Institute’s report on tax breaks and community benefits from nonprofit hospitals stipulates definitions for both.
Tax exemptions: The report calculates the value of federal and state corporate income taxes as well as local sales and property taxes that a hospital would owe as a for-profit entity.
There is also an exemption on federal unemployment taxes for the first $7,000 of an employee’s annual pay. The tax break calculation includes the value of tax-exempt charitable donations the hospital declares, but not government grants and in-kind donations.
When nonprofit hospitals issue tax-exempt bonds, they pay investors a lower interest rate than they would as a for-profit business. The Lown report calculates the difference between the tax-exempt interest rate and the standard corporate bond interest rate a hospital would otherwise pay, and includes that savings in the nonprofit hospital’s total tax break.
Community benefits: Lown’s definition of community benefits leaves out some items that hospitals represent as costs they also must bear.
Lown’s definition includes:

free and discounted care that hospitals provide;
clinical services that hospitals subsidize, such as primary care clinics, addiction treatment and neonatal care;
community health improvement programs, such as health fairs, free immunization services and interpreter services;
community programs that target social conditions related to health — addressing housing needs, providing community advocacy and undertaking environmental initiatives, for example;
contributions in cash or in kind to other nonprofits to improve health.

Hospital expenses that Lown doesn’t include in its calculation of direct community benefits include:

contributions to medical schools, physician groups and other hospitals;
a hospital’s Medicaid shortfall — the gap between what it costs the hospital to treat Medicaid beneficiaries and the payment it receives from Medicaid;
health professions education and research expenses, such as for training medical interns and residents, because “it is not clear that these investments have a direct impact on community health,” according to the report.

The majority of resident physicians, for example, don’t report practicing in underserved communities after their training, according to the report, and just over one-third “go on to practice primary care.” In addition, hospitals get medical education payments from Medicare to reimburse their training costs,  the report states.
Research funding “is a public good,” the report acknowledges, but “it is unlikely that a hospital’s research has a direct impact on community health.”
The Medicaid shortfall “represents nearly half of reported community benefit spending” as hospitals add it up, Lown reports. But the institute’s researchers find it a flawed measurement for several reasons.
The Medicaid shortfall “is an accounting measure, not direct spending,” according to the institute. When a hospital loses money on a Medicaid patient, that “is not funding that goes into the community to improve health.”
The shortfall doesn’t reflect the number of Medicaid patients treated, and if a hospital’s costs are higher, the shortfall increases “regardless of the number of Medicaid patients served.”
Hospitals also may charge other payors more to offset the Medicaid shortfall, and may benefit from other programs to offset the Medicaid shortfall. Hospitals also grant other insurers discounts, which the IRS does not treat as community benefits, the report states, so “it’s unclear why Medicaid should be different.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Regulators signal move towards stricter conservation standards for transmission corridor
description: Stricter environmental requirements seem to be on the horizon for the long-embattled New England Clean Energy Connect project. Despite a second marathon meeting on the project’s conservation plan, the Maine Board of Environmental Protection held off on making a final decision Thursday, but are poised to agree on a stronger definition of “mature forest” after[...]
text:
The $1.65 million iNew England Clean Energy Connect project owned by Central Maine Power parent company Iberdrola carries hydroelectric power from Quebec to several New England states.
(Photo of an unnamed transmission line in Maine by BWFolsom/ Getty Images)Stricter environmental requirements seem to be on the horizon for the long-embattled New England Clean Energy Connect project.
Despite a second marathon meeting on the project’s conservation plan, the Maine Board of Environmental Protection held off on making a final decision Thursday, but are poised to agree on a stronger definition of “mature forest” after staff make final revisions. 
Last year, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection approved the project’s conservation plan as part of the construction of 53 miles of new transmission line through western Maine. The $1.65 million interconnection project owned by Central Maine Power parent company Iberdrola carries hydroelectric power from Quebec to several New England states.
The citizen-led Board of Environmental Protection, an independent body that oversees the enforcement of environmental laws, met to consider an appeal of the department’s decision, filed by the Appalachian Mountain Club, Maine Audubon, Natural Resources Council of Maine and Trout Unlimited.
The groups have argued that the conservation area set aside by NECEC doesn’t meet the board’s earlier standards, and instead should be less fragmented, with more old-growth forest. 
Board members on Thursday were largely in agreement in their support of stricter requirements for what counted as “mature forest” in the area. 
Chair Robert Duchesne said the original agreement didn’t take into account standard commercial forestry practices in the area, like pre-commercial thinning, and how that would impact the forest even if it technically met the original definition of mature forest. 
“So I don’t fully accept the testimony as evidence for the licensee, that that mature standard that was advocated originally is actually being met because it didn’t take those impacts into effect,” he said. “That bothers me, and if you don’t have that, then you really don’t have mitigation.”
Duchesne said he was sympathetic to the challenge NECEC may have working with the landowner on any new requirement, but was not convinced it overruled other interests. 
“I am very sensitive about whether the landowner, of which there are very few in the area, would go along with any revisions to this, but that ultimately is not my problem,” he said. “We’re just setting the standards.”
The draft order before the board included other restrictions that the board members voted to remove, including additional no-harvest restrictions and prohibiting shifting of conservation areas over time. 
The strongest voice opposing the draft order was board member Brooke Barnes.
“The condition is that the primary goal is promoting habitat connectivity and promoting conservation of mature forest areas,” Barnes said. “I think there’s been some conflation between promoting and protecting, and so we’ve shifted into a mode where I’m seeing these conditions on the proposed board order, and they’re very much in protecting mode.”
But Barnes ultimately said he agreed with the new definition of mature forest, and supported a version of the order that eliminated the other restrictions — a change that the majority of the board supported.
David Kallin, an attorney representing the conservation groups, said they supported the draft order, and would like to see the board also order NECEC to purchase an additional 10,000 acres of mature forest to be managed by a conservation organization or state agency.
Kallin said the original restrictions were a “mirage” and “they didn’t actually create mature forests.”
Lisa Gilbreath, attorney for NECEC LLC, opposed the draft order, and said it “very blatantly exceeds the scope of the conditions.” She argued that the board should not be weighing whether the standards are adequate but whether the project has met their requirements, which she said it had.
“Rewriting the requirements now, as I said, it flips the proceeding on its head,” she said. “It throws out multiple years of work by multiple agencies who have followed their ordinary course in developing a conservation easement.”
But the board was not persuaded, and directed staff to further revise the draft order and bring it back to a future meeting, most likely in January.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Runoff in southwest Georgia becomes high-stakes battle after House Democrats claim narrow majority
description: Voters in eight southwest Georgia counties have one more trip to make to their polling places before they ring in the new year, and they’ll decide whether House Democrats expand their newly won majority or whether Republicans can save an incumbent lawmaker’s seat. Early voting starts Monday for residents of Georgia’s House District 151, which […]
text:
Starting next week, some voters in southwest Georgia will be headed back to their polling places to participate in a runoff election that could help grow Democrats' majority in the state House or give Republicans another hand in resisting their agenda. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderVoters in eight southwest Georgia counties have one more trip to make to their polling places before they ring in the new year, and they’ll decide whether House Democrats expand their newly won majority or whether Republicans can save an incumbent lawmaker’s seat.
Rep. Mike Cheokas and Ethan Wolfe are set to compete in a Dec. 1 runoff. Photos courtesy of Georgia House of Representatives and Ethan Wolfe campaign.
Early voting starts Monday for residents of Georgia’s House District 151, which includes parts of Chattahoochee, Dougherty, Marion, Schley, Stewart, Sumter, Terrell and Ware counties. Voters will choose between Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas and Democrat Ethan Wolfe, a retired military officer, after neither candidate surpassed 50% of the vote earlier this month. Election Day is Dec. 1.
Cheokas had the lead with 9,403 votes, good for about 47.9% to Wolfe’s 8,022 votes, or slightly under 41%. Independent candidate Travis Lockhart made up the difference.
Democrats claimed historic wins in this year’s election, flipping every statewide position on the ballot from governor to agriculture commissioner and gaining a majority in the state House, but only a slim one.
Democrats are set to hold 91 seats in the 180-member chamber, giving them the minimum number of seats required to claim majority status. With two other races still unresolved, Democrats expect to pick up at least one more seat when the dust settles.
“Anytime you get into margins that close, one vote can be the difference maker,” said Carmen Bergman, director of the Georgia House Republican Caucus. “We saw that with several pieces of consequential legislation over the years, whether it be tort reform or school choice legislation. So I expect both the Democrats and us are going to be fighting hard.”
Both of the bills Bergman referred to passed the House with 91 votes, the minimum needed to move out of the chamber.
“These legislators are still human,” said Democratic strategist Andrew Heaton. “People are going to get sick. People are going to have family emergencies. People are going to have deaths in the family. And so we’ve got to have every bit of cushion possible to ensure that all of our agenda goes through when it’s up for a vote.”
Cheokas said he’s been knocking on constituents’ doors until sundown ahead of the runoff and speaking directly with voters to stress the importance of turning out.
Cheokas, who chairs the House’s small business development committee, said his experience makes him the better man for the job.
“Most of all, it’s about the lives of the people living in my district,” he said. “No matter who has the gavel, our community is best suited to have a representative who’s been there, knows how it works, and has a track record of delivering results. Southwest Georgians don’t want a freshman who takes orders from DC Democrats.”
Cheokas was first sworn into the House in 2004 as a Democrat, but switched parties in 2010. He lost his seat to a Democrat in 2016 but won it back against a different opponent in 2018.
“As for the makeup of the House, whether it’s a gubernatorial appointment, a federal indictment or a couple of sick days, we’ve seen Democrats in the House lose members during session,” he added. “That threshold for a majority will be smaller after my victory.
Wolfe said he and his team have been hitting the campaign trail as well and working to remind voters that the election is not over.
He said he is pitching himself as an outsider candidate.
“We don’t need another 20 years of the same excuses,” he said. “We need someone who shows up with fresh ideas, real solutions and a willingness to fight for the people back home. I’m talking about bringing good-paying jobs to rural Georgia, keeping our hospitals open, investing in our public schools and making life more affordable for working families.
“I spent 30 years serving my country in the Air Force, and I know that leadership means taking responsibility and getting results,” he added. “I’m not running to build a political career. I’m running because I love this community, and I believe our best days can still be ahead of us. But we have to be willing to do something different.”
The last time Cheokas had a Democratic challenger was in 2022, and Cheokas won by nearly 10 percentage points that year, though the area, like most of the rest of the state, swung hard toward Democrats this year. House Democrats were able to pick up 10 seats, potentially more, this year.
That makes Heaton feel optimistic about Wolfe’s chances.
“The reasons that animated voters to go out in November haven’t changed in one month,” he said.
But what will change is the season. Early voting is set to last Nov. 23 to 25, the Monday through Wednesday of Thanksgiving week, when many voters will be traveling or getting ready to host family and friends and likely not thinking about who ought to represent them in the Georgia House of Representatives.
“It’s going to take a massive field and campaign operation to get our voters back out to the polls and help them understand why this is still so important,” Heaton said. “We can’t rest where we’re at. We’ve got to get this 93rd vote.”
Bergman said Republicans won’t be resting either and said it will come down to a “turnout game.”
And this time around, Bergman said, Republicans will be hungry for a victory.
“One of the best ways to know the mood of an electorate is through verbatims, what you’re hearing on the ground, what you’re hearing from people who can actually vote,” she said. “And, conservatives, Republicans in that area are motivated by what we’ve seen transpire and are excited for the chance to support their hometown guy, Mike Chokas, to go be a watchdog in Atlanta.”

title: Ohio’s bill banning child marriage will likely not pass, according to Ohio Senate president
description: The bill that would ban child marriage in Ohio will likely not pass this General Assembly, according to Ohio Republican Senate leadership.  Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon, said members of his Republican caucus raised questions about the need to raise the minimum age to get married to 18.  “Shouldn’t there be discussions about what […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal). The bill that would ban child marriage in Ohio will likely not pass this General Assembly, according to Ohio Republican Senate leadership. 
Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon, said members of his Republican caucus raised questions about the need to raise the minimum age to get married to 18.

“Shouldn’t there be discussions about what might be wrong with the current law, as opposed to maybe a bright line change?” McColley asked. 
“Because, as you might expect, there are individuals in our caucus who know people who were married before they were 18. Many of them might even be related to people who were married before they were 18 and have been happily married for, in many cases, decades.” 
Under current law in Ohio, 17-year-olds are able to marry someone up to four years older than them, as long as a juvenile court signs off on it. The current law took effect in 2019. 
Ohio Senate Bill 341 would require Ohioans to be 18 to get married.
“Our caucus looked at it and had a very long, thoughtful conversation about this. And again, it’s not to say that there shouldn’t be reforms put in the system,” McColley said. 
“The question remained: What problem are we trying to solve here that doesn’t already have the oversight in place? And if there’s a problem that we’re trying to solve without, under limited circumstances, allowing for this to occur with a great deal of oversight, then let’s talk about that problem.” 
McColley said last week he supported the bill. 
The Ohio Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously passed the bill in June just before the lawmakers went on break. 
More than 5,000 Ohio children have been married as minors since 2000 and nearly 300,000 minors nationally were married between 2000 and 2018, according to Unchained At Last, an organization dedicated to ending underage marriage.
Sixty minors were married in Ohio between 2020 and 2025 — most of them girls being married to adult men, according to Unchained At Last. 
“I’m hearing that unless something changes, there’s not an appetite (for the bill),” said Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio, D-Lakewood. 
“If there are real specific issues, then they should talk them out and let’s get something over the finish line.”
Ohio Senators Bill DeMora and Bill Blessing, introduced the bipartisan bill earlier this year. There has been no public opposition to the bill. 
“I don’t understand why it’s not brought up,” said DeMora, D-Columbus. 
“(McColley is) afraid of his own caucus. … It’s mind-boggling why they can’t bring it up because they’re scared of their own shadow.” 
There is no legitimate reason for a 17-year-old to get married, DeMora said. 
“Most of these young girls that get married under the age of 18 end up having issues like substance issues, battered women, sexual abuse,” he said. 
DeMora tried unsuccessfully to add the child marriage ban bill as an amendment to Ohio House Bill 58, which has to do with recovery housing. Ohio H.B. 58 unanimously passed the Senate on Wednesday and is headed to Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s desk for his signature. 
“I brought it up there because I’m thinking that there is a relationship between young girls who get married under 18 and the stuff they have to go through when they finally are able to get out of these things that don’t work,” he said. 
DeMora said he plans on continuing to try to add his bill as an amendment to other bills that are being voted on. 
“I promised the advocates I would do that, and I’m going to continue to do that,” he said. 
Eighteen states have a law banning child marriage — most recently California and Oklahoma, according to Unchained At Last. 
Any bill that does not pass before the end of the year must be reintroduced in the new General Assembly to be considered.
